**Member:** Commissioner Dwyer  **Date of order:** ………………………………

**Application:** Application in Existing Proceedings (Form 4) under r 64G, filed 18 June 2026

---

**UPON** the application of the Appellant under r 64G of the *Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011* for the Commission to decide the objection of MSH to the Notice of Non-Party Disclosure (Form 29) sealed by the Industrial Registry on 22 April 2026 ("the Notice");

**AND UPON** reading the Affidavit of Cory Lea Shepherd affirmed 18 June 2026 and the exhibits CS-1 to CS-4, MSH's letter of 5 June 2026 (ref K-LM26/729), and the Respondent's disclosure of 11 June 2026;

**THE COMMISSION ORDERS THAT:**

1. Pursuant to r 64G(2), the Notice is upheld as varied in the terms of Schedule A to the application — the pressed Items being 1, 2, 3(a), 3(b), 9, 10 and 19 (Item 10 confined to (a) an aggregate metadata-only count, (b)–(d) the phrase-family and bounded-correspondence exports, and (e) the bounded Payroll→Line-Manager AVAC correspondence) — the objection of MSH being otherwise overruled.

2. MSH produce the documents within that varied scope by native electronic export of the messages and records returned by the server-side filters described in the Notice (identified custodians, date-ranges and phrase-families), no inbox review, reading or relevance-assessment of any email being required, by 4:00 pm on ……………………………… (and in any event within 14 days of this order, or such further time as the Commission allows).

3. MSH, by its Chief Executive or a delegated Director, file and serve within seven (7) business days of this order a verification affidavit complying with the Schedule to this order, in respect of each pressed Item, the AVAC payroll export sought at Item 16, and each Item on which MSH asserts non-existence, destruction or irrelevance (Items 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 18 and 20).

4. The time for production at order 2 is fixed and is not contingent upon the supply of any pleading to MSH.

5. If any question of privacy or confidentiality is raised in respect of the production, the documents be produced to the Commission for its inspection in the first instance, with access to the parties as the Commission directs, and subject to any order under s 580 of the *Industrial Relations Act 2016*.

6. Pursuant to s 580 of the *Industrial Relations Act 2016*, there be no publication of any information identifying the fact or content of the Public Interest Disclosure (reference PID 24-ESU-1130) or the Ethical Standards Unit determination, giving effect to s 65 of the *Public Interest Disclosure Act 2010* (Qld).

7. Costs reserved.

8. There be liberty to apply, and such further or other orders as the Commission considers appropriate.

---

## SCHEDULE — REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE VERIFICATION AFFIDAVIT (order 3)
The verification affidavit is directed only to verifying, after a defined search, what exists and what is to be produced; it is not directed to any wider inquiry into MSH's conduct. So that a statement of non-existence is verified rather than asserted in the abstract, the affidavit must address the following.

**Part 1 — For every Item for which production is sought, or non-existence, destruction or irrelevance is asserted, the affidavit must depose:**

(1) that a search was in fact undertaken (a bare assertion of non-existence, unsupported by a deposed search, being insufficient); the name and position of the person who conducted the search, and whether that person had access to the systems searched; the systems, mailboxes, repositories and custodians searched; the search terms, filters and date-range applied; and the date on which the search was undertaken;

(2) whether the record exists as at the date of the affidavit; if it does not, whether it ever existed; and, if it once existed, when and by what means it ceased to exist (deletion, system migration, archiving, disposal or destruction), on whose authority or instruction, and under what retention policy or schedule;

(3) whether any copy, backup, archive, export, migrated instance, or version held on any superseding system exists, and if so its production;

(4) where any document already before the Commission, or disclosed in this proceeding, appears to fall within the Item, identification of that document and either its production or the precise basis on which it is said to fall outside the Item; and

(5) the name and position of any officer on whose knowledge the deponent relies for the above, that officer's account being exhibited or separately sworn.

**Part 2 — Item-specific matters, in addition to Part 1:**

- **Items 1–2 (SPOK emergency-code / paging records):** the date and nature of the SPOK "upgrade"; whether the pre-upgrade records were migrated to, retained in, or are retrievable from the upgraded system or any successor or backup, with the production of any that are retrievable and, for any that are not, the reason they are said to be irretrievable and the date and authority on which they ceased to be retained. As to the "spreadsheet of recorded MET calls" for 17–18 March 2024 — its identity, author, custodian and source system, and whether it is (a) an export from the SPOK system itself, (b) an MSH-maintained administrative record, or (c) the Appellant's own monthly call-statistics sheet (volume only) — together with its production. If it is (c), the affidavit must confirm that the SPOK system-level records (which clinician was paged, whether each page was received or acknowledged, whether any page was misdirected, and the associated timestamps) have been separately searched.
- **Item 3(c) (consequential changes):** each change to Switchboard operating procedures, reporting lines or systems over the noticed period, with its date — addressing in terms the SPOK upgrade, the Switchboard reporting-line reorganisation, the issue of a Queensland Health device to the Line Manager, and the introduction of a separate Switchboard Telecommunications Coordinator role together with any restriction of contact-number and directory-database updates to that role — or, if there was no such change, a statement to that effect on oath; and in either case the reconciliation of the answer with the statement that there were "no consequential changes".
- **Items 4 and 7 (fatigue risk-assessment / register):** whether any fatigue risk-assessment or register record referable to the Switchboard work area existed as at 17–18 March 2024 (as distinct from training records); if so, its production; if not, a statement on oath that none existed.
- **Item 5 (fatigue framework):** each fatigue-risk-management policy, directive, guideline or framework (including any under the Queensland Health Fatigue Risk Management System) that applied to the Switchboard work area, or to its non-clinical administrative staff, as at 17–18 March 2024 — identified by name and number — or, if none applied, a statement on oath to that effect; and in either case the date on which fatigue risk management was implemented at the Switchboard.
- **Item 16 (AVAC payroll export):** production of the AVAC payroll-system export for PRN 15397775 and PRN 15605601, or a sworn statement that no such export exists (the Daily Staffing Variance Forms already produced not being that export).
- **Item 18 (communication book; 15 November 2023 business-case minutes):** whether each record exists; and if either was destroyed, when, by whom, and under what authority.
- **Item 20 (operational / HR response, 13–31 May 2024):** whether records of the operational and human-resources response to the matters raised in that window exist, addressing in terms the correspondence of 15–16 May 2024 disclosed by the Respondent on 11 June 2026, independently of when the reference "PID24-ESU-1130" was assigned.

---

**Commissioner Dwyer**

# FORM 20 — AFFIDAVIT OF CORY LEA SHEPHERD

**QUEENSLAND INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION** — Matter No. WC/2024/227
*Workers' Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003 (Qld); Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011*

**BETWEEN:** CORY LEA SHEPHERD — **Appellant**
**AND:** WORKERS' COMPENSATION REGULATOR — **Respondent**
**NOMINATED PARTY (Notice of Non-Party Disclosure, Form 29):** METRO SOUTH HOSPITAL AND HEALTH SERVICE (the Line Manager and Director being the persons affected by the notice, by position title)

**AFFIDAVIT OF CORY LEA SHEPHERD** *(Form 20 — filed on behalf of the Appellant, in support of the Application in Existing Proceedings (Form 4) under r 64G)*

I, CORY LEA SHEPHERD, of 15 Edmond Street, Coomera in the State of Queensland, Administration Officer, do solemnly and sincerely affirm and declare:

## Purpose, and the Amended 9A
1. I make this affidavit in support of my application (Form 4) in this matter and of my Notice of Non-Party Disclosure (Form 29). I refer to my Amended Statement of Facts and Contentions filed 7 April 2026 ("the Amended 9A"). The facts below are within my own knowledge except where stated otherwise, and they go to the stressors pleaded in the Amended 9A and to the relevance and necessity of the documents sought in the Form 29. I set the facts out under the same structure as the Amended 9A.

2. I am aware that the statutory exclusion under s 32(5)(a) of the *Workers' Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003* is for the Respondent to establish. I make this affidavit because the practical task of proving the matters pleaded rests on me, and because the documents that prove them are held by Metro South Hospital and Health Service ("MSH"), not by me.

## PART A — MY POSITION
3. **Position.** I am employed by MSH as an Administration Officer, classification AO3, in Switchboard Services at Logan Hospital (organisational unit "MSH CI LOGH Switchboard Srvs"; position 32002276). I am commonly described as a Switchboard Operator.

4. **Permanent appointment.** I was converted from temporary to permanent employment with effect from 3 March 2021 under the temporary-to-permanent conversion directive. My appointment is permanent and I am classified as a Continuous Shift Worker (64 hours per fortnight on conversion; five weeks' recreation leave). My appointment and classification are recorded in MSH's myHR system.

5. **Full-time hours.** On 31 August 2023 I applied of my own initiative to increase my hours to full time on a rotational roster. My application was approved on 27 September 2023 and I commenced full-time hours on 16 October 2023. Annexed and marked "CS-3" is my application of 31 August 2023, in which I also recorded my intention to become the Switchboard union delegate.

## PART B — MY ROLE (THE FULL PICTURE)
6. **The importance of the role.** The Switchboard is the hospital's communications hub and a critical part of its patient-safety system. In an emergency (a Code Blue, a MET call, a security or clinical emergency) it is the Switchboard that activates and pages the response teams, through the SPOK messaging and paging system. Whether the right clinician is reached, and how quickly, depends on the Switchboard and on the information in SPOK being correct. The role is not peripheral administration; it is the point at which urgent help is summoned. An error or delay at the Switchboard is an error or delay in the emergency response itself. The Respondent admits that "[m]aintaining accurate contact details for medical staff is a critical function of the Switchboard to ensure effective clinical handover and patient safety" (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 8).

7. **The systems I operate.** In my application of 31 August 2023 I recorded, in my own words, the systems I operate. I operate concurrently and in real time a number of separate systems, including the Alcatel Switchboard console, the SPOK messaging and paging system, Cerner, HBCIS, EDIS (the Emergency Department web database), Microsoft 365, and spreadsheets used for rostering and call records. I move between these systems continuously while answering calls.

8. **The first point of contact.** The Switchboard is the first point of contact for Logan Hospital. The Switchboard number is the principal published telephone number for the hospital (the first number listed for the public) and it is also the number that staff throughout the hospital use and know to call. Calls from the public and from staff alike come to me in the first instance.

9. **Volume.** I handle approximately 200 to 300 calls per shift, a substantial proportion of which come from people who are distressed, frightened, in conflict, or in crisis. I am frequently the first person a caller reaches in an urgent or emergency situation. I maintain and author monthly call statistics ("Individual monthly stats") which tally volume only — the number of calls I handled and emergency codes activated. They do not record which clinicians were paged, whether a page was received or acknowledged, or whether a page was misdirected; that system-level data is held only by MSH in the SPOK system and I cannot produce it. I do not annex those statistics; the aggregate figures I state in this affidavit may be received in open evidence.

10. **Triage.** A core part of my function is to triage and connect — directing calls ward-to-ward and from one point of urgency to another, identifying which calls cannot wait, and routing them to the correct clinician or team without delay, while continuing to answer the queue and operate the systems above.

11. **Locating emergency callers.** In an emergency, a caller is sometimes unable to tell me where they are calling from. In those circumstances I must identify the source and location of the call so that help can be directed to the right place. Any delay in doing so may delay the emergency response.

12. **Emergency codes and concurrent urgencies.** A core part of my function is the activation of emergency codes. Between 15 and 50 emergency codes are sent out through the SPOK system by the Switchboard over a 24-hour period, each paged simultaneously to approximately 10 clinicians who together form the responding team. These, and other urgent matters, do not arrive one at a time; during a single shift I manage a number of urgencies concurrently (code calls, emergency and security responses, and time-critical clinical calls) escalating each to the correct clinician, team or responder while continuing to manage the remaining calls in the queue.

13. **Direct relay of urgent clinical results.** A core clinical function of my role is the direct relay of urgent pathology and other clinical results between doctors (doctor-to-doctor, including to and from external doctors and facilities (for example, Hibiscus)) where any delay may directly affect a patient's treatment. I also connect and coordinate with external agencies, including the Queensland Ambulance Service and the Queensland Police Service.

14. **The criticality of that function, illustrated.** The importance of this relay function is illustrated by occasions on which a doctor holding urgent results could not be connected to the on-call clinician until I identified the difficulty at the Switchboard and connected them directly. Where the on-call contact information on which the Switchboard depends is not kept current, the resulting delay falls on urgent clinical communications, and it is at the Switchboard (and on the operator) that the failure first appears and must be resolved in real time. I give this to illustrate the role; I do not rely on it as a stressor.

15. **The Direct Support Officer (DSO) function.** Each medical department has a Direct Support Officer ("DSO") — an administrative officer who provides direct support to that department, including in relation to its medical rostering and leave. When a department's DSO was not contactable, I performed that support function from the Switchboard, in addition to my own duties (resolving conflicts in doctors' leave and rostering, escalating matters to executives, and managing intra-hospital disputes) while continuing to answer the call queue.

16. **Roster and leave administration.** My role includes administrative responsibilities carried out alongside the live Switchboard work, including maintaining and updating doctor rosters and staffing numbers, and leave administration for doctors.

17. **The daily roster and the SPOK dependency.** The Switchboard runs the daily roster that is referred to and relied upon across the hospital. SPOK pages clinicians by reference to the on-call roster, so the accuracy of that roster determines whether an emergency page reaches the right, available clinician.

18. **Weekend coverage.** On weekends, the management structure that operates during business hours is not present. During those periods the Switchboard manages doctor leave, updates rosters, and carries out whatever else is required, in effect performing functions that would otherwise be performed by management.

19. **Complaints come to the Switchboard, and to me, in the first instance.** As the hospital's first point of contact (paragraph 8), the Switchboard is where complaints from the public, from clinicians, and from staff across the hospital first arrive — by telephone and to the Switchboard email inbox — and they come to me, as the operator on duty, frequently as accusations made directly to me. I receive and triage each such complaint at the Switchboard before it goes anywhere else. I action and resolve a substantial proportion of them myself; those requiring management action I escalate to my Line Manager or, where appropriate, to the dedicated complaints area. My Line Manager was frequently unavailable, however, and the complaints she did not action returned to, and accumulated at, the Switchboard, where they again fell to me. The complaints therefore came to me first, and the records of those escalated to management are held in my Line Manager's mailbox (Items 3(a) and 3(b) of the Form 29).

20. **Complaints about my own manager.** My manager was frequently not contactable or reachable, and did not action the complaints or issues that were raised with her. Two consequences followed. First, complaints about my own manager (her unavailability, her responses, and her inaction) came directly to the Switchboard, so that I was receiving and managing complaints concerning the very person to whom I would otherwise escalate them, and at times complaints that concerned the Switchboard itself. Second, the matters she did not action generated further complaints, which then fell to me to absorb and manage on top of the volume of calls and safety-critical work I was already carrying. These arose because my manager was not present in the fast-paced environment in which the complaints were generated, and because there was no one else to whom they could be directed; over the period this became a recurring pattern, the same unresolved matters returning to the Switchboard, and to me, to be managed again. By way of example, in my email of 15 May 2024 I recorded that clinicians and staff from other departments had sought updates on pager statuses and other requests which were, in the words I used at the time, "often left unresolved due to ambiguity around when [Ms Taylor] is available."

21. **My vantage point.** Because the Switchboard is the central point to which complaints are directed, I am positioned to observe directly, and over time, both the volume and the subject-matter of the complaints the hospital receives.

22. **The increase over the period, and a change that drove it.** From that vantage point I observed that, over the period pleaded in the Amended 9A, the volume and subject-matter of the unresolved complaints and requests coming to the Switchboard (including those concerning my manager's availability and the currency of the on-call roster and the telephone directory) increased. Part of that increase followed an operational change made during the period: a separate Switchboard Telecommunications Coordinator role was introduced, held by Ms Ellen Stibbard, and the updating of contact numbers in the Switchboard directory and the associated database was restricted to that role. In her email of 18 July 2023 Ms Stibbard stated that she would be "removing everyone's access to the database" and that any entry to be "amended, added or removed" was to be sent to her directly. Updates the Switchboard had previously been able to make or obtain promptly now had to await Ms Stibbard or, in her absence, the Line Manager; her attendance was limited to part of each week; numbers and directory entries fell out of date, and the resulting complaints about wrong or out-of-date numbers came to me at the Switchboard. The records that would establish the full extent of that increase, and of that change to how contact details were updated, are held by MSH (Items 3(a), 3(b) and 3(c) of the Form 29), and I cannot produce them.

23. **The baseline (the standing condition of the role).** The defining condition of my role is this: from the Switchboard I have a vantage point over everything that goes wrong in the hospital, and I am accused of, and held responsible for, much of it (including matters properly the responsibility of others (the medical departments' Direct Support Officers, doctor availability, the updating of SPOK, and decisions made at executive level)) regardless of where the fault actually lies. The volume is constant: approximately 200 to 300 calls per shift, a substantial proportion from people who are distressed, frightened, in conflict or in crisis, while I maintain the systems and the roster on which the hospital's emergency paging depends.

24. **The patient-safety function was performed at the Switchboard.** I was the operator through whom emergency codes were activated and urgent clinical and pathology results were relayed doctor-to-doctor. The patient-safety function of the hospital's emergency communications was performed by me at the Switchboard, and the conditions I describe in this Part applied to that function and to me as the person performing it.

25. That standing condition (bearing the patient-safety load of a hospital's communications, at constant volume, while absorbing the blame for failures across the whole system, and while the support above me was absent or unmaintained) is the condition in which I performed every duty described above.

## PART C — STRESSOR 1: COURSE OF MANAGEMENT CONDUCT (Amended 9A, Stressor 1)
26. **Erratic presence and unilateral directives without consultation [1(a)].** Throughout 2023 and 2024 my Line Manager, Ms Chloe Donovan-Taylor ("Ms Taylor"), maintained an erratic physical presence and imposed unilateral directives without consultation. Those directives were sent from her email account to the Logan Hospital Switchboard group distribution list (the shared Switchboard mailbox), and were frequently expressed to take effect "effective immediately" or with immediate effect. The objective record of her working presence is held in MSH's security-access system (Item 9 of the Form 29).

27. **The MASPER directive [1(a)].** The misrouted-call issues raised by the MASPER registrar and the medical department in May 2024 were, in substance, a problem of the roster not reflecting doctors' actual availability — a doctor, roster and coordination problem, not an error of the operators. Ms Taylor's own email of 9 May 2024 records that a doctor's hours were "not provided on the rosters" and that the contact number was "switched off." Rather than consult the Switchboard (which could have identified the cause) or check the roster herself, she directed a change to the Switchboard's call-handling process. Annexed and marked "CS-1" is that email chain.

28. **I raised the absence of consultation from the outset [1(a)].** On 16 June 2023 I wrote raising, among other workplace issues, "No consultation of the team members or the department when making major changes such as additional shift… commence/finish [times]." I raised it again on 15 May 2024, and the Director, Ms Tammy Reese, asked me on 21 May 2024 to identify the directives about which I had consultation concerns.

29. **Roster/SPOK errors and resulting delay [1(a)].** When the on-call roster in SPOK was not kept up to date, emergency and urgent pages were directed to the wrong or an unavailable clinician. Whether a page reached the correct clinician, was received or acknowledged, or was misdirected is recorded in MSH's SPOK system; that record is held only by MSH and I cannot produce it — my own statistics record volume only. These errors accumulated at the Switchboard and fell to me to identify and work around in real time. I raised them by complaint; to my knowledge and observation, no change to operating procedures, no investigation, and no remedial or safety action was taken in response, and the failure to address them resulted in direct delay, including to urgent clinical communications.

30. **The vocabulary of the complaints [1(a)].** The complaints about misdirected calls use a recognisable and recurring operational vocabulary — that a doctor or clinician was paged or directed to the "wrong ward", the "wrong location", the "wrong team" or the "wrong doctor"; that a page was "misdirected" or that there was a "pager error"; or that the "list", "directory" or "roster" was "out of date" and needed "updating". These are the actual words in which the complaints are made.

31. **Destruction of WHS records [1(b)].** On 6 June 2023 I recorded a critical operational instruction in the communication book regarding the need to verify and update doctors' on-call contact details. On that day my Line Manager, Ms Taylor, removed the page containing my handwritten entry from the Communication Book. The removal of a page from the communication book is admitted (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 6); the Respondent does not admit the contents of the entry, or that the page bore my handwriting, on the basis that it holds no copy of the page (Form 24, Para 7). The contents of the entry are within my own knowledge.

32. **Grievance and its handling [1(c)].** On 7 August 2023 I submitted a grievance regarding Ms Taylor's conduct, raising WHS concerns about unsafe rostering and fatigue. My grievance was not upheld and I was directed to continue reporting to Ms Taylor. In her email of 7 August 2023 Ms Reese acknowledged that "there was a rostering error that was accidentally made by Chloe with regards to night shifts" (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 5).

33. **COVID special pandemic leave obstruction [1(d)].** My application for COVID special pandemic leave (Process Reference 15480560) had to be submitted four times before it was approved — once by text message to my Line Manager's mobile and three times through myHR. On myHR the application was declined twice by my Line Manager, Ms Taylor, and was ultimately approved on the same supporting evidence I had already provided. The myHR records and audit trail recording those submissions and declines are the material the subject of Item 11 of the Form 29, disclosed by MSH with its letter of 5 June 2026 (see paragraph 51); I refer to that disclosure and do not annex it.

34. **Public Interest Disclosure [1(e)].** On 13 May 2024 I made a complaint concerning Ms Taylor and Ms Reese, which the Ethical Standards Unit determined on 24 December 2024 to constitute a Public Interest Disclosure (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 20); the determination bears reference PID 24-ESU-1130. I do not set out the content of that disclosure in this affidavit.

35. **Direction to retract within 48 hours [1(f)].** On 15 May 2024, within 48 hours of the matter referred to in the preceding paragraph, the Director, Ms Reese, directed me to retract an email I had sent inquiring about office hours (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 21). A substantively similar email sent by Ms Taylor on 9 May 2024 about another staff member's hours attracted no such direction; the Respondent denies that comparison, contending the circumstances were different (Form 24, Para 22).

36. **Suppression of union representation [1(g)].** On 11 August 2023 I notified Ms Taylor of my intention to become the Switchboard union delegate; the Respondent admits that I sent that text but characterises it as "not a formal notification" (Form 24, Para 18). My intention was also recorded in my full-time application of 31 August 2023 (Exhibit CS-3) and expressed directly to Ms Taylor. On 18 May 2024 I sent a request regarding union representation to the Together union (Ms Heather Hayes), and on 20 May 2024 Together confirmed it had "passed [my] correspondence on to [my] Health team." Annexed and marked "CS-2" is that correspondence. The Union Encouragement Policy (QH-POL-248) requires managers to take a "positive, supportive role" (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 17). Management did not facilitate the delegate appointment for a period exceeding 9 months — a matter the Respondent denies (Form 24, Para 19), and which the union-delegate correspondence sought under the Notice (Item 19) goes to — leaving the department without delegate representation while I was disputing unsafe rostering and fatigue practices.

## PART D — STRESSOR 2: REMUNERATION (Amended 9A, Stressor 2)
37. **Underpayment and the AVAC delay.** Between February and April 2024 I was not paid my correct entitlements. On 3 May 2024 Queensland Health Payroll (Payroll Officer Elaine Grant) instructed Ms Taylor to "submit an AVAC to correct these shifts" (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 40); the AVAC was not submitted until 28 May 2024, a 25-day delay (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 41).

## PART E — STRESSOR 3: STATUTORY FATIGUE BREACH (Amended 9A, Stressor 3)
38. **The 7-hour break.** On 17–18 March 2024 I was rostered to work consecutive shifts ending at 23:00 and recommencing at 06:00 — a 7-hour break (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 1), against the 10-hour minimum (or 8 hours only by written agreement) mandated by the Award and the FRMS (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 3). Factoring my established commute, the rest opportunity available to me was substantially less than that 7-hour gap.

39. **Coordinating emergency codes under exhaustion.** Under that exhaustion I was required to manage life-safety emergency codes and doctor pages through the SPOK system — the very function described in paragraph 6 above. Being required to control emergency clinical coordination in that state, after I had previously raised fatigue concerns, is the conduct pleaded at Stressor 3.

40. **Fatigue-leave refusal.** When I required recovery time, Ms Taylor relied on the 8-hour-break agreement I had signed on 17 June 2020 to deny paid fatigue leave, requiring me to exhaust my own personal leave on 19 March 2024.

41. **The Reviewing Officer's findings.** In the Review Decision dated 24 October 2024 the Regulator's own Reviewing Officer found that rostering me with the 7-hour break "amounted to unreasonable management action", and was "satisfied [my] employment was a significant contributing factor to the psychological injury". The Respondent admits the contents of that Review Decision — both findings — reserving only its relevance on the hearing de novo (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 37).

## PART F — POST-INJURY AGGRAVATION (Amended 9A)
42. **Meetings while on certified leave.** After the onset of my injury, and while I was on certified leave, I was required to attend meetings convened by management on 12 and 16 July 2024.

43. **Termination and reinstatement.** On 8 October 2024 my employment was terminated on the basis of "abandonment of employment." I applied for reinstatement (matter TD/2024/110) and was reinstated.

44. **Medical records obtained without a Notice served on me.** In the course of the proceeding, the Respondent obtained my medical records under a Notice of Non-Party Disclosure (Form 29) that was never served on me. The Respondent admits that it did not serve any such Notice on me before it obtained those records (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 25). I was not notified of that Notice before the records were obtained.

## PART G — MY INJURY AND CURRENT CAPACITY
45. **Injury and current capacity.** As pleaded in the Amended 9A, I suffered the onset of a psychiatric injury (Major Depressive Disorder with Anxious Distress) on 18 June 2024. I returned to work on medical advice and am currently working at 0.5 FTE, and I remain unable to perform the full duties of the role described above. The diagnosis, onset and causation of my injury are addressed in the medical evidence in the substantive appeal and in the Amended 9A; I do not annex or repeat that evidence here.

## PART H — THE DOCUMENTS, AND WHY DISCLOSURE IS NECESSARY
46. The matters in Parts C–F are recorded in documents held by MSH — its email system, its identity-management and security-access systems, its meeting and governance records, and its roster, payroll and HR systems. I am able to produce individual examples (such as those annexed), but I cannot export the complete record. I do not seek the review or reading of any email; I seek only the native electronic export of the messages returned by the keyword filters described in the Form 29 (identified custodians, date-ranges and phrase-families), which can be produced by MSH from its systems at minimal cost.

47. Because my injury developed over the course of the management conduct described above, the matter the documents go to is the cumulative volume and frequency of that conduct across the whole pleaded period — including the full corpus of directives sent from my Line Manager to the Switchboard. Individual examples show that the conduct occurred; only the complete export shows how much of it the role endured over the course of conduct.

48. Because the practical burden of proving these matters rests on me, and because I cannot prove their full extent without MSH's records, the production sought in the Form 29 is necessary. Where a document the Form 29 seeks does not exist, I ask that its non-existence be verified on oath.

49. On 5 June 2026 MSH responded to the Form 29 by letter signed by its Chief Executive (ref K-LM26/729). That letter is already before the Commission, and I therefore do not annex it but refer to it and rely upon it. In that letter MSH stated, among other things: that there had been "no consequential changes to operating procedures" over the period (Item 3(c)); that fatigue risk management at the Switchboard was implemented "after 30 June 2024 in connection with an organisational change related to the reporting lines for Switchboard" (Item 5); that the SPOK records "do not exist" because "records predating [the system] upgrade were not retained," while "a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls is available for the period 17–18 March 2024" (Items 1–2); and that the text messages between me and my manager were on her personal mobile device, no Queensland Health device having been issued to her until the third quarter of 2024 (Item 14). I depose only that the letter states these matters, and I rely on it as referred to above; their significance is addressed in the application and submissions.

50. As to Items 1 and 2 (the SPOK emergency-paging records), I operate the SPOK paging system as part of my daily duties, and it is the system through which the Switchboard activates and records emergency codes and pages. In its letter MSH states that those records "do not exist" because the SPOK system "was upgraded" and "records predating that upgrade were not retained," while in the same letter confirming that "a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls is available for the period 17–18 March 2024." I am not able to reconcile an upgrade of the system with the disposal of its emergency-code paging records. I therefore ask that the verification on oath I seek address, for Items 1 and 2: the date and nature of the SPOK upgrade; whether the records predating it were migrated, archived or destroyed; the basis on which they were "not retained"; and whether any backup or archive of those records exists.

51. With its letter of 5 June 2026, MSH also disclosed documents in answer to Items 6, 11, 12, 13, 15 and 16 of the Form 29. Those documents are before the Commission and I refer to them rather than annex them. They include: the Role Description for the Manager of Switchboard Services (Item 6); the HR sub-delegation instrument for paid special pandemic leave (the COVID-19 Pandemic Event Instrument) together with Pandemic Directive 01/20 and its Implementation Guideline (Item 13); my myHR leave records and AVAC history for the pandemic-leave period (Item 11); the pandemic-leave audit trail for the Logan Hospital Switchboard team (Item 12); my leave-takings report for 19 March 2024 (Item 15); and the daily staffing-variance forms for the periods 5–18 February and 19 February–3 March 2024 (Item 16).

52. On 11 June 2026 the Respondent disclosed in this proceeding correspondence dated 15–16 May 2024 concerning my complaint and the operational and human-resources response to it. That correspondence is contemporaneous operational and human-resources material falling within the 13–31 May 2024 date range that is the subject of Item 20 — the material MSH's letter states "does not exist" on the basis that the reference "PID24-ESU-1130" "commenced in November 2024"; the correspondence is dated within the Item 20 window irrespective of when that reference number was later assigned. Annexed and marked "CS-4" is the Respondent's disclosure of 11 June 2026. I rely on that disclosure in support of the matters deposed in Parts C to F; its significance for Item 20 is addressed in my submissions.

 BETWEEN: CORY LEA SHEPHERD — Appellant AND: WORKERS' COMPENSATION

 METRO SOUTH HOSPITAL AND HEALTH SERVICE (the Line Manager and Director being the persons
 affected by the notice, by position title)

 AFFIDAVIT OF CORY LEA SHEPHERD (Form 20 — filed on behalf of the Appellant, in support of the
 Application in Existing Proceedings (Form 4) under r 64G)

 I, CORY LEA SHEPHERD, of 15 Edmond Street, Coomera in the State of Queensland, Administration
 Officer, do solemnly and sincerely affirm and declare:



 Purpose, and the Amended 9A

  1. I make this affidavit in support of my application (Form 4) in this matter and of my Notice of Non-Party
  Disclosure (Form 29). I refer to my Amended Statement of Facts and Contentions filed 7 April 2026 ("the
  Amended 9A"). The facts below are within my own knowledge except where stated otherwise, and they go
  to the stressors pleaded in the Amended 9A and to the relevance and necessity of the documents sought in
  the Form 29. I set the facts out under the same structure as the Amended 9A.

  2. I am aware that the statutory exclusion under s 32(5)(a) of the Workers' Compensation and
  Rehabilitation Act 2003 is for the Respondent to establish. I make this affidavit because the practical task
  of proving the matters pleaded rests on me, and because the documents that prove them are held by Metro
  South Hospital and Health Service ("MSH"), not by me.


 PART A — MY POSITION

  3. Position. I am employed by MSH as an Administration Officer, classification AO3, in Switchboard
  Services at Logan Hospital (organisational unit "MSH CI LOGH Switchboard Srvs"; position 32002276). I
  am commonly described as a Switchboard Operator.

  4. Permanent appointment. I was converted from temporary to permanent employment with effect from 3
  March 2021 under the temporary-to-permanent conversion directive. My appointment is permanent and I
  am classified as a Continuous Shift Worker (64 hours per fortnight on conversion; five weeks' recreation
  leave). My appointment and classification are recorded in MSH's myHR system.

  5. Full-time hours. On 31 August 2023 I applied of my own initiative to increase my hours to full time on
  a rotational roster. My application was approved on 27 September 2023 and I commenced full-time hours
  on 16 October 2023. Annexed and marked "CS-3" is my application of 31 August 2023, in which I also
  recorded my intention to become the Switchboard union delegate.

 PART B — MY ROLE (THE FULL PICTURE)

  6. The importance of the role. The Switchboard is the hospital's communications hub and a critical part of
  its patient-safety system. In an emergency (a Code Blue, a MET call, a security or clinical emergency) it is
  the Switchboard that activates and pages the response teams, through the SPOK messaging and paging
  system. Whether the right clinician is reached, and how quickly, depends on the Switchboard and on the
  information in SPOK being correct. The role is not peripheral administration; it is the point at which urgent
  help is summoned. An error or delay at the Switchboard is an error or delay in the emergency response
  itself. The Respondent admits that "[m]aintaining accurate contact details for medical staff is a critical
  function of the Switchboard to ensure effective clinical handover and patient safety" (Admitted Fact: Form
  24, Para 8).

  7. The systems I operate. In my application of 31 August 2023 I recorded, in my own words, the systems
  I operate. I operate concurrently and in real time a number of separate systems, including the Alcatel
  Switchboard console, the SPOK messaging and paging system, Cerner, HBCIS, EDIS (the Emergency
  Department web database), Microsoft 365, and spreadsheets used for rostering and call records. I move
  between these systems continuously while answering calls.

  8. The first point of contact. The Switchboard is the first point of contact for Logan Hospital. The
  Switchboard number is the principal published telephone number for the hospital (the first number listed
  for the public) and it is also the number that staff throughout the hospital use and know to call. Calls from
  the public and from staff alike come to me in the first instance.

  9. Volume. I handle approximately 200 to 300 calls per shift, a substantial proportion of which come from
  people who are distressed, frightened, in conflict, or in crisis. I am frequently the first person a caller
  reaches in an urgent or emergency situation. I maintain and author monthly call statistics ("Individual
  monthly stats") which tally volume only — the number of calls I handled and emergency codes activated.
  They do not record which clinicians were paged, whether a page was received or acknowledged, or
  whether a page was misdirected; that system-level data is held only by MSH in the SPOK system and I
  cannot produce it. I do not annex those statistics; the aggregate figures I state in this affidavit may be
  received in open evidence.

  10. Triage. A core part of my function is to triage and connect — directing calls ward-to-ward and from
  one point of urgency to another, identifying which calls cannot wait, and routing them to the correct
  clinician or team without delay, while continuing to answer the queue and operate the systems above.

  11. Locating emergency callers. In an emergency, a caller is sometimes unable to tell me where they are
  calling from. In those circumstances I must identify the source and location of the call so that help can be
  directed to the right place. Any delay in doing so may delay the emergency response.

  12. Emergency codes and concurrent urgencies. A core part of my function is the activation of
  emergency codes. Between 15 and 50 emergency codes are sent out through the SPOK system by the
  Switchboard over a 24-hour period, each paged simultaneously to approximately 10 clinicians who
  together form the responding team. These, and other urgent matters, do not arrive one at a time; during a
  single shift I manage a number of urgencies concurrently (code calls, emergency and security responses,
  and time-critical clinical calls) escalating each to the correct clinician, team or responder while continuing
  to manage the remaining calls in the queue.

  13. Direct relay of urgent clinical results. A core clinical function of my role is the direct relay of urgent
  pathology and other clinical results between doctors (doctor-to-doctor, including to and from external
  doctors and facilities (for example, Hibiscus)) where any delay may directly affect a patient's treatment. I
  also connect and coordinate with external agencies, including the Queensland Ambulance Service and the
  Queensland Police Service.

  14. The criticality of that function, illustrated. The importance of this relay function is illustrated by
  occasions on which a doctor holding urgent results could not be connected to the on-call clinician until I
  identified the difficulty at the Switchboard and connected them directly. Where the on-call contact
  information on which the Switchboard depends is not kept current, the resulting delay falls on urgent
  clinical communications, and it is at the Switchboard (and on the operator) that the failure first appears and
  must be resolved in real time. I give this to illustrate the role; I do not rely on it as a stressor.

  15. The Direct Support Officer (DSO) function. Each medical department has a Direct Support Officer
  ("DSO") — an administrative officer who provides direct support to that department, including in relation
  to its medical rostering and leave. When a department's DSO was not contactable, I performed that support
  function from the Switchboard, in addition to my own duties (resolving conflicts in doctors' leave and
  rostering, escalating matters to executives, and managing intra-hospital disputes) while continuing to
  answer the call queue.

  16. Roster and leave administration. My role includes administrative responsibilities carried out
  alongside the live Switchboard work, including maintaining and updating doctor rosters and staffing
  numbers, and leave administration for doctors.

  17. The daily roster and the SPOK dependency. The Switchboard runs the daily roster that is referred to
  and relied upon across the hospital. SPOK pages clinicians by reference to the on-call roster, so the
  accuracy of that roster determines whether an emergency page reaches the right, available clinician.

  18. Weekend coverage. On weekends, the management structure that operates during business hours is not
  present. During those periods the Switchboard manages doctor leave, updates rosters, and carries out
  whatever else is required, in effect performing functions that would otherwise be performed by
  management.

  19. Complaints come to the Switchboard, and to me, in the first instance. As the hospital's first point of
  contact (paragraph 8), the Switchboard is where complaints from the public, from clinicians, and from staff
  across the hospital first arrive — by telephone and to the Switchboard email inbox — and they come to me,
  as the operator on duty, frequently as accusations made directly to me. I receive and triage each such
  complaint at the Switchboard before it goes anywhere else. I action and resolve a substantial proportion of
  them myself; those requiring management action I escalate to my Line Manager or, where appropriate, to
  the dedicated complaints area. My Line Manager was frequently unavailable, however, and the complaints
  she did not action returned to, and accumulated at, the Switchboard, where they again fell to me. The
  complaints therefore came to me first, and the records of those escalated to management are held in my
  Line Manager's mailbox (Items 3(a) and 3(b) of the Form 29).

  20. Complaints about my own manager. My manager was frequently not contactable or reachable, and
  did not action the complaints or issues that were raised with her. Two consequences followed. First,
  complaints about my own manager (her unavailability, her responses, and her inaction) came directly to the
  Switchboard, so that I was receiving and managing complaints concerning the very person to whom I

  would otherwise escalate them, and at times complaints that concerned the Switchboard itself. Second, the
  matters she did not action generated further complaints, which then fell to me to absorb and manage on top
  of the volume of calls and safety-critical work I was already carrying. These arose because my manager
  was not present in the fast-paced environment in which the complaints were generated, and because there
  was no one else to whom they could be directed; over the period this became a recurring pattern, the same
  unresolved matters returning to the Switchboard, and to me, to be managed again. By way of example, in
  my email of 15 May 2024 I recorded that clinicians and staff from other departments had sought updates
  on pager statuses and other requests which were, in the words I used at the time, "often left unresolved due
  to ambiguity around when [Ms Taylor] is available."

  21. My vantage point. Because the Switchboard is the central point to which complaints are directed, I am
  positioned to observe directly, and over time, both the volume and the subject-matter of the complaints the
  hospital receives.

  22. The increase over the period, and a change that drove it. From that vantage point I observed that,
  over the period pleaded in the Amended 9A, the volume and subject-matter of the unresolved complaints
  and requests coming to the Switchboard (including those concerning my manager's availability and the
  currency of the on-call roster and the telephone directory) increased. Part of that increase followed an
  operational change made during the period: a separate Switchboard Telecommunications Coordinator role
  was introduced, held by Ms Ellen Stibbard, and the updating of contact numbers in the Switchboard
  directory and the associated database was restricted to that role. In her email of 18 July 2023 Ms Stibbard
  stated that she would be "removing everyone's access to the database" and that any entry to be "amended,
  added or removed" was to be sent to her directly. Updates the Switchboard had previously been able to
  make or obtain promptly now had to await Ms Stibbard or, in her absence, the Line Manager; her
  attendance was limited to part of each week; numbers and directory entries fell out of date, and the
  resulting complaints about wrong or out-of-date numbers came to me at the Switchboard. The records that
  would establish the full extent of that increase, and of that change to how contact details were updated, are
  held by MSH (Items 3(a), 3(b) and 3(c) of the Form 29), and I cannot produce them.

  23. The baseline (the standing condition of the role). The defining condition of my role is this: from the
  Switchboard I have a vantage point over everything that goes wrong in the hospital, and I am accused of,
  and held responsible for, much of it (including matters properly the responsibility of others (the medical
  departments' Direct Support Officers, doctor availability, the updating of SPOK, and decisions made at
  executive level)) regardless of where the fault actually lies. The volume is constant: approximately 200 to
  300 calls per shift, a substantial proportion from people who are distressed, frightened, in conflict or in
  crisis, while I maintain the systems and the roster on which the hospital's emergency paging depends.

  24. The patient-safety function was performed at the Switchboard. I was the operator through whom
  emergency codes were activated and urgent clinical and pathology results were relayed doctor-to-doctor.
  The patient-safety function of the hospital's emergency communications was performed by me at the
  Switchboard, and the conditions I describe in this Part applied to that function and to me as the person
  performing it.

  25. That standing condition (bearing the patient-safety load of a hospital's communications, at constant
  volume, while absorbing the blame for failures across the whole system, and while the support above me
  was absent or unmaintained) is the condition in which I performed every duty described above.

 PART C — STRESSOR 1: COURSE OF MANAGEMENT CONDUCT (Amended 9A,
 Stressor 1)

  26. Erratic presence and unilateral directives without consultation [1(a)]. Throughout 2023 and 2024
  my Line Manager, Ms Chloe Donovan-Taylor ("Ms Taylor"), maintained an erratic physical presence and
  imposed unilateral directives without consultation. Those directives were sent from her email account to
  the Logan Hospital Switchboard group distribution list (the shared Switchboard mailbox), and were
  frequently expressed to take effect "effective immediately" or with immediate effect. The objective record
  of her working presence is held in MSH's security-access system (Item 9 of the Form 29).

  27. The MASPER directive [1(a)]. The misrouted-call issues raised by the MASPER registrar and the
  medical department in May 2024 were, in substance, a problem of the roster not reflecting doctors' actual
  availability — a doctor, roster and coordination problem, not an error of the operators. Ms Taylor's own
  email of 9 May 2024 records that a doctor's hours were "not provided on the rosters" and that the contact
  number was "switched off." Rather than consult the Switchboard (which could have identified the cause) or
  check the roster herself, she directed a change to the Switchboard's call-handling process. Annexed and
  marked "CS-1" is that email chain.

  28. I raised the absence of consultation from the outset [1(a)]. On 16 June 2023 I wrote raising, among
  other workplace issues, "No consultation of the team members or the department when making major
  changes such as additional shift… commence/finish [times]." I raised it again on 15 May 2024, and the
  Director, Ms Tammy Reese, asked me on 21 May 2024 to identify the directives about which I had
  consultation concerns.

  29. Roster/SPOK errors and resulting delay [1(a)]. When the on-call roster in SPOK was not kept up to
  date, emergency and urgent pages were directed to the wrong or an unavailable clinician. Whether a page
  reached the correct clinician, was received or acknowledged, or was misdirected is recorded in MSH's
  SPOK system; that record is held only by MSH and I cannot produce it — my own statistics record volume
  only. These errors accumulated at the Switchboard and fell to me to identify and work around in real time.
  I raised them by complaint; to my knowledge and observation, no change to operating procedures, no
  investigation, and no remedial or safety action was taken in response, and the failure to address them
  resulted in direct delay, including to urgent clinical communications.

  30. The vocabulary of the complaints [1(a)]. The complaints about misdirected calls use a recognisable
  and recurring operational vocabulary — that a doctor or clinician was paged or directed to the "wrong
  ward", the "wrong location", the "wrong team" or the "wrong doctor"; that a page was "misdirected" or that
  there was a "pager error"; or that the "list", "directory" or "roster" was "out of date" and needed "updating".
  These are the actual words in which the complaints are made.

  31. Destruction of WHS records [1(b)]. On 6 June 2023 I recorded a critical operational instruction in the
  communication book regarding the need to verify and update doctors' on-call contact details. On that day
  my Line Manager, Ms Taylor, removed the page containing my handwritten entry from the
  Communication Book. The removal of a page from the communication book is admitted (Admitted Fact:
  Form 24, Para 6); the Respondent does not admit the contents of the entry, or that the page bore my
  handwriting, on the basis that it holds no copy of the page (Form 24, Para 7). The contents of the entry are
  within my own knowledge.

  32. Grievance and its handling [1(c)]. On 7 August 2023 I submitted a grievance regarding Ms Taylor's
  conduct, raising WHS concerns about unsafe rostering and fatigue. My grievance was not upheld and I was
  directed to continue reporting to Ms Taylor. In her email of 7 August 2023 Ms Reese acknowledged that
  "there was a rostering error that was accidentally made by Chloe with regards to night shifts" (Admitted
  Fact: Form 24, Para 5).

  33. COVID special pandemic leave obstruction [1(d)]. My application for COVID special pandemic
  leave (Process Reference 15480560) had to be submitted four times before it was approved — once by text
  message to my Line Manager's mobile and three times through myHR. On myHR the application was
  declined twice by my Line Manager, Ms Taylor, and was ultimately approved on the same supporting
  evidence I had already provided. The myHR records and audit trail recording those submissions and
  declines are the material the subject of Item 11 of the Form 29, disclosed by MSH with its letter of 5 June
  2026 (see paragraph 51); I refer to that disclosure and do not annex it.

  34. Public Interest Disclosure [1(e)]. On 13 May 2024 I made a complaint concerning Ms Taylor and Ms
  Reese, which the Ethical Standards Unit determined on 24 December 2024 to constitute a Public Interest
  Disclosure (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 20); the determination bears reference PID 24-ESU-1130. I do
  not set out the content of that disclosure in this affidavit.

  35. Direction to retract within 48 hours [1(f)]. On 15 May 2024, within 48 hours of the matter referred to
  in the preceding paragraph, the Director, Ms Reese, directed me to retract an email I had sent inquiring
  about office hours (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 21). A substantively similar email sent by Ms Taylor on
  9 May 2024 about another staff member's hours attracted no such direction; the Respondent denies that
  comparison, contending the circumstances were different (Form 24, Para 22).

  36. Suppression of union representation [1(g)]. On 11 August 2023 I notified Ms Taylor of my intention
  to become the Switchboard union delegate; the Respondent admits that I sent that text but characterises it
  as "not a formal notification" (Form 24, Para 18). My intention was also recorded in my full-time
  application of 31 August 2023 (Exhibit CS-3) and expressed directly to Ms Taylor. On 18 May 2024 I sent
  a request regarding union representation to the Together union (Ms Heather Hayes), and on 20 May 2024
  Together confirmed it had "passed [my] correspondence on to [my] Health team." Annexed and marked
  "CS-2" is that correspondence. The Union Encouragement Policy (QH-POL-248) requires managers to
  take a "positive, supportive role" (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 17). Management did not facilitate the
  delegate appointment for a period exceeding 9 months — a matter the Respondent denies (Form 24, Para
  19), and which the union-delegate correspondence sought under the Notice (Item 19) goes to — leaving the
  department without delegate representation while I was disputing unsafe rostering and fatigue practices.


 PART D — STRESSOR 2: REMUNERATION (Amended 9A, Stressor 2)

  37. Underpayment and the AVAC delay. Between February and April 2024 I was not paid my correct

  Taylor to "submit an AVAC to correct these shifts" (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 40); the AVAC was not
  submitted until 28 May 2024, a 25-day delay (Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para 41).

# AFFIDAVIT OF CORY LEA SHEPHERD — FRONT SHEET

**QUEENSLAND INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION** — Matter No. WC/2024/227

# FORM 4 — APPLICATION IN EXISTING PROCEEDINGS

**QUEENSLAND INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION** — *Workers' Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003 (Qld)* — Matter No: WC/2024/227

**BETWEEN:** CORY LEA SHEPHERD (Appellant) **and** WORKERS' COMPENSATION REGULATOR (Respondent)

**APPLICATION IN EXISTING PROCEEDINGS** *(Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011, r 64G)*

## OVERVIEW
This is an application under r 64G for the Commission to decide MSH's objection to a sealed Notice of Non-Party Disclosure. The Appellant has narrowed the Notice, withdrawn what the record does not need, and seeks production by a single self-executing step — a server-side export of records MSH already holds, bounded by identified custodian, date-range and phrase-family, requiring no review or reading of any email. Where a record is said not to exist, the Appellant asks only that the non-existence be stated on oath after a defined search. The objection therefore reduces to one question: whether that bounded export and produce-or-swear verification should be ordered, or whether a non-party's un-sworn assertion that its emergency-code paging logs and fatigue records "do not exist" should instead be accepted. The Appellant does not seek any medical records, the financial or payroll data of other employees, or any patient or other sensitive personal or health information; where any such identifying information appears in the records produced, it may be redacted (Part B(d)).

## PART A — APPLICANT
Applicant: Cory Lea Shepherd, Appellant (Self-Represented). This application is supported by the Affidavit of Cory Lea Shepherd affirmed 18 June 2026 ("the Affidavit"), and is made in respect of the Notice of Non-Party Disclosure (Form 29) sealed by the Industrial Registry on 22 April 2026 ("the Form 29"). The Form 29 was served on Metro South Hospital and Health Service ("MSH") as the nominated party required to produce, and on the Line Manager (Logan Hospital Switchboard) and the Director responsible for the Switchboard function as the persons affected by the notice — each a non-party about whom information is sought, required to be served under r 64D(1)(a), identified by position title and served via the representative service address (Executive Director, Clinical Governance, Risk & Legal, Metro South HHS), MSH being served last as r 64C(2) requires.

## PART B — DISPOSITION SOUGHT
The Appellant respectfully applies, pursuant to r 64G of the *Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011*, for the objection of MSH to the Form 29 to be decided as follows:

(a) Pursuant to r 64G(2), the Notice be upheld as varied in the terms of Schedule A (the pressed Items being 1, 2, 3(a), 3(b), 9, 10 and 19 — Item 10 confined, per Schedule A, to (a) an aggregate metadata-only count, (b)–(d) the phrase-family and bounded-correspondence exports, and (e) the bounded Payroll→Line-Manager AVAC correspondence), the objection being otherwise overruled, and MSH be ordered to produce the documents within that varied scope by native electronic export of the messages and records returned by the server-side filters described in the Form 29 (identified custodians, identified date-ranges and identified phrase-families) — no inbox review, reading or relevance-assessment of any email being sought or required.

(b) **Verification affidavit (produce-or-swear).** MSH is ordered, by its Chief Executive or a delegated Director, to file and serve a single affidavit within seven (7) business days of the order which, in respect of each pressed Item (Items 1, 2, 3(a), 3(b), 9, 10 and 19), the AVAC payroll export sought at Item 16, and each Item on which MSH asserts non-existence, destruction or irrelevance (Items 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 18 and 20): (i) confirms on oath that the server-side export or search was in fact undertaken, identifying the name and position of the person who conducted it, and the custodian, system, date-range and method applied; (ii) produces the records returned by that search; (iii) where the search returns no record, states on oath that the document does not exist, deposing the basis on which it is said not to exist — and, where any document already before the Commission or disclosed in this proceeding appears to fall within an Item for which non-existence is maintained (in particular, as to Item 20, the correspondence of 15–16 May 2024 disclosed by the Respondent on 11 June 2026), identifies that document and either produces it or states on oath the basis on which it is said to fall outside the Item; and (iv) is given by the Chief Executive or delegated Director as the accountable deponent, who may depose to matters within the knowledge of a systems or eHealth officer — in particular, for the SPOK emergency-code records (Items 1–2), the date and nature of the system upgrade, whether the pre-upgrade records were migrated, archived or destroyed, and the identity, author, holder and source system of the "spreadsheet of recorded MET calls" referred to in MSH's letter — on information and belief from a named officer, identifying that officer's position and exhibiting or separately swearing that officer's account; and (v) addresses, in respect of each Item, the specific matters set out in Schedule C. If the Commission considers any element of this verification beyond what is appropriate to its decision of the objection, it may direct such lesser verification as it sees fit, the balance of these orders to stand.

(c) To the extent any extension is required, the time for the production at (a) is fixed at a date certain and not contingent upon the supply of any pleading to a non-party.

(d) **Privacy safeguard.** If any question of privacy or confidentiality is raised in respect of the export, the documents be produced to the Commission for its inspection in the first instance, with access to the parties as the Commission directs and subject to any order under s 580 of the *Industrial Relations Act 2016*.

(e) **Confidentiality of sensitive material (s 580 IR Act 2016) — non-publication (PID).** Non-publication of any information identifying the fact or content of the Public Interest Disclosure (reference PID 24-ESU-1130) and the Ethical Standards Unit determination, giving effect to the confidentiality required by s 65 of the *Public Interest Disclosure Act 2010* (Qld). (Any patient-identifying information appearing in the records produced may be redacted, and is in any event subject to the Commission-inspection safeguard at Part B(d); the Appellant seeks no order in respect of his own medical evidence, which is a matter for the substantive appeal.)

(f) Costs reserved.

(g) Such further or other orders as the Commission considers appropriate.

## SCHEDULE A — DISPOSITION OF THE TWENTY ITEMS
The Appellant does not press the Form 29 in full. He has narrowed and disposed of the twenty Items as set out in the overview table below, each pressed Item anchored to the stressor pleaded in the Amended 9A; the detail and the disposition notes follow.

**Disposition of all twenty Items (overview):**

| 3(b) | Pressed | Management discussion / action on those complaints |
