The scope and relevance of each pressed Item are set out in the Relevance Map at Schedule B; the Item 10 sub-sets (a)–(e) are summarised at Part B(a).

**Produce-or-swear (the Items so marked in the overview).** For each, the Appellant neither accepts nor rejects MSH's informal assertion of non-existence, destruction or irrelevance; he asks only that it be produced, or its non-existence (or destruction) sworn under Part B(b) and Schedule C after a defined search. A sworn statement that a hospital does not retain its emergency-code paging logs (Items 1–2), holds no fatigue risk assessment for the 17–18 March 2024 pairing (Item 4), or destroyed the communication-book record (Item 18) is of obvious significance to the s 32(5)(a) inquiry; the Appellant reserves any argument on the effect of a sworn negative until the verification affidavit is filed. As to **Item 18**, only the removal of a page is admitted (Form 24, Para 6; Stressor 1(b)); that admission does not establish the fate of the communication book or the 15 November 2023 business-case minutes.

**Already produced (no order needed) — Items 6, 11, 12 (audit trail), 13, 15** (disclosed with MSH's letter of 5 June 2026; Affidavit ¶51). As to **Item 16** (AVAC payroll export, PRN 15397775 and 15605601), what MSH produced are **Daily Staffing Variance Forms**, each signed by the Line Manager as "Switchboard Manager" — not the AVAC payroll-system export the Notice sought; the Appellant presses Item 16 only to the extent of that export, to be produced under Part B(b) (for PRN 15397775 and 15605601) or its non-existence sworn.

**Withdrawn — Items 8, 14 and 17, and the comparator balance of Item 12.** Item 8 (management-system login records) duplicates the presence point captured by Item 9; Item 14 (text messages) was exchanged on the Line Manager's personal mobile device and is outside MSH's possession or control (cf. r 64B); and the comparator payroll export (Item 17) and the balance of the comparator pandemic-leave material (Item 12) are not pressed, on the affected staff's privacy grounds (r 64E(4)(e)–(f)).

**Narrowing of Item 19 (date and scope).** Item 19 sought union-delegate correspondence over 1 March – 30 June 2024, confined to identified custodians (the Line Manager, the Director, the Logan Hospital health-team mailbox, and HR / People and Culture). The Appellant narrows the pressed period to 18 May 2024 (his email to Ms Heather Hayes of Together Queensland) through to the injury date, 18 June 2024 — capturing the union's forwarding of that request to MSH and MSH's handling of it. The earlier notification of intention (11 August 2023) is admitted as sent (Form 24, Para 18) and needs no disclosure; the failure to facilitate the appointment for over 9 months is denied (Form 24, Para 19) and is the contested fact this Item goes to. MSH's objection that Item 19 would require searching ~20,006 staff mailboxes mischaracterises it: the Item is confined to the custodians above — indeed the very custodians MSH itself proposed in its 5 June 2026 letter. As to date, MSH's suggested 17–18 March 2024 window predates the 18 May union request and so could not capture the correspondence at all; the apt and far narrower window is 18 May – 18 June 2024. The Item seeks only correspondence already held in those custodians' mailboxes (received from Together Queensland), not Together's own records, so no production notice to Together is required. The Appellant is content for MSH to satisfy Item 19 by a sworn statement of what was received from Together (Ms Hayes) and what action was taken.

## PART C — GROUNDS
1. **The matter in issue.** The Form 29 is directly relevant to the matter in issue in the appeal (the s 32(5)(a) "reasonable management action" defence) as articulated in the Amended Statement of Facts and Contentions filed 7 April 2026 ("the Amended 9A"). The Continuation Schedule to the Form 29 states that matter in issue and ties each Item, by a Relevance Anchor Table, to specified stressors pleaded in the Amended 9A and to the admitted facts in the Respondent's Form 24.

2. **The health dimension.** The documents are not collateral to a private dispute; they go to whether the patient-safety and clinical-governance functions of the Switchboard were compromised. As deposed (Affidavit, ¶¶6–25), the Switchboard is the hospital's communications hub — where emergency codes are activated and urgent pathology results relayed doctor-to-doctor. The misrouted-call corpus (Item 3(a)), the manager's presence record (Item 9) and her directives (Item 10) bear directly on whether those time-critical communications were delayed or misdirected — a patient-safety reality visible only from within MSH's own systems, and inseparable from the s 32(5)(a) evaluation.

3. **Possession and control.** As deposed (Affidavit, para 46), each pressed Item is recorded in documents within MSH's exclusive possession or control — its email system, its Active Directory / Entra / Citrix identity-management environment, its Security Access swipe-card system, its meeting and governance records, and its roster and HR systems. The Appellant, as the Switchboard operator, cannot produce them.

4. **No other reasonably simple, inexpensive way (r 64B).** The probative content of the documents is their completeness — the scale, frequency and pattern of the conduct pleaded. The Appellant can produce individual examples (and has annexed them to the Affidavit), but cannot export the complete corpus. There is no other reasonably simple, inexpensive way for the Appellant to prove what the documents show, save by bulk server-side export from MSH's systems, which is achievable at minimal cost and requires no inbox review.

5. **The period is the course of conduct — not a narrow window, and not unlimited.** Because the injury developed cumulatively over the course of management conduct, the documents go to the volume and frequency of that conduct. The Form 29 noticed the email-based Items (3(a), 3(b) and 10) for the period 1 December 2023 to 30 June 2024, and the Appellant presses no period earlier or broader than the Notice; the SPOK paging Item (Item 1) is confined to 17–18 March 2024. Confining disclosure to those two days alone would sample the conduct, not show it; the period the Notice fixes is the appropriate measure of the pleaded course (and see *Delaney v Q-COMP* [2005] QIC 11; 178 QGIG 197, where the composite course of conduct, not isolated shifts, is the unit of assessment). The volume of directives from the Line Manager to the Switchboard across the noticed period is sought not by producing the corpus but by an aggregate monthly count (sender, date, recipient-list and subject only — no message bodies: Schedule A, Item 10), which proves the scale without any review of content (Stressor 1(a)).

6. **The fatigue-governance records (Items 4, 5 and 7).** MSH's own letter states that fatigue risk management at the Switchboard was "implemented… after 30 June 2024 in connection with an organisational change related to the reporting lines for Switchboard" — which concedes that a fatigue risk-management framework applies to the Switchboard work area, and locates its implementation there only after the date of injury. That framework reflects the Queensland Health Fatigue Risk Management System (FRMS Implementation Guideline QH-GDL-401-3.3). MSH's objection that fatigue records do not exist because "Fatigue Risk Management System training only applies to health practitioners and clinical assistants" answers a different question: Item 5 concerns training, but Items 4 and 7 concern the fatigue risk-*assessment* and register records. Whether those records exist for the Switchboard as at 17–18 March 2024 is precisely what the verification on oath (Part B(b)) should establish.

7. **The objection cannot rest on non-existence.** MSH itself produced documents responsive to Items 6, 11, 12, 13, 15 and 16 with its 5 June 2026 letter, and the Respondent disclosed further responsive material on 11 June 2026 (the 15–16 May 2024 correspondence within the Item 20 window) — establishing that the classes of record sought are real and retrievable from MSH's systems. The Appellant has also annexed individual examples (the manager's 9 May 2024 email; the 18–20 May 2024 union correspondence) which show the same on their face.

8. **The application is not oppressive — it seeks an export, not a review.** The Appellant seeks only the native electronic export of the records returned by a self-executing server-side filter (the identified custodians, date-ranges and phrase-families in the Form 29); no inbox review, reading or relevance-assessment by MSH is sought or required. The relief is the antithesis of a general search, and is offered subject to nil-result discharge (Part B(b)). Any claim of legal professional privilege may be made item-by-item over a specific record and is no basis for resisting the export itself; and any question of privacy or confidentiality is met by production to the Commission in the first instance (Part B(d)). No question of privilege or privacy justifies refusing the export — at most it governs the manner of access, which is the Commission's to manage.

9. **The verification affidavit is the proportionate course.** Framed as produce-or-swear, the order leaves MSH a single, bounded step: it either produces the documents, or verifies their non-existence on oath after a defined search. Either course resolves the objection without an item-by-item production dispute. The power to make the order arises under r 64G(2), which empowers the Commission to make any order appropriate to its decision of the objection, together with the Commission's general power to give directions for the conduct of the proceeding; the order does no more than ensure the objection — production, or verified non-existence — is resolved on a proper evidentiary footing. For each Item, MSH must therefore either produce the record or swear, after a defined search, that it does not exist; there is no third answer, and an un-sworn assertion of non-existence in correspondence is not a basis on which the objection can be sustained. The Appellant respectfully submits this is the orderly and proportionate disposition.

10. **The model-litigant expectation.** In *State of Queensland (Queensland Police Service) v Workers' Compensation Regulator* [2025] QIRC 203 (O'Neill IC), the Commission applied the model-litigant principles to a State respondent in a disclosure dispute. While that duty binds the Regulator as a party, the same expectation of candour should inform how a government entity such as MSH approaches a bounded, self-executing export: it should facilitate production, and a bare assertion that its emergency-code logs or fatigue records "do not exist" should be tested on oath, not accepted.

11. **Evidentiary context.** The Respondent obtained the Appellant's medical records under a Form 29 never served on him; the Respondent admits the non-service, saying it was not required to serve him as a party (Form 24, Para 25). The Appellant does not agitate the merits of that course here, but the contrast is instructive: he cannot simply obtain MSH's records — he must serve a sealed Notice on MSH and the persons affected (rr 64C, 64D), absorb their objection (r 64E) and bring this application (r 64G); his own records were taken from a third party without the Notice ever reaching him.

## PART C2 — MSH'S OBJECTIONS ANSWERED (letter of 5 June 2026, K-LM26/729, signed by the Chief Executive)
MSH's objections reduce to three refrains, each of which the Notice already answers — and the letter itself supplies several of the answers the disclosure was designed to obtain.

1. *"We have not received the Form 9A, so we cannot assess relevance."* The Notice does not depend on the supply of the parties' pleadings to a non-party. The Continuation Schedule states the matter in issue and ties each Item, by a Relevance Anchor Table, to a specified Stressor and an admitted Form 24 fact on its face (r 64C). Relevance is demonstrable from the Notice itself; the absence of the Form 9A in MSH's hands is not a ground under r 64E(4).

2. *"Compliance would require eHealth to review and search individual staff email accounts" (Items 3(a), 10).* It would not. The Appellant seeks a server-side export (a self-executing filter bounded by identified custodian, identified date-range and identified phrase-family) and expressly disclaims any inbox review (Notice, Administrative Concessions; Part B(a)). MSH's "expense and inconvenience" objection rests on a characterisation of the request as a manual account-by-account search, which is incorrect. As to Item 3(a) in particular, MSH's own letter records that complaints about Switchboard operational errors "are made directly to the Line Manager of Switch Board and managed solely via email" — i.e. a single identified mailbox, not a hospital-wide trawl.

3. *"The matter in issue relates only to the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024."* It does not — Stressor 1(a) pleads a course of conduct, of which the 7-hour break (Stressor 3) is one part. The Notice fixes the email-Items at 1 December 2023 – 30 June 2024; confining disclosure to two days would sample that course, not show it (ground 5; *Delaney v Q-COMP* [2005] QIC 11).

4. *"Item 19 would require searching the emails of ~20,006 staff."* It would not. Item 19 is confined to identified custodians (the Line Manager, the Director, the Logan Hospital health-team mailbox and HR) and is narrowed to 18 May – 18 June 2024 (Schedule A), adopting the custodians MSH itself proposed; MSH's suggested 17–18 March 2024 date predates the 18 May 2024 union request and so could not capture the correspondence.

5. *"Item 9 (building access) lacks relevance and particularity, and the Switchboard office has no swipe access."* The Appellant does not seek a Switchboard-office swipe. He seeks the Line Manager's own security access-card records (by her card identity) for the collocated office area and the building — records MSH's access-control system holds — confined to the pleaded-conduct windows (Schedule A). Particularity is satisfied (one identified person; identified dates); relevance is direct (whether the manager was on site when a directive issued or a complaint was left unactioned, going to Stressor 1(a)); and any effect on the Line Manager is managed by the Commission-inspection-first safeguard (Part B(d)), which governs the manner of access, not refusal.

6. **The letter supplies the answers, under the Chief Executive's hand.** In responding, MSH has stated: (a) *No remedial change* — MSH states there have been "no 'consequential' changes to operating procedures over the period requested" (Item 3(c)): nothing was changed to remedy the misroute complaints — although operational changes that worsened the position were in fact made during the period (the unilateral "effective immediately" directives altering call-handling, and the restriction of contact-number and directory updates to the new Switchboard Telecommunications Coordinator role: Affidavit ¶¶22, 26–27) — changes the verification (Schedule C, Item 3(c)) should reconcile with the "no consequential changes" statement. (b) *No fatigue framework at the time, and a restructure* — fatigue risk management at the Switchboard "occurred after 30 June 2024 in connection with an organisational change related to the reporting lines for Switchboard" (Item 5): no FRMS framework was in place at the date of injury. (c) *Emergency-code logs not retained* — the SPOK records "do not exist… records predating [the system] upgrade were not retained," yet "a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls is available for the period 17–18 March 2024" (Items 1–2). Whether that spreadsheet is a SPOK export, a separate MSH record, or the monthly call-statistics sheet the Appellant himself authors cannot be told from the letter (Schedule C requires the verification to classify it). If it is the Appellant's own sheet, it records call and code *volume* only and does not satisfy Item 1, which seeks the SPOK system-level paging data — which clinician was paged, whether each page was received or acknowledged, and any misdirection, with timestamps — that MSH alone holds (Affidavit, ¶9). If it is a separate MSH or SPOK record, it is a contemporaneous record for the exact pleaded shift and should be produced under Item 1. Either way the matter goes to the s 32(5)(a) inquiry, not to refusing production.

7. **The verification affidavit should formalise these statements.** Where MSH states a record does not exist (Items 1–2, 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 18, 20), the order at Part B(b) requires that to be sworn by the Chief Executive or a delegated Director, after a defined search by a named person and with the required contents set out Item by Item in Schedule C — so the statements made informally in the letter are placed on the evidentiary footing the appeal requires. The Item 20 answer illustrates why a sworn answer matters: MSH says that material "does not exist" because "PID24-ESU-1130" commenced in November 2024, yet the Respondent disclosed correspondence of 15–16 May 2024 — squarely within the Item 20 window — on 11 June 2026 (Affidavit, ¶52). MSH cannot swear non-existence consistently with that disclosure; the reference number is a later-assigned identifier, not the date the material came into existence. So too the Item 18 "already conceded" answer (Form 24, Para 14): only the removal of a page is admitted (Form 24, Para 6), not the fate of the communication book or the 15 November 2023 business-case minutes. Each such answer should be sworn, not asserted.

## SCHEDULE C — REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE VERIFICATION AFFIDAVIT (Part B(b))
This Schedule states what the verification affidavit must depose to. It is directed only to verifying, after a defined search, what exists and what is to be produced; it is not directed to any wider inquiry into MSH's conduct. So that a statement of non-existence is verified rather than asserted in the abstract, the affidavit must address the following.

**Part 1 — For every Item for which production is sought, or non-existence, destruction or irrelevance is asserted, the affidavit must depose:**

(1) that a search was in fact undertaken (a bare assertion of non-existence, unsupported by a deposed search, being insufficient); the name and position of the person who conducted the search, and whether that person had access to the systems searched; the systems, mailboxes, repositories and custodians searched; the search terms, filters and date-range applied; and the date on which the search was undertaken;

(2) whether the record exists as at the date of the affidavit; if it does not, whether it ever existed; and, if it once existed, when and by what means it ceased to exist (deletion, system migration, archiving, disposal or destruction), on whose authority or instruction, and under what retention policy or schedule;

(3) whether any copy, backup, archive, export, migrated instance, or version held on any superseding system exists, and if so its production;

(4) where any document already before the Commission, or disclosed in this proceeding, appears to fall within the Item, identification of that document and either its production or the precise basis on which it is said to fall outside the Item; and

(5) the name and position of any officer on whose knowledge the deponent relies for the above, that officer's account being exhibited or separately sworn.

**Part 2 — Item-specific matters, in addition to Part 1:**

- **Items 1–2 (SPOK emergency-code / paging records — "not retained" must be sworn):** the date and nature of the SPOK "upgrade"; whether the pre-upgrade records were migrated to, retained in, or are retrievable from the upgraded system or any successor or backup, with the production of any that are retrievable and, for any that are not, the reason they are said to be irretrievable and the date and authority on which they ceased to be retained. As to the "spreadsheet of recorded MET calls" for 17–18 March 2024 — its identity, author, custodian and source system, and whether it is (a) an export from the SPOK system itself, (b) an MSH-maintained administrative record, or (c) the Appellant's own monthly call-statistics sheet (which tallies call and emergency-code *volume* only) — together with its production. If it is (c), the affidavit must confirm that the SPOK *system-level* records — which clinician was paged, whether each page was received or acknowledged, whether any page was misdirected, and the associated timestamps — have been separately searched, those system-level records being held only by MSH and not by the Appellant (Affidavit ¶9).
- **Item 3(c) (consequential changes — "no changes" must be sworn):** each change to Switchboard operating procedures, reporting lines or systems over the noticed period, with its date — addressing in terms the SPOK upgrade, the Switchboard reporting-line reorganisation, the issue of a Queensland Health device to the Line Manager, and the introduction of a separate Switchboard Telecommunications Coordinator role together with any restriction of contact-number and directory-database updates to that role — or, if there was no such change, a statement to that effect on oath; and in either case the reconciliation of the answer with the statement in the letter that there were "no consequential changes".
- **Items 4 and 7 (fatigue risk-assessment / register — "none exist" must be sworn):** whether any fatigue risk-assessment or register record referable to the Switchboard work area existed as at 17–18 March 2024 (as distinct from training records); if so, its production; if not, a statement on oath that none existed.
- **Item 5 (fatigue framework — identify the policy, or swear none applied):** each fatigue-risk-management policy, directive, guideline or framework (including any under the Queensland Health Fatigue Risk Management System) that applied to the Switchboard work area, or to its non-clinical administrative staff, as at 17–18 March 2024 — identified by name and number — or, if none applied, a statement on oath to that effect; and in either case the date on which fatigue risk management was implemented at the Switchboard, reconciled with MSH's statement that it occurred only "after 30 June 2024".
- **Item 16 (AVAC payroll export):** production of the AVAC payroll-system export for PRN 15397775 and PRN 15605601, or a sworn statement that no such export exists (the Daily Staffing Variance Forms already produced not being that export).
- **Item 18 (communication book; 15 November 2023 business-case minutes):** whether each record exists; and if either was destroyed, when, by whom, and under what authority.
- **Item 20 (operational / HR response, 13–31 May 2024):** whether records of the operational and human-resources response to the matters raised in that window exist, addressing in terms the correspondence of 15–16 May 2024 disclosed by the Respondent on 11 June 2026, independently of when the reference "PID24-ESU-1130" was assigned.

 PART C — GROUNDS

  1. The matter in issue. The Form 29 is directly relevant to the matter in issue in the appeal (the s 32(5)(a)
  "reasonable management action" defence) as articulated in the Amended Statement of Facts and
  Contentions filed 7 April 2026 ("the Amended 9A"). The Continuation Schedule to the Form 29 states that
  matter in issue and ties each Item, by a Relevance Anchor Table, to specified stressors pleaded in the
  Amended 9A and to the admitted facts in the Respondent's Form 24.

  2. The health dimension. The documents are not collateral to a private dispute; they go to whether the
  patient-safety and clinical-governance functions of the Switchboard were compromised. As deposed
  (Affidavit, ¶¶6–25), the Switchboard is the hospital's communications hub — where emergency codes are
  activated and urgent pathology results relayed doctor-to-doctor. The misrouted-call corpus (Item 3(a)), the
  manager's presence record (Item 9) and her directives (Item 10) bear directly on whether those time-critical
  communications were delayed or misdirected — a patient-safety reality visible only from within MSH's
  own systems, and inseparable from the s 32(5)(a) evaluation.

  3. Possession and control. As deposed (Affidavit, para 46), each pressed Item is recorded in documents
  within MSH's exclusive possession or control — its email system, its Active Directory / Entra / Citrix
  identity-management environment, its Security Access swipe-card system, its meeting and governance
  records, and its roster and HR systems. The Appellant, as the Switchboard operator, cannot produce them.

  4. No other reasonably simple, inexpensive way (r 64B). The probative content of the documents is their
  completeness — the scale, frequency and pattern of the conduct pleaded. The Appellant can produce
  individual examples (and has annexed them to the Affidavit), but cannot export the complete corpus. There
  is no other reasonably simple, inexpensive way for the Appellant to prove what the documents show, save
  by bulk server-side export from MSH's systems, which is achievable at minimal cost and requires no inbox
  review.

  5. The period is the course of conduct — not a narrow window, and not unlimited. Because the injury
  developed cumulatively over the course of management conduct, the documents go to the volume and
  frequency of that conduct. The Form 29 noticed the email-based Items (3(a), 3(b) and 10) for the period 1
  December 2023 to 30 June 2024, and the Appellant presses no period earlier or broader than the Notice; the
  SPOK paging Item (Item 1) is confined to 17–18 March 2024. Confining disclosure to those two days
  alone would sample the conduct, not show it; the period the Notice fixes is the appropriate measure of the
  pleaded course (and see Delaney v Q-COMP [2005] QIC 11; 178 QGIG 197, where the composite course
  of conduct, not isolated shifts, is the unit of assessment). The volume of directives from the Line Manager
  to the Switchboard across the noticed period is sought not by producing the corpus but by an aggregate


WC/2024/227 — Shepherd v Workers' Compensation Regulator                       Form 4 (Application, r 64G) — Page 5 of 12

>>> lodgement/WC2024227_Form4_FINAL.pdf :: page 6
  monthly count (sender, date, recipient-list and subject only — no message bodies: Schedule A, Item 10),
  which proves the scale without any review of content (Stressor 1(a)).

  6. The fatigue-governance records (Items 4, 5 and 7). MSH's own letter states that fatigue risk
  management at the Switchboard was "implemented… after 30 June 2024 in connection with an
  organisational change related to the reporting lines for Switchboard" — which concedes that a fatigue risk-
  management framework applies to the Switchboard work area, and locates its implementation there only
  after the date of injury. That framework reflects the Queensland Health Fatigue Risk Management System
  (FRMS Implementation Guideline QH-GDL-401-3.3). MSH's objection that fatigue records do not exist
  because "Fatigue Risk Management System training only applies to health practitioners and clinical
  assistants" answers a different question: Item 5 concerns training, but Items 4 and 7 concern the fatigue
  risk-assessment and register records. Whether those records exist for the Switchboard as at 17–18 March
  2024 is precisely what the verification on oath (Part B(b)) should establish.

  7. The objection cannot rest on non-existence. MSH itself produced documents responsive to Items 6,
  11, 12, 13, 15 and 16 with its 5 June 2026 letter, and the Respondent disclosed further responsive material
  on 11 June 2026 (the 15–16 May 2024 correspondence within the Item 20 window) — establishing that the
  classes of record sought are real and retrievable from MSH's systems. The Appellant has also annexed
  individual examples (the manager's 9 May 2024 email; the 18–20 May 2024 union correspondence) which
  show the same on their face.

  8. The application is not oppressive — it seeks an export, not a review. The Appellant seeks only the
  native electronic export of the records returned by a self-executing server-side filter (the identified
  custodians, date-ranges and phrase-families in the Form 29); no inbox review, reading or relevance-
  assessment by MSH is sought or required. The relief is the antithesis of a general search, and is offered
  subject to nil-result discharge (Part B(b)). Any claim of legal professional privilege may be made item-by-
  item over a specific record and is no basis for resisting the export itself; and any question of privacy or
  confidentiality is met by production to the Commission in the first instance (Part B(d)). No question of
  privilege or privacy justifies refusing the export — at most it governs the manner of access, which is the
  Commission's to manage.

  9. The verification affidavit is the proportionate course. Framed as produce-or-swear, the order leaves
  MSH a single, bounded step: it either produces the documents, or verifies their non-existence on oath after
  a defined search. Either course resolves the objection without an item-by-item production dispute. The
  power to make the order arises under r 64G(2), which empowers the Commission to make any order
  appropriate to its decision of the objection, together with the Commission's general power to give
  directions for the conduct of the proceeding; the order does no more than ensure the objection —
  production, or verified non-existence — is resolved on a proper evidentiary footing. For each Item, MSH
  must therefore either produce the record or swear, after a defined search, that it does not exist; there is no
  third answer, and an un-sworn assertion of non-existence in correspondence is not a basis on which the
  objection can be sustained. The Appellant respectfully submits this is the orderly and proportionate
  disposition.

  10. The model-litigant expectation. In State of Queensland (Queensland Police Service) v Workers'
  Compensation Regulator [2025] QIRC 203 (O'Neill IC), the Commission applied the model-litigant
  principles to a State respondent in a disclosure dispute. While that duty binds the Regulator as a party, the
  same expectation of candour should inform how a government entity such as MSH approaches a bounded,


WC/2024/227 — Shepherd v Workers' Compensation Regulator                        Form 4 (Application, r 64G) — Page 6 of 12

>>> lodgement/WC2024227_Form4_FINAL.pdf :: page 7
  self-executing export: it should facilitate production, and a bare assertion that its emergency-code logs or
  fatigue records "do not exist" should be tested on oath, not accepted.

  11. Evidentiary context. The Respondent obtained the Appellant's medical records under a Form 29 never
  served on him; the Respondent admits the non-service, saying it was not required to serve him as a party
  (Form 24, Para 25). The Appellant does not agitate the merits of that course here, but the contrast is
  instructive: he cannot simply obtain MSH's records — he must serve a sealed Notice on MSH and the
  persons affected (rr 64C, 64D), absorb their objection (r 64E) and bring this application (r 64G); his own
  records were taken from a third party without the Notice ever reaching him.


 PART C2 — MSH'S OBJECTIONS ANSWERED (letter of 5 June 2026, K-LM26/729,
 signed by the Chief Executive)
 MSH's objections reduce to three refrains, each of which the Notice already answers — and the letter itself
 supplies several of the answers the disclosure was designed to obtain.


  1. "We have not received the Form 9A, so we cannot assess relevance." The Notice does not depend on the
  supply of the parties' pleadings to a non-party. The Continuation Schedule states the matter in issue and ties
  each Item, by a Relevance Anchor Table, to a specified Stressor and an admitted Form 24 fact on its face (r
  64C). Relevance is demonstrable from the Notice itself; the absence of the Form 9A in MSH's hands is not
  a ground under r 64E(4).

  2. "Compliance would require eHealth to review and search individual staff email accounts" (Items 3(a),
  10). It would not. The Appellant seeks a server-side export (a self-executing filter bounded by identified
  custodian, identified date-range and identified phrase-family) and expressly disclaims any inbox review
  (Notice, Administrative Concessions; Part B(a)). MSH's "expense and inconvenience" objection rests on a
  characterisation of the request as a manual account-by-account search, which is incorrect. As to Item 3(a)
  in particular, MSH's own letter records that complaints about Switchboard operational errors "are made
  directly to the Line Manager of Switch Board and managed solely via email" — i.e. a single identified
  mailbox, not a hospital-wide trawl.

  3. "The matter in issue relates only to the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024." It does not — Stressor
  1(a) pleads a course of conduct, of which the 7-hour break (Stressor 3) is one part. The Notice fixes the
  email-Items at 1 December 2023 – 30 June 2024; confining disclosure to two days would sample that
  course, not show it (ground 5; Delaney v Q-COMP [2005] QIC 11).

  4. "Item 19 would require searching the emails of ~20,006 staff." It would not. Item 19 is confined to
  identified custodians (the Line Manager, the Director, the Logan Hospital health-team mailbox and HR)
  and is narrowed to 18 May – 18 June 2024 (Schedule A), adopting the custodians MSH itself proposed;
  MSH's suggested 17–18 March 2024 date predates the 18 May 2024 union request and so could not capture
  the correspondence.

  5. "Item 9 (building access) lacks relevance and particularity, and the Switchboard office has no swipe
  access." The Appellant does not seek a Switchboard-office swipe. He seeks the Line Manager's own
  security access-card records (by her card identity) for the collocated office area and the building — records
  MSH's access-control system holds — confined to the pleaded-conduct windows (Schedule A).
  Particularity is satisfied (one identified person; identified dates); relevance is direct (whether the manager

  was on site when a directive issued or a complaint was left unactioned, going to Stressor 1(a)); and any
  effect on the Line Manager is managed by the Commission-inspection-first safeguard (Part B(d)), which
  governs the manner of access, not refusal.

  6. The letter supplies the answers, under the Chief Executive's hand. In responding, MSH has stated:
  (a) No remedial change — MSH states there have been "no 'consequential' changes to operating procedures
  over the period requested" (Item 3(c)): nothing was changed to remedy the misroute complaints —
  although operational changes that worsened the position were in fact made during the period (the unilateral
  "effective immediately" directives altering call-handling, and the restriction of contact-number and
  directory updates to the new Switchboard Telecommunications Coordinator role: Affidavit ¶¶22, 26–27)
  — changes the verification (Schedule C, Item 3(c)) should reconcile with the "no consequential changes"
  statement. (b) No fatigue framework at the time, and a restructure — fatigue risk management at the
  Switchboard "occurred after 30 June 2024 in connection with an organisational change related to the
  reporting lines for Switchboard" (Item 5): no FRMS framework was in place at the date of injury. (c)
  Emergency-code logs not retained — the SPOK records "do not exist… records predating [the system]
  upgrade were not retained," yet "a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls is available for the period 17–18
  March 2024" (Items 1–2). Whether that spreadsheet is a SPOK export, a separate MSH record, or the
  monthly call-statistics sheet the Appellant himself authors cannot be told from the letter (Schedule C
  requires the verification to classify it). If it is the Appellant's own sheet, it records call and code volume
  only and does not satisfy Item 1, which seeks the SPOK system-level paging data — which clinician was
  paged, whether each page was received or acknowledged, and any misdirection, with timestamps — that
  MSH alone holds (Affidavit, ¶9). If it is a separate MSH or SPOK record, it is a contemporaneous record
  for the exact pleaded shift and should be produced under Item 1. Either way the matter goes to the s 32(5)
  (a) inquiry, not to refusing production.

  7. The verification affidavit should formalise these statements. Where MSH states a record does not
  exist (Items 1–2, 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 18, 20), the order at Part B(b) requires that to be sworn by the Chief
  Executive or a delegated Director, after a defined search by a named person and with the required contents
  set out Item by Item in Schedule C — so the statements made informally in the letter are placed on the
  evidentiary footing the appeal requires. The Item 20 answer illustrates why a sworn answer matters: MSH
  says that material "does not exist" because "PID24-ESU-1130" commenced in November 2024, yet the
  Respondent disclosed correspondence of 15–16 May 2024 — squarely within the Item 20 window — on
  11 June 2026 (Affidavit, ¶52). MSH cannot swear non-existence consistently with that disclosure; the
  reference number is a later-assigned identifier, not the date the material came into existence. So too the
  Item 18 "already conceded" answer (Form 24, Para 14): only the removal of a page is admitted (Form 24,
  Para 6), not the fate of the communication book or the 15 November 2023 business-case minutes. Each
  such answer should be sworn, not asserted.

 SCHEDULE C — REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE VERIFICATION AFFIDAVIT
 (Part B(b))
 This Schedule states what the verification affidavit must depose to. It is directed only to verifying, after a
 defined search, what exists and what is to be produced; it is not directed to any wider inquiry into MSH's
 conduct. So that a statement of non-existence is verified rather than asserted in the abstract, the affidavit
 must address the following.

 Part 1 — For every Item for which production is sought, or non-existence, destruction or irrelevance is
 asserted, the affidavit must depose:

 (1) that a search was in fact undertaken (a bare assertion of non-existence, unsupported by a deposed search,
 being insufficient); the name and position of the person who conducted the search, and whether that person
 had access to the systems searched; the systems, mailboxes, repositories and custodians searched; the search
 terms, filters and date-range applied; and the date on which the search was undertaken;

 (2) whether the record exists as at the date of the affidavit; if it does not, whether it ever existed; and, if it
 once existed, when and by what means it ceased to exist (deletion, system migration, archiving, disposal or
 destruction), on whose authority or instruction, and under what retention policy or schedule;

 (3) whether any copy, backup, archive, export, migrated instance, or version held on any superseding system
 exists, and if so its production;

 (4) where any document already before the Commission, or disclosed in this proceeding, appears to fall
 within the Item, identification of that document and either its production or the precise basis on which it is
 said to fall outside the Item; and

 (5) the name and position of any officer on whose knowledge the deponent relies for the above, that officer's

A. Application and Orders Sought
1.     By correspondence dated 5 June 2026, signed by its Chief Executive and provided in accordance with the
       direction issued from the Chambers of Commissioner Dwyer on 22 May 2026, Metro South Hospital and
       Health Service (“MSH”) responded to the Appellant’s Form 29 Notice of Non-Party Disclosure sealed 22

       seven further Items do not exist or are not in MSH’s possession; and objects under rule 64E(4) of the
       Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011 (“the Rules”) to the remainder. This application accepts the
       greater part of that response. It asks the Commission to decide only the objections that remain, on terms
       the Appellant has himself narrowed (in one instance to the very scope MSH proposed), and to require
       verification of one answer that a document already before the Commission contradicts.
2.     TAKE NOTICE that the Appellant applies under rule 64G(1) for the following orders:
       (a)      the objections to Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10 and 19 of the Notice are overruled, and MSH is to
                produce the documents described in Schedule A (items 1 to 6) within fourteen (14) days of the
                order;
       (b)      MSH is to produce within fourteen (14) days the spreadsheet of recorded MET calls for the period
                17–18 March 2024 identified in its response to Items 1 and 2, against which no ground of objection
                is raised;
       (c)      pursuant to rule 64G(2), MSH is to verify by affidavit of an officer with direct knowledge of the
                searches undertaken, within fourteen (14) days, its statements that documents responsive to Items
                1–2 (non-retention following the SPOK upgrade), 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20 do not exist or are not in
                its possession or control, identifying in each case the systems searched, the searches undertaken,
                and the basis for the statement, and, as to Item 14, the date on which a Queensland Health mobile
                device was issued to the Line Manager, and otherwise in the terms of order 6 of the accompanying
                draft order (including the governance-search particulars for Items 4, 5 and 7, the basis for any
                maintained non-possession as to Item 20 having regard to Annexure C, and the process references
                for the Item 16 enclosures);
       (d)      as to Item 18, noting MSH’s statement that the destruction of the record is conceded on the
                pleadings, production is not pressed upon MSH confirming that statement in the affidavit referred
                to in order (c);
       (e)      Items 12 (balance) and 17 of the Notice are not pressed, in light of the privacy considerations MSH
                has raised;
       (f)      each party bear its own costs of the application, in accordance with rule 64G(3); and
       (g)      such further or other orders as the Commission considers appropriate.
B. Jurisdiction and Timeliness
3.     The Notice was sealed by the Industrial Registry on 22 April 2026 and served on MSH by email at 5:08
       PM that day. By direction issued from Chambers on 22 May 2026 (in effect, leave under rule 64E(1) for
                                                    Page 1

>>> lodgement/WC2024227_Form_4_Application_Rule_64G.pdf :: page 2
     objection at a later time), MSH was directed to provide any objections by 4:00 PM on 5 June 2026.
     MSH’s objection was served by email at 3:02 PM on 5 June 2026. Rule 64G(1) permits this application
     within seven days after service of the objection; it is made within that period. Service of the objection
     operates as a stay of the Notice (rule 64F); this application brings the objected-to Items before the
     Commission for decision.
C. The Character of MSH’s Response
4.   The response falls into three categories. First, compliance: MSH has produced documents responsive to
     Items 6, 11, 12 (in part), 13, 15 and 16. That compliance is acknowledged; the enclosed records materially
     advance the appeal. Secondly, answers: for Items 1–2, 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20, MSH states that
     responsive documents do not exist or are not in its possession or control. Those are answers to the Notice
     rather than objections under rule 64E(4); they are addressed in Sections G and H. Thirdly, objections:
     for Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10, 12 (balance), 17, 18 and 19, MSH objects on grounds of expense and
     inconvenience (rule 64E(4)(a)), relevance (4(b)), particularity (4(c)), confidentiality (4(e)) and effect on
     a person (4(f)). Of these nine, the Appellant presses six, each on narrowed terms, and does not press three.
     None of the objections is put on the basis that the documents do not exist.
D. The Role of the Non-Party and the Matter in Issue
5.   Subdivision 7A allocates functions. The party issuing a notice must state in it the matter in issue (rule
     64C(1)). The non-party’s part is to produce (rule 64B(1)) or to object on the grounds rule 64E(4)
     provides. Where an objection is contested, the decision belongs to the Commission (rule 64G). Nothing
     in the subdivision asks the non-party to settle the scope of the appeal, or to measure relevance against its
     own restatement of the issues. That involves no criticism of MSH, whose reading is naturally operational;
     but it frames what the Commission is asked to decide.
6.   The standard the Rules apply is direct relevance: a notice may require production of documents directly
     relevant to a matter in issue in the proceeding. In practical terms, a document answers that standard where
     it is capable of tending to prove or disprove an allegation in issue, having regard to the matters pleaded
     and the issues those matters raise. Annexure B identifies, for each contested Item, the allegation the
     records tend to prove or disprove. Several objections instead test the Items against admissibility, or
     against the non-party’s view of what the evidence will show; neither is the question at the disclosure
     stage.
7.   Several of the objections proceed from such a restatement. The response treats the matter in issue, “as
     pleaded in the Notice”, as confined to the “consecutive shifts of 17 to 18 March 2024”, and tests each date
     range against that confined reading. The Notice states the matter in issue in materially wider terms: a
     psychiatric injury with onset in June 2024, sustained in the course of employment at the Logan Hospital
     Switchboard, in a de novo appeal in which the Appellant bears the onus of establishing the injury,
     including that the employment was a significant contributing factor to it, and that it did not arise out of
     reasonable management action taken in a reasonable way within s 32(5)(a) of the Workers’
     Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003. The consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024 are the
     keystone stressor; they are not the perimeter of the inquiry. The pleadings themselves sharpen the point:
     the Regulator’s own Independent Review Office has found that the 7-hour rest break constituted
     unreasonable management action (Form 24, ¶37). A restatement that confines disclosure to 17–18 March
     2024 confines it to the one event already the subject of that finding. On the pleadings and admitted facts
     presently before the Commission, the inquiry under s 32(5)(a) is broader than that single shift pairing; it
     extends to the course of conduct pleaded from June 2023 to June 2024, and the records sought bear
     directly on that broader inquiry.
8.   There is a further reason the restatement does not govern relevance. To confine disclosure to the events a
     non-party considers caused the injury is to treat the non-party’s opinion of causation as settled. The cause
     of a psychiatric injury is not a matter on which MSH, or any party, holds privileged insight; it is the
     question the appeal exists to decide. The degree, duration and density of the pleaded stressors are
     themselves facts in issue under s 32(5)(a): the reasonableness of management action, and the manner of
     its taking, fall to be weighed against the conduct’s extent, not a single instance of it. The Notice seeks
                                                    Page 2

>>> lodgement/WC2024227_Form_4_Application_Rule_64G.pdf :: page 3
      records of fact; the objections that resist it proceed on assumptions about what those records are likely to
      show or not show. The Appellant’s entitlement is correspondingly modest: to have the case as pleaded,
      including causation as pleaded, heard and determined on the evidence that bears upon it, not on a
      restatement that reduces it to a single shift pairing.
9.    The onus intensifies, rather than diminishes, the necessity of production. On a de novo appeal the
      Appellant bears the onus of establishing each element of s 32(1) and of excluding s 32(5)(a). The
      reasonableness of the management action over the pleaded course, and the degree, duration and density of
      the conduct said to have contributed to the injury, are accordingly matters the Appellant must prove,
      going both to whether the employment significantly contributed to the injury and to whether the action
      was reasonable and reasonably taken. The contemporaneous records of that conduct exist, if at all, in the
      non-party’s systems. A party required to prove the character of conduct cannot reasonably be left without
      the records of it, held solely by the author of that conduct; production allows the matters in issue to be
      determined on what the systems recorded rather than on contested recollection: a course that serves the
      parties and the Commission equally, whichever way the records fall. The burden objections have a force
      the Appellant accepts in part: some date ranges in the Notice were broad. Where that is so, a proportionate
      answer may lie in narrowed production on conditions rather than refusal; the Appellant has done the
      narrowing himself. Schedule A confines every contested Item by custodian, system and date before the
      Commission is asked to rule.
E. Expense, Inconvenience and the Delivery of Health Care
10.   Each rule 64E(4)(a) objection states that compliance would detract from MSH’s core function of
      providing health care; no order sought requires the Commission to weigh disclosure against patient care.
      The Schedule A terms confine every electronic search to identified corporate systems (a single Exchange
      mailbox custodian set, directory sign-in records, one access-control system), held by role-based
      custodians within defined windows, and performed by corporate and information services rather than
      clinical staff. That such searches are neither prohibitively expensive nor operationally disruptive is
      demonstrated, not merely asserted, by the Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026, addressed at Section
      G. Rule 64I entitles MSH to its reasonable expenses of production.
11.   Nor is the subject matter of the Notice opposed to the value MSH invokes; it is, in significant part, the
      same value. The Appellant shares that concern; the operational complaints the subject of Items 3(a) and
      3(b) were themselves directed to the safe operation of that function. The pleaded role is the coordination
      of Logan Hospital’s life-safety emergency codes (Code Blue and MET calls) through the Switchboard,
      and the fatigue governance of that function during the pleaded period is within the matter in issue, not
      adjacent to it. Patient safety is therefore not a consideration weighing against production; it is among the
      matters the records evidence.
F. The Items Pressed
12.   Items 1 and 2 (order (b)). MSH states the SPOK records were not retained following a system upgrade,
      but identifies “a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls” available for 17–18 March 2024. That spreadsheet
      does not appear among the enclosures. No ground of objection is raised against it; order (b) seeks its
      production.
13.   Items 3(a) and 3(b). The ground is expense (rule 64E(4)(a)). The response states that all employee
      complaints concerning Switchboard operational errors are made directly to the Line Manager and
      managed by email or verbally. That account itself supplies the cure: a single-custodian, keyword-limited
      search of the Line Manager’s mailbox over twelve weeks (Schedule A items 1 and 2), in place of the
      seven-month, multi-account search the objection describes. The burden of a search so confined is modest,
      and rule 64I meets its cost.
14.   Item 8. The grounds are expense and particularity. The particularity point is accepted and cured:
      Schedule A item 3 identifies the system (Windows Active Directory / Microsoft Entra ID sign-in audit
      records) and a single named account, over a defined window spanning the operational complaints the
      subject of Items 3(a) and 3(b) and the lead-up to the pleaded onset. Sign-in audit records are extracted by
      date-range query, not by review of content, so the window does not alter the character of the task. As to
                                                      Page 3

>>> lodgement/WC2024227_Form_4_Application_Rule_64G.pdf :: page 4
      expense, the passage in the response appears to have been carried across from the email-search
      objections: it describes reviewing “individual staff member email accounts”, which Item 8 does not seek.
      A directory sign-in export for one account is a standard administrative query against existing audit
      records.
15.   Item 9. The grounds are relevance, particularity and effect on a person (rule 64E(4)(b), (c), (f)). The
      response clarifies that the Switchboard has no dedicated swipe access but is collocated within an access-
      controlled office area; the Appellant accepts that clarification and re-specifies the Item accordingly
      (Schedule A item 4). As to relevance, the records serve four connected purposes: the Form 24 admissions
      place the seven-hour break between the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024 at the centre of the s
      32(5)(a) inquiry, and whether that action was taken in a reasonable way turns in part on what supervision
      was present when it occurred; and the Line Manager’s pattern of attendance across the period of the
      operational complaints, through to the pleaded onset, bears on the support available to the Switchboard
      while those complaints were being received, itself a component of the manner inquiry. Thirdly, the
      Amended Form 9A pleads as a material fact that the Line Manager “maintained an erratic physical
      presence” during the pleaded period (Part B, Stressor 1(a)); a record of attendance is the direct
      documentary answer to that pleaded fact. Fourthly, the window spans a further contested fact: the
      response admits the payroll instruction of 3 May 2024 and the submission of the AVAC on 28 May 2024
      (Form 24, ¶¶40–41) while denying any want of diligence in the twenty-five days between them (¶¶47–
      49); the Line Manager’s attendance across that period is direct evidence on that contest. A record of
      workplace attendance, in the form sought here, is not intrinsically private in the way medical, financial or
      family information would be; the “effect on a person” the response anticipates is the ordinary effect of
      relevant evidence, which rule 64E(4)(f) does not exist to prevent. Documents produced may in any event
      be used only for the purposes of this proceeding, and for Items 8 and 9 the Appellant proposes the
      concrete regime in the accompanying draft order: production to the Registry marked confidential,
      inspection confined to the parties for the purposes of this proceeding, and non-responsive personal
      information redacted: a regime that materially reduces any legitimate concern. The relevance objection
      was, moreover, advanced expressly subject to MSH’s stated limitation in assessing relevance without the
      pleadings; Annexure B removes that limitation.
16.   Item 10. The ground is expense. The Item is narrowed to the Line Manager and the Director as
      custodians, keyword-limited in the Notice’s own terms, over two months (Schedule A item 5). The
      ground is answered in the same way as for Items 3(a) and 3(b).
17.   Item 19. The grounds are expense and effect (rule 64E(4)(a), (f)). MSH proposed the cure in its own
      response: narrowing to 17–18 March 2024, limited to emails received from Together Queensland by the
      Line Manager, the Director, or members of the Logan Hospital Human Resources team who remain
      employed by MSH. The Appellant adopts that proposal without amendment (Schedule A item 6). The
      draft order makes the Item 19 order subject to notice to Together Queensland, with liberty to apply.
18.   Item 20. The response states that responsive documents do not exist because reference PID 24-ESU-1130
      commenced in November 2024, outside the 13–31 May 2024 window. That is accepted so far as it goes:
      the reference number post-dates the events. The disclosures themselves are pleaded, and both their
      character as a Public Interest Disclosure and the immediate response to them are admitted (Form 24,
      ¶¶20–21). The Item is re-specified by subject matter rather than reference number (Schedule A item 7):
      records of operational or human-resources action during 13–31 May 2024 responsive to the disclosures
      the Appellant made in that period. Properly understood, the Item always sought that subject matter: the
      contemporaneous operational and human-resources response within MSH, during 13–31 May 2024, to
      the disclosures the Appellant made in that period. The reference number, which on MSH’s own answer
      was assigned only in November 2024, was descriptive, not definitional; an item is not sensibly confined
      to a reference that did not exist during the period the item addresses. That such records exist is established
      by the Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026, addressed in Section G below. Annexure C accordingly
      demonstrates that the non-existence answer was mistaken, incomplete, or based on an unduly narrow
      construction of the Item as originally framed; Because MSH answered the Item rather than objecting to it
      under rule 64E(4), the primary relief sought is verification: the affidavit in the accompanying draft order
                                                      Page 4

>>> lodgement/WC2024227_Form_4_Application_Rule_64G.pdf :: page 5
      is to state, should non-possession be maintained, the precise basis on which it is maintained having regard
      to the correspondence at Annexure C. Should the Commission be satisfied that the Item, properly
      understood, sought the re-specified subject matter at Schedule A item 7, the Appellant respectfully
      invites an order for production on those terms under the further-orders limb (order (g)); the documents the
      Annexure evidences are, on their face, already assembled.
G. The Respondent’s Disclosure of 11 June 2026
19.   On 11 June 2026 the Respondent disclosed to the Appellant documents which, on its own description,
      were “received through Notice of Non-Party Disclosure request and conferencing”. That disclosure bears
      directly on the objections now before the Commission, and the Appellant relies on it as part of the
      material on this application (Annexure C). First, it establishes that records sought by the Notice exist.
      Among the documents disclosed is internal MSH correspondence of 15 and 16 May 2024 routing the
      Appellant’s disclosures within Logan Hospital Human Resources and to the Director, recording that the
      Ethical Standards Unit’s assessment was on foot. That is operational and human-resources action taken
      during the 13–31 May 2024 window, by the custodians identified in Schedule A item 7: precisely the
      subject matter of Item 20, to which MSH answered that documents do not exist. The correspondence
      originates from MSH human-resources officers within Logan Hospital; it is accordingly within MSH’s
      own systems, or accessible to it through Queensland Health records infrastructure. The answer is difficult
      to reconcile with the document and requires explanation, whether by production or affidavit verification.
20.   Second, it establishes that production is neither prohibitively expensive nor operationally
      disruptive. The documents disclosed are of the same character as a number of the email-based and
      administrative Items to which MSH objects on the ground of expense (internal email correspondence
      held by identified custodians, and complete records of administrative processes), assembled and
      produced through ordinary means; and rule 64I in any event provides for MSH’s reasonable expenses of
      compliance to be met. Where the same documents, held by the same custodians, have already been
      gathered and provided in this proceeding, an objection that gathering them is unduly burdensome is
      difficult to sustain; and rule 64B(2) is not engaged, there being no other reasonably simple and
      inexpensive way for the Appellant to prove matters that sit only with the non-party. Third, it confirms
      the breadth of the matter in issue. The disclosed material concerns mid-May 2024, two months before
      onset, and outside the “consecutive shifts of 17 to 18 March 2024” to which MSH would confine
      relevance. That the Respondent itself treats it as disclosable is inconsistent with the confined reading on
      which the objections depend.
H. Verification of the Non-Existence Answers
21.   For Items 1–2 (non-retention), 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20, MSH answers that documents do not exist or are
      not in its possession or control. The Appellant does not suggest those answers are other than honestly
      made. They are, however, presently statements in correspondence: unsworn, and in several instances
      statements on which the conduct of the appeal will rest. Rule 64G(2) empowers the Commission to make
      any order it considers appropriate; an order that the answers be verified by affidavit, identifying the
      systems searched, the searches undertaken and the basis for each statement, is a conventional and
      proportionate way of giving them a form on which the parties and the Commission can act.
22.   Verification has particular utility for the fatigue-management Items. The response states, for Items 4 and
      7, that Fatigue Risk Management System training applies only to health practitioners and clinical
      assistants, so that no such requirement applied to Switchboard staff; and, for Item 5, that fatigue risk
      management assessment was implemented at the Switchboard after 30 June 2024. Each statement may be
      accurate. Read together, they tend to indicate that no fatigue-management requirement applied to
      Switchboard staff before 30 June 2024, a period that includes the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024
      and the pleaded onset of the injury. The records the Items seek go to the manner in which the rostering
      decisions were taken (whether any fatigue-management requirement governed the function within which
      those decisions were made), and not merely to whether fatigue caused the injury; the latter is a medical
      question, but the former is a question about the manner of the management action, squarely within s 32(5)
      (a). The verifying affidavit should therefore identify the governance registers, policy repositories and

                                                     Page 5

>>> lodgement/WC2024227_Form_4_Application_Rule_64G.pdf :: page 6
      training records searched in connection with Items 4, 5 and 7, the result of those searches, and whether
      those searches identified any fatigue risk management training requirement, fatigue risk management
      assessment process, or other fatigue-management requirement applying to Logan Hospital Switchboard
      staff before 30 June 2024. For Item 14, the verifying affidavit should state the date on which a
      Queensland Health device was issued to the Line Manager and confirm whether any responsive
      communications exist on MSH systems. The affidavit should also identify the process references to
      which the Item 16 enclosures correspond: the Notice cited references 15397775 and 15605601, and the
      Item 11 report for 1 February to 31 May 2024 lists neither. The references cited in the Notice were drawn
      from records provided to the Appellant; the discrepancy lies within MSH’s own production, and the
      affidavit is the means of resolving it.
I. Items Not Pressed; the Pleadings Point
23.   The Appellant does not press the balance of Item 12 or Item 17. The privacy considerations MSH raises
      (sensitive health information of other staff, and re-identification risk within a small team) are genuine; the
      audit trail and variance records already produced serve the comparator purpose. Nor does the Appellant
      press production under Item 18: MSH objects on the footing that the destruction of the record “appears to
      have already been conceded” on the pleadings, and the Appellant is content to proceed on that
      concession, confirmed in the affidavit referred to in order (c).
24.   The response renews the observation that MSH has not received the Appellant’s Amended Form 9A, and
      submits its capacity to assess relevance was limited. Rule 64C(1) requires the notice to state the matter in
      issue, and this Notice does so; the objections MSH has in fact articulated, ground by ground, demonstrate
      that it conveyed what the rule requires. In any event the point is spent: the Appellant provides at
      Annexure B a Relevance Map setting out, for each contested Item, the pleaded matter and the Form 24
      admission to which it answers, and will provide a sealed copy of the Amended Form 9A on request or as
      the Commission directs. No contested Item falls to be decided on an asserted inability to assess relevance.
J. Disposition, Material and Service
25.   The orders sought confine production to documents a non-party can extract through standard
      administrative processes, within defined date windows, with reasonable expenses met under rule 64I, and
      with the privacy objections accommodated by the withdrawal of the Items that engaged them. The
      application is brought to narrow the field, not to enlarge it: the greater part of the Notice is resolved by
      MSH’s compliance, by its answers, and by the Appellant’s withdrawals, and what remains is confined by
      Schedule A to a materially narrower set of documents than the Notice as originally served sought. The
      Appellant relies upon the Notice, the direction of 22 May 2026, MSH’s correspondence of 5 June 2026
      (with enclosures) and the Respondent’s Statement of Facts and Contentions (Form 9C), each already
      before the Commission, together with the Relevance Map at Annexure B and the extract of the
      Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026 at Annexure C. This application is to be served on the
      Respondent and on MSH (attention: Principal Lawyer, Metro South Legal Services), and the Appellant
      will give notice of order (a), so far as it concerns Item 19, to Together Queensland. A draft of the orders
      sought (including the Items 8–9 confidentiality regime, the Together Queensland notice mechanism, and
      liberty to apply as to mechanics) accompanies this application. The Appellant is content for the
      application to be determined on the papers, and seeks orders in the terms of the draft.

>>> lodgement/_md2html.py :: text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Minimal Markdown -> HTML for the WC/2024/227 lodgement docs.
Handles: headings, bold/italic, blockquotes, hr, pipe tables,
ordered/unordered lists (with 4-space nested bullets)."""
import re, sys, html

def inline(t):
    t = html.escape(t)
    t = re.sub(r'\*\*(.+?)\*\*', r'<strong>\1</strong>', t)
    t = re.sub(r'(?<!\*)\*(?!\s)(.+?)(?<!\s)\*(?!\*)', r'<em>\1</em>', t)
    return t

def render(md):
    lines = md.split('\n')
    out, i = [], 0
    n = len(lines)
    pending_cols = None
    pending_break = False
    while i < n:
        ln = lines[i]
        # column-width hint for the next table, e.g. <!--cols:6,28,16,26,24-->
        mcols = re.match(r'^\s*<!--\s*cols:\s*([\d,\s.]+)\s*-->\s*$', ln)
        if mcols:
            pending_cols = [w.strip() for w in mcols.group(1).split(',') if w.strip()]
            i += 1; continue
        # forced page break — applied to the next block element
        if re.match(r'^\[newpage\]\s*$', ln):
            pending_break = True; i += 1; continue
        # red banner: [[banner:TEXT]]
        mb = re.match(r'^\[\[banner:(.+)\]\]\s*$', ln)
        if mb:
            out.append(f'<p class="banner">{inline(mb.group(1))}</p>'); i += 1; continue
        # table block
        if ln.strip().startswith('|') and i+1 < n and re.match(r'^\s*\|[\s:|-]+\|\s*$', lines[i+1]):
            header = [c.strip() for c in ln.strip().strip('|').split('|')]
            i += 2
            rows = []
            while i < n and lines[i].strip().startswith('|'):
                rows.append([c.strip() for c in lines[i].strip().strip('|').split('|')])
                i += 1
            ncol = len(header)
            widths = pending_cols if (pending_cols and len(pending_cols) == ncol) else None
            pending_cols = None
            if widths is None:
                widths = ['6', '28', '16', '26', '24'] if ncol == 5 else [str(round(100 / ncol, 2))] * ncol
            colgroup = '<colgroup>' + ''.join(f'<col style="width:{w}%">' for w in widths) + '</colgroup>'
            out.append('<table>' + colgroup + '<thead><tr>' + ''.join(f'<th>{inline(h)}</th>' for h in header) + '</tr></thead><tbody>')
            for r in rows:
                out.append('<tr>' + ''.join(f'<td>{inline(c)}</td>' for c in r) + '</tr>')
            out.append('</tbody></table>')
            continue
        # headings
        m = re.match(r'^(#{1,6})\s+(.*)$', ln)
        if m:
            lvl = len(m.group(1))
            brk = ' style="page-break-before:always"' if pending_break else ''
            pending_break = False
            out.append(f'<h{lvl}{brk}>{inline(m.group(2))}</h{lvl}>'); i += 1; continue
        # hr
        if re.match(r'^---+\s*$', ln):
            out.append('<hr>'); i += 1; continue
        # blockquote
        if ln.strip().startswith('>'):
            buf = []
            while i < n and lines[i].strip().startswith('>'):
                buf.append(inline(re.sub(r'^\s*>\s?', '', lines[i]))); i += 1
            out.append('<blockquote>' + '<br>'.join(buf) + '</blockquote>'); continue
        # numbered paragraph — preserve the LITERAL number (legal affidavit / grounds
        # paragraphs must keep their authored numbers; do NOT auto-renumber via <ol>)
        m2 = re.match(r'^(\d+[A-Z]?)\.\s+(.*)$', ln)
        if m2:
            num, item = m2.group(1), m2.group(2)
            i += 1
            sub = []
            while i < n and re.match(r'^\s{2,}[-*]\s+', lines[i]):
                sub.append(inline(re.sub(r'^\s+[-*]\s+', '', lines[i]))); i += 1
            out.append(f'<p class="num"><span class="n">{num}.</span> {inline(item)}</p>')
            if sub:
                out.append('<ul class="sub">' + ''.join(f'<li>{s}</li>' for s in sub) + '</ul>')
            continue
        # unordered list
        if re.match(r'^[-*]\s+', ln):
            out.append('<ul>')
            while i < n and re.match(r'^[-*]\s+', lines[i]):
                txt = re.sub(r'^[-*]\s+', '', lines[i])
                out.append('<li>' + inline(txt) + '</li>'); i += 1
            out.append('</ul>'); continue
        # blank
        if ln.strip() == '':
            i += 1; continue
        # paragraph (gather until blank)
        buf = [ln]; i += 1
        while i < n and lines[i].strip() != '' and not re.match(r'^(#{1,6}\s|>|---+\s*$|\d+[A-Z]?\.\s|[-*]\s|\|)', lines[i]):
            buf.append(lines[i]); i += 1
        out.append('<p>' + inline(' '.join(buf)) + '</p>')
    return '\n'.join(out)

CSS = """

th, td { border:0.75pt solid #000; padding:3pt 5pt; vertical-align:top; text-align:left; word-wrap:break-word; overflow-wrap:break-word; line-height:1.2; }

.sig { margin-top:14pt; }
.banner { color:#c00000; font-weight:bold; text-align:center; border:1.5pt solid #c00000; padding:5pt; margin:4pt 0 8pt 0; font-size:11pt; }
"""

src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
md = open(src, encoding='utf-8').read()
body = render(md)

open(dst, 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(doc)

>>> lodgement/_stamp.py :: text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Stamp a matter footer + 'Page X of Y' onto each page of a PDF.
Usage: _stamp.py input.pdf "Form label" output.pdf [sign]
Pass a 4th arg "sign" to add a per-page deponent/witness signing footer
(QIRC affidavits: each page is signed by the deponent and the witness,
rr 50-57 Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011)."""
import sys, subprocess, re, os
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import A4

inp, label, outp = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
sign = len(sys.argv) > 4 and sys.argv[4] == "sign"

# page count
info = subprocess.check_output(['pdfinfo', inp]).decode()
pages = int(re.search(r'Pages:\s+(\d+)', info).group(1))

W, H = A4
cm = 28.35
dots = "…" * 22
overlay = inp + '.ovl.pdf'
c = canvas.Canvas(overlay, pagesize=A4)
matter = "WC/2024/227  —  Shepherd v Workers' Compensation Regulator"
for i in range(1, pages + 1):
    c.setStrokeGray(0.6); c.setLineWidth(0.4)
    if sign:
        # per-page signing band (deponent + witness), above the matter line
        c.line(1.8 * cm, 1.9 * cm, W - 1.8 * cm, 1.9 * cm)
        c.setFont('Times-Roman', 8); c.setFillGray(0.15)
        c.drawString(1.8 * cm, 1.45 * cm, f"Deponent: {dots}")
        c.drawRightString(W - 1.8 * cm, 1.45 * cm, f"Witness (JP / C.dec / Lawyer): {dots}")
        c.setFont('Times-Roman', 7); c.setFillGray(0.4)
        c.drawString(1.8 * cm, 0.78 * cm, matter)
        c.drawRightString(W - 1.8 * cm, 0.78 * cm, f"{label}  —  Page {i} of {pages}")
    else:
        c.line(1.8 * cm, 1.4 * cm, W - 1.8 * cm, 1.4 * cm)
        c.setFont('Times-Roman', 8); c.setFillGray(0.35)
        c.drawString(1.8 * cm, 1.0 * cm, matter)
        c.drawRightString(W - 1.8 * cm, 1.0 * cm, f"{label}  —  Page {i} of {pages}")
    c.showPage()
c.save()

subprocess.check_call(['qpdf', '--overlay', overlay, '--', inp, outp])
os.remove(overlay)
print(f"stamped {pages}pp -> {outp}")

  Kind regards,
  The Claim Process
  It is important that you understand the process of how WorkCover will assess your claim and
what
your obligations are during this process.
  Psychological injury claims usually follow the following three stages:
  1. Submission of Nominated Factors:
  This is where you provide substantiating information to WorkCover regarding the recent and
significant events that you and your treating medical team attribute as the cause for you to
seek
treatment. The information provided at this stage provides the substantive grounds for your
application.
  2. Employers Response:
  WorkCover provides your nominated factors to your employer for them to respond to.? This stage
generally takes 5 business days but can extend longer depending on the investigations being
completed.
  3. Natural Justice:
  After your employer?s response is received it will be passed on to you.? The purpose of this
stage is to provide you with an opportunity to review all information received from your
employer.? This is also a final opportunity to provide WorkCover with any further evidence that
you wished to have considered as part of your application.
  After this I will review your claim and all of the information available and make a decision
as
to whether or not your claim is acceptable under the legislation.
  The claim process can take up to 20 business days, but should there be a delay meaning that it
will take longer, I will send a letter outlining the reasons for this delay.
  For further information on how your claim is determined please refer to the WorkCover website
.
If you wish to watch a video on the claim process please refer to the Claim process webpage .

>>> corpus/README.md :: text
# CORPUS — the whole correspondence record, in one place

> Built 31 July 2026 from the six mailbox packs at `documents/correspondence-packs/`.
> **154 unique messages, 2020–2026.** Deduplicated across packs on (date, subject, sender).

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| **`FULL_CORPUS.md`** | ⭐ **Every message, full text, chronological.** Grouped by month. This is the pull-from file. |
| **`MESSAGE_INDEX.tsv`** | One row per message: `date · pack · page · from · to · cc · subject`. Sort or filter it. |

## How to use it

**Search the text:**
```
grep -n -i "on call"      wc2024227/corpus/FULL_CORPUS.md
grep -n -B2 -A20 "26 June" wc2024227/corpus/FULL_CORPUS.md
```
**Find every message from one person, or in a window:**
```
grep -i "hughes"   wc2024227/corpus/MESSAGE_INDEX.tsv
grep "^2025-03"    wc2024227/corpus/MESSAGE_INDEX.tsv
```

## ⚠️ Read these before quoting anything

1. **Times are UTC as exported. Add 10 hours for AEST.** The 26 June email shows `00:42:50` — that
   is **10:42 AEST**. Every time in the corpus and the index needs the same conversion.
2. **Never quote from the corpus into a filing.** Every entry cites `pack NN p.NNN` — **open the PDF
   and verify the words there.** The corpus is a finding aid, not a source. This is the cardinal
   habit in `CLAUDE.md`.
3. **Bodies are truncated at 6,000 characters.** Long items are complete in the PDF only.
4. **Attachments are not here.** Where an item is attachment-only, the body reads
   `(no body captured)` — 4 messages. Several missing attachments matter:
   MSH's employer responses of **16 Aug** and **6 Sep 2024**; Cory's WorkCover statements of
   **12 and 15 July 2024**.
5. **Images are not here.** Screenshots and text-message captures carry content no grep will find —
   the 14 Jan 2024 DFV thread is the example. **Render the PDF page** where an item mentions
   `IMG_*`, a screenshot, or a text message.
6. **Boilerplate was stripped** — disclaimers, acknowledgements of country, "Get Outlook for iOS",
   external-sender warnings. Nothing substantive was removed, but the PDF is authoritative.

## What the shape of it shows

| Year | Messages |
|---|---|
| 2020 | 2 |
| 2021 | 1 |
| 2022 | 15 |
| 2023 | 3 |
| **2024** | **37** |
| **2025** | **78** |
| **2026** | 17 |

Two years of low-volume roster traffic, then **37 messages in 2024** (the claim year) and
**78 in 2025** — the year of the return, the DFV leave, the attendance letter and the complaint.

## Coverage — be honest about it
The corpus contains **every message the packs captured**. It does **not** contain: the attachments,
the images, anything from OneDrive, or packs **06–09**, which have never been supplied.
