RETURN TO WORK AND WORKPLACE CONTROLS — PROPOSALS FOR CONSULTATION

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
August 2026 — tabled for discussion; nothing in this document is a demand, an allegation,
or a variation of any request or notice already on foot.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 1 — WHAT I HAVE ASKED FOR, AND HOW I PROPOSE EACH BE DONE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  RETURN TO WORK. Under the Proposal for Return to Work of 3 August 2026: a staged return
    on the pattern certified in the Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026, with the
    controls set out in that proposal, the Checklist's own review date of 28 August 2026 as
    the first checkpoint, a support person present at the return discussion, and the plan
    recorded in writing.

2.  PAY AND LEAVE. Corrected through the ordinary payroll machinery: the rostered shifts
    processed by AVAC, the leave debited since 3 July 2026 re-credited, and the codings
    confirmed in writing.

3.  THE PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK ASSESSMENT (clause 7.2; Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards
    at work Code of Practice 2022). A scoping meeting with me, my union representative and
    any Health and Safety Representative; the hazard categories to include those identified
    in the Health Service's letter of 7 July 2026 together with organisational justice and
    job insecurity; the data sources the Code identifies (complaints, absence, turnover,
    EAP usage); an assessor independent of Corporate Services; a written scope and timeline;
    findings shared; controls selected in consultation in the order the WHS Regulation
    requires.

4.  THE MEDICAL INFORMATION. Per my response of 3 August 2026: the Health Service confirms
    the questions it presses; the questions are put through the allocation in that response;
    costs as the Health Service has committed in writing.

5.  THE PROCESS, NAMED. The instrument, steps, decision-maker and end-decision of the
    process I am being managed under, in writing; or, if none applies, a documented
    return-to-work plan agreed with me, with review dates, per the Workplace Rehabilitation
    Standard.

6.  SEPARATION OF FUNCTIONS. Decisions concerning my attendance, duties and pay made by an
    officer outside Corporate Services, with the delegation recorded in writing. This is the
    ordinary separation; it requires no restructuring and no finding about anyone.

7.  FEEDBACK (clause 7.1.11). A short written response to each work health and safety matter
    I have raised: received, assessed, outcome.

8.  RECORDS. Copies of preserved HR policies E12 and E13, and the roster and payroll record
    for the twelve months preceding 3 July 2026.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 2 — THE SWITCHBOARD OPERATING MODEL (PROPOSED CONTROLS)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

These are offered as controls for discussion in the assessment and under clause 7.1.5. Each
concerns the design of the work, not any person. Implementation cost is near zero: rostering
and process changes only.

A.  PATIENT SAFETY AS THE DESIGN PRINCIPLE. The Switchboard activates the hospital's
    emergency codes and relays urgent clinical results; whether the right clinician is
    reached, and how quickly, depends on the Switchboard and the accuracy of the on-call
    information it relies on. I propose: (i) clear ownership, with a backup, for the accuracy
    of the on-call roster and the paging system; (ii) directory updates restored to a
    workable pathway with a backup when the responsible officer is unavailable; and (iii) a
    defined escalation path for when a department's support officer or the manager cannot
    be reached.

2.  CONSULTATION BEFORE OPERATIONAL CHANGE. No change to Switchboard operating processes
    takes effect until the operators who work the board have been consulted. The Switchboard
    is a real-time environment operating multiple concurrent systems; the operators hold the
    working knowledge of it. This is the consultation the Work Health and Safety Act already
    requires, applied systematically.

3.  A ROTATIONAL, INTEGRATED MANAGER. The manager of Switchboard Services works a regular
    rostered rotation on the board — on the phones, in the room. Management of a fast-paced,
    direct, real-time environment is soundest when management holds direct current knowledge
    of it; presence also ensures supervision and support are available where the work
    happens. This is the standard model in emergency communications settings.

4.  A COMPLAINT-RESPONSE STANDARD. Complaints and escalations sent to Switchboard management
    are acknowledged within one business day and substantively answered within three; where
    the manager is unavailable, the matter escalates automatically to the established Client
    Liaison pathway rather than returning to the operators' console.

5.  ONE RULEBOOK FOR THE ROOM. The manager working in rotation is subject to the same
    frameworks as the operators — rostering rules, minimum notice, fatigue breaks, and leave
    processes — applied consistently. Consistency of process is itself a psychosocial
    control.

6.  A 24/7 ON-SHIFT SUPERVISOR FUNCTION, ROTATING WITHIN THE TEAM. The design principle is
    that in a real-time environment, escalation is delay: a decision the board needs now
    cannot wait on a chain to an off-site or after-hours contact. Authority therefore
    follows the clock. On every shift, one rostered operator holds the shift-supervisor
    function — the real-time decision-maker for operational matters arising on the board —
    while continuing to work the board with the team. The supervisor is not a second
    manager: the manager holds the frameworks, administration and business-hours functions;
    the supervisor holds the shift, so that after hours, on weekends, and at 3am the room
    is never waiting on an escalation that cannot answer in time. Only matters that can
    properly wait are escalated to the manager in hours. The function rotates among
    operators trained and assessed for it, and carries a classification increment or
    in-charge allowance for the shifts on which it is held — a development pathway and
    recognition for competence within the room, with shared capability across several
    trained operators rather than dependence on any one person. When the supervisor makes a
    real-time decision, the operators present are consulted there and then — consultation at
    the speed of the room — and the decision is carried forward through the handover below.
    This is the standard model in emergency communications centres. The cost is a modest
    per-shift allowance, ordinarily offset by reduced turnover and absence.

8.  STRUCTURED HANDOVER AND DECISION LOG. Each shift hands over to the next through a
    structured record: operational status, live issues, and the decisions made on shift with
    their reasons. Context transfers instead of evaporating at shift change — a recognised
    failure point in continuous operations — and decisions become consistent and auditable
    across the roster. The log also gives the manager, in hours, a complete account of the
    room's operation without interrupting it.

7.  EVIDENCE-BASED ROSTERING. Rosters designed from the demand data the Switchboard already
    generates — call volumes by hour and day, and emergency-code activity — so that coverage
    matches the actual peaks; with fatigue rules (minimum breaks) built into the roster
    design rather than checked afterwards; published with proper notice; and with equity
    across operators visible on the face of the roster. The data required is already
    collected; this proposal only asks that the roster be built from it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 3 — HOW I PROPOSE THE CONSULTATION ITSELF RUN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

(a)  I will attend any discussion at any time, with a support person and my union
     representative present.

(b)  Discussions occur alongside, not instead of, written responses; anything agreed is
     confirmed in writing before it is treated as resolved.

(c)  My participation in any discussion waives nothing and does not pause any process
     already on foot, unless recorded otherwise in writing by agreement.

I table this because I would rather build the fix than continue the dispute. Every item in it
is capable of being implemented from existing resources, this month.

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital
0417 400 227 · coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

------------------------------------------------------------------

  I'd rather this hour be about my health."

WHY THIS WORKS
- Every personal item he wants addressed (the doors, what would help) IS a Form B
  question — candour and the report requirements point the same direction.
- The doctor forms his opinions from the patient's account + MSH's own letter + the
  factual workplace package — three sources, none of them coaching.
- The A/B wall and the billing wall are stated once, in the room, and then live in the
  two scope documents — clean on paper, clean in cross.

⛔ KEEPING IT OUT OF MSH'S HANDS (added 4 Aug — Cory's question)
------------------------------------------------------------------
WHAT MSH ACTUALLY GETS: the REPORT ONLY, answering the questions put. They have no
access to the clinical file. He adopted option 1 on 3 Aug and expressly refused the

permits only what is "necessary" to identify/assess adjustments. If MSH ever asks for
records rather than a report: decline, in one line, citing the same clause.

⚠ THE REAL LEAK IS THE OTHER TRACK: clinical NOTES can reach the Regulator in
WC/2024/227 through Form 29 / NNPD notices — that channel is already active. There is
no doctor-patient privilege in Australian courts. So the room is not a vault: assume
anything recorded in the clinical notes may one day be produced in the APPEAL (not to
MSH as employer, but to the Regulator).

⇒ THE PRACTICAL RULE FOR THE CONSULT:
- SAY FREELY (and fully): symptoms, function, sleep, mood, the doors, the shutdowns,
  what the exclusion and non-payment have done to him, treatment, what would help.
  Clinically necessary, and it reads exactly as what it is if ever produced.
- KEEP OUT: legal strategy, tactics, predictions, opinions about MSH's motives, what
  the other side is trying to do. No clinical value, fully producible, and it converts
  a treating record into a strategy document.
- Report B instruction is HANDED OVER as a medico-legal instruction for the appeal
  (created for that dominant purpose); keep it distinct from the treating file, and
  never discussed in the same breath as the MSH report.

FOUR PROTECTIONS TO ASK FOR, IN THE ROOM:
1. "Please confine the employer's report to the questions on the form" — no aetiology,
   no extraneous history, no third-party/family material.
2. "May I read it before it goes to the employer?" — a patient may review for scope and
   accuracy (never to change an opinion). Legitimate, and it catches over-disclosure.
3. "My consent is for this report only, not for release of my clinical records."
   Say it, and confirm it in one line to the clinic when the report is being prepared.
4. If the employer contacts the clinic directly: ask that he be told, and that nothing
   be released without his written consent.

   separate (high) price — never folded into the compensation resolution.
 • Verify the three para-6 facts against source before sending (Form 24 Response;
   the Review Decision finding; MSH's 5 June letter Items 4/5/7). Name documents,
   not paragraph numbers.
 • Pitch quantum at FULL value — little spread in a statutory claim; no gain in
   discounting for speed.
 • Timing is the real determinant: this exact letter gets "no" before production
   (see February) and "yes" after it. Hold to the trigger. -->

⛔ THE THREE-CHANNEL RULE (added 4 Aug — Cory asked whether to voice the contest to the
doctor): The PAPER carries the questions. The ROOM carries the truth. The MSH TRACK
carries the fight. Never mixed.
- No contest, commentary or "inappropriate" language EVER in writing to a practice —
  it enters the clinical file, the clinical file is what Form 29s produce, and one
  cross-examination question ("your patient told you the request was inappropriate
  before you wrote this, didn't he?") converts the doctor's independent opinion into a
  briefed one. Report A and Report B both bleed.
- The contest is ALREADY filed where it wins: the 3 Aug response, the allocation, the
  dispute, the CE letter. Form A/B ARE the contest in procedural form — that is how the
  objection reaches the doctor: through structure, not adjectives.
- In the room, as his patient, he says everything: what the letter did to him, the
  distress, the shutdown, the month unpaid. That is symptomatology, not strategy.
- The one flag sentence, ORAL ONLY: "I've raised concerns about how this request was
  made — I'm handling those separately with the employer. What I want from you is your
  own opinion, entirely yours, on the questions in front of you." (Insists on
  independence — the opposite of coaching, unattackable if it ever surfaces.)

SUBJECT: Logan Switchboard: never risk assessed — draft submission attached

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dear Emily and Heath,

IN SHORT

  * Logan Hospital Switchboard activates every emergency code and MET call in
    the hospital. It has never had a psychosocial risk assessment of any kind,
    and it was left out of the Fatigue Risk Management System on the basis that
    it is non-clinical.

  * A union submission and a costed provider proposal are drafted and attached.
    Adopting them is a matter of minutes, not hours.

  * One thing is near term. I refer my dispute to Stage 2 on Monday 10 August,
    and clause 1.11.2(b) requires the Health Service to arrange a conference.

  * I am not asking the union to take carriage of my own dispute. I am content
    to keep running that myself.

Heath, thank you for taking this through to the industrial team. Emily, thank
you for picking it up. I know the team's time is stretched, so I have set this
out under six headings and kept each one short.


1. WHY I AM WRITING

I am writing about the Switchboard, not about my own dispute.

So far as I am aware Switchboard Services at Logan Hospital has never had a
psychosocial risk assessment of any kind. It was not brought into the Fatigue
Risk Management System on the basis that it is non-clinical, and fatigue risk
management was introduced there in the second half of 2024.

The work itself is not non-clinical in any practical sense. The Switchboard
activates and pages every emergency code and MET call in the hospital, relays
urgent doctor to doctor results, and is the first point of contact for the public
and for staff across the site.

The fatigue is also not only a question of the break between shifts. A ten hour
break can be entirely compliant and the shift itself still be exhausting. On high
volume days the load is continuous: two to three hundred calls, code activation
and paging, urgent clinical relay, and complaints from across the hospital
arriving at the first point of contact. On those days breaks are deferred because
there is no relief rostered to take the console. A break entitlement is not a
break taken.

I have obtained an indicative proposal from an occupational psychology provider
for an independent psychosocial risk assessment of the service. It is attached.
The work would be commissioned and funded by the Health Service. My own
involvement would be limited to being consulted, in the same way as any other
affected worker, and the report should go to the Health Service and the union
rather than to me.


WHAT I HAVE ATTACHED, AND WHY THIS PROVIDER

I have attached two things:

  1. A short submission setting out what an assessment of the Switchboard would
     need to cover and why. Two pages.

  2. The provider's indicative proposal. The range quoted is $10,000 to $30,000
     depending on scope.

I approached more than one provider. I chose this one on a simple test: they
answered the questions in writing before being engaged, on independence, on
method and on scope. The others asked for a call and would not put anything on
paper. I took that as the difference between an assessment and a sales process.

Three things seem to me to matter more than who does the work, and the union may
see it differently:

  * Independence. The assessor should not be engaged by, or report to, the part
    of the service being assessed.

  * Method. Direct observation across high volume and low volume days and across
    the shift pattern, not a room and a questionnaire. A survey only assessment
    of a small team produces a nil finding by design.

  * Terms of reference agreed in writing before it starts, and provided to the
    union.

I am not attached to this provider and I have no arrangement with them. If the
union or the Health Service would rather use someone else, that is entirely
sensible. I obtained the proposal so that the cost and the scope were known
rather than hypothetical, and so that nobody could say the idea was vague.


2. WHY I HAVE COPIED THE UNION INTO MY CORRESPONDENCE

Since 3 August I have copied the union into my Stage 1 dispute under clause 1.11,
my request under clause 10.3.2, my response to the Request for Medical
Information, and my letter to the Chief Executive.

Three reasons. So the union holds the record as it happens rather than
reconstructed later. So nothing I send comes as a surprise to you, and nothing
the union says on my behalf is undercut by something I have already put in
writing. And because several of the issues raised in it are not only mine.

I am not asking anyone to adopt what I have written. I am asking that the union
have it.


3. THE SUPPORT I AM ASKING FOR

  (a) What came out of the industrial officer conference in July, and who holds
      carriage. I am content to keep running the correspondence myself with the
      union's support rather than the union taking carriage, but I would like
      that to be clear between us.

  (b) Attendance at the Stage 2 conference. I intend to refer the dispute to
      Stage 2 on Monday 10 August. Clause 1.11.2(b) requires the Health Service
      to arrange a conference. I would rather not be in that room on my own.

# Request for workplace psychosocial risk assessment — Switchboard Services (Logan Hospital)

**DRAFT — not sent**  
**File:** MSH-INJ-5795  
**Date:** 4 August 2026  

**To:** Manager, Work Health and Safety / Safety and Wellbeing  
Metro South Health  
*(please allocate to the unit that commissions and coordinates psychosocial risk assessments under the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022)*  

**Copy (for information only — not a medical request):**  
- LBH Injury Management — `LBH_InjuryManagement@health.qld.gov.au`  
- CS.Logan — `CS.Logan@health.qld.gov.au` *(please forward if the WHS mailbox differs)*  
- Heath Moran, Together *(optional)*  

**From:** Cory Lea Shepherd  
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health  
`coryshepherd1@hotmail.com` · 0417 400 227  

**Subject:** Request for psychosocial risk assessment of Switchboard work systems — rostering, fatigue, leave-as-control, organisational factors — parallel to medical process (MSH-INJ-5795)

---

Dear Manager / Safety and Wellbeing team,

## 1. What I am asking, and what I am not

I ask that Metro South Health commission a **workplace psychosocial risk assessment of Switchboard Services at Logan Hospital** — that is, of **how the work is designed and managed** — under the *Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022* and sections 17, 19 and 47–49 of the *Work Health and Safety Act 2011* (Qld).

I am **not**:

- making a personal complaint about any named individual, or asking for any finding about anyone;  
- asking WHS to run or replace the Request for Medical Information (RFMI) process;  
- authorising release of my clinical records to Corporate Services or to this assessment;  
- abandoning my employment or any entitlement.

I **am** engaging with the RFMI and Injury Management process. That process goes to **my** capacity and adjustments. This letter is **parallel**: it concerns assessment of the **department’s work systems**.

On 3 August 2026 I wrote to the Chief Executive under section 89 of the *Public Sector Act 2022* about conflict management, separation of clinical material from operational decision-making, and the fact that the matters treated as “psychosocial” cannot be answered by a medical practitioner writing about me. This letter does not repeat that disclosure. It asks the unit that looks after **WHS / psychosocial risk** to do the assessment that those workplace matters require.

## 2. Why WHS is the right department

Correspondence from Injury Management and Human Resources (including 7, 13, 15 and 29 July 2026 and the RFMI of 31 July 2026) has framed my hold-out and return by reference to:

- whether matters identified on the Employee Capability Checklist present any **psychosocial hazards or risks**;  
- **safe** return / health and safety of workers and others;  
- **Work Health and Safety Act 2011** sections 17 and 19 (and G3 Reasonable Adjustment).

The RFMI letter confirms MSH will meet **reasonable costs of preparing the medical report** about me. That funds a **medical** enquiry. It does **not** fund or substitute for a Code-compliant **psychosocial risk assessment of the work unit**.

The Code identifies psychosocial hazards by reference to **features of work and its management** (including job demands, remote/isolated work patterns, fatigue, organisational justice and change management). Those are **PCBU / department** matters. They are not cured by further diagnosis of one employee.

The letter of 7 July 2026 records that the Health Service did not have sufficient information to understand “unresolved workplace matters involving line management” or to assess whether they present psychosocial hazards. I take that at face value. That gap is one **only the Health Service can close** — by assessing the **workplace**, not by asking my doctor to investigate the department.

## 3. Workplace matters already put on the record (not medical)

I set these out in my letter to the Chief Executive (3 August 2026). They concern **how work is organised and decided**, not the character of any officer:

(a) how **patient-safety concerns** raised at Switchboard are escalated and answered;  
(b) how changes to the **work, roster and on-call arrangements** are introduced, and whether affected staff are consulted;  
(c) **fatigue and recovery** between shifts, and how rostering is managed against it;  
(d) the ability of staff to have genuine **input into decisions** that affect the work (organisational justice under the Code).

None of those can be answered by a medical practitioner writing about me.

## 4. Work-system indicators drawn from my sworn Form 20 and the operational role

I am an AO3 Switchboard Operator at Logan Hospital. In my Form 20 affidavit in WC/2024/227 I have deposed, among other things, to the following **work-system** features (summarised here for WHS; the full affidavit is available on request — I do not attach clinical material):

**Role and demand**

- Switchboard is the hospital’s **communications hub** and a critical part of **patient-safety** response (code activation and paging via SPOK; concurrent systems; high call volume; concurrent urgencies).  
- Operators absorb **complaints and blame** for failures that often originate in upstream roster/directory/departmental systems, not in operator error.  
- The role includes **roster and leave administration** functions and weekend coverage of work that is management-owned on weekdays.

**Rostering and fatigue**

- I was rostered with a **7-hour break** between consecutive shifts (17–18 March 2024), against the Award / FRMS minimum (10 hours, or 8 only by written agreement) — a matter the Regulator’s own Review Decision treated as **unreasonable management action**.  
- Under that exhaustion I was required to manage **life-safety emergency codes** and doctor paging.  
- When I needed recovery, I was required to use **my own personal leave** rather than paid fatigue leave.  
- I had previously raised **WHS concerns about unsafe rostering and fatigue** (including a grievance on 7 August 2023; a rostering error on night shifts was acknowledged in writing).

**Leave as a way of managing the work**

- Leave is not only personal recovery. In this environment, **staff using leave to manage workload, fatigue and the work environment** is a **system signal** (informal fatigue and demand control), not a reason to treat the hazard as located only in one employee’s medical file.  
- MSH’s own Form 29 response (Chief Executive letter K-LM26/729, 5 June 2026) is already on the Commission file and records, among other things, that **fatigue risk management at Switchboard** was implemented only **after 30 June 2024** in connection with an organisational reporting-line change, and that there had been **no consequential changes to operating procedures** over the earlier period. I refer to that letter as MSH’s own record; I do not re-argue it here.

**Change and consultation**

- Operational changes (including restriction of directory/database access and “effective immediately” directives) have been experienced at the console without the consultation the WHS Act contemplates when work affecting health and safety is redesigned.

These are the kinds of data sources the Code expects a **workplace** assessment to use (rosters, leave patterns, demand, complaints vocabulary, incident history, consultation record) — not a further diagnosis of me.

## 5. Independent psychosocial examination of the department

I have engaged with an **independent psychosocial assessment framework / mapping** for Switchboard against the 2022 Code (work-as-designed, work-as-done, rostering/fatigue, leave–demand signals, organisational justice). That material is for **consultation and scoping**. It is **not** a substitute for the Health Service’s own PCBU assessment, and I do not present it as a concluded external audit of Metro South Health unless and until a third-party assessor is commissioned under Health Service control.

I consider a formal assessment **necessary** because:

1. HR/IM have already invoked **psychosocial hazard** and **WHS** in connection with my return;  
2. the operational record (including rostering, fatigue, leave used to manage work, and patient-safety critical demand at Switchboard) points to **work-system** risk; and  
3. holding one employee out of the workplace while those system matters remain unassessed does not discharge the duty to identify and control psychosocial hazards **so far as is reasonably practicable**.

## 6. Separation from the medical process (important)

| Process | Object | Owner | Funding / information |
|--------|--------|--------|------------------------|
| RFMI / medical report | My capacity, restrictions, adjustments **for me** | Injury Management | MSH has stated it will meet reasonable costs of **that report**; clinical material medical-in-confidence |
| This request | Psychosocial risks in **Switchboard work systems** | **WHS / Safety and Wellbeing** (this letter) | PCBU assessment cost; **no clinical file** required |

I ask that:

(a) this assessment **not** be treated as answered by the RFMI medical report;  
(b) **no medical records** about me be sought or shared for the department assessment (system data only: rosters, leave aggregates, demand, procedures, consultation records, de-identified team patterns);  
(c) Corporate Services receive, if anything, **controls and adjustments to implement**, not clinical reasoning about me — consistently with the separation I proposed to the Chief Executive.

## 7. Consultation

Sections 47–49 of the WHS Act require consultation with workers who are, or are likely to be, directly affected when identifying hazards, deciding controls, and proposing changes affecting health or safety. That consultation has **not** occurred with me in relation to the psychosocial characterisation of my hold-out since late June / early July 2026.

I ask to be included in scoping consultation, and that other Switchboard operators and any health and safety representative be offered participation in the ordinary way. My union is available to assist.

## 8. What I ask you to do

Please:

1. **Confirm** that this request has been received by the unit responsible for psychosocial risk assessment under the Code.  
2. **Identify** the responsible officer and the proposed method (e.g. People at Work / Code methodology; independent assessor if used; timeline).  
3. **Scope** at least: rostering and break compliance (including FRMS); fatigue; leave patterns as demand/fatigue signal; job demands and concurrent critical tasks at Switchboard; organisational justice / change consultation; patient-safety critical communications load.  
4. **Confirm in writing** that the RFMI medical process is **not** treated as that assessment.  
5. Advise how workers will be **consulted** and when scoping will start.

I remain certified fit with restrictions, ready and willing to return within those restrictions, and willing to cooperate with a proper workplace assessment.

Yours sincerely,

**Cory Lea Shepherd**  
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital  
Metro South Health · MSH-INJ-5795  
0417 400 227 · coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

THE SPINE
A decision "based on the available information" requires two halves: the worker's
condition and the role's conditions. The service procured the first (funded, invoiced).
The assessment supplies the second. Same decision, same funding principle, same invoice
address. Refusal requires explaining in writing why the funding principle applies to
information about the worker but not information about the work.

SEQUENCING GUARDRAILS (the 4 Aug addition — Cory's insight)
- The logic: a fitness-for-work opinion is only as good as its job-demands information
  (standard occupational medicine). The assessment IS the job-demands analysis for the
  role's psychological demands. Assessment first → doctors answer the nine questions
  against the role as assessed. Their own instrument (the RFMI) thereby becomes the
  reason the assessment must happen.
- ⛔ NEVER framed as a precondition or refusal. The rebooking machinery from the 3 Aug
  Response is UNCHANGED (rebook within 3 business days of question-set confirmation, or
  at day 7 regardless). The assessment is an input that improves the answers, not a gate
  that delays them. If the appointment lands before the assessment completes, the doctors
  answer on what exists and may note that opinions on adjustments can be refined against
  the assessment findings — staged answers, never withheld answers.
- Report A / Report B separation intact: the assessment findings feed REPORT A (capacity,
  restrictions, adjustments — the nine-questions vehicle). Report B (appeal causation)
  stays separate and is never mentioned to MSH.
- The pincer inversion, for the strategy record: the RFMI was built to produce an
  incapacity answer against the paper role. Sequenced this way, it produces a
  conditions-dependent answer against the real role — and the service cannot object to
  better information without disowning its own "available information" standard.

THE GRACIOUS REGISTER — banked 4 Aug 2026
=========================================
The courteous-contributor voice for any MSH/HR engagement on the assessment or consultation.
Courtesy costs nothing, concedes nothing, and makes their silences louder by contrast.

THE THREE RULES
1. Thank for the PROCESS, never the outcome or the entitlement.
   ✔ "Thank you for the opportunity to contribute input."
   ✘ "Thank you for allowing me to..." — entitlements are not permissions.
2. Frame everything as service to the room and its patients, not to the matter.
   "To assist the service" / "in the interests of the room and the patients it serves."
3. Warm words never touch the machinery. No thank-you extends a deadline, withdraws a
   dispute, or softens a clock (Stage 1/2, 24 Aug deemed refusal, dispute limbs all run
   untouched). The two layers never meet in one sentence.

PHRASE BANK
- "Thank you for the opportunity to provide input — I appreciate the Health Service
  engaging on this."
- "I'm glad to assist with what I see as a genuine operational need."
- "I've tried to make my contribution as practical and ready-to-use as possible."
- "Offered in the hope it's useful to the process."
- "I'm happy to be guided by the process from here."
- "I remain available at any time, with my support person and union representative."
- "I appreciate the time being made for this."

READY REPLY — when HR invites input on the assessment/consultation
------------------------------------------------------------------
Dear [name],

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute — I genuinely appreciate the Health Service
engaging on this, and I'm glad to assist.

My aim throughout is a practical one: to help the service meet a need in the Switchboard
room, in the interests of the operators and the patients the room serves. To make the
discussion as productive as possible, I've prepared an integrated package — the hazard
mapping, proposed controls, a proposed assessment methodology, and information on
independent providers available locally — which I'll bring to table at our discussion.
It's offered as an input for consultation, nothing more; I'm happy to be guided by the
process from here.

I remain available at any time, with my support person and union representative, and I
look forward to it.

Kind regards,
Cory
------------------------------------------------------------------
NOTES
- The reply thanks, offers, and defers — while tabling the whole package with
  "for consultation" stamped on it.
- The record it builds: one side offering and assisting; the other deciding what to do
  about it. That is the exhibit.
- Use the register in every future engagement email unless a document is a formal notice
  (disputes/referrals keep their procedural voice).

WHAT THE JANUARY 2024 POLICE INSTRUMENT LIKELY WAS (and why it can stay vague)

Your recollection — "less than a PPN, a must-behave, not a protection order" —
is consistent with the statutory architecture. Under the DFVP Act 2012 a
domestic violence order or police protection notice could not have been made
against your sister at all: she was 15, and the Act does not permit orders
against a child respondent in a FAMILY relationship (child respondents are
reachable only in intimate-personal or informal-care relationships). So
whatever the police issued was necessarily non-DFVP-Act: most likely a caution
or warning under the Youth Justice Act 1992 (Part 2), or an informal
good-behaviour direction recorded in the QPS occurrence. That is EXACTLY why
the email says "no protection order was made" and goes no further — it is true,
it is verifiable, and it does not require naming the instrument or the child.
(Verify the DFVP Act child-respondent limitation against the current
consolidation before relying on it in anything filed.)

WHY THIS EMAIL IS WORTH SENDING (the strategic ledger)

- If they agree: the non-work-stressor material physically leaves the working
  file of a Respondent whose SOFC (13 May 2026, para 8) already pleads a
  pre-existing history. The material the over-supply put in reach of the
  causation fight is neutralised before the hearing.
- If they refuse or go silent: from that day the Respondent knowingly retains
  irrelevant material about a child after a written request grounded in the
  QPPs and the HR Act — which makes the preserved over-supply point (see
  skill/references/taylor-DFV-disclosure-to-Matheson.md §4A) stronger, not
  weaker, and gives the OIC or the Commission a clean record if it ever needs
  one.
- Either way: it is a restrained, child-protective, non-accusatory letter from
  a self-represented appellant — entirely in character with the rest of the
  file Dwyer will one day read.

THE COST, honestly: it tells the Regulator you regard the material as
significant. That is why the letter gives them a face-saving exit ("I make no
criticism... I do not suggest the Respondent has done anything with it") and
asks only for what a model litigant should do unprompted.

TIMING: after the 7 August mention. Not before, and not on 3 August — the
Monday package is employment-track and this is Regulator-track; keep the
channels clean. Suggested: Monday 10 August, the same day you refer the
Stage 1 dispute to Stage 2.

operative paragraphs more than the section header requires; cite the IR Act
s 296 point, the reprisal track, or anything from the strategy layer. The
letter asks for stewardship of a child's information. That is its entire face.

# WC/2024/227 — OUTLINE OF ARGUMENT
## The definitive Part C. Architecture, not a filing draft.
> Built 6 August 2026 under `elite-legal-drafting` + `au-legal-counsel`.
> ⛔ **NOT FOR FILING IN THIS STATE.** Seven of the eight authorities are unread — see Schedule 2.

> change, so nothing needs amending, and re-opening the pleadings risks the Form 24 admissions.

# PART I — THE METHOD (how the definitive version gets built)

Ten passes. Each one is finished before the next begins. **Nothing is drafted until pass 3.**

| # | Pass | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Authority acquisition.** Obtain and read all eight cases in full. | ⛔ **No case is cited that has not been read to its ratio.** Pinpoint paragraph numbers, verbatim quotes, and the facts each decision actually turned on |
| **2** | **Admissions audit.** Every *"Admitted Fact: Form 24, Para X"* tag re-checked against the **rendered** Response. | ⛔ `pdftotext` drops every exhibit reference and quoted phrase in this document — **`pdftoppm -r 150 -png`, always** |
| **3** | **The kill list.** Every limb unsupported by a held document, or defeated on the rule's own words, is **deleted** — not softened | ⭐ *"Being prepared to kill your babies."* Three limbs go. See Part III |
| **4** | **Anchor selection.** One item of evidence carries the case. Every other fact threads back to it | Anchor = **Form 24 ¶1 + ¶3** |
| **5** | **Thematic re-architecture.** A list of grievances becomes **one mechanism with one proven instance** | The list is what invites dilution. See Part II |
| **6** | **Bind construction.** Find the propositions where either choice costs the Respondent | ⭐⭐ The 7 < 8 < 10 bind. See ¶¶24–27 |
| **7** | **Concession pass.** Every genuine weakness conceded **before** the Respondent reaches it | Onus · some conduct was reasonable · the Review Decision does not bind · competing stressors exist |
| **8** | **Red team.** The Regulator's best case run against every paragraph | Documented at Part IV |
| **9** | **Tone audit.** Every adverb of assertion struck; understatement substituted | *"objectively reckless"*, *"flagrant"*, *"capriciously"*, *"manifestly"* — all go |
| **10** | **Silk test.** *Would senior counsel sign this and file it without amendment?* | If no, it is not finished |

# PART II — THE ARCHITECTURAL MOVE

## The problem with the pleading as it stands
It is a **list**: Stressor 1(a)–(g), Stressor 2(a)–(b), Stressor 3(a)–(d). Thirteen items.

⛔ **A list is the shape the Regulator needs.** It picks items off one at a time — *the grievance
was answered; the roster was equitable; the delegate process was followed; the AVAC was corrected*
— and then runs *Delaney*: **globally, the management action was reasonable.** Twelve reasonable
items outvote one unreasonable one. **The list arms the dilution argument.**

## The move
⭐⭐⭐ **Recast thirteen grievances as ONE MECHANISM with ONE ADMITTED INSTANCE.**

> **The mechanism: responsibility imposed, and the means to discharge it withheld.**

| Element | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|
| The function is **critical to patient safety** | Form 24 **¶8** | ⭐ **ADMITTED** |
| Maintaining the directory is **his responsibility** | AO3 Role Description — *"Collate information and maintain Omnivista database… to ensure information held within Switchboard Services is accurate"* | **MSH's own document, served 31 Jul 2026** |
| His **access to the database was removed** | Stibbard, 18 Jul 2023 — *"removing everyone's access to the database"* | Documentary |
| Changes were **imposed without consultation**, though the Role Description requires him to *"support and participate in change initiatives"* | Role Description; 16 Jun 2023 | **MSH's own document** |
| When he raised it, **the response came back at him** | Form 24 **¶21** — directed to retract, 48 hours later | ⭐ **ADMITTED** |
| When he grieved it, he was **sent back to the same manager** | 7 Aug 2023; Form 24 **¶5** | ⭐ **ADMITTED** (the rostering error) |
| ⭐⭐ **The one measurable breach of the employer's own rule** | Form 24 **¶1** and **¶3** — the 7-hour break | ⭐⭐ **ADMITTED** |

⇒ **Not thirteen complaints. One exposure, and one instance of it that the Respondent has admitted
and its own delegate called unreasonable.**

⭐ **This is also what solves the three-month gap** (17–18 March → 18 June 2024). Causation attaches
to a **continuing exposure of which the March roster is the proven instance** — which keeps the
specificity *Mahaffey* requires while explaining the interval, and does **not** hand the Regulator
a global-course case to dilute.

## The anchor, and the thread
⭐ **ANCHOR: the seven-hour break.** It is admitted (¶1), the standard is admitted (¶3), it is
**arithmetic rather than impression**, and the Respondent's own Review Unit characterised it as
unreasonable. **Every other fact is threaded back to it as context, never advanced as an
independent ground.**

# PART IV — THE OUTLINE ITSELF (skeleton, ~45 paragraphs)

## Section 1 — Framing and relief (¶¶1–4)

**¶1 — the loaded issue. Drafted last, placed first.**
> On 17–18 March 2024 the Respondent's insured rostered the Appellant to finish at 23:00 and
> recommence at 06:00. That is a seven-hour break. The minimum was ten hours, or eight by written
> agreement. **Both facts are admitted.** The Appellant was required, on that break, to operate the
> console through which every emergency code at Logan Hospital is activated — a function the
> Respondent admits is critical to patient safety. The Respondent's own Review Unit has already
> characterised the rostering as unreasonable management action. **The single question on this
> appeal is whether an admitted breach of the employer's own minimum rest standard, in a
> patient-safety-critical role, is management action taken in a reasonable way.**

⭐ **Hoffmann move — what the case is NOT about (¶2):** it is not about whether every management
decision over three years was reasonable; not about the Appellant's perception; and not about
whether the Review Decision binds the Commission. It does not.

**¶3 — relief.** **¶4 — posture:** decision under review, s 550(4) de novo, procedural history.

## Section 2 — Issues for determination (¶5)
1. Did the Appellant sustain a **personal injury** (s 32(1))?
2. Was **employment a significant contributing factor**? ⛔ **"A significant" — never "major."**
3. Does **s 32(5)(a)** exclude the injury?
4. If some management action was reasonable, does that **restore** the exclusion?

## Section 3 — Legal framework (¶¶6–14) — *the meta-tool: draft the judgment for the bench*
- **¶6** s 32(1) — the elements, separately stated.
- **¶7** ⛔ **The test is *"a significant contributing factor."*** The *"major significant"* test for
  psychiatric injury was **repealed in 2019**, before this injury. Competing causes need not be
  outweighed.
- **¶8** ⭐ **Onus, conceded squarely.** The Appellant bears it on the balance of probabilities,
  including that s 32(5) does not apply. *(Correcting the filed pleading, which asserted the
  Respondent bore it "under Prizeman" — a proposition Prizeman does not contain.)*
- **¶9** s 32(5)(a) — the two limbs: **reasonable management action**, taken in a **reasonable way**.
- **¶¶10–13** The authorities, in a **hierarchy**: Industrial Court first, then QIRC.
- **¶14** ⭐ **The dilution point, stated as a rule of law:** the presence of reasonable management
  action does not restore the exclusion where unreasonable management action with a sufficient
  causal connection is established; and it is an error to ask whether it was the *"dominant"* cause
  or to outnumber one causative unreasonable stressor with others said to be reasonable.

## Section 4 — Facts, thematically (¶¶15–30) — *the evidence weave*
Four themes. **Not thirteen items.** Each theme: proposition → admission → corroboration → the
concession the Respondent must make.

- **Theme A (¶¶15–18) — The function and its criticality.** ¶8 admitted · Role Description ·
  15–50 codes/24h · 269–444 calls per shift, average 360.
- **Theme B (¶¶19–22) — Responsibility without the means.** Role Description requires him to
  maintain the directory · access removed · changes imposed without consultation against a Role
  Description that requires participation in change.
- **Theme C (¶¶23–27) — ⭐⭐ THE ANCHOR: the seven-hour break.** *(the bind sits here)*
- **Theme D (¶¶28–30) — Raising it produced a response directed at him.** 7 Aug 2023 grievance,
  returned to the same manager · ¶21 retraction direction · the AVAC delay, ¶¶40–41.

### ⭐⭐⭐ ¶¶24–27 — THE LOGICAL BIND. The centrepiece.
> **¶24.** The Respondent admits the Appellant was rostered to a **seven-hour** break (¶1).
> **¶25.** The Respondent admits the minimum was **ten hours, or eight by written agreement** (¶3).
> **¶26.** The Respondent **positively asserts** that in June 2020 the Appellant **signed an
> agreement permitting an eight-hour break** (¶4 — pleaded as a denial *"as untrue"*, which is an
> affirmative case the Respondent must prove).
> **¶27.** ⭐⭐ **The Respondent's affirmative case does not answer the breach. It only changes its
> size.**
>
> | If ¶4 is made out | If ¶4 is not made out |
> |---|---|
> | Minimum **8 hours**. Break was **7**. **Short by 1 hour** | Minimum **10 hours**. Break was **7**. **Short by 3 hours** |
>
> **On the Respondent's own best case, the break was short. There is no version of the admitted
> facts in which it was not.** The Respondent must either produce a 2020 agreement said to govern a
> permanent full-time employee four years later — or accept the ten-hour minimum. **Either route
> ends at a breach.**

⭐ **This is what replaces the current overstatement.** The pleading presently asserts a ten-hour
minimum as an *"Admitted Fact"* when ¶4 denies it. **Conceding the contest and pleading the bind is
stronger than asserting the contest away** — and it cannot be attacked, because it runs on the
Respondent's own pleading.

⭐ **Understatement discipline for ¶23:** *"The Appellant finished at 23:00 and recommenced at
06:00. The commute is approximately two hours each way. No fatigue assessment was conducted. On
19 March 2024 the application for fatigue leave was refused."* **No characterisation. Let the
bench do the arithmetic.**

## Section 5 — Application (¶¶31–40) — *layered*
- **¶¶31–32 · LAYER 1 (primary).** The seven-hour break is management action, and it was not taken
  in a reasonable way: it breached the employer's own minimum on any view (¶27), in a
  patient-safety-critical role, after the Appellant had raised the identical risk in writing on
  7 August 2023, and with fatigue leave refused the following day.
- **¶¶33–35 · LAYER 2 (alternative).** Even if the seven-hour break stands alone as reasonable, the
  exclusion still fails: the pleaded course, evaluated in all the circumstances, was not reasonable
  management action taken in a reasonable way.
- **¶36 · LAYER 3 (residual).** To the extent any part of the pleaded course is not **management
  action** at all, s 32(5)(a) has nothing upon which to operate.
- **¶¶37–38 · The pre-emptive strikes.** ⭐ **Both raised by us, first:**
  - **Reality, not perception** — *Prizeman*. The case is grounded in **admitted** facts (¶¶1, 3, 5,
    8, 14, 21, 40, 41). A misperception case has nothing to attach to: **the break is arithmetic.**
  - **Competing causes** — the 2024 cessation of employment (**employer conduct, later reversed**)
    and the litigation **both post-date the 18 June 2024 onset** and cannot bear on causation.
    ⭐ **And s 32(1) requires employment to be *a* significant factor, not the only one.**
- **¶¶39–40 · Concessions, made openly.** Much of the management action was reasonable. The Review
  Decision does not bind. The Appellant does not say every decision over three years was
  unreasonable. ⭐ **He does not need to** — that is precisely the point at ¶14.

## Section 6 — Admissions and evidentiary tension (¶¶41–44)
- **¶41** — the admissions table: ¶1, ¶3, ¶5, ¶8, ¶14, ¶20, ¶21, ¶40, ¶41, ¶46.
- **¶42** ⭐ **¶8 was admitted with no exhibit at all** — the patient-safety criticality is
  established without a document.
- **¶43** — the Review Decision: **contents admitted (¶37)**, characterisation for the Commission
  de novo. ⚠ *"tension"*, never *"contradiction"*.
- **¶44** ⭐ The Respondent's own Review Unit reached its conclusions in **October 2024** — before
  the appeal existed, on the Respondent's own material. **Stated once. Not pressed.**

## Section 7 — Relief (¶45)
Specific. Jurisdictionally anchored to **s 558 WCRA**. ⚠ **Verify the section before filing.**

---

# PART V — RED TEAM (pass 8)

| The Regulator's best point | Answer |
|---|---|
| *Global dilution — twelve reasonable items, one contested* | ⭐ **¶14 + ¶27.** The architecture no longer offers twelve items, and the one it does offer is admitted arithmetic |
| *Three-month gap between March and June 2024* | Continuing exposure, of which the March roster is the **proven instance**; ECC records symptoms *"exacerbated on exposure"* |
| *He worked 14 months afterwards* | **~29% FTE at 269–444 calls per shift.** Fewer shifts, same intensity |
| *Pre-existing anxiety/ADHD from 26 Oct 2022* | ⛔ **Do not run a clean baseline.** Run **aggravation** — s 32 covers it, and pre-morbid **function** answers pre-morbid **diagnosis** |
| *The 8 Sep 2025 attendance letter — 34 occasions* | Post-dates onset by 15 months. **Every occasion involves notification.** ⚠ Not a Part C matter; keep it out |
| *He perceived unreasonableness where there was none* | ⭐ **¶37.** A seven-hour break is not a perception |
| *The Review Decision does not bind* | ⭐ **Conceded at ¶43 before they say it** |

# PART VI — SCHEDULE 2: THE CITATION GATE ⛔
**Eight authorities are cited. ONE is held.**

| Authority | Cited for | Status |
|---|---|---|
| *Prizeman v Q-COMP* [2005] QIC 53; (2005) 180 QGIG 481 | Reality, not perception | ✅ **HELD** — `documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf`. ⛔ Read it and pinpoint before citing |
| ⭐⭐ **Davis v Blackwood [2014] ICQ 009** (Martin J, P) + **Bowers** (Hall P) | ⚠ **THE RESPONDENT'S BEST AUTHORITY — blemishes / a system that miscarried is not necessarily unreasonable.** ⛔ **NOT HELD. ACQUIRE FIRST.** Answer: *Bowers* protects a system that miscarried; **MSH's Items 4, 5 and 7 admit there was no fatigue system at all** |
| **Briginshaw v Briginshaw [1938] 60 CLR 336** | Standard of persuasion for serious allegations — **named in the QIRC's own appeal guide** | ⭐⭐ **Use at ¶8. It is the doctrinal reason to run the admitted break and drop the reprisal adjectives** |
| *Q-COMP v Hochen* (C/2009/47) | The two-limb test; sufficient causal connection | ⛔ **NOT HELD.** ⚠ The citation format is a **file number, not a medium-neutral citation** — verify it exists in that form |
| *Simon Blackwood (WCR) v Mahaffey* [2016] ICQ 10 at [51], [54]–[57] | Single unreasonable stressor suffices | ⛔ **NOT HELD.** Pinpoints unverified |
| *Simon Blackwood (WCR) v Adams* [2015] ICQ 1 at [23] | No dominant-cause test; no outnumbering | ⛔ **NOT HELD.** ⭐ **The most load-bearing pinpoint in the outline. Obtain first** |
| *Delaney v Q-COMP* [2005] QIC 11 | Global evaluation | ⛔ **NOT HELD.** ⚠ **Double-edged — it is also the Respondent's best authority. Read it as an opponent would** |
| *Carr v WCR* [2022] QIRC 059 | Individual assessment of each stressor | ⛔ **NOT HELD** |
| *Read v WCR* [2017] QIRC 72 | Management action is a confined concept | ⛔ **NOT HELD** |
| *Allwood v WCR* [2017] QIRC 88 | Same | ⛔ **NOT HELD** |

⛔⛔ **THE RULE: no authority is cited in a filed document until it has been read to its ratio and
the pinpoint checked on the page.** A self-represented appellant who miscites is not forgiven the
way a silk is — and the filed pleading already carries one misattribution (**Prizeman for onus**).
⭐ **Obtain all eight from AustLII / QIRC before any version of this is filed.**

Cory Shepherd · 0417 400 227

THE CHAIN THIS ENQUIRY OPENS (added 4 Aug — Cory's sequencing)
1. Enquiry (now, his): quote + the provider's written confirmation that deliverables can
   include a practitioner-usable statement of the role's demands/conditions. That
   confirmation is itself a document: independent proof an assessment of this kind
   supplies the job-demands information the nine RFMI questions are missing.
2. Funding mirror (HOLD): MSH commissions and pays the provider directly. Only MSH can
   commission — the assessor needs site access, data and staff; a worker-commissioned
   report never enters the room and reads as a private expert (independence destroyed).
3. Appointment (whenever it occurs): doctors briefed with the nine questions + allocation,
   MSH's role description, and the integrated package as Cory's account of conditions.
   Staged answers if the assessment is incomplete — never withheld answers.
4. Findings land: Report A finalises restrictions/adjustments against the role AS
   ASSESSED. Division of labour stays absolute: the assessor answers "what is this role,
   actually"; only the doctors answer capacity/restrictions/adjustments; neither steps
   over the line. Report B (appeal) stays in its own lane, never fed to this chain.

WHY THE WORDING IS LOAD-BEARING
1. "I table it as an input; engagement is a matter for the Health Service" — Cory never
   steps into the commissioning role; the assessor's independence stays untainted.
2. s 18 WHS Act: cost is relevant to "reasonably practicable" only after likelihood and
   severity, and only if grossly disproportionate. A real quote converts "expensive and
   hard to arrange" from an argument into a documented untruth.
3. A "no" given against a tabled quote is a no recorded against a known price and
   confirmed availability — documented in the consultation record.

   ⛔ **Do not assert a clean baseline.** Use the aggravation route:

>>> drafts/PSYCHOSOCIAL_MAPPING_WHS.txt :: text
PSYCHOSOCIAL HAZARD MAPPING — SWITCHBOARD SERVICES
Prepared under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld), the Work Health and Safety
Regulation 2011 (Qld), and the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of
Practice 2022

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
August 2026 — prepared for the risk assessment under clause 7.2 of the certified agreement,
and for consultation under sections 47 to 49 of the Act. Companion to "Return to Work and
Workplace Controls — Proposals for Consultation". Nothing in this document is an allegation
against any person; every hazard is described as a feature of the work and its systems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 1 — THE FRAMEWORK THIS MAPPING SITS IN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  Section 19 of the Act places the primary duty on the person conducting the business to
    ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health of workers — health is defined
    to include psychological health.

2.  The Regulation requires psychosocial risks to be managed: hazards identified, risks
    assessed, controls implemented in the order of the hierarchy, and controls reviewed —
    including when a hazard is identified or on request.

3.  Sections 47 to 49 require consultation with the workers who are, or are likely to be,
    directly affected — at each step: identification, assessment, control selection, and
    review.

4.  The Code of Practice 2022 identifies the recognised psychosocial hazard categories and
    the data sources for assessing them, including complaints records, absence and turnover
    data, and workload data. This mapping uses the Code's categories and terminology.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 2 — THE MAPPING: HAZARD, PRESENTATION, RISK, PROPOSED CONTROL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  HIGH JOB DEMANDS.
    How it presents: sustained call volume (in the order of 200 to 300 calls per shift), a
    substantial proportion from distressed or urgent callers; concurrent operation of
    multiple systems; emergency code activations through the shift; additional functions
    absorbed when other support is unavailable.
    Risk: cognitive overload, sustained hyper-vigilance, exhaustion.
    Proposed controls: evidence-based rostering matched to demand peaks (Proposal 7);
    defined escalation and backup pathways so absorbed functions return to their owners
    (Proposals 1 and 4 of the operating model).

2.  LOW JOB CONTROL.
    How it presents: operational changes taking effect without consultation with the
    operators who work the board; no operator input into rostering design.
    Risk: helplessness in a high-demand role — the demand/control combination the Code
    identifies as high risk.
    Proposed controls: consultation before operational change (Proposal 2); operator
    consultation in roster design (Proposal 7).

3.  POOR SUPPORT.
    How it presents: supervision and decision-support not reliably available in real time,
    particularly after hours and on weekends, in a room whose work is continuous.
    Risk: unsupported decision-making in safety-critical moments; accumulated strain.
    Proposed controls: the rotational integrated manager in hours (Proposal 3); the 24/7
    on-shift supervisor function — authority follows the clock (Proposal 6).

4.  LOW ROLE CLARITY.
    How it presents: functions accreting to the Switchboard without documented boundaries
    (complaint handling, departmental support, roster administration); uncertainty as to
    what is, and is not, the operator's responsibility.
    Risk: role overload and blame absorption for matters outside the role.
    Proposed controls: documented boundaries and escalation paths (operating model
    Proposals 1 and 4); the complaint-response standard returning escalated matters to
    the accountable function.

5.  POOR ORGANISATIONAL CHANGE MANAGEMENT.
    How it presents: changes to processes and system access made without consultation with
    affected operators, with downstream effects discovered in operation.
    Risk: preventable failures experienced at the console; erosion of trust.
    Proposed control: consultation before operational change (Proposal 2), applied
    systematically as the Act already requires.

6.  INADEQUATE REWARD AND RECOGNITION.
    How it presents: no development pathway within the room; competence and additional
    responsibility carrying no recognition in classification or progression.
    Risk: effort-reward imbalance, disengagement, loss of experienced staff.
    Proposed control: the rotating on-shift supervisor function with in-charge recognition
    and a trained pathway (Proposal 6).

7.  POOR ORGANISATIONAL JUSTICE.
    How it presents: inconsistency between the timeframes and process standards applied to
    operators and those observed in matters affecting them; complaints and workplace
    matters raised without acknowledgment, outcome, or feedback.
    Risk: the perception and experience of unfairness — a recognised psychosocial hazard in
    its own right; escalating distress in those affected.
    Proposed controls: the complaint-response standard (Proposal 4); one rulebook for the
    room (Proposal 5); written feedback on WHS matters raised (Part 1, item 7 of the
    companion document).

8.  REMOTE OR ISOLATED WORK (AFTER HOURS).
    How it presents: after-hours and weekend shifts performed without present supervision
    or management support, while the room's functions continue unchanged.
    Risk: unsupported exposure to all other hazards during the periods of least support.
    Proposed control: the 24/7 on-shift supervisor function (Proposal 6).

9.  EXPOSURE TO DISTRESSED AND AGGRESSIVE CALLERS.
    How it presents: the Switchboard is the hospital's first point of contact; a
    substantial proportion of contacts are made in distress, fear, conflict or crisis, and
    complaints are frequently expressed as accusations to the operator answering.
    Risk: cumulative exposure to occupational violence and aggression in verbal form.
    Proposed controls: the complaint-response standard and escalation pathway so the
    operator's exposure ends at triage (Proposals 1 and 4); acknowledgment of this
    exposure in the assessment's scope.

10. FATIGUE.
    How it presents: rostering patterns capable of producing breaks below the mandated
    minimum; and — observable across the team, not any one operator — fatigue currently
    managed informally by staff themselves, through personal leave taken on and after
    high-volume periods. The pattern is visible on the face of the rosters when read
    against the leave records and the demand data: the cost of the unmanaged hazard is
    being transferred to workers' own leave balances.
    Risk: impaired performance in a safety-critical function; cumulative harm; depletion
    of leave entitlements as the de facto fatigue control.
    Proposed control: fatigue rules built into roster design — minimum breaks enforced
    structurally, not checked after the fact — so that recovery is provided by the roster,
    not purchased by the worker (Proposal 7).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 3 — CONSULTATION AND REVIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  This mapping is offered as a worker's contribution to hazard identification under
    sections 47 to 49 — the first step of the process the Regulation requires. It is not a
    substitute for the assessment; it is an input to it.

2.  I ask that the assessment: adopt the Code's categories; draw on the Code's data sources
    (complaints records, absence and turnover data, EAP usage, workload and call-volume
    data); specifically, map the team's leave usage against the rosters and the demand data,
    which will show whether fatigue is presently being absorbed through personal leave; be
    conducted by an assessor independent of the functions being assessed; and select
    controls in consultation, in the order the Regulation requires.

3.  I ask that controls, once implemented, carry review dates, and that the review include
    the operators affected — consistent with the Regulation's review triggers.

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital
0417 400 227 · coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

Subject: RE: Notice of dispute — clause 1.11 — attendance, roster, leave and pay from
26 June 2026

Dear Chloe,

Thank you for responding, and for confirming the dispute has been received and is under
review. Thank you also for the information about the Employee Assistance Program. I
appreciate you writing to me directly, and I would like to resolve this with you at Stage 1
if we possibly can.

Answering before the payroll cut-off

I do not consent to my recreation leave balance being applied to the period 20 July to
2 August 2026, or to any part of that period being recorded as sick leave without pay. That
balance is my own accrued entitlement, and once it is consumed it cannot be restored except
by re-credit. I am not asking the Health Service to withhold payment from me: if leave is
applied, I ask only that it be recorded as applied at the Health Service's initiative,
without my consent, without prejudice to the dispute, and subject to re-credit as the
dispute seeks.

My understanding of the position

So that we are working from the same facts, my understanding is:

1. On 26 June 2026 I was advised that I could not attend work until medical clearance was
   received.
2. On 3 July 2026 I provided the Employee Capabilities Checklist, which certified me fit
   for work with restrictions.
3. Within the hour I was advised that I could not attend.
4. My pay ceased from 13 July 2026, and leave has been debited since.
5. I have asked on several occasions for the instrument under which I am being kept from
   work, and I have not yet received an answer.

Your letter refers to the position since 3 July 2026; the dispute concerns the position
from 26 June 2026, which is why the dates above matter to the leave and pay in question.
If any part of my understanding is inaccurate, please tell me and I will correct my own
records.

Six questions, so the correct arrangement can be applied

I ask these in good faith. My concern is simply that whatever arrangement applies to me is
the right one under the instruments, so that it can be administered correctly and I am not
disadvantaged while the dispute is being resolved. If it is easier, you are very welcome to
answer them inline in a reply to this email, and if any of them are better answered by
someone else, I am happy for that person to respond directly.

1. Your letter refers to "the decision that has prevented you from attending your rostered
   shifts". Could you please tell me what that decision was made under — which instrument,
   policy or directive — who made it, and on what date?

2. If the arrangement is a suspension under section 101 of the Public Sector Act 2022,
   could I please be given the notice that section requires, stating when it starts and ends
   and whether I am entitled to remuneration? I would also be grateful to know what
   reasonable alternatives were considered beforehand, as section 101(3) requires — I
   proposed several, including the restrictions certified on 3 July and my return to work
   proposal of 3 August.

3. If the arrangement is recreation leave, section 33 of the Industrial Relations Act 2016
   provides that timing is agreed between employee and employer, and that where there is no
   agreement the employer may decide but must give at least eight weeks' written notice. I
   have not agreed, and I have not received that notice. Could you let me know which
   provision is being relied on?

4. If any part of the period is to be recorded as sick leave, could you let me know the
   basis? The Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026 certified me fit for work with
   restrictions, and I have been ready, willing and able to attend throughout. I would not
   want the Health Service's records to show an absence through illness when the position is
   that I have not been permitted to attend.

5. If the arrangement is none of these, then I remain ready, willing and able to work, and I
   would be grateful to know when I can return.

6. Could you also let me know who is conducting the review, and the date by which it is
   expected to be completed?

If the answer to question 1 is that no instrument applies to the period, I would ask that
the leave simply be re-credited and the period corrected, without the need for any further
process.

For completeness: my availability to work is unqualified, and has been throughout. My
separate request of 3 August under clause 10.3.2 is a request for a prospective change to be
agreed for the future; it does not qualify my present availability, and it is not part of
this dispute. It continues on its own timeframe under clause 10.3.

The status quo while we resolve this

Clause 1.11.4 provides that while the dispute procedure is being followed, the status quo
existing before the emergence of the dispute is to continue, and that no party is to be
prejudiced as to the final settlement. The position before the matters in dispute arose —
that is, before 26 June 2026 — was that I was rostered, working and paid. My leave and pay
are the subject matter of the dispute, so I ask that no further leave be debited and no
further unpaid absence recorded until it is resolved. If that decision sits above your
delegation, I am content for it to be referred upward — I am not asking you personally to
carry it.

I should also mention, simply as a fact relevant to timing, that I have been without wages
since 13 July 2026.

Timing, so we both know where we stand

Clause 1.11.2(a) contemplates that the Stage 1 procedure should not extend beyond seven
days, which falls on Monday 10 August. I would much rather resolve this with you before then
than move to the next stage. I am available:

   • today, any time before 5:00pm;
   • Wednesday 5 August, 9:00am to 5:00pm;
   • Thursday 6 August, 9:00am to 5:00pm;

and I can make other times work, including outside business hours, if that is easier. I
would have my support person and union representative present. So that the discussion is
productive, it would help if the answers to the questions above could be available at it.

If a discussion is not possible this week, could the answers to the six questions please be
provided in writing by Monday 10 August, so that we are not held up by diary availability.

If the dispute is unresolved by 10 August I will refer it to Stage 2 as the clause provides,
which I mention only so that the timing is not a surprise.

Where I stand

I want to come back to work. My return to work proposal of 3 August stands, as does my
request that a psychosocial assessment of the work area be conducted in consultation. If
there is anything further you need from me to progress the review, please tell me and I will
provide it the same day.

WHY THIS WORKS
- Q1 asks for the instrument/decision-maker/date using HER OWN word ("decision").
- Q2-Q4 close every available characterisation: suspension (s 101 notice, remuneration,
  alternatives), recreation leave (s 33 agreement or 8 weeks notice), sick leave (certified
  FIT — records point). Q5 leaves only "he should be at work".
- Every question is answerable only by producing a document they do not have, or by
  conceding. Neither is an accusation.
- "I am not asking you personally to carry it" removes her personal defensiveness and
  invites upward referral — which is where the answer actually lives.
- The 10 August line pre-announces Stage 2 as courtesy, not threat, and makes the referral
  unsurprising and unprovocative when it lands.
- Closes on return-to-work and the assessment: constructive, and it keeps the record
  showing one side solving and the other deciding.
⛔ NOT INCLUDED: delegate status (Stage 2 referral), the CE conflict letter (already with
her office), the 24-hour admission (it is in her letter — never argue with a gift), the
28-day gap (held for Stage 2/submissions), any WHS or protected-act citation.

   3 July 2026" — MSH's FIRST written acknowledgment that a DECISION exists. He has asked
   since June who made it and under what instrument. It is now named by his line manager.
3. "I am required to process leave on your behalf" — asserts a requirement, identifies no
   instrument, and does it while the dispute is on foot (cl 1.11.4 status quo).
4. Payroll pressure: PP04 cut-off today; silence = they apply the 41.21 hours anyway.

⚠ THE TRAP: consenting to apply his last recreation leave (a) exhausts the final paid
entitlement, and (b) characterises the absence as HIS leave rather than an employer
decision — which is the exact issue in dispute and would undercut the wages claim.
⚠ THE COUNTER-TRAP: flatly refusing may stop the payment and leave him with nothing this
fortnight, with no income since 13 July.

⭐ THE ANSWER: NEITHER CONSENT NOR REFUSE — RESERVE. He does not authorise it; if the
Health Service applies leave it does so on its own initiative, without his consent, and
subject to re-credit as sought in the dispute. She has already said she will apply it if
he does not respond — so the money still arrives, and consent is expressly withheld.

>>> drafts/STAGE1_MEETING_RECORD_PROTOCOL.txt :: text
STAGE 1 / STAGE 2 MEETING RECORD PROTOCOL — the one proofing gap. Banked 4 Aug 2026.
====================================================================================
IDENTIFIED BY RESPONSE-TREE TEST: every MSH reply branch is covered EXCEPT the branch
where they meet him and bring nothing. An undocumented meeting is the only way the
six questions can be made to disappear.

BEFORE THE MEETING
- Support person + union representative present (already offered in writing).
- Bring: the six questions, the ECC (3 Jul), the dispute notice, the RTW proposal.
- Ask at the start: "may I take notes?" — always yes; write times, names, roles.

IN THE MEETING
- Ask the six questions IN ORDER. If an answer is not given, ask: "is that something
  that can be provided, and by when?" Record the answer to THAT question too.
- Never argue. Never raise motive, the CE letter, the appeal, or the assessment cost.
- If a new characterisation is offered ("special leave", "leave without pay",
  "directed absence"), do not accept or reject it in the room: "thank you — I'll
  consider that and respond in writing."
- If pressed to agree to anything: "I'd like to take that away and respond in writing."

⭐ SAME DAY, IN WRITING (the step that closes the gap)
Send within hours, to the same recipients, subject "Record of Stage 1 discussion —
[date]":

  Dear Chloe,
  Thank you for meeting with me today at [time]. Present were [names].
  My record of the discussion is:
  1. [Question 1 — the answer given, or "no answer was given"].
  2. [ … each question, each answer or non-answer … ]
  6. [ … ]
  [Anything agreed, with dates.] [Anything to be provided, with the date promised.]
  If my record is inaccurate or incomplete in any respect, please let me know and I
  will correct it.
  Kind regards, Cory Shepherd

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE MEETING ITSELF
- An unanswered question in an email is a gap. An unanswered question recorded in an
  agreed minute is a FINDING.
- "Please correct me if I am wrong" converts their silence into acceptance of his
  record — the same mechanism that made the 3 August package work.
- It is courteous, standard practice, and impossible to object to.
- Do the same after ANY Stage 2 conference, any phone call, any corridor conversation.
STANDING RULE: nothing that happens orally in this matter stays oral.

I refer the dispute lodged on 3 August 2026 to Stage 2 under clause 1.11.2(b) of EB12,

clause shall arrange a conference of the parties. Given the matters set out in my letter

independent of the matters in dispute.

1  Why the referral is made

Stage 1 has concluded unresolved. The record is short:

1.1  The dispute was acknowledged as validly lodged on 4 August ("Your dispute has been
     lodged in accordance with clause 1.11.2(a)").

     "the 24-hour timeframe specified in the clause will not be achieved."

     corrected. It asked seven questions so the correct arrangement could be applied;
     [SLOT: none / only questions X] have been answered.

     was debited and that it was reserved, without consent, subject to re-credit.]
1.6  [SLOT: any response to the special leave request under Directive 12/24 — or its

For completeness, I note that I hold office as a delegate of Together Queensland, as the
