# Rule 64G Application v5R — Validation & Stress-Test Report

Rebuilt 11 June 2026 from the v5 specification (`skill/references/documents-and-64g.md`)
and the verified record only. "v5R" = rebuild; the original v5 FINAL was never
recovered. Files: `WC2024-227_Rule64G_FILING_v5R_FINAL.pdf` (7 pp, A4 — the
lodgement document) and `WC2024-227_Rule64G_Application_v5R_NOCASELAW.docx`
(editable master, body only; Annexure C is merged into the PDF).

## Validation — 33/33 PASS

- **Checklist item 1 (Form 24 pinpoints):** every pinpoint verified against the
  in-repo response (`documents/2026-02-18_Form24_Response...pdf`): ¶1, ¶3,
  ¶34 (cited with the offset handled: "Response ¶34, responding to Notice ¶37"),
  ¶39 ("the roster was equitable", cited as Response ¶39 / Notice ¶¶42–45), ¶21, ¶23.
- **Checklist item 2 (IRO framing):** "persuasive material identifying the matters
  in issue"; the de novo point is adopted, not resisted. The word "binding" does
  not appear.
- **Checklist item 3 (onus):** Appellant-onus stated and accepted (D1); used as the
  necessity argument (D2). No Respondent-onus relic.
- **Checklist item 4 (Hawes):** no "1 July 2024" anywhere (the certificate is not
  relied on in this application at all).
- **Discipline rules:** no case law; no "fraud"; no "reprisal"; no
  conspiracy/coordination language; Items 8–9 anchored ONLY to Stressor 1(a) +
  the ¶39 equitable-roster denial; PID complaint form NOT annexed; Annexure C =
  the single headed McGinley page only.
- **Mechanics:** orders summary matches the filed Draft Order exactly; Schedule A
  carries the re-specified Item 20; placeholders filled; 7 pages (< 30, PD 3/2021); A4.
- **Checklist item 6 (no conflicting live direction):** on the integrated corpus the
  only live directions are the 7 Apr 2026 FDO (timetable complete) and the 22 May
  direction (spent on 5 June). Nothing conflicts with the Items 8–9 regime.

## Stress test — how each likely attack lands

1. **r 64B(2) (simpler means exist):** defeated by D2 — the records exist only in
   MSH systems; no alternative source is identified anywhere in the corpus.
2. **Relevance confinement ("17–18 March only"):** D3 answers from the pleading
   itself — the Amended SOFC was filed with leave granted by Dwyer C on 7 April
   2026; the confined reading contradicts the pleading the Commission itself
   admitted to the record.
3. **Expense:** three layers — E2 confinement, r 64I costs, G3 practice. G3 is
   qualified ("so far as appears from the material") and asserts only from the
   face of the disclosure. The full asymmetry reply stays in the drawer
   (working-theories §7) for the ~12.5% case where MSH maintains the ground.
4. **Particularity:** Schedule A re-specifies Item 20 by subject and window;
   custodians and windows are defined for every item.
5. **Privacy / effect on persons (Items 8–9):** pre-empted — the application
   itself offers the confidentiality regime (Registry-confidential, parties-only,
   credential/date/timestamp fields, redactions). A privacy objection is hard to
   maintain against field-confined metadata under a protective order.
6. **Collateral-purpose attack:** the danger zone, fully sterilised — Items 8–9
   tied to two pleaded, contested facts and nothing else (D5 closes with "No
   broader use is made of these Items"); the disclosure-response language in
   Item 20/B-20 is institutional and neutral.
7. **Section G overreach:** G4's "cannot stand with" is carried by the annexed
   document itself (an internal MSH email squarely within Item 20's subject and
   window, located and produced). Provenance inferences (who supplied it, why)
   appear nowhere.
8. **Item 19 natural justice (TQ):** handled by the 7-day notice + liberty to
   apply, in both the application and the order.
9. **Order (c) proportionality:** framed as verification of answers MSH has
   already given — "asks nothing of MSH that its response does not already
   assert." The reconciliation engine (Item 14 device date; Item 16 process
   references) is stated as bookkeeping, not accusation.
10. **Tone:** zero adjectives of complaint; concessions lead (C5, I1); every
    assertion carries a pinpoint or an annexure.

                        Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011 — rule 4(2)
                  QUEENSLAND INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION
                      Workers’ Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003 (Qld)

Non-party to whom this application relates: METRO SOUTH HOSPITAL AND HEALTH SERVICE

A. APPLICATION AND ORDERS SOUGHT
A1. TAKE NOTICE that the Appellant applies to the Commission under rule 64G(1) of the Industrial
Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011 for a decision about the objection of MSH dated 5 June 2026 (ref K-
LM26/729) to the Appellant’s Form 29 – Notice of Non-Party Disclosure, sealed by the Industrial
Registry on 22 April 2026 (“the Notice”).
A2. The orders sought are set out in the draft order filed with this application. In summary: (a) the
objections to Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10 and 19 be overruled, and the documents described in Schedule
A be produced within 14 days in native electronic format; (b) the spreadsheet of recorded MET calls
for 17–18 March 2024, identified in MSH’s response to Items 1 and 2, be produced; (c) production
under Items 8 and 9 be subject to the confidentiality regime in the draft order; (d) the order concerning
Item 19 take effect seven days after written notice to Together Queensland, which has liberty to apply;
(e) MSH file and serve a verification affidavit of an officer with direct knowledge of the searches
undertaken, in the terms of the draft order; (f) each party bear its own costs of the application, in
accordance with rule 64G(3); and (g) liberty to apply as to the mechanics of production.

B. JURISDICTION AND TIMELINESS
B1. The Notice was sealed by the Industrial Registry on 22 April 2026 and served on MSH the same
day. By the direction of the Commission communicated on 22 May 2026, MSH was to provide any
objections to the Notice by 4:00 pm on Friday, 5 June 2026.
B2. MSH’s objection was served by email at 3:02 pm on 5 June 2026. By rule 64F, the objection
operates as a stay of the Notice. By rule 64G(1), a party may, within seven days of service of an
objection, apply to the Commission for a decision about the objection. This application is filed on 12
June 2026, within time.
B3. By rule 64G(2), the Commission may make any order it considers appropriate, including an order
lifting the stay, varying the Notice, or setting aside the Notice or part of it.

C. THE CHARACTER OF MSH’S RESPONSE — WHAT IS, AND IS NOT, IN DISPUTE
C1. MSH’s response of 5 June 2026 takes three forms, and the greater part of it is not in dispute.
C2. First, MSH has produced documents in answer to Items 6, 11, 12 (in part), 13, 15 and 16. The
Appellant acknowledges that production.
C3. Second, MSH answers that documents responsive to Items 1–2, 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20 do not
exist or are not retained — in the case of Items 1–2, by reason of a system upgrade. Each such answer
records that a search was undertaken. Those answers are addressed in Sections G and H.

>>> drafts/WC2024-227_Rule64G_FILING_v5R_FINAL.pdf :: page 2
C4. Third, MSH objects to Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10, 12 (balance), 17, 18 and 19, on grounds within
rule 64E(4)(a) (expense and inconvenience), (b) (relevance), (c) (particularity), and (e)–(f) (privacy
and effect on persons).
C5. The Appellant does not press Items 12 (balance) and 17. The Appellant does not press Item 18,
upon MSH’s confirmation in the verification affidavit sought that destruction of the record the subject
of that Item is conceded. What remains — Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10 and 19, with Item 20 as re-
specified in Schedule A — is the confined set of records the pleaded issues require.

D. THE ROLE OF THE NON-PARTY AND THE MATTER IN ISSUE
D1. The appeal is brought under s 550(4) of the Workers’ Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003
against the Respondent’s review decision. The Appellant bears the onus of establishing that he
sustained an injury within s 32 of that Act — including that his employment was a significant
contributing factor to the injury, and that the injury did not arise out of, or in the course of, reasonable
management action taken in a reasonable way (s 32(5)(a)). The Appellant accepts that onus and seeks
to discharge it on records of fact rather than contested recollection.
D2. That onus shapes this application. A party required to prove the character of management conduct
cannot fairly be left without the records of that conduct, where those records exist only in the systems
of the entity whose conduct is in question. MSH is not a stranger to this proceeding: it is the
employing authority whose management action is the subject of s 32(5)(a), and the sole custodian of
the systems — mail, rostering, attendance, payroll and human-resources case management — in which
that conduct was recorded as it occurred.
D3. MSH’s response restates the matter in issue as confined to “the consecutive shifts of 17–18
March 2024.” That is not the pleaded case. The Appellant’s Amended Statement of Facts and
Contentions, filed 8 April 2026 pursuant to leave, pleads a course of management conduct between
June 2023 and June 2024 comprising three stressors: a hostile course of management conduct,
including the Line Manager’s erratic physical presence (Stressor 1(a)); systemic failures of
remuneration between February and April 2024 (Stressor 2); and the rostering of consecutive shifts
separated by a 7-hour break on 17–18 March 2024 (Stressor 3). The 17–18 March events are the
anchor of the pleaded period, not its perimeter.
D4. The Respondent’s Form 24 response dated 18 February 2026 admits the 7-hour break (Response
¶1) and admits that the applicable industrial instruments require a minimum break of 10 hours between
shifts, or 8 hours by written agreement (Response ¶3). The Respondent admits the contents of the
review decision dated 24 October 2024 — which found the rostering of those two shifts to be
unreasonable management action — while submitting that the appeal is a hearing de novo and that the
question is for the Commission to determine (Response ¶34, responding to Notice ¶37). The Appellant
relies on that finding as persuasive material identifying the matters in issue; the Commission will
determine the question afresh, on the records this Notice seeks.
D5. Items 8 and 9 — the Line Manager’s system sign-in export and access-control records — are
directly relevant in the sense the rules require: they tend to prove or disprove allegations in issue. Two
such allegations are live on the pleadings. First, Stressor 1(a) pleads, and the Respondent contests, the
Line Manager’s erratic physical presence; the records measure presence. Secondly, the Respondent
denies the pleaded pay disparity on the footing that “the roster was equitable” (Response ¶39,
responding to Notice ¶¶42–45); the same records test that assertion. No broader use is made of these
Items.

E. EXPENSE AND INCONVENIENCE (RULE 64E(4)(a))
E1. The expense ground rests on the asserted need for Chief Executive approval, engagement of
eHealth Queensland, and diversion of resources from the delivery of health care.

>>> drafts/WC2024-227_Rule64G_FILING_v5R_FINAL.pdf :: page 3
E2. The Items as pressed are confined: keyword searches of two identified custodians’ mailboxes
across defined windows (Items 3(a), 3(b), 10); two system-generated exports of a kind produced in the
ordinary course for audit purposes (Items 8, 9); a two-day window of correspondence with a named
industrial organisation (Item 19); and a re-specified, subject-confined Item 20. Rule 64I separately
entitles MSH to its reasonable expenses of production, on notice given within one month.
E3. As to what production of records of this class involves in practice, see Section G.

F. ITEMS PRESSED
F1. The Items pressed, the records sought and the windows are set out in Schedule A. The matter in
issue about which each Item is directly relevant is stated, Item by Item, in Annexure B, in accordance
with rule 64C(1).
F2. As to the windows for Items 8 and 9: the irreducible floor is 16–19 March 2024, anchored to the
admitted 7-hour break (Response ¶1). The continuous window sought (1 March – 30 June 2024) is
what allows the records to be read neutrally: a continuous series across the roster periods either side of
those events, scored against the ordinary Monday-to-Friday working pattern, is pattern evidence. A
hand-picked set of dates would invite the objection it avoids.

G. THE RESPONDENT’S DISCLOSURE OF 11 JUNE 2026 — THE RECORDS EXIST AND
PRODUCTION IS AVAILABLE
G1. On 11 June 2026 at 11:03 am, the Respondent made supplementary disclosure to the Appellant of
a ten-page bundle, described in its covering email as documentation “received through Notice of Non-
Party Disclosure request and conferencing.” Three features of that bundle bear directly on this
application. A single page of the bundle is annexed (Annexure C); the bundle as a whole can be
provided to the Commission on request.
G2. The records exist. The bundle reproduces the complete electronic record of the Appellant’s leave
form 15480560 in MSH’s myHR system — the request, the certification chain, and the Attachments,
Comments, Process Flow and History tabs, the last with timestamps to the second. The records sought
under Items 8 and 9 are system records of the same character, from the same environment. The
enclosures to MSH’s own response of 5 June 2026 include a myHR report generated from a native
spreadsheet. These are extant, exportable system records.
G3. Production is available without the apparatus the objection describes. Documents of this class,
from these custodians, were collected and provided to the Respondent in the ordinary course of the
Respondent’s engagement with MSH officers — without, so far as appears from the material, Chief
Executive approval, the engagement of eHealth Queensland, or any diversion from the delivery of
health care. The expense ground falls to be assessed against what production has in fact involved.
G4. The breadth of searchable material is confirmed. Annexure C is an email of 16 May 2024 sent by
an MSH human resources officer, addressed to the Director and another officer and copied to three
further officers. It was not addressed to the Appellant; it is internal MSH correspondence of precisely
the class sought by Items 3(a), 3(b) and 10. It exists; it was located; and it was produced — to the
Respondent. The answer that documents responsive to Item 20 “do not exist” cannot stand with the
existence of internal responsive correspondence of this kind. Schedule A re-specifies Item 20 by
subject and window, so that no question of particularity remains.

H. VERIFICATION OF THE NON-EXISTENCE ANSWERS
H1. Each “does not exist / not retained” answer in MSH’s response records that a search was
undertaken. The Appellant seeks no more than that those answers be placed on affidavit by an officer
with direct knowledge of the searches: the systems searched, the searches undertaken, and the basis for
each statement.

H2. Two specific matters require reconciliation in that affidavit. First, as to Item 14: the date on

report.
H3. Verification in these terms is the ordinary means of giving the Commission, and the Appellant, a

I. ITEMS NOT PRESSED

confinement.

7.   Each party bear its own costs of the application, in accordance with rule 64G(3).

APPLICATION FOR A DECISION ABOUT OBJECTION — RULE 64G(1) — AND INTEGRATED
                         OUTLINE OF SUBMISSIONS
A. Application and Orders Sought
1.   By correspondence dated 5 June 2026, signed by its Chief Executive and provided in accordance with the
     direction issued from the Chambers of Commissioner Dwyer on 22 May 2026, Metro South Hospital and
     Health Service (“MSH”) responded to the Appellant’s Form 29 Notice of Non-Party Disclosure sealed 22
     April 2026 (“the Notice”). The response complies with six Items; states that documents responsive to
     seven further Items do not exist or are not in MSH’s possession; and objects under rule 64E(4) of the
     Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011 (“the Rules”) to the remainder. This application accepts the
     greater part of that response. It asks the Commission to decide only the objections that remain — on terms
     the Appellant has himself narrowed, in one instance to the very scope MSH proposed — and to require
     verification of one answer that a document already before the Commission contradicts.
2.   TAKE NOTICE that the Appellant applies under rule 64G(1) for the following orders:
     (a) the objections to Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10 and 19 of the Notice are overruled, and MSH is to
            produce the documents described in Schedule A (items 1 to 6) within fourteen (14) days of the
            order;
     (b) MSH is to produce within fourteen (14) days the spreadsheet of recorded MET calls for the period
            17–18 March 2024 identified in its response to Items 1 and 2, against which no ground of objection
            is raised;
     (c) pursuant to rule 64G(2), MSH is to verify by affidavit of an officer with direct knowledge of the

            1–2 (non-retention following the SPOK upgrade), 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20 do not exist or are not in
            its possession or control, identifying in each case the systems searched, the searches undertaken,

            maintained non-possession as to Item 20 having regard to Annexure C, and the process references

     (d) as to Item 18, noting MSH’s statement that the destruction of the record is conceded on the

     (e) Items 12 (balance) and 17 of the Notice are not pressed, in light of the privacy considerations MSH
            has raised;
     (f)    each party bear its own costs of the application, in accordance with rule 64G(3); and
     (g) such further or other orders as the Commission considers appropriate.
B. Jurisdiction and Timeliness
3.   The Notice was sealed by the Industrial Registry on 22 April 2026 and served on MSH by email at 5:08
     PM that day. By direction issued from Chambers on 22 May 2026 — in effect, leave under rule 64E(1) for
     objection at a later time — MSH was directed to provide any objections by 4:00 PM on 5 June 2026.
     MSH’s objection was served by email at 3:02 PM on 5 June 2026. Rule 64G(1) permits this application
     within seven days after service of the objection; it is made within that period. Rule 64F stays the Notice as
     to the documents objected to; this application brings the stayed Items before the Commission for
     decision.
C. The Character of MSH’s Response
4.   The response falls into three categories. First, compliance: MSH has produced documents responsive to
     Items 6, 11, 12 (in part), 13, 15 and 16. That compliance is acknowledged; the enclosed records materially
     advance the appeal. Secondly, answers: for Items 1–2, 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20, MSH states that
     responsive documents do not exist or are not in its possession or control. Those are answers to the Notice
     rather than objections under rule 64E(4); they are addressed in Sections G and H. Thirdly, objections:
     for Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10, 12 (balance), 17, 18 and 19, MSH objects on grounds of expense and
     inconvenience (rule 64E(4)(a)), relevance (4(b)), particularity (4(c)), privacy (4(e)) and effect on a

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5.1_FINAL_CLEAN.pdf :: page 2
    person (4(f)). Of these nine, the Appellant presses six, each on narrowed terms, and does not press three.
    None of the objections is put on the basis that the documents do not exist.
D. The Role of the Non-Party and the Matter in Issue
5.  Subdivision 7A allocates functions. The party issuing a notice must state in it the matter in issue (rule
    64C(1)). The non-party’s part is to produce (rule 64D) or to object on the grounds rule 64E(4) provides.
    Where an objection is contested, the decision belongs to the Commission (rule 64G). Nothing in the
    subdivision asks the non-party to settle the scope of the appeal, or to measure relevance against its own
    restatement of the issues. That involves no criticism of MSH, whose reading is naturally operational; but
    it frames what the Commission is asked to decide.
6.  The standard the Rules apply is direct relevance: a notice may require production of documents directly
    relevant to a matter in issue in the proceeding. In practical terms, a document answers that standard where
    it is capable of tending to prove or disprove an allegation in issue, having regard to the matters pleaded
    and the issues those matters raise. Annexure B identifies, for each contested Item, the allegation the
    records tend to prove or disprove. Several objections instead test the Items against admissibility, or
    against the non-party’s view of what the evidence will show — neither is the question at the disclosure
    stage.
7.  Several of the objections proceed from such a restatement. The response treats the matter in issue, “as
    pleaded in the Notice”, as confined to the “consecutive shifts of 17 to 18 March 2024”, and tests each date
    range against that confined reading. The Notice states the matter in issue in materially wider terms: a
    psychiatric injury with onset in June 2024, sustained in the course of employment at the Logan Hospital
    Switchboard, in a de novo appeal in which the Appellant bears the onus of establishing the injury —
    including that the employment was a significant contributing factor to it, and that it did not arise out of
    reasonable management action taken in a reasonable way within s 32(5)(a) of the Workers’
    Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003. The consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024 are the
    keystone stressor; they are not the perimeter of the inquiry. The pleadings themselves sharpen the point:
    the Regulator’s own Independent Review Office has found that the 7-hour rest break constituted
    unreasonable management action (Form 24, ¶37). A restatement that confines disclosure to 17–18 March
    2024 confines it to the one event already the subject of that finding. On the pleadings and admitted facts
    presently before the Commission, the inquiry under s 32(5)(a) is broader than that single shift pairing —
    it extends to the course of conduct pleaded from June 2023 to June 2024 — and the records sought bear
    directly on that broader inquiry.
8.  There is a further reason the restatement does not govern relevance. To confine disclosure to the events a
    non-party considers caused the injury is to treat the non-party’s opinion of causation as settled. The cause
    of a psychiatric injury is not a matter on which MSH — or any party — holds privileged insight; it is the
    question the appeal exists to decide. The degree, duration and density of the pleaded stressors are
    themselves facts in issue under s 32(5)(a): the reasonableness of management action, and the manner of
    its taking, fall to be weighed against the conduct’s extent, not a single instance of it. The Notice seeks
    records of fact; the objections that resist it proceed on assumptions about what those records are likely to
    show or not show. The Appellant’s entitlement is correspondingly modest: to have the case as pleaded —
    including causation as pleaded — heard and determined on the evidence that bears upon it, not on a
    restatement that reduces it to a single shift pairing.
9.  The onus intensifies, rather than diminishes, the necessity of production. On a de novo appeal the
    Appellant bears the onus of establishing each element of s 32(1) and of excluding s 32(5)(a). The
    reasonableness of the management action over the pleaded course — and the degree, duration and density
    of the conduct said to have contributed to the injury — are accordingly matters the Appellant must prove,
    going both to whether the employment significantly contributed to the injury and to whether the action
    was reasonable and reasonably taken. The contemporaneous records of that conduct exist, if at all, in the
    non-party’s systems. A party required to prove the character of conduct cannot reasonably be left without
    the records of it, held solely by the author of that conduct; production allows the matters in issue to be
    determined on what the systems recorded rather than on contested recollection — a course that serves the
    parties and the Commission equally, whichever way the records fall. The burden objections have a force
    the Appellant accepts in part: some date ranges in the Notice were broad. Where that is so, a proportionate
    answer may lie in narrowed production on conditions rather than refusal — and the Appellant has done
    the narrowing himself. Schedule A confines every contested Item by custodian, system and date before
    the Commission is asked to rule.
E. Expense, Inconvenience and the Delivery of Health Care
10. Each rule 64E(4)(a) objection states that compliance would detract from MSH’s core function of
    providing health care; no order sought requires the Commission to weigh disclosure against patient care.
    The Schedule A terms confine every electronic search to identified corporate systems — a single
    Exchange mailbox custodian set, directory sign-in records, one access-control system — held by role-
    based custodians within defined windows, and performed by corporate and information services rather
    than clinical staff. That such searches are neither prohibitively expensive nor operationally disruptive is

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5.1_FINAL_CLEAN.pdf :: page 3
     demonstrated, not merely asserted, by the Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026, addressed at Section
     G. Rule 64I entitles MSH to its reasonable expenses of production.
11. Nor is the subject matter of the Notice opposed to the value MSH invokes — it is, in significant part, the
     same value. The Appellant shares that concern; the operational complaints the subject of Items 3(a) and
     3(b) were themselves directed to the safe operation of that function. The pleaded role is the coordination
     of Logan Hospital’s life-safety emergency codes — Code Blue and MET calls — through the
     Switchboard, and the fatigue governance of that function during the pleaded period is within the matter in
     issue, not adjacent to it. Patient safety is therefore not a consideration weighing against production; it is
     among the matters the records evidence.
F. The Items Pressed
12. Items 1 and 2 (order (b)). MSH states the SPOK records were not retained following a system upgrade,
     but identifies “a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls” available for 17–18 March 2024. That spreadsheet
     does not appear among the enclosures. No ground of objection is raised against it; order (b) seeks its
     production.
13. Items 3(a) and 3(b). The ground is expense (rule 64E(4)(a)). The response states that all employee
     complaints concerning Switchboard operational errors are made directly to the Line Manager and
     managed by email or verbally. That account itself supplies the cure: a single-custodian, keyword-limited
     search of the Line Manager’s mailbox over twelve weeks (Schedule A items 1 and 2) — in place of the
     seven-month, multi-account search the objection describes. The burden of a search so confined is modest,
     and rule 64I meets its cost.
14. Item 8. The grounds are expense and particularity. The particularity point is accepted and cured:
     Schedule A item 3 identifies the system (Windows Active Directory / Microsoft Entra ID sign-in audit
     records) and a single named account, over a defined window spanning the operational complaints the
     subject of Items 3(a) and 3(b) and the lead-up to the pleaded onset. Sign-in audit records are extracted by
     date-range query, not by review of content, so the window does not alter the character of the task. As to
     expense, the passage in the response appears to have been carried across from the email-search objections
     — it describes reviewing “individual staff member email accounts”, which Item 8 does not seek. A
     directory sign-in export for one account is a standard administrative query against existing audit records.
15. Item 9. The grounds are relevance, particularity and effect on a person (rule 64E(4)(b), (c), (f)). The
     response clarifies that the Switchboard has no dedicated swipe access but is collocated within an access-
     controlled office area; the Appellant accepts that clarification and re-specifies the Item accordingly
     (Schedule A item 4). As to relevance, the records serve four connected purposes: the Form 24 admissions
     place the seven-hour break between the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024 at the centre of the s
     32(5)(a) inquiry, and whether that action was taken in a reasonable way turns in part on what supervision
     was present when it occurred; and the Line Manager’s pattern of attendance across the period of the
     operational complaints, through to the pleaded onset, bears on the support available to the Switchboard
     while those complaints were being received — itself a component of the manner inquiry. Thirdly, the
     Amended Form 9A pleads as a material fact that the Line Manager “maintained an erratic physical
     presence” during the pleaded period (Part B, Stressor 1(a)); a record of attendance is the direct
     documentary answer to that pleaded fact. Fourthly, the window spans a further contested fact: the
     response admits the payroll instruction of 3 May 2024 and the submission of the AVAC on 28 May 2024
     (Form 24, ¶¶40–41) while denying any want of diligence in the twenty-five days between them (¶¶47–
     49); the Line Manager’s attendance across that period is direct evidence on that contest. A record of
     workplace attendance, in the form sought here, is not intrinsically private in the way medical, financial or
     family information would be; the “effect on a person” the response anticipates is the ordinary effect of
     relevant evidence, which rule 64E(4)(f) does not exist to prevent. Documents produced may in any event
     be used only for the purposes of this proceeding, and for Items 8 and 9 the Appellant proposes the
     concrete regime in the accompanying draft order: production to the Registry marked confidential,
     inspection confined to the parties for the purposes of this proceeding, and non-responsive personal
     information redacted — a regime that materially reduces any legitimate concern. The relevance objection
     was, moreover, advanced expressly subject to MSH’s stated limitation in assessing relevance without the
     pleadings; Annexure B removes that limitation.
16. Item 10. The ground is expense. The Item is narrowed to the Line Manager and the Director as
     custodians, keyword-limited in the Notice’s own terms, over two months (Schedule A item 5). The
     ground is answered in the same way as for Items 3(a) and 3(b).
17. Item 19. The grounds are expense and effect (rule 64E(4)(a), (f)). MSH proposed the cure in its own
     response: narrowing to 17–18 March 2024, limited to emails received from Together Queensland by the
     Line Manager, the Director, or members of the Logan Hospital Human Resources team who remain
     employed by MSH. The Appellant adopts that proposal without amendment (Schedule A item 6). The
     draft order makes the Item 19 order subject to notice to Together Queensland, with liberty to apply.
18. Item 20. The response states that responsive documents do not exist because reference PID 24-ESU-1130
     commenced in November 2024, outside the 13–31 May 2024 window. That is accepted so far as it goes:
     the reference number post-dates the events. The disclosures themselves are pleaded, and both their

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5.1_FINAL_CLEAN.pdf :: page 4
    character as a Public Interest Disclosure and the immediate response to them are admitted (Form 24,
    ¶¶20–21). The Item is re-specified by subject matter rather than reference number (Schedule A item 7):
    records of operational or human-resources action during 13–31 May 2024 responsive to the disclosures
    the Appellant made in that period. Properly understood, the Item always sought that subject matter: the
    contemporaneous operational and human-resources response within MSH, during 13–31 May 2024, to
    the disclosures the Appellant made in that period. The reference number — which, on MSH’s own
    answer, was assigned only in November 2024 — was descriptive, not definitional; an item is not sensibly
    confined to a reference that did not exist during the period the item addresses. That such records exist is
    established by the Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026, addressed in Section G below. Annexure C
    accordingly demonstrates that the non-existence answer was mistaken, incomplete, or based on an unduly
    narrow construction of the Item as originally framed; Because MSH answered the Item rather than
    objecting to it under rule 64E(4), the primary relief sought is verification: the affidavit in the
    accompanying draft order is to state, should non-possession be maintained, the precise basis on which it
    is maintained having regard to the correspondence at Annexure C. Should the Commission be satisfied
    that the Item, properly understood, sought the re-specified subject matter at Schedule A item 7, the
    Appellant respectfully invites an order for production on those terms under the further-orders limb (order
    (g)); the documents the Annexure evidences are, on their face, already assembled.
G. The Respondent’s Disclosure of 11 June 2026
19. On 11 June 2026 the Respondent disclosed to the Appellant documents which, on its own description,
    were “received through Notice of Non-Party Disclosure request and conferencing”. That disclosure bears
    directly on the objections now before the Commission, and the Appellant relies on it as part of the
    material on this application (Annexure C). First, it establishes that records sought by the Notice exist.
    Among the documents disclosed is internal MSH correspondence of 15 and 16 May 2024 routing the
    Appellant’s disclosures within Logan Hospital Human Resources and to the Director, recording that the
    Ethical Standards Unit’s assessment was on foot. That is operational and human-resources action taken
    during the 13–31 May 2024 window, by the custodians identified in Schedule A item 7 — precisely the
    subject matter of Item 20, to which MSH answered that documents do not exist. The correspondence
    originates from MSH human-resources officers within Logan Hospital; it is accordingly within MSH’s
    own systems, or accessible to it through Queensland Health records infrastructure. The answer is difficult
    to reconcile with the document and requires explanation, whether by production or affidavit verification.
20. Second, it establishes that production is neither prohibitively expensive nor operationally
    disruptive. The documents disclosed are of the same character as a number of the email-based and
    administrative Items to which MSH objects on the ground of expense — internal email correspondence
    held by identified custodians, and complete records of administrative processes — assembled and
    produced through ordinary means; and rule 64I in any event provides for MSH’s reasonable expenses of
    compliance to be met. Where the same documents, held by the same custodians, have already been
    gathered and provided in this proceeding, an objection that gathering them is unduly burdensome is
    difficult to sustain; and rule 64B(2) is not engaged, there being no other reasonably simple and
    inexpensive way for the Appellant to prove matters that sit only with the non-party. Third, it confirms
    the breadth of the matter in issue. The disclosed material concerns mid-May 2024 — two months
    before onset, and outside the “consecutive shifts of 17 to 18 March 2024” to which MSH would confine
    relevance. That the Respondent itself treats it as disclosable is inconsistent with the confined reading on
    which the objections depend.
H. Verification of the Non-Existence Answers
21. For Items 1–2 (non-retention), 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20, MSH answers that documents do not exist or are
    not in its possession or control. The Appellant does not suggest those answers are other than honestly
    made. They are, however, presently statements in correspondence — unsworn, and in several instances
    statements on which the conduct of the appeal will rest. Rule 64G(2) empowers the Commission to make
    any order it considers appropriate; an order that the answers be verified by affidavit, identifying the
    systems searched, the searches undertaken and the basis for each statement, is a conventional and
    proportionate way of giving them a form on which the parties and the Commission can act.
22. Verification has particular utility for the fatigue-management Items. The response states, for Items 4 and
    7, that Fatigue Risk Management System training applies only to health practitioners and clinical
    assistants, so that no such requirement applied to Switchboard staff; and, for Item 5, that fatigue risk
    management assessment was implemented at the Switchboard after 30 June 2024. Each statement may be
    accurate. Read together, they tend to indicate that no fatigue-management requirement applied to
    Switchboard staff before 30 June 2024 — a period that includes the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March
    2024 and the pleaded onset of the injury. The records the Items seek go to the manner in which the
    rostering decisions were taken — whether any fatigue-management requirement governed the function
    within which those decisions were made — and not merely to whether fatigue caused the injury; the latter
    is a medical question, but the former is a question about the manner of the management action, squarely
    within s 32(5)(a). The verifying affidavit should therefore identify the governance registers, policy
    repositories and training records searched in connection with Items 4, 5 and 7, the result of those searches,

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5.1_FINAL_CLEAN.pdf :: page 5
      and whether those searches identified any fatigue risk management training requirement, fatigue risk
      management assessment process, or other fatigue-management requirement applying to Logan Hospital
      Switchboard staff before 30 June 2024. For Item 14, the verifying affidavit should state the date on which
      a Queensland Health device was issued to the Line Manager and confirm whether any responsive
      communications exist on MSH systems. The affidavit should also identify the process references to
      which the Item 16 enclosures correspond: the Notice cited references 15397775 and 15605601, and the
      Item 11 report for 1 February to 31 May 2024 lists neither. The references cited in the Notice were drawn
      from records provided to the Appellant; the discrepancy lies within MSH’s own production, and the
      affidavit is the means of resolving it.
I. Items Not Pressed; the Pleadings Point
23. The Appellant does not press the balance of Item 12 or Item 17. The privacy considerations MSH raises
      — sensitive health information of other staff, and re-identification risk within a small team — are
      genuine; the audit trail and variance records already produced serve the comparator purpose. Nor does the
      Appellant press production under Item 18: MSH objects on the footing that the destruction of the record
      “appears to have already been conceded” on the pleadings, and the Appellant is content to proceed on that
      concession, confirmed in the affidavit referred to in order (c).
24. The response renews the observation that MSH has not received the Appellant’s Amended Form 9A, and
      submits its capacity to assess relevance was limited. Rule 64C(1) requires the notice to state the matter in
      issue, and this Notice does so; the objections MSH has in fact articulated, ground by ground, demonstrate
      that it conveyed what the rule requires. In any event the point is spent: the Appellant provides at
      Annexure B a Relevance Map setting out, for each contested Item, the pleaded matter and the Form 24
      admission to which it answers, and will provide a sealed copy of the Amended Form 9A on request or as
      the Commission directs. No contested Item falls to be decided on an asserted inability to assess relevance.
J. Disposition, Material and Service
25. The orders sought confine production to documents a non-party can extract through standard
      administrative processes, within defined date windows, with reasonable expenses met under rule 64I, and
      with the privacy objections accommodated by the withdrawal of the Items that engaged them. The
      application is brought to narrow the field, not to enlarge it: the greater part of the Notice is resolved by
      MSH’s compliance, by its answers, and by the Appellant’s withdrawals, and what remains is confined by
      Schedule A to a materially narrower set of documents than the Notice as originally served sought. The
      Appellant relies upon the Notice, the direction of 22 May 2026, MSH’s correspondence of 5 June 2026
      (with enclosures) and the Respondent’s Statement of Facts and Contentions (Form 9C), each already
      before the Commission, together with the Relevance Map at Annexure B and the extract of the
      Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026 at Annexure C. This application is to be served on the
      Respondent and on MSH (attention: Principal Lawyer, Metro South Legal Services), and the Appellant
      will give notice of order (a), so far as it concerns Item 19, to Together Queensland. A draft of the orders
      sought — including the Items 8–9 confidentiality regime, the Together Queensland notice mechanism,
      and liberty to apply as to mechanics — accompanies this application. The Appellant is content for the
      application to be determined on the papers, and seeks orders in the terms of the draft.

                   FORM 4 — APPLICATION IN EXISTING PROCEEDINGS
                           Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011 — rule 4(2)
                      QUEENSLAND INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION
                        Workers’ Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003 (Qld)
                                      Matter No: WC/2024/227
  CORY LEA SHEPHERD (Appellant / Applicant) and WORKERS’ COMPENSATION REGULATOR
                                               (Respondent)
   Non-party to whom this application relates: METRO SOUTH HOSPITAL AND HEALTH SERVICE
APPLICATION FOR A DECISION ABOUT OBJECTION — RULE 64G(1) — AND INTEGRATED
                         OUTLINE OF SUBMISSIONS
A. Application and Orders Sought
1.   By correspondence dated 5 June 2026, signed by its Chief Executive and provided in accordance with the
     direction issued from the Chambers of Commissioner Dwyer on 22 May 2026, Metro South Hospital and
     Health Service (“MSH”) responded to the Appellant’s Form 29 Notice of Non-Party Disclosure sealed 22
     April 2026 (“the Notice”). The response complies with six Items; states that documents responsive to
     seven further Items do not exist or are not in MSH’s possession; and objects under rule 64E(4) of the
     Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011 (“the Rules”) to the remainder. This application accepts the
     greater part of that response. It asks the Commission to decide only the objections that remain — on terms
     the Appellant has himself narrowed, in one instance to the very scope MSH proposed — and to require
     verification of one answer that a document already before the Commission contradicts.
2.   TAKE NOTICE that the Appellant applies under rule 64G(1) for the following orders:
     (a) the objections to Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10 and 19 of the Notice are overruled, and MSH is to
            produce the documents described in Schedule A (items 1 to 6) within fourteen (14) days of the
            order;
     (b) MSH is to produce within fourteen (14) days the spreadsheet of recorded MET calls for the period
            17–18 March 2024 identified in its response to Items 1 and 2, against which no ground of objection
            is raised;
     (c) pursuant to rule 64G(2), MSH is to verify by affidavit of an officer with direct knowledge of the
            searches undertaken, within fourteen (14) days, its statements that documents responsive to Items
            1–2 (non-retention following the SPOK upgrade), 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20 do not exist or are not in
            its possession or control, identifying in each case the systems searched, the searches undertaken,
            and the basis for the statement, and, as to Item 14, the date on which a Queensland Health mobile
            device was issued to the Line Manager, and otherwise in the terms of order 6 of the accompanying
            draft order (including the governance-search particulars for Items 4, 5 and 7, the basis for any
            maintained non-possession as to Item 20 having regard to Annexure C, and the process references
            for the Item 16 enclosures);
     (d) as to Item 18, noting MSH’s statement that the destruction of the record is conceded on the
            pleadings, production is not pressed upon MSH confirming that statement in the affidavit referred
            to in order (c);
     (e) Items 12 (balance) and 17 of the Notice are not pressed, in light of the privacy considerations MSH
            has raised;
     (f)    each party bear its own costs of the application, in accordance with rule 64G(3); and
     (g) such further or other orders as the Commission considers appropriate.
B. Jurisdiction and Timeliness
3.   The Notice was sealed by the Industrial Registry on 22 April 2026 and served on MSH by email at 5:08
     PM that day. By direction issued from Chambers on 22 May 2026 — in effect, leave under rule 64E(1) for
     objection at a later time — MSH was directed to provide any objections by 4:00 PM on 5 June 2026.
     MSH’s objection was served by email at 3:02 PM on 5 June 2026. Rule 64G(1) permits this application
     within seven days after service of the objection; it is made within that period. Rule 64F stays the Notice as
     to the documents objected to; this application brings the stayed Items before the Commission for
     decision.
C. The Character of MSH’s Response
4.   The response falls into three categories. First, compliance: MSH has produced documents responsive to
     Items 6, 11, 12 (in part), 13, 15 and 16. That compliance is acknowledged; the enclosed records materially
     advance the appeal. Secondly, answers: for Items 1–2, 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20, MSH states that
     responsive documents do not exist or are not in its possession or control. Those are answers to the Notice
     rather than objections under rule 64E(4); they are addressed in Sections G and H. Thirdly, objections:
     for Items 3(a), 3(b), 8, 9, 10, 12 (balance), 17, 18 and 19, MSH objects on grounds of expense and
     inconvenience (rule 64E(4)(a)), relevance (4(b)), particularity (4(c)), privacy (4(e)) and effect on a

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5_FINAL_original.pdf :: page 2
    person (4(f)). Of these nine, the Appellant presses six, each on narrowed terms, and does not press three.
    None of the objections is put on the basis that the documents do not exist.
D. The Role of the Non-Party and the Matter in Issue
5.  Subdivision 7A allocates functions. The party issuing a notice must state in it the matter in issue (rule
    64C(1)). The non-party’s part is to produce (rule 64D) or to object on the grounds rule 64E(4) provides.
    Where an objection is contested, the decision belongs to the Commission (rule 64G). Nothing in the
    subdivision asks the non-party to settle the scope of the appeal, or to measure relevance against its own
    restatement of the issues. That involves no criticism of MSH, whose reading is naturally operational; but
    it frames what the Commission is asked to decide.
6.  The standard the Rules apply is direct relevance: a notice may require production of documents directly
    relevant to a matter in issue in the proceeding. In practical terms, a document answers that standard where
    it is capable of tending to prove or disprove an allegation in issue, having regard to the matters pleaded
    and the issues those matters raise. Annexure B identifies, for each contested Item, the allegation the
    records tend to prove or disprove. Several objections instead test the Items against admissibility, or
    against the non-party’s view of what the evidence will show — neither is the question at the disclosure
    stage.
7.  Several of the objections proceed from such a restatement. The response treats the matter in issue, “as
    pleaded in the Notice”, as confined to the “consecutive shifts of 17 to 18 March 2024”, and tests each date
    range against that confined reading. The Notice states the matter in issue in materially wider terms: a
    psychiatric injury with onset in June 2024, sustained in the course of employment at the Logan Hospital
    Switchboard, in a de novo appeal in which the Appellant bears the onus of establishing the injury —
    including that the employment was a significant contributing factor to it, and that it did not arise out of
    reasonable management action taken in a reasonable way within s 32(5)(a) of the Workers’
    Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003. The consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024 are the
    keystone stressor; they are not the perimeter of the inquiry. The pleadings themselves sharpen the point:
    the Regulator’s own Independent Review Office has found that the 7-hour rest break constituted
    unreasonable management action (Form 24, ¶37). A restatement that confines disclosure to 17–18 March
    2024 confines it to the one event already the subject of that finding. On the pleadings and admitted facts
    presently before the Commission, the inquiry under s 32(5)(a) is broader than that single shift pairing —
    it extends to the course of conduct pleaded from June 2023 to June 2024 — and the records sought bear
    directly on that broader inquiry.
8.  There is a further reason the restatement does not govern relevance. To confine disclosure to the events a
    non-party considers caused the injury is to treat the non-party’s opinion of causation as settled. The cause
    of a psychiatric injury is not a matter on which MSH — or any party — holds privileged insight; it is the
    question the appeal exists to decide. The degree, duration and density of the pleaded stressors are
    themselves facts in issue under s 32(5)(a): the reasonableness of management action, and the manner of
    its taking, fall to be weighed against the conduct’s extent, not a single instance of it. The Notice seeks
    records of fact; the objections that resist it proceed on assumptions about what those records are likely to
    show or not show. The Appellant’s entitlement is correspondingly modest: to have the case as pleaded —
    including causation as pleaded — heard and determined on the evidence that bears upon it, not on a
    restatement that reduces it to a single shift pairing.
9.  The onus intensifies, rather than diminishes, the necessity of production. On a de novo appeal the
    Appellant bears the onus of establishing each element of s 32(1) and of excluding s 32(5)(a). The
    reasonableness of the management action over the pleaded course — and the degree, duration and density
    of the conduct said to have contributed to the injury — are accordingly matters the Appellant must prove,
    going both to whether the employment significantly contributed to the injury and to whether the action
    was reasonable and reasonably taken. The contemporaneous records of that conduct exist, if at all, in the
    non-party’s systems. A party required to prove the character of conduct cannot reasonably be left without
    the records of it, held solely by the author of that conduct; production allows the matters in issue to be
    determined on what the systems recorded rather than on contested recollection — a course that serves the
    parties and the Commission equally, whichever way the records fall. The burden objections have a force
    the Appellant accepts in part: some date ranges in the Notice were broad. Where that is so, a proportionate
    answer may lie in narrowed production on conditions rather than refusal — and the Appellant has done
    the narrowing himself. Schedule A confines every contested Item by custodian, system and date before
    the Commission is asked to rule.
E. Expense, Inconvenience and the Delivery of Health Care
10. Each rule 64E(4)(a) objection states that compliance would detract from MSH’s core function of
    providing health care; no order sought requires the Commission to weigh disclosure against patient care.
    The Schedule A terms confine every electronic search to identified corporate systems — a single
    Exchange mailbox custodian set, directory sign-in records, one access-control system — held by role-
    based custodians within defined windows, and performed by corporate and information services rather
    than clinical staff. That such searches are neither prohibitively expensive nor operationally disruptive is

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5_FINAL_original.pdf :: page 3
     demonstrated, not merely asserted, by the Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026, addressed at Section
     G. Rule 64I entitles MSH to its reasonable expenses of production.
11. Nor is the subject matter of the Notice opposed to the value MSH invokes — it is, in significant part, the
     same value. The Appellant shares that concern; the operational complaints the subject of Items 3(a) and
     3(b) were themselves directed to the safe operation of that function. The pleaded role is the coordination
     of Logan Hospital’s life-safety emergency codes — Code Blue and MET calls — through the
     Switchboard, and the fatigue governance of that function during the pleaded period is within the matter in
     issue, not adjacent to it. Patient safety is therefore not a consideration weighing against production; it is
     among the matters the records evidence.
F. The Items Pressed
12. Items 1 and 2 (order (b)). MSH states the SPOK records were not retained following a system upgrade,
     but identifies “a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls” available for 17–18 March 2024. That spreadsheet
     does not appear among the enclosures. No ground of objection is raised against it; order (b) seeks its
     production.
13. Items 3(a) and 3(b). The ground is expense (rule 64E(4)(a)). The response states that all employee
     complaints concerning Switchboard operational errors are made directly to the Line Manager and
     managed by email or verbally. That account itself supplies the cure: a single-custodian, keyword-limited
     search of the Line Manager’s mailbox over twelve weeks (Schedule A items 1 and 2) — in place of the
     seven-month, multi-account search the objection describes. The burden of a search so confined is modest,
     and rule 64I meets its cost.
14. Item 8. The grounds are expense and particularity. The particularity point is accepted and cured:
     Schedule A item 3 identifies the system (Windows Active Directory / Microsoft Entra ID sign-in audit
     records) and a single named account, over a defined window spanning the operational complaints the
     subject of Items 3(a) and 3(b) and the lead-up to the pleaded onset. Sign-in audit records are extracted by
     date-range query, not by review of content, so the window does not alter the character of the task. As to
     expense, the passage in the response appears to have been carried across from the email-search objections
     — it describes reviewing “individual staff member email accounts”, which Item 8 does not seek. A
     directory sign-in export for one account is a standard administrative query against existing audit records.
15. Item 9. The grounds are relevance, particularity and effect on a person (rule 64E(4)(b), (c), (f)). The
     response clarifies that the Switchboard has no dedicated swipe access but is collocated within an access-
     controlled office area; the Appellant accepts that clarification and re-specifies the Item accordingly
     (Schedule A item 4). As to relevance, the records serve four connected purposes: the Form 24 admissions
     place the seven-hour break between the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March 2024 at the centre of the s
     32(5)(a) inquiry, and whether that action was taken in a reasonable way turns in part on what supervision
     was present when it occurred; and the Line Manager’s pattern of attendance across the period of the
     operational complaints, through to the pleaded onset, bears on the support available to the Switchboard
     while those complaints were being received — itself a component of the manner inquiry. Thirdly, the
     Amended Form 9A pleads as a material fact that the Line Manager “maintained an erratic physical
     presence” during the pleaded period (Part B, Stressor 1(a)); a record of attendance is the direct
     documentary answer to that pleaded fact. Fourthly, the window spans a further contested fact: the
     response admits the payroll instruction of 3 May 2024 and the submission of the AVAC on 28 May 2024
     (Form 24, ¶¶40–41) while denying any want of diligence in the twenty-five days between them (¶¶47–
     49); the Line Manager’s attendance across that period is direct evidence on that contest. A record of
     workplace attendance, in the form sought here, is not intrinsically private in the way medical, financial or
     family information would be; the “effect on a person” the response anticipates is the ordinary effect of
     relevant evidence, which rule 64E(4)(f) does not exist to prevent. Documents produced may in any event
     be used only for the purposes of this proceeding, and for Items 8 and 9 the Appellant proposes the
     concrete regime in the accompanying draft order: production to the Registry marked confidential,
     inspection confined to the parties for the purposes of this proceeding, and non-responsive personal
     information redacted — a regime that materially reduces any legitimate concern. The relevance objection
     was, moreover, advanced expressly subject to MSH’s stated limitation in assessing relevance without the
     pleadings; Annexure B removes that limitation.
16. Item 10. The ground is expense. The Item is narrowed to the Line Manager and the Director as
     custodians, keyword-limited in the Notice’s own terms, over two months (Schedule A item 5). The
     ground is answered in the same way as for Items 3(a) and 3(b).
17. Item 19. The grounds are expense and effect (rule 64E(4)(a), (f)). MSH proposed the cure in its own
     response: narrowing to 17–18 March 2024, limited to emails received from Together Queensland by the
     Line Manager, the Director, or members of the Logan Hospital Human Resources team who remain
     employed by MSH. The Appellant adopts that proposal without amendment (Schedule A item 6). The
     draft order makes the Item 19 order subject to notice to Together Queensland, with liberty to apply.
18. Item 20. The response states that responsive documents do not exist because reference PID 24-ESU-1130
     commenced in November 2024, outside the 13–31 May 2024 window. That is accepted so far as it goes:
     the reference number post-dates the events. The disclosures themselves are pleaded, and both their

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5_FINAL_original.pdf :: page 4
    character as a Public Interest Disclosure and the immediate response to them are admitted (Form 24,
    ¶¶20–21). The Item is re-specified by subject matter rather than reference number (Schedule A item 7):
    records of operational or human-resources action during 13–31 May 2024 responsive to the disclosures
    the Appellant made in that period. Properly understood, the Item always sought that subject matter: the
    contemporaneous operational and human-resources response within MSH, during 13–31 May 2024, to
    the disclosures the Appellant made in that period. The reference number — which, on MSH’s own
    answer, was assigned only in November 2024 — was descriptive, not definitional; an item is not sensibly
    confined to a reference that did not exist during the period the item addresses. That such records exist is
    established by the Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026, addressed in Section G below. Annexure C
    accordingly demonstrates that the non-existence answer was mistaken, incomplete, or based on an unduly
    narrow construction of the Item as originally framed; Because MSH answered the Item rather than
    objecting to it under rule 64E(4), the primary relief sought is verification: the affidavit in the
    accompanying draft order is to state, should non-possession be maintained, the precise basis on which it
    is maintained having regard to the correspondence at Annexure C. Should the Commission be satisfied
    that the Item, properly understood, sought the re-specified subject matter at Schedule A item 7, the
    Appellant respectfully invites an order for production on those terms under the further-orders limb (order
    (g)); the documents the Annexure evidences are, on their face, already assembled.
G. The Respondent’s Disclosure of 11 June 2026
19. On 11 June 2026 the Respondent disclosed to the Appellant documents which, on its own description,
    were “received through Notice of Non-Party Disclosure request and conferencing”. That disclosure bears
    directly on the objections now before the Commission, and the Appellant relies on it as part of the
    material on this application (Annexure C). First, it establishes that records sought by the Notice exist.
    Among the documents disclosed is internal MSH correspondence of 15 and 16 May 2024 routing the
    Appellant’s disclosures within Logan Hospital Human Resources and to the Director, recording that the
    Ethical Standards Unit’s assessment was on foot. That is operational and human-resources action taken
    during the 13–31 May 2024 window, by the custodians identified in Schedule A item 7 — precisely the
    subject matter of Item 20, to which MSH answered that documents do not exist. The correspondence
    originates from MSH human-resources officers within Logan Hospital; it is accordingly within MSH’s
    own systems, or accessible to it through Queensland Health records infrastructure. The answer is difficult
    to reconcile with the document and requires explanation, whether by production or affidavit verification.
20. Second, it establishes that production is neither prohibitively expensive nor operationally
    disruptive. The documents disclosed are of the same character as a number of the email-based and
    administrative Items to which MSH objects on the ground of expense — internal email correspondence
    held by identified custodians, and complete records of administrative processes — assembled and
    produced through ordinary means; and rule 64I in any event provides for MSH’s reasonable expenses of
    compliance to be met. Where the same documents, held by the same custodians, have already been
    gathered and provided in this proceeding, an objection that gathering them is unduly burdensome is
    difficult to sustain; and rule 64B(2) is not engaged, there being no other reasonably simple and
    inexpensive way for the Appellant to prove matters that sit only with the non-party. Third, it confirms
    the breadth of the matter in issue. The disclosed material concerns mid-May 2024 — two months
    before onset, and outside the “consecutive shifts of 17 to 18 March 2024” to which MSH would confine
    relevance. That the Respondent itself treats it as disclosable is inconsistent with the confined reading on
    which the objections depend.
H. Verification of the Non-Existence Answers
21. For Items 1–2 (non-retention), 3(c), 4, 5, 7, 14 and 20, MSH answers that documents do not exist or are
    not in its possession or control. The Appellant does not suggest those answers are other than honestly
    made. They are, however, presently statements in correspondence — unsworn, and in several instances
    statements on which the conduct of the appeal will rest. Rule 64G(2) empowers the Commission to make
    any order it considers appropriate; an order that the answers be verified by affidavit, identifying the
    systems searched, the searches undertaken and the basis for each statement, is a conventional and
    proportionate way of giving them a form on which the parties and the Commission can act.
22. Verification has particular utility for the fatigue-management Items. The response states, for Items 4 and
    7, that Fatigue Risk Management System training applies only to health practitioners and clinical
    assistants, so that no such requirement applied to Switchboard staff; and, for Item 5, that fatigue risk
    management assessment was implemented at the Switchboard after 30 June 2024. Each statement may be
    accurate. Read together, they tend to indicate that no fatigue-management requirement applied to
    Switchboard staff before 30 June 2024 — a period that includes the consecutive shifts of 17–18 March
    2024 and the pleaded onset of the injury. The records the Items seek go to the manner in which the
    rostering decisions were taken — whether any fatigue-management requirement governed the function
    within which those decisions were made — and not merely to whether fatigue caused the injury; the latter
    is a medical question, but the former is a question about the manner of the management action, squarely
    within s 32(5)(a). The verifying affidavit should therefore identify the governance registers, policy
    repositories and training records searched in connection with Items 4, 5 and 7, the result of those searches,

>>> drafts/WC2024227_Rule64G_FILING_v5_FINAL_original.pdf :: page 5
      and whether those searches identified any fatigue risk management training requirement, fatigue risk
      management assessment process, or other fatigue-management requirement applying to Logan Hospital
      Switchboard staff before 30 June 2024. For Item 14, the verifying affidavit should state the date on which
      a Queensland Health device was issued to the Line Manager and confirm whether any responsive
      communications exist on MSH systems. The affidavit should also identify the process references to
      which the Item 16 enclosures correspond: the Notice cited references 15397775 and 15605601, and the
      Item 11 report for 1 February to 31 May 2024 lists neither. The references cited in the Notice were drawn
      from records provided to the Appellant; the discrepancy lies within MSH’s own production, and the
      affidavit is the means of resolving it.
I. Items Not Pressed; the Pleadings Point
23. The Appellant does not press the balance of Item 12 or Item 17. The privacy considerations MSH raises
      — sensitive health information of other staff, and re-identification risk within a small team — are
      genuine; the audit trail and variance records already produced serve the comparator purpose. Nor does the
      Appellant press production under Item 18: MSH objects on the footing that the destruction of the record
      “appears to have already been conceded” on the pleadings, and the Appellant is content to proceed on that
      concession, confirmed in the affidavit referred to in order (c).
24. The response renews the observation that MSH has not received the Appellant’s Amended Form 9A, and
      submits its capacity to assess relevance was limited. Rule 64C(1) requires the notice to state the matter in
      issue, and this Notice does so; the objections MSH has in fact articulated, ground by ground, demonstrate
      that it conveyed what the rule requires. In any event the point is spent: the Appellant provides at
      Annexure B a Relevance Map setting out, for each contested Item, the pleaded matter and the Form 24
      admission to which it answers, and will provide a sealed copy of the Amended Form 9A on request or as
      the Commission directs. No contested Item falls to be decided on an asserted inability to assess relevance.
J. Disposition, Material and Service
25. The orders sought confine production to documents a non-party can extract through standard
      administrative processes, within defined date windows, with reasonable expenses met under rule 64I, and
      with the privacy objections accommodated by the withdrawal of the Items that engaged them. The
      application is brought to narrow the field, not to enlarge it: the greater part of the Notice is resolved by
      MSH’s compliance, by its answers, and by the Appellant’s withdrawals, and what remains is confined by
      Schedule A to a materially narrower set of documents than the Notice as originally served sought. The
      Appellant relies upon the Notice, the direction of 22 May 2026, MSH’s correspondence of 5 June 2026
      (with enclosures) and the Respondent’s Statement of Facts and Contentions (Form 9C), each already
      before the Commission, together with the Relevance Map at Annexure B and the extract of the
      Respondent’s disclosure of 11 June 2026 at Annexure C. This application is to be served on the
      Respondent and on MSH (attention: Principal Lawyer, Metro South Legal Services), and the Appellant
      will give notice of order (a), so far as it concerns Item 19, to Together Queensland. A draft of the orders
      sought — including the Items 8–9 confidentiality regime, the Together Queensland notice mechanism,
      and liberty to apply as to mechanics — accompanies this application. The Appellant is content for the
      application to be determined on the papers, and seeks orders in the terms of the draft.

                               Spacer, Table, TableStyle, KeepTogether)

OUT = "/home/user/Personalproject/wc2024227/drafts/out/LIST_OF_DOCUMENTS_WC2024227.pdf"

bodyb = ParagraphStyle("bodyb", fontName=BOLD, fontSize=7.4, leading=9.4)
head  = ParagraphStyle("head",  fontName=BOLD, fontSize=7.4, leading=9.4,

class Numbered(pdfcanvas.Canvas):
    def __init__(self, *a, **k):
        super().__init__(*a, **k); self._pages = []

    def showPage(self):
        self._pages.append(dict(self.__dict__)); self._startPage()

    def save(self):
        n = len(self._pages)
        for st in self._pages:
            self.__dict__.update(st); self._foot(n); super().showPage()
        super().save()

    def _foot(self, n):
        self.setFont(FONT, 6.8)
        self.setFillColor(colors.HexColor("#555555"))
        self.drawString(14 * mm, 9 * mm,
                        "C Shepherd · WC/2024/227 · Appellant's List of Documents "
                        "· 5 August 2026")
        self.drawRightString(PW - 14 * mm, 9 * mm,
                             "Page %d of %d" % (self._pageNumber, n))
        self.setStrokeColor(colors.HexColor("#bbbbbb")); self.setLineWidth(0.4)
        self.line(14 * mm, 12 * mm, PW - 14 * mm, 12 * mm)


def P(t, s=body):
    return Paragraph(t, s)


COLS = [12 * mm, 22 * mm, 104 * mm, 40 * mm, 34 * mm, 14 * mm, 34 * mm]
HEADERS = ["Item", "Date", "Description", "Author / From", "Recipient / To",
           "Pages", "Status"]

TSTYLE = TableStyle([
    ("BACKGROUND", (0, 0), (-1, 0), colors.HexColor("#2f3b52")),
    ("VALIGN",     (0, 0), (-1, -1), "TOP"),
    ("GRID",       (0, 0), (-1, -1), 0.35, colors.HexColor("#9aa3b0")),
    ("LEFTPADDING",(0, 0), (-1, -1), 3),
    ("RIGHTPADDING",(0, 0), (-1, -1), 3),
    ("TOPPADDING", (0, 0), (-1, -1), 2.5),
    ("BOTTOMPADDING",(0, 0), (-1, -1), 2.5),
    ("ROWBACKGROUNDS", (0, 1), (-1, -1),
     [colors.white, colors.HexColor("#f2f4f7")]),
])


def table(rows):
    data = [[P(h, head) for h in HEADERS]]
    for r in rows:
        data.append([P(str(c)) for c in r])
    t = Table(data, colWidths=COLS, repeatRows=1)
    t.setStyle(TSTYLE)
    return t

def build():
    doc = BaseDocTemplate(TMP, pagesize=landscape(A4),
                          leftMargin=14 * mm, rightMargin=14 * mm,
                          topMargin=13 * mm, bottomMargin=16 * mm,
                          title="Appellant's List of Documents — WC/2024/227",
                          author="Cory L Shepherd", subject="", creator="", producer="")
    frame = Frame(doc.leftMargin, doc.bottomMargin, doc.width, doc.height, id="f")
    doc.addPageTemplates([PageTemplate(id="p", frames=[frame])])

    s = []
    s.append(P("QUEENSLAND INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION", meta))
    s.append(P("Matter No. WC/2024/227 · <i>Workers' Compensation and Rehabilitation "
               "Act 2003</i> (Qld)", meta))
    s.append(Spacer(1, 3))
    s.append(P("BETWEEN: CORY LEA SHEPHERD (Appellant) &nbsp;&nbsp;AND: "
               "WORKERS' COMPENSATION REGULATOR (Respondent)", meta))
    s.append(Spacer(1, 7))
    s.append(P("APPELLANT'S LIST OF DOCUMENTS", h1))
    s.append(P("Served on the Respondent · 5 August 2026", meta))
    s.append(Spacer(1, 5))
    s.append(P("This list is given in discharge of the Appellant's disclosure obligation in "
               "this proceeding. It lists documents in the Appellant's possession or under "
               "his control that are directly relevant to a matter in issue. Disclosure is "
               "continuing: this list will be supplemented as further documents come into "
               "the Appellant's possession, including the medical reports referred to at "
               "Part 5.", note))
    s.append(Spacer(1, 4))

    s.append(P("PART 1 — DOCUMENTS IN THE APPELLANT'S POSSESSION, PRODUCED WITH THIS LIST", h2))
    s.append(table(PART1))

    s.append(P("PART 2 — DOCUMENTS ALREADY BEFORE THE COMMISSION OR PREVIOUSLY EXCHANGED", h2))
    s.append(table(PART2))

    s.append(P("PART 3 — DOCUMENTS FOR WHICH PRIVILEGE OR STATUTORY PROTECTION IS CLAIMED", h2))
    s.append(table(PART3))

    s.append(P("PART 4 — DOCUMENTS ONCE IN, OR NEVER IN, THE APPELLANT'S POSSESSION", h2))
    s.append(table(PART4))

    s.append(P("PART 5 — DOCUMENTS NOT YET IN EXISTENCE", h2))
    s.append(P("The Appellant will disclose, upon receipt, the report of his treating "
               "psychiatrist addressing diagnosis, causation and chronology, and any further "
               "medical certificate or capacity advice issued after the date of this list.",
               body))

    s.append(Spacer(1, 8))
    s.append(P("Cory Lea Shepherd, Appellant (Self-Represented)", bodyb))
    s.append(P("15 Edmond Street, Coomera QLD 4209 · 0417 400 227 · "
               "coryshepherd1@hotmail.com", body))
    doc.build(s, canvasmaker=Numbered)

    with pikepdf.open(TMP, allow_overwriting_input=True) as pdf:
        for k in list(pdf.docinfo.keys()):
            del pdf.docinfo[k]
        pdf.docinfo["/Author"] = "Cory L Shepherd"
        pdf.docinfo["/Title"] = "Appellant's List of Documents — WC/2024/227"
        if pdf.Root.get("/Metadata") is not None:
            del pdf.Root["/Metadata"]
        pdf.save(OUT, encryption=pikepdf.Encryption(
            owner="", user="", allow=pikepdf.Permissions(
                modify_other=False, modify_annotation=False, modify_assembly=False,
                modify_form=False, extract=True, print_lowres=True, print_highres=True)))
    print("built:", OUT)


build()

class Numbered(pdfcanvas.Canvas):

    def save(self):

        super().save()
    def _f(self, n):

])

def tbl(rows, h=("Date / time", "Event", "Source · significance")):
    d = [[P(h[0], hd), P(h[1], hd), P(h[2], hd)]]
    for r in rows:
        d.append([P(r[0], bb), P(r[1]), P(r[2])])
