def build():
    doc = BaseDocTemplate(TMP, pagesize=landscape(A4), leftMargin=13*mm, rightMargin=13*mm,
                          topMargin=12*mm, bottomMargin=16*mm,
                          title="Master Log — WC/2024/227",
                          author="Cory L Shepherd", subject="", creator="", producer="")
    doc.addPageTemplates([PageTemplate(id="p", frames=[
        Frame(doc.leftMargin, doc.bottomMargin, doc.width, doc.height, id="f")])])
    s = []
    s.append(P("MASTER LOG — THE PID, THE ACTORS, THE FORM 29, THE 64G, "
               "THE LOCKOUT AND WHAT FOLLOWED", h1))
    s.append(P("WC/2024/227 · Shepherd v Workers' Compensation Regulator · "
               "compiled 5 August 2026", mt))
    s.append(Spacer(1, 3))
    s.append(P("⚠ INTERNAL WORKING DOCUMENT. NOT FOR SERVICE AND NOT FOR DISCLOSURE. "
               "Contains entries referable to a public interest disclosure (s 65 PID Act) and "
               "one restricted category. Nothing in this log is an allegation of coordination "
               "or improper purpose; entries are recorded in date order only.", warn))
    s.append(Spacer(1, 5))

    for title, rows in [
        ("PHASE 1 — THE STANDING CONDITION (2023)", PH1),
        ("PHASE 2 — THE PLEADED PERIOD (Feb–May 2024)", PH2),
        ("PHASE 3 — ⭐ THE PID AND THE SHARED HR MAILBOX (13–28 May 2024)", PH3),
        ("PHASE 4 — INJURY, TERMINATION, REVIEW, DETERMINATION (Jun–Dec 2024)", PH4),
        ("⭐⭐ THE DISMISSAL, THE LETTER AND THE DISAGREEMENT (Jun 2024 – 2025)", PH_DISMISSAL),
        ("PHASE 5 — REINSTATEMENT AND THE GRADUATED ARRANGEMENT (2025 – Jun 2026)", PH5),
        ("⭐⭐ THE MATERIAL SUPPLY CHAIN — MSH → THE REGULATOR (Jan 2024 – Jun 2026)", PH_SUPPLY),
        ("⭐ THE QIRC FILE — PLEADINGS, ADMISSIONS AND SUBMISSIONS", PH_QIRC),
        ("⭐⭐ FORM 24 LEDGER (18 Feb 2026) — WHAT IS ADMITTED", F24_ADMIT),
        ("⛔ FORM 24 LEDGER — WHAT IS DENIED OR NOT ADMITTED (the live contests)", F24_DENY),
        ("PHASE 6 — THE FORM 29, THE OBJECTION AND THE 64G (Feb–Jun 2026)", PH6),
        ("PHASE 7 — ⭐ THE LOCKOUT AND WHAT FOLLOWED (26 Jun – 31 Jul 2026)", PH7),
        ("PHASE 8 — THE PACKAGE AND THE RESPONSE (3–5 Aug 2026)", PH8),
        ("PHASE 9 — THE FORWARD CALENDAR", PH9),
        ("⭐⭐ VERIFIED FROM SOURCE, 5 AUGUST 2026", PH_VERIFIED),
        ("OUTSTANDING", OUTSTANDING),
    ]:
        if rows in (F24_ADMIT, F24_DENY):
            s.append(P(title, h2))
            s.append(tbl(rows, ("Notice ¶", "What was pleaded",
                                "The Respondent's answer")))
        else:
            s.append(P(title, h2)); s.append(tbl(rows))

    s.append(Spacer(1, 7))
    s.append(P("Compiled from source documents. Admissions are cited to the Form 24; MSH's "
               "statements to the objection of 5 June 2026 (ref K-LM26/729); the 15–16 May "
               "2024 entries to the Respondent's disclosure of 11 June 2026.", nt))
    doc.build(s, canvasmaker=Numbered)

    with pikepdf.open(TMP, allow_overwriting_input=True) as pdf:
        for k in list(pdf.docinfo.keys()):
            del pdf.docinfo[k]
        pdf.docinfo["/Author"] = "Cory L Shepherd"
        pdf.docinfo["/Title"] = "Master Log — WC/2024/227"
        if pdf.Root.get("/Metadata") is not None:
            del pdf.Root["/Metadata"]
        pdf.save(OUT, encryption=pikepdf.Encryption(
            owner="", user="", allow=pikepdf.Permissions(
                modify_other=False, modify_annotation=False, modify_assembly=False,
                modify_form=False, extract=True, print_lowres=True, print_highres=True)))
    print("built:", OUT)


build()

>>> drafts/CEILING_SET/01_REPORT_B_INSTRUCTION_LETTER.txt :: text
⛔ HOLD — send/hand to the psychiatrist AT OR AFTER the rebooked consultation, never before
   the question-set position with MSH is settled. THE single highest-impact document in the
   matter: conditional on a strong report, appeal-at-hearing moves ~36% → ~57%.

To:      Dr [Krishnaiah], Consultant Psychiatrist
From:    Cory Lea Shepherd — Appellant, QIRC matter WC/2024/227 (self-represented)
Re:      Letter of instruction — medico-legal report (the "appeal report")

Dear Doctor,

I am the appellant in WC/2024/227 (Shepherd v Workers' Compensation Regulator), an appeal
against the rejection of my workers' compensation claim for a psychological injury. I ask
you to prepare a medico-legal report for that proceeding. This report is SEPARATE from any
information provided to Metro South Health for return-to-work purposes: this report may
address causation; the workplace documents must not.

I enclose: (1) a chronology of the workplace events; (2) the pleaded stressors (Amended
Statement of Facts and Contentions, 7 April 2026); (3) the admitted facts extract (Form 24),
including that I was rostered a 7-hour break between shifts on 17–18 March 2024 against a
10-hour minimum, and that the Regulator's own Reviewing Officer found that rostering
"amounted to unreasonable management action" and was "satisfied [my] employment was a
significant contributing factor"; (4) your own clinical records as you hold them.

The legal test: an injury is compensable if employment is "A SIGNIFICANT contributing
factor" (s 32(1), Workers' Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003). Employment need not
be the only or main factor; other contributors may coexist.

I ask that your report address, in your own clinical judgment:

1.  Diagnosis, and the date of onset as best the clinical record establishes it (I note
    your record of 24 October 2024 and the escalation of medication at that time).

2.  Whether my employment — in particular the pleaded matters: the rostering and fatigue
    events (including the 17–18 March 2024 break), the sustained workload and
    complaint-exposure conditions of the Switchboard role, and the non-response to the
    concerns and reports I raised — was A SIGNIFICANT contributing factor to the onset of
    the condition, and your clinical reasoning.

3.  CHRONOLOGY, expressly: the diagnosis was recorded on 24 October 2024. The personal
    events sometimes referred to in my history (a separation and related matters) began in
    December 2024 and after. Please state plainly the significance, if any, those later
    events could have for the ONSET of a condition diagnosed before they occurred, and
    distinguish (if you consider it clinically appropriate) between the CAUSE of onset and
    factors affecting the subsequent COURSE of the condition.

4.  Any clinical observations relevant to the reliability of my account — including that I
    continued working a reduced pattern against clinical advice through 2025, funding the
    shortfall from my own leave.

5.  The mechanism: from a clinical perspective, how conditions of the kind described in the
    enclosures (sustained high demand, low control, absent support, unresolved complaints,
    fatigue) contribute to conditions of this kind.

Please do not address current work capacity or adjustments in this report — those are dealt
with separately. I am responsible for your fee for this report; please provide an estimate.
I am conscious you may be asked to produce your file in the proceeding; please write on the
basis that the report and its reasoning may be tested.

Yours sincerely,
Cory Lea Shepherd · 0417 400 227 · coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

 B2 Question 2 — lawful and reasonable directions; performance and conduct

 The Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026 records "Understanding instructions: Normal" and "Carrying out
 instructions accurately: Normal".

 The record of compliance is as follows: the Checklist was requested on 5 May 2026; I advised on 21 May 2026 that an
 appointment was booked for 5 June; the completed Checklist was provided to Injury Management on 3 July 2026; and
 on 3 July 2026 I asked the Health Service to confirm whether I was to attend. I have complied with each request made
 of me.

 As to the premise that "the Health Service is not aware of any concerns being raised for appropriate management": the
 Health Service's objection of 5 June 2026, signed by the Chief Executive, refers to a public interest disclosure by its
 reference number. A complaint was made on 4 October 2025 and a further complaint in February 2026.

 Whether the directions given have been lawful and reasonable is a matter for the Health Service to state, together with
 the instrument relied on. I have asked for that instrument and it has not been identified.

 B3 Question 5 — the meaning of “complaint handling”
 The Role Description provided as Attachment 2 contains no complaint-handling responsibility. The letter itself states
 the position: "established process for client complaints received by Switchboard employees is for immediate escalation
 and management by the Health Service Client Liaison Officer and/or Manager, Switchboard Services".

 The restriction asks that complaints be logged and redirected rather than actioned, resolved or absorbed. That is the
 process the Health Service describes as its own.

 B4 Question 6 — the inherent requirements test
 The question asks whether I can fulfil the requirements of the role "without restrictions or modifications to duties". That
 is not the test under the policy the same letter cites.

    HR Policy G03 (QH-POL-210) exists "to assist employees … to meet the genuine occupational requirements of
    their role by applying principles of reasonable adjustment", and cl 3 provides that adjustments "should support the
    employee to undertake the genuine occupational requirements of their role". Section 34 of the Anti-Discrimination Act
    1991 is to the same effect.
 I ask the Health Service to identify the genuine occupational requirements of the role which it says are not met, and
 the adjustment considered in respect of each. The Checklist records that "usual switchboard operational duties remain
 suitable".

 B5 Question 9 — accommodation and onus
 The question assumes an inability to accommodate which has not been assessed or communicated. G03 cl 2
 provides:

    unjustifiable hardship "is tested against the whole organisation, not a division or unit within the organisation …
    the onus is on Queensland Health, as the employer, to prove an adjustment is unreasonable, not on the
    person to prove that it is reasonable".
 I ask the Health Service to identify what adjustment has been assessed, by whom, against what part of the
 organisation, and on what basis it was found unreasonable.

 PART C — THE CONSULTATION FRAMEWORK
 The Checklist identifies, among the matters relevant to a return, "unresolved workplace matters involving line
 management". Under s 55A of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 a psychosocial hazard is one arising from
 or relating to "the design or management of work" or "workplace interactions or behaviours". Matters of that kind are
 assessed and controlled under Part 3.1 of the Regulation.

>>> drafts/out/ANNOTATED_SCHEDULE_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 3
    Section 55C(1) provides that a person conducting a business or undertaking "must manage psychosocial risks
    under part 3.1". Section 36(3) requires that risks be minimised by substituting the hazard, isolating the hazard
    from any person exposed to it, or engineering controls, before administrative controls are considered.
 Section 47(1) of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 requires consultation with workers directly affected by a matter
 relating to work health or safety, and s 48(1) requires that information be shared, that workers have a reasonable
 opportunity to contribute to the decision-making process, that their views be taken into account, and that they be
 advised of the outcome.

 My position is that the matters I have raised — changes to work arrangements made without consultation,
 responsibility for patient safety without corresponding input, and the handling of concerns once raised — fall within the
 hazard categories described in the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022: poor
 organisational change management, low job control, poor support, and poor organisational justice. Each is a feature of
 the work. I ask that they be assessed as such.

 I have raised consultation as a patient safety matter since 2024. Switchboard Services routes emergency and
 after-hours calls on a continuous 24/7 roster. My concern is that changes to those arrangements made without
 consulting the operators who action them carry risk. That concern is unchanged and it is the reason I seek to be
 included in decisions affecting the work for which I am accountable.

PROPOSED METHODOLOGY — PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK ASSESSMENT,
SWITCHBOARD SERVICES
Cory Lea Shepherd

AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health

August 2026 — a worker's proposal for how the clause 7.2 assessment be conducted, offered in

consultation under sections 47 to 49 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011. Companion to the

ISO 45003, and recognised practice in emergency communications settings.

Psychosocial Hazard Mapping and the Proposals for Consultation. Nothing in this document is a demand
or an allegation; the method proposed is drawn from the Code of Practice 2022,

PART 1 — THE EIGHT PHASES PROPOSED
1. GOVERNANCE. An assessor independent of the functions being assessed; published terms of
reference; a small steering group including an operator representative, any Health and Safety
Representative, and the union. The Code of Practice 2022 and ISO 45003 stated as the methods frame.

2. THE RECORDED DATA (work as recorded). Call volumes by hour and day; emergency-code activity;
the rosters audited against the fatigue rules; the team's leave usage mapped against the rosters and the
demand data; turnover, vacancy and backfill data; the complaints correspondence; EAP usage; incident
history; overtime.

3. THE SURVEY (work as experienced). The "People at Work" instrument — the validated, benchmarked
psychosocial risk survey developed with the Queensland regulator, available without cost — offered to all
operators with anonymity protected.

4. OBSERVATION (work as done). The assessor attends the room across shift types, including night and
weekend shifts, and observes the work as it is actually performed — the concurrency, the interruptions, the
emergency activations.

5. INTERVIEWS. An interview offered to every operator; structured prompts; and exit interviews sought
from operators who have recently left the area.

6. CONVERGENCE AND RISK RATING. The data, survey, observation and interview findings
triangulated; each hazard rated by duration, frequency and severity as the Code provides; the resulting risk
register shared with the operators.

7. CONTROL SELECTION IN CONSULTATION. A controls workshop with the operators; controls
considered in the order the Regulation requires; each adopted control given an owner and an
implementation date. The Proposals for Consultation are offered as a starting set.

8. REVIEW. Implemented controls carry review dates; a small set of indicators is tracked (fatigue-rule
compliance, complaint response times, leave-against-demand correlation); the survey repeated at twelve
months.

PART 2 — MATTERS PROPOSED FOR INCLUSION IN SCOPE
(a) A critical-incident debrief and peer-support step following defined trigger events (emergency codes,
deaths, abusive or distressing calls), as is standard in comparable emergency communications settings.

(b) Post-call recovery arrangements — a short off-queue recovery after distressing calls — and a defined
surge protocol for periods when demand exceeds capacity.

(c) The physical work environment of the room: headset acoustic protection, noise, console ergonomics,
screen-based work breaks, and lighting.

>>> drafts/out/Assessment_Methodology_Proposal_Shepherd_Aug2026.pdf :: page 2
(d) A quality-assurance framework including call-recording review, introduced in consultation and framed
as protective — an objective record that resolves complaints and accusations without them resting on the
operator.

(e) An evidence-based occupancy standard, so that sustained utilisation remains within recognised
bounds for call-handling work.

(f) Service standards on departments for the supply of roster and contact-detail updates to the
Switchboard, addressing the recurring cause of misdirected calls at its source.

(g) A documented training and competency framework for the room's functions, including any
shift-supervision function.

(h) A standing, anonymous route for operators to raise hazards, with feedback guaranteed, measured at
the twelve-month review.

PART 3 — CONSULTATION
I offer this methodology as an input to the scoping of the assessment, and ask that the scoping discussion
address each phase and each proposed scope item, with the outcome recorded. I will attend any
discussion at any time, with a support person and my union representative present.

RETURN TO WORK AND WORKPLACE CONTROLS — PROPOSALS
FOR CONSULTATION
Cory Lea Shepherd

AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health

August 2026 — tabled for discussion; nothing in this document is a demand, an allegation,

or a variation of any request or notice already on foot.

PART 1 — WHAT I HAVE ASKED FOR, AND HOW I PROPOSE EACH BE DONE
1. RETURN TO WORK. Under the Proposal for Return to Work of 3 August 2026: a staged return on the
pattern certified in the Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026, with the controls set out in that
proposal, the Checklist's own review date of 28 August 2026 as the first checkpoint, a support person
present at the return discussion, and the plan recorded in writing.

2. PAY AND LEAVE. Corrected through the ordinary payroll machinery: the rostered shifts processed by
AVAC, the leave debited since 3 July 2026 re-credited, and the codings confirmed in writing.

3. THE PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK ASSESSMENT (clause 7.2; Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at
work Code of Practice 2022). A scoping meeting with me, my union representative and any Health and
Safety Representative; the hazard categories to include those identified in the Health Service's letter of 7
July 2026 together with organisational justice and job insecurity; the data sources the Code identifies
(complaints, absence, turnover, EAP usage); an assessor independent of Corporate Services; a written
scope and timeline; findings shared; controls selected in consultation in the order the WHS Regulation
requires.

4. THE MEDICAL INFORMATION. Per my response of 3 August 2026: the Health Service confirms the
questions it presses; the questions are put through the allocation in that response; costs as the Health
Service has committed in writing.

5. THE PROCESS, NAMED. The instrument, steps, decision-maker and end-decision of the process I am
being managed under, in writing; or, if none applies, a documented return-to-work plan agreed with me,
with review dates, per the Workplace Rehabilitation Standard.

6. SEPARATION OF FUNCTIONS. Decisions concerning my attendance, duties and pay made by an
officer outside Corporate Services, with the delegation recorded in writing. This is the ordinary separation;
it requires no restructuring and no finding about anyone.

7. FEEDBACK (clause 7.1.11). A short written response to each work health and safety matter I have
raised: received, assessed, outcome.

8. RECORDS. Copies of preserved HR policies E12 and E13, and the roster and payroll record for the
twelve months preceding 3 July 2026.

PART 2 — THE SWITCHBOARD OPERATING MODEL (PROPOSED CONTROLS)
These are offered as controls for discussion in the assessment and under clause 7.1.5. Each concerns the
design of the work, not any person. Implementation cost is near zero: rostering and process changes only.

A. PATIENT SAFETY AS THE DESIGN PRINCIPLE. The Switchboard activates the hospital's emergency
codes and relays urgent clinical results; whether the right clinician is reached, and how quickly, depends
on the Switchboard and the accuracy of the on-call information it relies on. I propose: (i) clear ownership,
with a backup, for the accuracy of the on-call roster and the paging system; (ii) directory updates restored
to a workable pathway with a backup when the responsible officer is unavailable; and (iii) a defined
escalation path for when a department's support officer or the manager cannot be reached.

2. CONSULTATION BEFORE OPERATIONAL CHANGE. No change to Switchboard operating processes
takes effect until the operators who work the board have been consulted. The Switchboard is a real-time

>>> drafts/out/Consultation_Proposals_Shepherd_Aug2026.pdf :: page 2
environment operating multiple concurrent systems; the operators hold the working knowledge of it. This is
the consultation the Work Health and Safety Act already requires, applied systematically.

3. A ROTATIONAL, INTEGRATED MANAGER. The manager of Switchboard Services works a regular
rostered rotation on the board — on the phones, in the room. Management of a fast-paced, direct,
real-time environment is soundest when management holds direct current knowledge of it; presence also
ensures supervision and support are available where the work happens. This is the standard model in
emergency communications settings.

4. A COMPLAINT-RESPONSE STANDARD. Complaints and escalations sent to Switchboard
management are acknowledged within one business day and substantively answered within three; where
the manager is unavailable, the matter escalates automatically to the established Client Liaison pathway
rather than returning to the operators' console.

5. ONE RULEBOOK FOR THE ROOM. The manager working in rotation is subject to the same
frameworks as the operators — rostering rules, minimum notice, fatigue breaks, and leave processes —
applied consistently. Consistency of process is itself a psychosocial control.

6. A 24/7 ON-SHIFT SUPERVISOR FUNCTION, ROTATING WITHIN THE TEAM. The design principle is
that in a real-time environment, escalation is delay: a decision the board needs now cannot wait on a chain
to an off-site or after-hours contact. Authority therefore follows the clock. On every shift, one rostered
operator holds the shift-supervisor function — the real-time decision-maker for operational matters arising
on the board — while continuing to work the board with the team. The supervisor is not a second manager:
the manager holds the frameworks, administration and business-hours functions; the supervisor holds the
shift, so that after hours, on weekends, and at 3am the room is never waiting on an escalation that cannot
answer in time. Only matters that can properly wait are escalated to the manager in hours. The function
rotates among operators trained and assessed for it, and carries a classification increment or in-charge
allowance for the shifts on which it is held — a development pathway and recognition for competence
within the room, with shared capability across several trained operators rather than dependence on any
one person. When the supervisor makes a real-time decision, the operators present are consulted there
and then — consultation at the speed of the room — and the decision is carried forward through the
handover below. This is the standard model in emergency communications centres. The cost is a modest
per-shift allowance, ordinarily offset by reduced turnover and absence.

8. STRUCTURED HANDOVER AND DECISION LOG. Each shift hands over to the next through a
structured record: operational status, live issues, and the decisions made on shift with their reasons.
Context transfers instead of evaporating at shift change — a recognised failure point in continuous
operations — and decisions become consistent and auditable across the roster. The log also gives the
manager, in hours, a complete account of the room's operation without interrupting it.

7. EVIDENCE-BASED ROSTERING. Rosters designed from the demand data the Switchboard already
generates — call volumes by hour and day, and emergency-code activity — so that coverage matches the
actual peaks; with fatigue rules (minimum breaks) built into the roster design rather than checked
afterwards; published with proper notice; and with equity across operators visible on the face of the roster.
The data required is already collected; this proposal only asks that the roster be built from it.

PART 3 — HOW I PROPOSE THE CONSULTATION ITSELF RUN
(a) I will attend any discussion at any time, with a support person and my union representative present.

(b) Discussions occur alongside, not instead of, written responses; anything agreed is confirmed in writing
before it is treated as resolved.

(c) My participation in any discussion waives nothing and does not pause any process already on foot,
unless recorded otherwise in writing by agreement.

I table this because I would rather build the fix than continue the dispute. Every item in it is capable of
being implemented from existing resources, this month.

Dear Human Resources team,

I refer to the email from Injury Management of Friday 31 July 2026 at 11:43am and the two
letters of the same date signed by Mr Scott Hughes, Director, Corporate Services. I have
directed this response to Human Resources, and copied Injury Management so that it is received
within the timeframe the letter set.

Nothing in this response is a personal complaint about any individual, and I ask for no finding
about anyone. My concern is with how the process is being run, and with the support and
adjustment that ordinarily apply when an employee is certified fit with restrictions. I have
copied my union, and I have written separately to the Chief Executive today about the conflict
of interest and the handling of my personal information.

I am engaging with this process and will obtain the information sought. My response is attached,
with a proposed allocation of the nine questions and my proposal for return to work. In summary:

  - Questions 1(d), 4, 5 and 8 I will obtain from my general practitioner; Questions 7, 1(a),
    1(d) and 8 from my treating psychiatrist. Please confirm which questions the Health Service
    presses, and the invoices will be directed to you under the arrangement in your letter.
  - Questions 2, 3, 6 and 9 are not medical questions: they ask my doctor to answer matters
    which G03 and the Work Health and Safety Act place with the Health Service. I ask that the
    Health Service answer those itself; the medical part of each can then be put to my
    practitioners.
  - Question 1(a) is answered openly in the attachment: the diagnosis was made on 24 October
    2024, with the clinical context to come from my psychiatrist.
  - Question 1(c) I consent to, and the answer is in Dr Ma's own file: his understanding of my
    condition derives from my psychiatrist's correspondence, not my self-report.
  - Question 1(b) alone I ask be withdrawn. G03 clause 3 permits medical information "where
    necessary" to identify or assess adjustments; a causal formulation does neither, and it goes
    to a matter in issue in WC/2024/227.

I adopt option 1 and will obtain the information myself. I do not provide an authority under
option 2.

Three matters are dealt with in the attachment and I flag them here.

First, timing. I met the 2:00pm deadline of 3 July; the checklist certified me fit with
restrictions; within the hour I was told I could not attend, and I have been held out for five
weeks without an instrument being identified or a date given. Your letter arrived two hours
before a consultation with Dr Ma of which the Health Service had notice; I cancelled it rather
than waste a cost, and will rebook once the question set is settled. I ask for the extension
your letter contemplates, and for a date by which the Health Service will tell me whether I am
returning to work. I also ask what decision is meant by "a decision regarding your ability to
perform your role", and under what instrument it would be made — this is the second occasion an
adverse position has been foreshadowed without one.

Second, my exclusion. The Health Service's own letter confirms complaints are escalated to the
Client Liaison Officer and/or Manager, and the Role Description contains no complaint-handling
duty. There is no identified restriction preventing my performance of the role. I ask to be
returned to my roster, and that the leave debited since 3 July 2026 be reversed.

Third, delegation and conflict. I previously asked who is making decisions about me and whether
any conflict has been identified and managed; I have not been answered. Part 6 of the attachment
asks again and proposes the ordinary separation of functions.

>>> drafts/out/LETTER_Conflict_and_Information_Handling_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 1
 Conflict of interest, delegation, and the handling of my personal
 information
 Section 89, Public Sector Act 2022 · Code of Conduct clause 1.2
 Cory Lea Shepherd
 AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
 Employee reference MSH-INJ-5795
 To:   Ms Noelle Cridland, Chief Executive, Metro South Health
 Date: 3 August 2026


 1. WHAT I AM ASKING, AND WHAT I AM NOT
 I am asking that the decisions being made about my capacity, my attendance and my return to duty be made by an
 officer outside Corporate Services, and that the clinical material be held only by the Injury Management team.

 I address this letter to you because section 89 of the Public Sector Act 2022 makes the chief executive the person to
 whom a conflict is disclosed, and the only person who may authorise an officer to continue to act in a matter affected by
 one. I do not raise it with you in order to escalate it. I raise it with you because, on the terms of the section, there is no
 one else who can answer the questions at Part 3.

 I am not asking that anyone be removed from the management of my employment. I am not asking that anyone be
 stood aside, investigated, or found to have done anything wrong. I make no allegation against any individual and I seek
 no finding about anyone.

 This is not a personal complaint. It is about how the process is being run when an employee is diagnosed with an illness
 and needs managerial support and reasonable adjustment.

 Clause 1.2 of the Code of Conduct for the Queensland Public Service records that having a conflict of interest is not of
 itself wrongdoing, and that what matters is whether it is disclosed and managed. I proceed on that basis, and I ask these
 questions in that spirit.

 2. THE POSITION AS I UNDERSTAND IT
   (a) The letters of 31 July 2026 are written in the first person of the decision-maker — "I am seeking further
      clarification", "I require further information", "I will make a decision regarding your ability to perform your role" — and
      are signed by Mr Scott Hughes, Director, Corporate Services.
   (b) Question 3 of the attached request asks my general practitioner to advise whether I am fit to return "under the
      existing reporting arrangements, including working with and reporting to [my] current line manager". Those reporting
      arrangements sit within Corporate Services.
   (c) The Manager, Switchboard Services — who on 2 July 2026 advised that my return could not be facilitated, and
      asked me to wait for advice as to my next returning shift — reports within that same directorate.
   (d) On 3 October 2025 I made a formal written request for review to the A/Director, Human Resources Business
      Partnering, concerning a process initiated by the officer who has signed the letters of 31 July 2026. My union was
      copied. I do not reopen that matter and I make no submission about it. I record it only because it bears on whether a
      conflict exists and how it must be managed.
   (e) The letter of 7 July 2026 records that my treating practitioner had advised of "unresolved workplace matters
      involving line management", and that the Health Service did not have sufficient information to assess whether they
      presented psychosocial hazards.
 The officer determining my return to duty is therefore the Director of the directorate in which the advice of 2 July 2026
 was given, to whom the officer who gave it reports, and whose own directorate is the subject matter of the
 reporting-arrangements question at question 3.

 I say only that this is a set of circumstances in which a conflict may exist. Whether it does, and how it has been
 managed, is not something I can determine.

 2A. WHAT THE "UNRESOLVED WORKPLACE MATTERS" ARE, AND WHY THEY ARE WORKPLACE MATTERS




Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Conflict of interest, delegation and information handling                                Page 1

>>> drafts/out/LETTER_Conflict_and_Information_Handling_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 2
 The letter of 7 July 2026 records that the Health Service does not have sufficient information to understand the nature of
 the unresolved matters involving line management, or to assess whether they present psychosocial hazards. I take that
 at face value, and I would rather close the gap than argue about it.

 The matters concern how the work is organised and decided, not the character of any officer. They are, in substance:

   (a) how patient safety concerns raised at the switchboard are escalated and answered;
   (b) how changes to the work, the roster and the on-call arrangements have been introduced, and whether affected
      staff were consulted before rather than told afterwards;
   (c) fatigue and recovery between shifts, and how rostering is managed against it; and
   (d) the ability of staff to have genuine input into decisions that affect the work — which the Managing the risk of
      psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 treats as a matter of work design and organisational justice,
      and therefore as a psychosocial hazard in its own right where it is absent.
 Each of those is a workplace matter. None of them can be answered by a medical practitioner writing about me.
 Sections 47 to 49 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 require the Health Service to consult workers who are directly
 affected when identifying hazards, when deciding how to control them, when proposing changes affecting health or
 safety, and when deciding the procedures for monitoring the health of workers. That consultation has not occurred at
 any point since 26 June 2026.

 I record, without argument, that the information gap the Health Service identifies is one only the Health Service can
 close, and that it is being used in the meantime to maintain my exclusion.

 2B. MANAGERIAL SUPPORT AND ADJUSTMENT WHILE I AM UNWELL

 When an employee is certified fit with restrictions, the Health Service's own policies contemplate managerial support
 and reasonable adjustment: G03 clause 1.1 (temporary adjustments so an employee may "continue work during their
 recovery"; clause 1.1.1 extends this to a "health management case" with no compensation claim), and QH-IMP-401-5
 (suitable duties identified and actively sought and "made available wherever reasonably practicable"; the worker's
 connection with the workplace maintained; the dispute resolution process advised — for "either a work or
 non-work-related injury/illness").

 I obtained the checklist the Health Service required in order to facilitate my return. It certified me fit with restrictions.
 What followed was exclusion rather than adjustment: interim duties were declined in any capacity on 15 July 2026, and
 no adjustment plan has been identified to me. The Health Service may seek medical information — but a medical
 process clarifies functional limits; it does not displace the duty to consider adjustments in the meantime. I ask that
 interim adjustments be identified and implemented under the restrictions already certified.

 2C. DUE PROCESS — HOW THE DECISIONS ARE MADE

 Support and adjustment are the substance; due process is how the decisions about them are made: being told what
 power is being used and who decides; a fair opportunity to respond before a serious consequence; a decision-maker
 independent of the matters in issue; consultation as sections 47 to 49 of the Work Health and Safety Act require; and
 deadlines that are not one-sided. On the last point I record only this: I was given seven calendar days on 7 July and
 again on 31 July, each with a consequence attached, while the Health Service advised on 15 July that it was unable to
 commit to a timeframe of its own and on 30 July that it was unable to guarantee my return. I have asked several times
 for a date and have not been given one.

 The Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 calls this organisational justice, and
 treats its absence — including a lack of procedural fairness — as a psychosocial hazard. I do not say any tribunal has
 found a denial of fair process. I say the process described has not been applied to me, and I ask that it be — which is
 what the separation at Part 4 is for.

 3. THE QUESTIONS I ASK
 Section 89(1) of the Public Sector Act 2022 provides that if a public sector employee has an interest that conflicts or
 may conflict with the discharge of the employee's duties, the employee:

      "(a) must disclose the nature of the interest and conflict to the employee's chief executive as soon as practicable
      after the relevant facts come to the employee's knowledge; and (b) must not take action or further action concerning
      a matter that is, or may be, affected by the conflict unless authorised by the employee's chief executive."




Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Conflict of interest, delegation and information handling                             Page 2

>>> drafts/out/LETTER_Conflict_and_Information_Handling_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 3
 I ask the Health Service to confirm:

   (a) whether any disclosure has been made under section 89(1)(a) in relation to the decisions concerning my
      attendance, my pay and my return to duty;
   (b) whether any authorisation has been given under section 89(1)(b) for an officer to take, or to continue to take, action
      concerning those matters;
   (c) who holds the delegation for those decisions, and the source and instrument of that delegation;
   (d) whether the advice of 2 July 2026 and the decision of 3 July 2026 were made with the knowledge or approval of the
      officer now determining my return to duty; and
   (e) whether any conflict has been identified and recorded, and if so, how it is being managed.
 I ask these questions in writing because I have asked them before, in my email of 28 July 2026, and have not received
 an answer.

 If no authorisation has been given under section 89(1)(b), I ask that you consider the direction contemplated by section
 89(2), and that in the meantime the decisions described at Part 2 be allocated to an officer outside Corporate Services.

 I am conscious that this is a request that you exercise a function under the Act, and not a request that anything be found
 about anyone. If the answer to each of (a) to (e) is that the matter has been dealt with, that answer will resolve it entirely
 and I will take it no further.

 4. THE SEPARATION I PROPOSE
 I propose the ordinary separation of functions. It requires no restructuring, removes no one from the management of my
 employment, and requires no finding to be made about anyone.

   (a) THE CLINICAL MATERIAL — held exclusively by the Injury Management team, Human Resources, on a
      medical-in-confidence basis. Corporate Services would not hold, and would not have access to, the clinical material.
      This is what the Employee Capabilities Checklist itself recommends at Additional Comments 4(c): "return-to-work
      coordination and correspondence through the Injury Management team, Human Resources."
   (b) THE DECISION — any decision concerning my capacity or my return to duty made by an officer outside Corporate
      Services.
   (c) IMPLEMENTATION — Corporate Services retains the operational role: rostering me, putting in place whatever
      adjustments are decided, and the ordinary day-to-day management of my work. My line manager would receive the
      adjustments to be implemented, not the clinical information behind them.
 The officer steps out of the decision, not out of the workplace.

 Metro South Health is a large organisation and I do not anticipate that this would present any difficulty.

 5. MY PERSONAL INFORMATION
 The information sought by the request of 31 July 2026 is sensitive health information about me. I ask:

   (a) that it be held by the Injury Management team, used only for the purpose for which it was collected, and not
      provided to Corporate Services — what Corporate Services requires in order to roster me and implement
      adjustments is the adjustments themselves, not the diagnosis or the clinical reasoning behind them;
   (b) to be told who has had access to the medical material already held about me, who will have access to the further
      material, and whether it is proposed to provide any of it to any person outside the Health Service, and for what
      purpose; and
   (c) that it not be used in connection with any other proceeding. I do not consent to that.
 I make these requests under the Information Privacy Act 2009 and the Queensland Privacy Principles, and consistently
 with the consent I have given, which is scoped in my response of the same date.

 6. WHY IT MATTERS TO THE DECISION ITSELF
 I raise one further matter, neutrally.

 A decision on my request for a change in the way I work may only be made, or refused, on reasonable grounds.
 Whether grounds are reasonable is not only a question of what was decided; it is also a question of who decided it and


Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Conflict of interest, delegation and information handling                              Page 3

>>> drafts/out/LETTER_Conflict_and_Information_Handling_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 4
 on what material. If the decision is made by an officer within the arrangements the decision concerns, that is a matter
 which can be raised later, by either of us, and I would rather it were dealt with now.

 I would also note that the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 identifies poor
 organisational justice — including a lack of procedural fairness — as a psychosocial hazard in its own right, and that HR
 Policy G03 requires proper consideration to be given to that Code.

 I therefore ask that this be resolved before the decisions are made, rather than after.

 6.1 ONE MATTER I RECORD FOR THE FILE
 I record the following once, neutrally, and I do not develop it here.

 In the course of my employment I have raised concerns about patient safety, about changes to the work and the roster,
 about fatigue, and about the ability of staff to have input into decisions affecting the work. I am entitled to raise those
 matters, and to be consulted on work health and safety matters that affect me.

 Since 3 July 2026 I have been held out of the workplace, my accrued leave has been debited, and from 13 July 2026 I
 have been without wages, while those matters remain unassessed by the Health Service and while the decisions about
 my return sit within the directorate they concern. That is a serious detriment to me.

 I am not making a claim in this letter and I ask for no finding. I record it because it is a matter I have raised with my
 union, and because I would rather it be dealt with by the Health Service now than become an issue later. I do not
 abandon my employment or any entitlement.

 7. WHAT THIS LETTER DOES NOT DO
   (a) It makes no allegation against any individual and asks for no finding about anyone.
   (b) It does not ask that anyone be removed from the workplace, stood aside or investigated.
   (c) It is separate from my response of the same date to the Request for Medical Information, from my request under
      clause 10.3.2, and from my notice of dispute under clause 1.11. A decision on any of those is not an answer to this.
   (d) It is not a complaint under any Act, and it is not a grievance.
 I confirm again that I am engaging with this process and want to return to work.

 Arrangements for the medical appointments, and costs
 Request for Medical Information dated 31 July 2026 · MSH-INJ-5795
 Cory Lea Shepherd
 AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
 To:   Human Resources, Logan Bayside Health Network
      LBH.HRTeam1@health.qld.gov.au
 Date: 3 August 2026


 1. THE APPOINTMENTS, AND WHAT PRECEDES THEM
 The letter of 31 July 2026 asks that the information sought be returned within seven calendar days, and states that if it is
 not received a decision will be made regarding my ability to perform my role on the information then available.

 I am ready to obtain that information, and one step precedes it — a step which sits with the Health Service. My
 response of today's date proposes an allocation of the nine questions and asks that one be withdrawn. Before I put
 questions to my practitioners and incur costs on the Health Service's account, I ask the Health Service to confirm which
 questions it presses and to whom each is directed.

 On that confirmation I will rebook both consultations — with Dr Ma, and with my treating psychiatrist — within three
 business days, and I will advise the Health Service of both appointment dates the day they are made. The consultation
 with Dr Ma of 31 July 2026, of which the Health Service had notice, was cancelled only because the letter arrived two
 hours before it and put the question set in issue; I did not consider it reasonable to incur a cost, on the Health Service's
 account, on questions the Health Service may not press.

 If I have not received confirmation within seven days of this notice, I will rebook both consultations in any event and put
 the questions as allocated in my response, and I will tell the Health Service what was asked of whom. The information
 will follow as soon as the reports are received.

 2. THE TIMEFRAME
 The seven-day period runs to 7 August 2026. Reports of this kind cannot ordinarily be obtained within seven days of
 being asked, and the Health Service will know that from its own experience: its letter of 7 July 2026 also set a seven-day
 period, and on 15 July 2026 it advised that it was itself unable to commit to a timeframe for the same information.

 I ask that no decision be made regarding my ability to perform my role on the basis that information has not been
 provided, while the step which precedes it — the Health Service's confirmation of the question set — remains
 outstanding, and while the reports it makes necessary are then obtained. If the Health Service intends to make such a
 decision earlier, I ask to be told in advance, and to be told what decision is contemplated and under what instrument.

 3. COSTS
 I do not ask for anything under this heading. The position is already settled by the Health Service's own letter, and I
 record it only so that the arrangement is clear.

 The letter of 31 July 2026 states:

     "MSH will meet your reasonable costs of preparing this report and we appreciate your assistance with this request.
     Please send invoices to Michelle Harrison, Injury Management Consultant, Human Resources, Logan and
     Beaudesert Health Services via email at lbh_InjuryManagement@health.qld.gov.au."

 I accept that arrangement and will proceed on it: when the consultations are rebooked, each practitioner will be
 instructed to render their account directly to Ms Harrison at that address, quoting MSH-INJ-5795, and not to me. I will
 advise the expected fees once confirmed.

 For completeness, and because they are separate matters:

   (a) THE REPORTS NOW SOUGHT. The arrangement above covers them. The questions I propose to put to my
      treating psychiatrist are questions from the Health Service's own request, allocated as set out in my response, and I
      proceed on the basis that they fall within it. If the Health Service takes a different view as to any part, I ask to be told
      before the appointments so that no cost is incurred on a footing that is not agreed.

 Cory Lea Shepherd

 Subject: Notice of dispute under clause 1.11 — application of the certified agreement to my
      attendance, roster, leave and pay from 26 June 2026


 1. WHAT THIS NOTICE IS
 This notice informs you, as my immediate supervisor, of the existence of a dispute, in accordance with clause 1.11.2(a)
 of the certified agreement.

 Clause 1.11.2 provides that where there is "any disagreement between the parties as to the interpretation, application or
 implementation of this Agreement", the procedure in that clause applies. Clause 1.11.1 records that the objectives are
 "the avoidance and resolution of any disputes … by measures based on the provision of information and explanation,
 consultation, co-operation and negotiation", and that "the emphasis will be on finding a resolution at the earliest possible
 stage in the process".

 That is what I am seeking. I would prefer this resolved at Stage 1 and I am available to discuss it at any time.

 2. THE SUBJECT MATTER OF THE DISPUTE
 The dispute concerns the application and implementation of the certified agreement to my employment from 26 June
 2026, in the following respects.

 2.1 ATTENDANCE AND ROSTERED DUTY
 I have not been permitted to attend my rostered shifts since 3 July 2026. On 2 July 2026 I was advised that the Health
 Service was "unable to facilitate" my return until a completed Employee Capacity Certificate was received, and asked to
 "wait for my advice to when your next returning shift will be".

 The Employee Capability Checklist was returned to the Injury Management team on 3 July 2026 at 2:30pm and, a
 section having been identified as missing, resubmitted at 3:06pm that afternoon. The letter of 7 July 2026 records both
 times. The same letter records that "you have been certified fit to return to work effective from 3 July 2026". I asked the
 same afternoon to be told whether I should attend. I have not received an answer to that question.

 The condition on which the advice of 2 July 2026 was expressed has therefore been satisfied. I have asked which
 instrument is relied on to maintain the position since, and have not received an answer.

 2.2 LEAVE
 Since 3 July 2026 my accrued leave has been debited, and from 13 July 2026 I have been recorded as absent without
 pay, in respect of a period in which I have been willing and available to work and have said so in writing. I dispute the
 application of the leave provisions of the certified agreement to that period.

 2.3 ROSTER
 I dispute the position, so far as it is taken, that my rostered pattern over the preceding twelve months is inconsistent with
 the requirements of my role. That pattern was set by the Health Service and worked without any concern being raised
 with me.

 2.4 WORK HEALTH AND SAFETY MATTERS RAISED
 Clause 7.1.11 provides that "the parties commit to ensure that appropriate feedback is provided to employees who raise
 workplace health and safety matters". Clause 7.1.5 records the parties' agreement to address, among other issues,
 "management of ill or injured employees", "psychosocial issues and implementation of Managing the risk of
 psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022", and "injured workers to have the opportunity to be re-trained in

 alternative areas/departments". I have raised matters within each of those descriptions and have not received feedback
 on them.

 2.5 PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK ASSESSMENT
 Clause 7.2 provides for psychosocial risk assessments conducted using the resources in the Managing the risk of
 psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022, "in consultation with workers and Health and Safety
 Representatives". I have asked for a workplace risk assessment and none has been provided.

 I record that the Health Service identified this itself. The letter of 7 July 2026 states:

     "it is noted that your treating medical practitioner has advised that there are unresolved workplace matters involving
     line management. At this stage, the Health Service does not have sufficient information to understand the nature of
     these matters or assess whether they present any psychosocial hazards or risks that may affect your proposed
     return to work."

 That was written on 7 July 2026, with further information said to be required "to enable the Health Service to assess any
 identified risks". So far as I am aware, no assessment has been undertaken in the four weeks since. I ask that one be
 conducted, and that I be consulted in it, as clause 7.2.2 contemplates.

 2.6 THE PROCESS ITSELF
 Since 26 June 2026 I have been asked to provide medical information about myself, held out of my rostered shifts, had
 my accrued leave debited and then been recorded as absent without pay, and told that a decision will be made
 regarding my ability to perform my role.

 The letter of 15 July 2026 refers to employees "being managed through Health Management processes". That is the
 only description of this process I have been given.

 I have a phrase. I do not have a process.

 I ask to be told, in relation to it:

   (a) the instrument under which it is conducted — the Act, directive, clause of the certified agreement, or policy;
   (b) what its steps are, and where they are published;
   (c) who the decision-maker is; and
   (d) what decision it ends in.
 I am not raising this as a complaint about anyone. I raise it because I cannot follow a process properly, or exercise
 whatever rights attach to it, without knowing those four things. If the answer to any of them is that there is none, that is
 also something I need to know.

 The Workplace rehabilitation standard (QH-IMP-401-5) requires that a worker be informed of "the appropriate dispute
 resolution process to follow"; I have not been informed of any. Clause 1.11.1 makes "the provision of information and
 explanation" an objective of this procedure — this is a request for exactly that, and it is the first one I make.

 3. THE STATUS QUO WHILE THE PROCEDURE IS FOLLOWED
 Clause 1.11.4 provides:

     "Subject to legislation, while the dispute procedure is being followed, normal work is to continue except in the case of
     a genuine safety issue. The status quo existing before the emergence of a dispute is to continue whilst the
     procedure is being followed. No party shall be prejudiced as to the final settlement by the continuation of work."

 The status quo before the emergence of this dispute was that I was rostered and working. I ask that I be returned to my
 rostered shifts while the procedure is followed, in accordance with that clause. I am not asking for anything to be
 decided in my favour by doing so; clause 1.11.4 expressly provides that no party is prejudiced as to the final settlement
 by the continuation of work.

 I anticipate the Health Service may say that the exception for "a genuine safety issue" applies. If that position is taken, I
 ask that it be put in writing and that the following be identified, so that it can be discussed at Stage 1:

   (a) the hazard identified, and the assessment on which it was identified;
   (b) the control measures considered, in the order required by section 36 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation
      2011, and why each was rejected; and

 Proposal for Return to Work
 Accompanying the Response to the Request for Medical Information · MSH-INJ-5795
 Cory Lea Shepherd
 AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
 To:   Human Resources, Logan Bayside Health Network
      LBH.HRTeam1@health.qld.gov.au
 Date: 3 August 2026


 1. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS
 This document sets out my proposal for returning to work. It accompanies my response of today's date to the Request
 for Medical Information, and is presented separately so that it can be considered — and, internally, routed — on its own.
 The confirmations I seek are listed at Part 9 of the response. The proposal at section 3 below is also the subject of my
 separate request of today's date under clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement.

 2. THE PROPOSAL
 I have been held out of the workplace since 3 July 2026 without wages, with my accrued leave debited, and self-funding
 the medical costs of this process. G03 clause 1.1 contemplates temporary adjustments which allow an employee to
 "continue work during their recovery," and clause 1.1.1 confirms that workplace rehabilitation support is available to
 employees "who have an injury/illness impacting their current ability to perform their role, with no claim or entitlement to
 compensation (health management case)." Clause 1 provides that "Managers are responsible for ensuring work
 environments and work, do not unreasonably prevent employment for people."

 The Health Service's Workplace rehabilitation standard (QH-IMP-401-5, 7 January 2026) is also engaged. It provides
 that the line manager or delegate shall "identify and actively seek ... meaningful suitable duties, and ensure suitable
 duties are made available wherever reasonably practicable"; that the line manager "is best placed to be the primary
 contact for the worker wherever possible and facilitate the injured workers on-going connection with the workplace"; that
 "regular, transparent and timely communication" be maintained with the worker "whether at work or off work"; and that
 the worker be informed of "the appropriate dispute resolution process to follow in such cases where the worker does not
 agree with elements of a proposed workplace rehabilitation plan or suitable duties program". The standard applies to a
 worker requiring rehabilitation "for either a work or non-work-related injury/illness".

 I have been offered no suitable duties — interim duties were declined in any capacity. I have been held away from the
 workplace rather than connected to it. I have not been informed of any dispute resolution process. I ask that each of
 those be addressed.

 I also record that I was not consulted before the decision of 3 July 2026, or since. Section 47 of the Work Health and
 Safety Act 2011 requires consultation with workers who are "directly affected by a matter relating to work health or
 safety". Section 48 requires that I be given a reasonable opportunity "to contribute to the decision-making process
 relating to the matter". Section 49 requires consultation when identifying hazards and assessing risks, when deciding
 how to eliminate or minimise them, when proposing changes that may affect the health or safety of workers, and when
 making decisions about the procedures for monitoring the health of workers. The present request is a procedure for
 monitoring my health.

 I propose the following. Each item is within the Health Service's existing processes and, so far as I can see, requires no
 material expenditure and no restructuring.

   (a) RETURN TO DUTY. That I return to my rostered shifts now, on the restrictions certified in the Employee
      Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026, while the balance of this inquiry is completed. If the exclusion is maintained,
      that the instrument relied on be identified, that the period be treated as paid special leave, and that the leave
      debited since 3 July 2026 be reversed.
   (b) COMPLAINT HANDLING. That the Health Service confirm in writing that complaints received by Switchboard staff
      are escalated in accordance with the process it has itself described. This requires no change to anything.
   (c) ROSTER PREDICTABILITY. That my roster be published in accordance with the certified agreement and not
      altered without my agreement other than in an emergency.




Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Proposal for Return to Work                                                          Page 1

>>> drafts/out/PROPOSAL_Return_to_Work_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 2
   (d) ORDINARY PROCEDURAL FAIRNESS. That any concern about my performance or conduct be raised with me in
      writing, with particulars, in accordance with the applicable directive, and that I be afforded a support person.
   (e) A SEPARATE CONTACT POINT. That leave, injury management and human resources matters concerning me be
      handled by an officer outside Switchboard Services rather than by my line manager, who wrote to me on 2 July
      2026 concerning leave types and my return to duty. This does not alter day-to-day supervision and involves no
      change to reporting lines.
   (f) WORKPLACE RISK ASSESSMENT. As set out at Part 4.2.
   (g) REVIEW. That the arrangements be reviewed at six weeks, or earlier if either party considers it necessary.
   (h) GRADUATED RETURN. If the Health Service prefers, I am willing to return on a graduated basis by agreement. I
      am not seeking to avoid any part of my role.
 If any part of this proposal cannot be accommodated, I ask that the Health Service identify which part and its reasons,
 having regard to G03 clause 2.

 3. CONTROLS I WOULD BE WILLING TO SEE PUT IN PLACE
 I record these subject to two qualifications I do not waive: identifying hazards and determining controls is a function of
 the Health Service under Part 3.1 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011, not of the worker; and the controls
 that are appropriate are ultimately a matter for clinical opinion, which question 1(d) of the Health Service's own request
 seeks.

   (a) A telephone call one hour before each rostered shift, to confirm I am attending; if unanswered or attendance is not
      confirmed, a second call; if still not confirmed, the on-call operator is contacted and cover arranged. The measure is
      contingent, not standing: on the shifts I attend — most of them — it costs one telephone call, and where I am not
      attending, that is established an hour ahead rather than at start time. An on-call arrangement has existed in the unit
      since 15 April 2024; this applies it, and would have addressed a substantial part of the attendance history recorded
      in the correspondence of 8 September 2025. It is a confirmation of attendance, not an assessment of my condition
      — no colleague needs to know anything about my health for it to work.
   (b) A defined escalation pathway I may initiate during a shift if my condition is acutely exacerbated — who assumes
      the board, how the shift is closed out — so the response is planned rather than improvised.
   (c) Continuation of the existing complaint-handling arrangement recorded in the Health Service's own letter: immediate
      escalation to the Client Liaison Officer and/or Manager. This requires no change to anything.
   (d) Continuation of the rostered pattern that has applied over the preceding twelve months. The Checklist records it as
      "the pattern Mr Shepherd has in fact worked and tolerated over the past twelve months without deterioration" and a
      "continuation of existing arrangement". The Health Service set that roster; where my condition was exacerbated I
      managed it myself, from my own sick and annual leave — which is why, on 3 July 2026, my paid sick leave was
      exhausted. I am not asking for the pattern to be reduced. I am asking that it continue, with the variability managed
      by a process rather than by the exhaustion of my entitlements. If it is now said the role requires something different,
      I ask what changed, and when.
   (e) Injury management correspondence directed through the Injury Management team, consistent with the Checklist's
      own recommendation.
 The only conduct matter ever raised with me is attendance and lateness; the measures at (a) and

   (b) are directed at precisely that. If any measure cannot be accommodated I ask that the Health
 Service identify which and why, noting G03 clause 2: unjustifiable hardship is "tested against the whole organisation, not
 a division or unit", and "the onus is on Queensland Health, as the employer, to prove an adjustment is unreasonable".

 4. THE STATUS OF THIS PROPOSAL — A REQUEST UNDER CLAUSE 10.3
 So that the Health Service is not left to determine for itself what kind of document this is, I identify the provision the
 proposal is made under.

 Clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement provides that, in accordance with the Industrial Relations Act 2016, an
 employee "may ask the employer for a change in the way the employee works, including the employee's ordinary hours
 of work." Section 27(1)(c) of that Act puts the matter beyond doubt for a case such as this one: the request may be for
 "a change to the way the employee works, for example, the use of different equipment as a result of a disability, illness

 The measures at sections 2 and 3 are a change in the way I work, sought as a result of an illness. I have made that
 request formally, by a separate letter of today's date headed "Request for a change in the way I work", so that there is
 no question about what it is or when it was received. That letter sets the change out in the form clause 10.3.3 requires
 and states the reasons for it. Sections 2 and 3 of this document are the fuller explanation of the same proposal.

 I ask that the two be read together, and that the request be dealt with under clauses 10.3.4 to 10.3.6. Nothing in this

 5. MY SUBSTANTIVE POSITION
 The letters of 31 July 2026 describe my employment as "Administration Officer (AO), Switchboard Operations,

 fortnight."

 I ask the Health Service to confirm:

   (a) that the position so described continues to be held for me, and that no permanent appointment to it has been made
      or is proposed to be made while I am held out of the workplace;
   (b) whether the shifts I would ordinarily work are being performed by another employee. I ask because it bears directly
      on Question 9. The Health Service has asked my doctor to advise whether I can safely return if it is "not able to
      accommodate the restrictions". If the duties I would perform are being performed by someone else, the work is
      available, and the premise of that question requires examination before it is put to anyone; and
   (c) what, if anything, has been communicated within the workplace about my absence.
 I raise (c) because my absence has been the subject of enquiry among colleagues. I would prefer that whatever is said
 about it is accurate.

 I raise these matters only to have the position confirmed in writing.

PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK ASSESSMENT — INTEGRATED PACKAGE — SWITCHBOARD SERVICES, LOGAN HOSPITAL
Risk report · hazard matrix · proposed controls · assessment methodology · scope · conduct of the assessment · recommended assessor
Cory Lea Shepherd, AO3 Switchboard Services · August 2026 · Prepared under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld), the WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld), the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work
Code of Practice 2022, and consistent with ISO 45003. This document consolidates, as one integrated package, the worker's contribution offered under ss 47–49 for the clause 7.2 assessment: the risk report and
hazard matrix, the proposed controls, the proposed methodology, the matters proposed for scope, the proposed conduct of the assessment, and providers available to perform it. Every hazard is described as a
feature of the work and its systems; the 'existing controls' column records the position as known to me as an operator of the room; nothing in this document is a demand or an allegation against any person.

PART 1 — FRAMEWORK
Section 19 of the Act requires the health of workers — expressly including psychological health — to be ensured so far as reasonably practicable. The Regulation requires psychosocial hazards to be
identified, the risks assessed, controls implemented in the order of the hierarchy, and controls reviewed, in consultation with affected workers (ss 47–49). The Code supplies the recognised hazard
categories, the assessment factors (duration, frequency and severity of exposure), and the data sources. Risk ratings below apply the Code's factors; where a category of harm has already materialised in
a diagnosed psychological injury within the room, the consequence limb is treated as established rather than speculative.

PART 3 — WHAT THE MATRIX DISCLOSES
Read as a whole, the matrix records a single consistent position: each identified hazard has been operating without documented identification, without assessment, without controls selected through the
hierarchy, and without the consultation sections 47–49 require — over a sustained period, in a room performing a patient-safety function, in which a psychological injury of the kind these hazards produce
has already occurred. The only control identified anywhere in the matrix is informal and worker-funded (personal leave operating as the de facto fatigue control). This is recorded factually, from the
operator's vantage point, and is exactly the question the clause 7.2 assessment exists to examine: the assessment can confirm, correct, or complete this matrix — and I ask that it do so with the operators
consulted.

PART 4 — THE PROPOSED CONTROLS, INTEGRATED
P1 Patient-safety design (ownership and backup for on-call/paging accuracy; workable directory pathway; defined escalation) · P2 Consultation before operational change · P3 The rotational integrated
manager (in hours, on the phones, in the room) · P4 Complaint-response standard (1 business day acknowledgment / 3 days response / automatic escalation) · P5 One rulebook for the room · P6 The
24/7 rotating on-shift supervisor — authority follows the clock; real-time decisions consulted with the room; recognition and a trained pathway · P7 Evidence-based rostering — coverage from the demand
data, fatigue rules built into design, equity visible · P8 Structured handover and decision log. Implementation is from existing resources except the P6 allowance; each control maps to the matrix rows
above; controls to be selected and sequenced in consultation, with owners, dates and review.

PART 5 — STRUCTURAL ROSTERING RECOMMENDATIONS (P7 IN DETAIL)
(i) Coverage built from the demand curve. The demand data (call volumes by hour, day and month; emergency-code activity) is used to identify the room's high-volume and low-volume days and
periods. Staffing profiles are then set to the identified pattern — heavier coverage and defined surge cover on high-volume days; baseline coverage on low-volume days — rather than a flat roster applied
to a variable workload.
(ii) Rostered admin time. Protected off-queue admin blocks are built into the roster — scheduled by preference on identified low-volume days — for the work the room currently absorbs while on the
queue: training and competency maintenance, directory and contact-data upkeep, complaint follow-up, quality review and handover documentation. Work that has no rostered home is work performed
under call pressure or not at all.
(iii) Relief and break cover on high-volume days — fatigue within the shift. The fatigue that presents in this room arises principally from long continuous runs on the queue during high-volume
periods, where breaks are deferred, shortened or taken late because the queue does not stop and no relief is rostered to cover them. A rostered break is not a taken break unless someone is rostered to
hold the queue. It is proposed that high-volume days carry a named relief or rotation arrangement so that breaks are covered and taken as rostered, that time on the queue between breaks be bounded
by an occupancy standard, and that both be measured — rostered break time against off-queue time actually taken.
(iv) Fatigue rules built into the design — recovery between shifts. Separately from within-shift fatigue, minimum break requirements between shifts are enforced by the roster system at the point of
construction, so a non-compliant line cannot be published; turnarounds below the minimum become structurally impossible rather than discouraged.
(v) Leave built into the establishment. The roster's baseline is set to include a planned-leave allowance, so approved leave does not strip coverage below the demand profile and leave approval does
not depend on colleagues absorbing the gap. Leave handling is visible and equitable, and the leave-against-demand correlation — the current pattern in which personal leave clusters on and after
high-volume periods — is monitored as a standing indicator that fatigue is being managed by the roster rather than purchased by workers.
(vi) Equity visible. The distribution of nights, weekends, high-volume days and admin blocks across the team is published with the roster, so equity is observable rather than asserted.

>>> drafts/out/Psychosocial_Assessment_Package_Integrated_Shepherd_Aug2026.pdf :: page 3
(vii) Consulted and published in advance. Roster design and any change to the pattern are consulted with the operators before taking effect, and rosters are published with the notice the Award
requires.

PART 6 — THE EIGHT PHASES PROPOSED FOR THE ASSESSMENT
1. GOVERNANCE. An assessor independent of the functions being assessed; published terms of reference; a small steering group including an operator representative, any Health and Safety
Representative, and the union. The Code of Practice 2022 and ISO 45003 stated as the methods frame.
2. THE RECORDED DATA (work as recorded). Call volumes by hour, day and month, profiled into the room's high-volume and low-volume days; emergency-code activity; time on queue and occupancy
through the day; rostered break times compared with off-queue time actually taken; the rosters audited against the fatigue rules; the team's leave usage mapped against the rosters and the demand data;
turnover, vacancy and backfill data; the complaints correspondence; EAP usage; incident history; overtime.
3. THE SURVEY (work as experienced). The "People at Work" instrument — the validated, benchmarked psychosocial risk survey developed with the Queensland regulator, available without cost —
offered to all operators with anonymity protected.
4. OBSERVATION (work as done). The assessor attends the room across shift types, including night and weekend shifts, and observes the work as it is actually performed — the concurrency, the
interruptions, the emergency activations.
5. INTERVIEWS. An interview offered to every operator; structured prompts; and exit interviews sought from operators who have recently left the area.
6. CONVERGENCE AND RISK RATING. The data, survey, observation and interview findings triangulated; each hazard rated by duration, frequency and severity as the Code provides; the resulting risk
register shared with the operators.
7. CONTROL SELECTION IN CONSULTATION. A controls workshop with the operators; controls considered in the order the Regulation requires; each adopted control given an owner and an
implementation date. The proposed controls at Part 4 are offered as a starting set.
8. REVIEW. Implemented controls carry review dates; a small set of indicators is tracked (fatigue-rule compliance, complaint response times, leave-against-demand correlation); the survey repeated at
twelve months.

PART 7 — MATTERS PROPOSED FOR INCLUSION IN SCOPE
(a) A critical-incident debrief and peer-support step following defined trigger events (emergency codes, deaths, abusive or distressing calls), as is standard in comparable emergency communications
settings.
(b) Post-call recovery arrangements — a short off-queue recovery after distressing calls — and a defined surge protocol for periods when demand exceeds capacity.
(c) The physical work environment of the room: headset acoustic protection, noise, console ergonomics, screen-based work breaks, and lighting.
(d) A quality-assurance framework including call-recording review, introduced in consultation and framed as protective — an objective record that resolves complaints and accusations without them
resting on the operator.
(e) An evidence-based occupancy standard, so that sustained utilisation remains within recognised bounds for call-handling work.
(f) Service standards on departments for the supply of roster and contact-detail updates to the Switchboard, addressing the recurring cause of misdirected calls at its source.
(g) A documented training and competency framework for the room's functions, including any shift-supervision function.
(h) A standing, anonymous route for operators to raise hazards, with feedback guaranteed, measured at the twelve-month review.

PART 8 — THE CONDUCT OF THE ASSESSMENT (worker recommendations)
Independence of the assessor. It is recommended that the assessor be external to the health service, led by registered organisational psychologists with work health and safety capability, without prior
engagement with the health service on this subject matter, and with a reporting line to a level of the organisation above the functions being assessed. Findings reported to the functions under assessment
cannot serve the review step the Regulation requires.
Observation protocol. Observation under Phase 4 is recommended to be conducted across the full operating cycle — day, evening, night and weekend shifts, and across identified high-volume and
low-volume days, so the room is seen both under strain and at baseline — with attendance unannounced within an agreed assessment window, under a written protocol settled in consultation before
observation begins, recording at minimum: call volumes and concurrency, single-operator periods, interruptions, escalation attempts and their response times, emergency activations, handover practice,
and whether any off-queue or administrative time exists or is absorbed on the queue. An assessment of a 24-hour room conducted in business hours only assesses a different room.

>>> drafts/out/Psychosocial_Assessment_Package_Integrated_Shepherd_Aug2026.pdf :: page 4
The survey instrument. "People at Work" is nominated as the Phase 3 instrument: it is validated, benchmarked across industries, developed with WorkSafe Queensland, and available without cost
(peopleatwork.gov.au). Anonymity protected; all operators offered participation.
Interview themes. It is recommended the Phase 5 interviews include, at minimum: what a difficult shift looks like and what happens afterwards; whom the operator would tell about a hazard and what
happened on the last occasion they did; and what, if anything, operators have stopped reporting and why. The last question is the standard test for normalisation in high-exposure work environments and
is best asked by an independent assessor.
Indicators and review. A small leading-indicator set tracked from completion: fatigue-rule compliance in rosters as published; complaint acknowledgment and response times; the leave-against-demand
correlation; and the survey repeated at twelve months, with results shared with the room.
