 Request for a change in the way I work
 Clause 10.3.2, Certified Agreement (No. 12) 2025 · s 27, Industrial Relations Act 2016 (Qld)
 Cory Lea Shepherd
 AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
 Employee reference MSH-INJ-5795
 To:   Human Resources, Logan Bayside Health Network
      LBH.HRTeam1@health.qld.gov.au
 Date: 3 August 2026


 1. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS
 This is a request under clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement for a change in the way I work.

 I make it as a separate document, rather than within my response to the Request for Medical Information of 31 July
 2026, so that there is no question about what it is or when it was received.

 Clause 10.3.2 provides that, in accordance with the Industrial Relations Act 2016, an employee "may ask the employer
 for a change in the way the employee works, including the employee's ordinary hours of work". Section 27(1)(c) of that
 Act provides that the request may be for "a change to the way the employee works, for example, the use of different
 equipment as a result of a disability, illness or injury".

 Clause 10.3.3 requires that the request be in writing, state the change in sufficient detail to allow a decision to be made,
 and state the reasons. Parts 2 and 3 below do each of those things.

 I make the request under two separate limbs of section 27(1), and I ask that they be considered separately.

   (a) ORDINARY HOURS — Part 2.1. This is made under section 27(1)(a), which concerns "the employee's ordinary
      hours of work", and under clause 10.3.2, which is in the same terms. That limb stands on its own. It does not
      depend on illness or injury, and neither section 27, nor section 28, nor clause 10.3 makes medical information a
      precondition to making such a request or to deciding one. My reasons for it are matters of rostering history and are
      set out at Part 3.
   (b) THE WAY I WORK — Parts 2.2 to 2.5. These are made under section 27(1)(c), which concerns "a change to the
      way the employee works, for example, the use of different equipment as a result of a disability, illness or injury".
 I separate them because a decision on one is not a decision on the other, and because the question of my ordinary
 hours does not require, and should not await, information sought for a different purpose. If the Health Service is not in a
 position to decide (b) at present, I ask that it decide (a), and say so.

 2. THE CHANGE I AM ASKING FOR

 2.1 MY ORDINARY HOURS
 That my rostered pattern continue at the level at which it has in fact operated over the twelve months preceding the
 Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026 — approximately 0.6 of the shifts of my full-time permanent line of 76
 hours per fortnight, worked from within that line, being the average I have actually worked across those twelve months,
 with the precise figure to be established from the Health Service's own roster and payroll records as set out below. My
 appointment to that line is not varied by this request.

 The Employee Capabilities Checklist describes that level, at Additional Comments 3, as a "reduced pattern of
 approximately six shifts per fortnight", and records that it "is the pattern Mr Shepherd has in fact worked and tolerated
 over the past twelve months without deterioration, and maintaining rather than increasing it best supports recovery while

 anything about my health for (a) to (c) to work. They need only know whether the shift is confirmed.

 Clause 10.3.4 provides that the Health Service may grant this request, grant it in part or subject to conditions, or refuse

 5. THE FRAMEWORK THE DECISION SITS IN
 I set this out for one reason only. Clause 10.3.5 permits the Health Service to grant the request in part or subject to
 conditions, or refuse it, "only on reasonable grounds". Grounds are reasonable against the whole of the law that applies,
 not against the agreement alone. If the request is refused in whole or in part, I would like to be able to understand the
 reasons given under clause 10.3.6 by reference to the same framework the Health Service is applying.

 5.1 THE OBLIGATION
 The Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 provides at section 15(1) that a person must not discriminate "in any variation of the
 terms of work", or "by treating a worker unfavourably in any way in connection with work". Section 15(2) provides that
 "dismissing includes ending the particular work of a person by forced retirement, failure to provide work or otherwise".

 Section 11 provides that indirect discrimination happens if a person imposes a term with which a person with an
 attribute does not or is not able to comply, and which is not reasonable. Impairment is a protected attribute under
 section 7.

 5.2 THE EXEMPTIONS, AND WHAT THEY REQUIRE
 Sections 35 and 36 provide that it is not unlawful to discriminate on the basis of impairment where the person would
 require special services or facilities and supplying them would impose unjustifiable hardship, or where the
 circumstances of the impairment would impose unjustifiable hardship.

 Those provisions are exemptions, and each of them turns on unjustifiable hardship. Section 5 provides that whether
 something would impose unjustifiable hardship depends on all the relevant circumstances of the case, including the
 nature of the services or facilities, their cost and the number of people who would benefit or be disadvantaged, the



Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Request under clause 10.3.2 — decision due within 21 days (cl 10.3.6)                 Page 3

>>> drafts/out/REQUEST_Change_in_the_way_I_work_cl10.3_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 4
 financial circumstances of the person, the disruption that supplying them might cause, and the nature of any benefit or
 detriment to all people concerned.

 HR Policy G03 puts the same test in the Health Service's own words, at clause 2: unjustifiable hardship is "tested
 against the whole organisation, not a division or unit within the organisation", and "the onus is on Queensland Health, as
 the employer, to prove an adjustment is unreasonable, not on the person to prove that it is reasonable".

 I would add that the Health Service is a public entity for the purposes of the Human Rights Act 2019, and section 58 of
 that Act requires a public entity to act and make decisions compatibly with human rights and to give proper
 consideration to relevant human rights in doing so.

 5.3 WHY I RAISE IT, AND WHAT I AM NOT DOING
 I have made no complaint under the Anti-Discrimination Act, and this letter is not one. I make no allegation against
 anyone and I ask for no finding to be made about anyone.

 I raise it because the measures at Part 2 are modest ones, and I would like the reasons for any refusal to engage with
 that. On the shifts I attend, the arrangement at 2.2 costs one telephone call. The roster at 2.1 is the roster the Health
 Service already sets. The complaint-handling arrangement at 2.4 is the Health Service's own established process. The
 correspondence routing at 2.5 is what the Employee Capabilities Checklist itself recommends.

 If the Health Service considers that any of the measures would impose unjustifiable hardship, I ask only that it identify
 which measure, and what the hardship is. That is the same thing clause 10.3.6 requires, expressed in the language of
 the Act.

 6. THE TIME FOR THE DECISION
 Clause 10.3.6 provides:

     "The employer must give the employee written notice about its decision within 21 days after receiving the request. If
     the employer decides to grant the request in part or subject to conditions or to refuse the request, the written notice
     about the decision must state the reasons for the decision, outlining the reasonable grounds for granting the request
     in part or subject to conditions or for the refusal."

 Section 28(3) of the Industrial Relations Act 2016 is in the same terms. Section 28(4) provides that a notice granting the
 request in part or subject to conditions, or refusing it, must state the written reasons outlining the reasonable grounds,
 and must state that the Commission has jurisdiction to hear and decide a dispute over the request under chapter 6.
 Section 29 provides that if the written notice is not given within 21 days after the request is received, the employer is
 taken to have decided to refuse the request.

 Twenty-one days from the date of this letter is Monday 24 August 2026.

 I record these provisions because a date has not been available in this matter at any stage. I have asked several times
 to be told when I would know whether I am returning to work, and I have not been given a date. The certified agreement
 provides one, and I would much prefer that the request be dealt with by agreement well before it.

 I record this because it bears directly on the present request. The Health Service now seeks further information about a
 document it required me to obtain in order to work, and which certified that I could.

 I am willing to provide clarification of that document. I ask that the clarification be directed to identifying the adjustments
 which allow me to work — the purpose for which the document was obtained, the purpose stated in the letter of 31 July
 2026, and the purpose contemplated by Human Resources Policy G03.

 1.2 THE TEST APPLIED
 The letter to Dr Ma states the purpose of the request:

     "to identify and implement any appropriate workplace controls or reasonable adjustments to support a safe and
     sustainable return to his substantive position."

 Human Resources Policy G03 (QH-POL-210), which the Health Service has cited, sets the limit at clause 3:

     "Reasonable adjustment may need to be supported by medical or rehabilitation information, where necessary, to
     either identify required workplace adjustments and/or assess the suitability of proposed adjustments."

 I have applied that test to each question: is this information necessary to identify a required adjustment, or to assess the
 suitability of a proposed one — and is the person being asked the right person to answer it?

 Applying that test, the nine questions divide four ways. I am not declining to provide information. I am proposing that
 each question be directed to whoever is able to answer it.

 1.3 THE CHECKLIST ALREADY ANSWERS MOST OF WHAT IS NOW ASKED
 The Employee Capabilities Checklist is Attachment 1 to the Health Service's own letter. Read in full, it already answers,
 in substance, most of the nine questions.

 Q1(d) foreseeable risk and necessary controls — answered at Additional Comments 3 and 4, which set out the
 recommended work pattern with clinical reasoning for each shift type, and five specific workplace
 modifications.
 Q4 restrictions, clinical basis in functional terms, duration and review — answered at Additional Comments 2:
 "Episodic, with symptom exacerbation linked to stressor exposure. The restrictions below are expected to
 remain necessary for at least the next 3-6 months, subject to treatment response and 8-weekly review." The
 review date is given on the first page as 28 August 2026.
 Q5 what "complaint handling" encompasses — answered: "complaints received at the Switchboard are to be
 logged and redirected to management/the dedicated complaints area, not actioned, resolved or absorbed by Mr
 Shepherd."
 Q6 the requirements of the role — answered: "Usual switchboard operational duties remain suitable;
 complaint-handling duties are excluded as below."
 Q7 working memory in functional terms — addressed under Memorising information ("Working memory
 affected under stress") and at Additional Comments 1 ("reduced concentration and working memory under
 sustained high-demand load"), with the roster controls which manage it.
 Q8 tasks and environments which exacerbate the condition — answered at Additional Comments 1 and in the
 foreseeable-stressors response.
 Q2 capacity to follow a direction — the checklist records "Understanding instructions: Normal" and "Carrying
 out instructions accurately: Normal."
 I do not raise this to refuse further clarification. I have set out at Part 3 what my practitioners will provide. I raise it
 because I have been excluded from the workplace for five weeks while information the Health Service has held since 3
 July 2026 is sought again.

 PART 4 — QUESTIONS FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE
 These four questions ask a doctor to answer matters which the Health Service's own policy and the Work Health and
 Safety Act 2011 place with the Health Service. I ask that the Health Service answer them, after which the properly
 medical component of each can be put to my practitioners.

 4.1 QUESTION 2 — is there a performance or conduct process?
 The question asks whether I can "follow a reasonable and lawful direction issued by [my] supervisor" and "participate in
 discussions in relation to [my] workplace performance and/or conduct."

 These are not questions about capacity to perform the genuine occupational requirements of my role. They concern
 readiness for a management process. Either such a process is on foot concerning me — in which case I am entitled to
 be told of it, given particulars, and afforded procedural fairness — or there is not, in which case the questions do not
 serve the stated purpose of this inquiry.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: please confirm whether any performance or conduct process concerning me
     is on foot or contemplated, and if so provide particulars.
    → THEN, IF APPROPRIATE, FOR MY PRACTITIONER: "Does the employee have capacity to participate in
     ordinary workplace meetings and supervision, and are any supports required?"
 The premise of Question 2 is separately incorrect and is addressed at Part 5.

 4.2 QUESTION 3 — is the workplace safe?
 The question asks whether I am "medically fit to return to their substantive role under the existing reporting
 arrangements, including working with and reporting to their current line manager." That asks a treating doctor to certify
 that a workplace arrangement is safe. Under section 19 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 that duty rests with the



Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Response to Request for Medical Information of 31 July 2026                        Page 4

>>> drafts/out/RFMI_Response_and_Allocation_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 5
 Health Service; under the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 a psychosocial
 hazard is a feature of the work, identified and controlled by the PCBU; and G03 clause 1 requires proper consideration
 of that Code. A doctor can advise on me; a doctor cannot assess the Health Service's reporting arrangements.

 The letter of 7 July 2026 records that the Health Service "does not have sufficient information to understand the nature
 of these matters or assess whether they present any psychosocial hazards or risks". That gap is real, and it is closed by
 the Health Service consulting and assessing — sections 47 to 49 require consultation with workers directly affected, and
 none has occurred since 26 June 2026. For completeness, the matters concern how work in the unit is organised and
 decided: how patient safety concerns raised at the switchboard are escalated; how changes to work and roster have
 been introduced; fatigue and recovery between shifts; and staff input into decisions affecting the work. They are
 workplace matters, which is why the assessment belongs with the Health Service.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: a risk assessment of the Switchboard work environment addressing the
     psychosocial hazards identified. Clause 7.2.1 of the certified agreement provides the mechanism.
    → THEN FOR MY PRACTITIONER: "Are any adjustments recommended in relation to supervision
     arrangements, and if so, what are they in functional terms?"

 4.3 QUESTION 6 — what are the genuine occupational requirements?
 The question asks whether I can "fulfill the full inherent requirements of [my] Role ... without restrictions or modifications
 to duties."

 This applies the wrong test. G03 states its purpose as assisting employees "to meet the genuine occupational
 requirements of their role by applying principles of reasonable adjustment," and at clause 3 provides that adjustments
 "should support the employee to undertake the genuine occupational requirements of their role, without risk to their own
 health and safety or that of others in the workplace." Section 34 of the Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 is to the same effect.
 Neither asks whether an employee can perform a role without adjustment.

 A clinician also cannot determine which duties are genuine occupational requirements. That is the employer's
 determination. The Health Service has itself already made part of it: its letter states that "established process for client
 complaints received by Switchboard employees is for immediate escalation and management by the Health Service
 Client Liaison Officer and/or Manager, Switchboard Services," and the Role Description at Attachment 2 contains no
 complaint-handling responsibility.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: identify which duties of the role it says are genuine occupational
     requirements, having regard to the Role Description at Attachment 2.
    → THEN FOR MY PRACTITIONER: "Can the employee perform the genuine occupational requirements of the
     role with the adjustments you have recommended?"

 4.4 QUESTION 9 — can the adjustments be accommodated?
 The question asks: "If we are not able to accommodate the restrictions you have recommended, is Mr Shepherd able to
 safely return to the workplace?"

 This presupposes an inability to accommodate before any accommodation has been assessed. G03 clause 2 provides
 that unjustifiable hardship "is tested against the whole organisation, not a division or unit within the organisation," and
 that "the onus is on Queensland Health, as the employer, to prove an adjustment is unreasonable, not on the person to
 prove that it is reasonable."

 The question therefore asks my doctor to answer the final step first, on a hypothetical the Health Service has
 constructed and not yet tested, and on which the onus is not mine.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: assess the recommended adjustments against the whole organisation. If it
     considers any cannot be accommodated, identify which and its reasons.
    → THEN, IF NECESSARY, the question can be put to my practitioner properly.

 PART 6 — DELEGATION AND CONFLICT OF INTEREST
 This is not a personal complaint about any individual. I make no allegation and I ask for no finding about anyone. My
 concern is with how the process is being run — who is deciding, on what material, and under what instrument — and
 with the support and adjustment that ordinarily apply when an employee is certified fit with restrictions. G03 clause 1.1
 provides for temporary adjustments so an employee may "continue work during their recovery"; the Workplace
 rehabilitation standard requires suitable duties to be actively sought and the worker's connection with the workplace
 maintained, for "either a work or non-work-related injury/illness". I obtained the checklist the Health Service required for
 that purpose. It certified me fit with restrictions. What followed was exclusion rather than adjustment.

 Due process is the other half: being told what power is being used and who decides; a fair opportunity to respond before
 a serious employment consequence; consultation on the matters in issue; deadlines that are not one-sided; and
 decisions made by an officer independent of the matters they concern — what the Managing the risk of psychosocial
 hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 calls organisational justice. I do not say any tribunal has found a denial of fair
 process; I say that process has not been applied, and I ask that it be.

 I asked on 28 July 2026 who is making decisions about me and whether any conflict of interest has been identified. I
 have not received a response. Both letters of 31 July 2026 are written in the first person of the decision-maker and
 signed by Mr Hughes, Director, Corporate Services; question 3 asks my doctor about the reporting arrangements within
 that same directorate, and the Manager who gave the advice of 2 July 2026 reports within it. The officer determining my
 return therefore sits within the arrangements in issue. I ask the Health Service to confirm: (a) the source and instrument
 of the delegation; (b) whether any conflict has been identified, declared and managed, and how; and (c) whether the
 decisions of 2 and 3 July 2026 were made with the knowledge or approval of the officer now determining my return.

 6.1 A PROPOSED MANAGEMENT OF THE CONFLICT
 I propose the ordinary separation of functions: the clinical material held exclusively by the Injury Management team on a
 medical-in-confidence basis — which is what the Checklist itself recommends at Additional Comments 4(c); any
 decision concerning my capacity or return made by an officer outside Corporate Services; and implementation —
 rostering, and putting the adjustments in place — retained within Corporate Services. The officer steps out of the
 decision, not out of the workplace. I record, because it bears on the assessment, that on 3 October 2025 I made a
 formal written request for review to the A/Director, HR Business Partnering concerning a process initiated by the officer
 who has signed the letters of 31 July 2026; I do not reopen it here. Code of Conduct clause 1.2 provides that a conflict is
 not wrongdoing in itself — failing to disclose and manage one is likely to be.

 Submission to Together Queensland
 Request that the union seek an independent psychosocial risk assessment of Switchboard Services, Logan
 Hospital, Metro South Health
 Submitted by Cory Lea Shepherd, AO3 Switchboard Services, workplace delegate · 6 August 2026

 1 What I am asking the union to do
 I ask that Together Queensland request Metro South Health to commission an independent
 psychosocial risk assessment of Switchboard Services at Logan Hospital, under the Managing the risk
 of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 and consistently with ISO 45003, with the
 operators consulted.

 I ask that the request be made by the union, signed by the appropriate officer, and raised with the Chief
 Executive and through the Health Consultative Forum or its equivalent. I am the workplace delegate and
 I am the person raising it, but I do not think it should be my request alone: the matters are collective,
 they affect operators who are still at work, and a request that belongs to the union will outlast whatever
 happens in my own circumstances.

 I also ask the union to consider whether a work group should be determined and a health and safety
 representative election facilitated for the area. I am not seeking that role. I am asking that the room have
 one.

 2 Why the work area needs it
 Switchboard is the hospital's communications hub. Operators activate emergency codes and page
 clinicians, handle a high daily call volume including callers in distress, work across day, evening, night
 and weekend shifts, and after hours work without supervision present. Operators are also the first point
 of contact when information held elsewhere in the organisation (rosters, on-call arrangements, contact
 directories) is out of date, and they absorb the complaints that follow.

 Matters that have been raised over several years, and which I understand continue, include:

    2.1 rostering practice and the adequacy of recovery between and within shifts;
    2.2 fatigue on high-volume days, and the extent to which staff manage it using their own personal
       leave;
    2.3 how complaints and concerns raised by operators are acknowledged, answered and closed;
    2.4 the absence of supervision and decision support after hours and on weekends;
    2.5 operational changes taking effect without consultation with the operators affected;
    2.6 the absence of any debrief or recovery step following emergency codes, deaths, or abusive calls.
 To my knowledge no psychosocial risk assessment has ever been conducted for this work area, or for
 the wider line it sits within. I may be wrong about that, and an assessment is the way to find out.

 3 My own position, stated plainly
 My own matters are entwined with this, and I want the union to have that in front of it rather than
 discover it later. I sustained a psychological injury in June 2024. I have an appeal on foot in the
 Commission, and I am currently in a dispute with the Health Service about attendance, roster, leave and
 pay. I have been away from the workplace since late June 2026.

 I raise that for two reasons, and neither is that I want something from this request. The first is that it is
 the evidence: what happened to me is one operator's experience of the same work, and I would not be
 able to describe the room accurately without it. The second is that it is how I know my colleagues need
 something like this. I have worked beside people managing the same demands with the same absence
 of supports, and I do not want another operator to arrive where I have arrived.

 I am not asking the union to advance my dispute through this request, and I do not want the assessment
 used for that purpose. If it assists the union to make the request without reference to me at all, I would


C Shepherd, Delegate · Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital · 6 August 2026                           Page 1 of 2

>>> drafts/out/SUBMISSION_Delegate_to_Together_Switchboard_Assessment.pdf :: page 2
 prefer that. My concern is the room.

 4 What I propose the union put forward
    4.1 An independent assessor, external to the Health Service, psychologist-led, reporting to a level
       above the functions being assessed.
    4.2 The data reviewed: call demand by hour, day and month; rosters audited against the fatigue
       rules; leave patterns read against demand; turnover and vacancies; the complaints record and
       response times; incident history; overtime; time on the queue between breaks.
    4.3 The People at Work survey, the validated instrument developed with the Queensland regulator,
       available at no cost, offered to all operators with anonymity protected.
    4.4 Observation across the full operating cycle, including night and weekend shifts and both
       high- and low-volume days, under a written protocol agreed in consultation.
    4.5 Interviews offered to every operator, and exit interviews sought from operators who have
       recently left the area.
    4.6 A risk register shared with the operators, not only with management, and controls selected in
       consultation with owners and dates.
    4.7 A review point at twelve months, with a small set of indicators tracked: fatigue-rule
       compliance, complaint response times, and the leave-against-demand pattern.

 5 Provider proposal already obtained
 So that cost and availability are not unknowns, I asked two providers for indicative proposals.
 Psychgroup (Sarah Hellwege, Director and Principal Psychologist) has replied in writing. Their
 Psychosocial Risk Infrastructure Audit reviews the organisation's own data, surveys, reporting systems,
 claims, rosters, policies, and interviews stakeholders across work health and safety, human resources,
 senior executives, health and safety representatives and workers, reporting against the Code of
 Practice and the ISO standards. The indicative cost is $10,000 to $30,000 depending on scope and the
 number of interviews. A psychosocial risk assessment (an independently facilitated survey with
 qualitative interviews) is included at no cost within their Partner Program. Ms Hellwege invited the
 details to be passed to the relevant contact within the hospital for definitive scoping.

 I have no association with the provider and no interest in who is engaged. Selection of an assessor is a
 matter for the Health Service in consultation. I obtained the proposal only so that the request could not
 be answered with uncertainty about cost or availability.

 6 Material available to the union
 I have prepared, as a worker's contribution, a psychosocial hazard mapping for the work area, a set of
 proposed controls, and a proposed assessment methodology. They are offered to the union to use,
 adapt or discard entirely as it sees fit. Nothing in them is a claim against any individual.

 Cory Lea Shepherd

      not require of me in any event.
   6. I ask for an extension of the seven days, and explain at Part 7 why that period cannot be met on the Health Service's

 PART 1 — THE ORIGIN OF THE REQUEST, AND THE TEST APPLIED

 1.1 THE ORIGIN AND STATED PURPOSE OF THE EMPLOYEE CAPABILITIES CHECKLIST
 The letter of 31 July 2026 records the origin of the checklist in the Health Service's own words:

     "your recently completed Employee Capabilities Checklist (ECC) (Attachment 1) completed by Dr Day Hong Ma on
     the 3 July 2026 which was provided to us to facilitate a Return to Work Plan."

 That is correct, and the sequence was as follows.

   (a) On 5 May 2026 the Manager, Switchboard Services asked me to arrange for the Employee Capabilities Checklist to
      be completed, so that the Health Service could "provide the most appropriate support in the workplace" and
      "discuss the next steps to ensure you are supported and working safely". No condition was attached to my
      attendance.
   (b) On 21 May 2026 I advised that an appointment was booked for 5 June 2026. In the same email I arranged a swap
      for a shift I was rostered on the following day. I remained rostered and at work with the checklist outstanding, and no
      suggestion was made that I could not attend.
   (c) On 26 June 2026 the position changed. I was advised that "until we receive appropriate medical clearance,
      including a completed Employee Capacity Certificate (ECC), we are unable to facilitate your return to work", by
      reference to section 19 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011, and that without the documentation I "will be unable
      to return to work".
   (d) That position was repeated on 2 July 2026, with a leave-type deadline of 2:00pm on Friday 3 July 2026.
   (e) I obtained the checklist and provided it on 3 July 2026 at 2:32pm. It certified me fit to work with restrictions.

 1.2 THE TEST APPLIED
 The letter to Dr Ma states the purpose of the request:

     "to identify and implement any appropriate workplace controls or reasonable adjustments to support a safe and
     sustainable return to his substantive position."

 Human Resources Policy G03 (QH-POL-210), which the Health Service has cited, sets the limit at clause 3:

     "Reasonable adjustment may need to be supported by medical or rehabilitation information, where necessary, to
     either identify required workplace adjustments and/or assess the suitability of proposed adjustments."

 I have applied that test to each question: is this information necessary to identify a required adjustment, or to assess the
 suitability of a proposed one — and is the person being asked the right person to answer it?

 Applying that test, the nine questions divide four ways. I am not declining to provide information. I am proposing that
 each question be directed to whoever is able to answer it.

 1.3 THE CHECKLIST ALREADY ANSWERS MOST OF WHAT IS NOW ASKED
 The Employee Capabilities Checklist is Attachment 1 to the Health Service's own letter. Read in full, it already answers,
 in substance, most of the nine questions.

 Q1(d) foreseeable risk and necessary controls — answered at Additional Comments 3 and 4, which set out the
 recommended work pattern with clinical reasoning for each shift type, and five specific workplace
 modifications.
 Q4 restrictions, clinical basis in functional terms, duration and review — answered at Additional Comments 2:
 "Episodic, with symptom exacerbation linked to stressor exposure. The restrictions below are expected to
 remain necessary for at least the next 3-6 months, subject to treatment response and 8-weekly review." The
 review date is given on the first page as 28 August 2026.
 Q5 what "complaint handling" encompasses — answered: "complaints received at the Switchboard are to be
 logged and redirected to management/the dedicated complaints area, not actioned, resolved or absorbed by Mr
 Shepherd."
 Q6 the requirements of the role — answered: "Usual switchboard operational duties remain suitable;
 complaint-handling duties are excluded as below."
 Q7 working memory in functional terms — addressed under Memorising information ("Working memory
 affected under stress") and at Additional Comments 1 ("reduced concentration and working memory under
 sustained high-demand load"), with the roster controls which manage it.
 Q8 tasks and environments which exacerbate the condition — answered at Additional Comments 1 and in the
 foreseeable-stressors response.
 Q2 capacity to follow a direction — the checklist records "Understanding instructions: Normal" and "Carrying
 out instructions accurately: Normal."
 I do not raise this to refuse further clarification. I have set out at Part 3 what my practitioners will provide. I raise it
 because I have been excluded from the workplace for five weeks while information the Health Service has held since 3
 July 2026 is sought again.

 The sequence bears on the timeframe: I cannot instruct either practitioner until the question set is settled, and none of
 that can occur within seven calendar days. The only step which cannot presently begin is the one which depends on the

 medical examination under chapter 3 part 8 division 5 of the Public Sector Act 2022, which has not been invoked.

 PART 4 — QUESTIONS FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE
 These four questions ask a doctor to answer matters which the Health Service's own policy and the Work Health and
 Safety Act 2011 place with the Health Service. I ask that the Health Service answer them, after which the properly
 medical component of each can be put to my practitioners.

 4.1 QUESTION 2 — is there a performance or conduct process?
 The question asks whether I can "follow a reasonable and lawful direction issued by [my] supervisor" and "participate in
 discussions in relation to [my] workplace performance and/or conduct."

 These are not questions about capacity to perform the genuine occupational requirements of my role. They concern
 readiness for a management process. Either such a process is on foot concerning me — in which case I am entitled to
 be told of it, given particulars, and afforded procedural fairness — or there is not, in which case the questions do not
 serve the stated purpose of this inquiry.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: please confirm whether any performance or conduct process concerning me
     is on foot or contemplated, and if so provide particulars.
    → THEN, IF APPROPRIATE, FOR MY PRACTITIONER: "Does the employee have capacity to participate in
     ordinary workplace meetings and supervision, and are any supports required?"
 The premise of Question 2 is separately incorrect and is addressed at Part 5.

 4.2 QUESTION 3 — is the workplace safe?
 The question asks whether I am "medically fit to return to their substantive role under the existing reporting
 arrangements, including working with and reporting to their current line manager." That asks a treating doctor to certify
 that a workplace arrangement is safe. Under section 19 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 that duty rests with the



Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Response to Request for Medical Information of 31 July 2026                        Page 4

>>> drafts/out/Shepherd_Documents_MSH-INJ-5795_3Aug2026.pdf :: page 5
 Health Service; under the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 a psychosocial
 hazard is a feature of the work, identified and controlled by the PCBU; and G03 clause 1 requires proper consideration
 of that Code. A doctor can advise on me; a doctor cannot assess the Health Service's reporting arrangements.

 The letter of 7 July 2026 records that the Health Service "does not have sufficient information to understand the nature
 of these matters or assess whether they present any psychosocial hazards or risks". That gap is real, and it is closed by
 the Health Service consulting and assessing — sections 47 to 49 require consultation with workers directly affected, and
 none has occurred since 26 June 2026. For completeness, the matters concern how work in the unit is organised and
 decided: how patient safety concerns raised at the switchboard are escalated; how changes to work and roster have
 been introduced; fatigue and recovery between shifts; and staff input into decisions affecting the work. They are
 workplace matters, which is why the assessment belongs with the Health Service.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: a risk assessment of the Switchboard work environment addressing the
     psychosocial hazards identified. Clause 7.2.1 of the certified agreement provides the mechanism.
    → THEN FOR MY PRACTITIONER: "Are any adjustments recommended in relation to supervision
     arrangements, and if so, what are they in functional terms?"

 4.3 QUESTION 6 — what are the genuine occupational requirements?
 The question asks whether I can "fulfill the full inherent requirements of [my] Role ... without restrictions or modifications
 to duties."

 This applies the wrong test. G03 states its purpose as assisting employees "to meet the genuine occupational
 requirements of their role by applying principles of reasonable adjustment," and at clause 3 provides that adjustments
 "should support the employee to undertake the genuine occupational requirements of their role, without risk to their own
 health and safety or that of others in the workplace." Section 34 of the Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 is to the same effect.
 Neither asks whether an employee can perform a role without adjustment.

 A clinician also cannot determine which duties are genuine occupational requirements. That is the employer's
 determination. The Health Service has itself already made part of it: its letter states that "established process for client
 complaints received by Switchboard employees is for immediate escalation and management by the Health Service
 Client Liaison Officer and/or Manager, Switchboard Services," and the Role Description at Attachment 2 contains no
 complaint-handling responsibility.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: identify which duties of the role it says are genuine occupational
     requirements, having regard to the Role Description at Attachment 2.
    → THEN FOR MY PRACTITIONER: "Can the employee perform the genuine occupational requirements of the
     role with the adjustments you have recommended?"

 4.4 QUESTION 9 — can the adjustments be accommodated?
 The question asks: "If we are not able to accommodate the restrictions you have recommended, is Mr Shepherd able to
 safely return to the workplace?"

 This presupposes an inability to accommodate before any accommodation has been assessed. G03 clause 2 provides
 that unjustifiable hardship "is tested against the whole organisation, not a division or unit within the organisation," and
 that "the onus is on Queensland Health, as the employer, to prove an adjustment is unreasonable, not on the person to
 prove that it is reasonable."

 The question therefore asks my doctor to answer the final step first, on a hypothetical the Health Service has
 constructed and not yet tested, and on which the onus is not mine.

    → FOR THE HEALTH SERVICE: assess the recommended adjustments against the whole organisation. If it
     considers any cannot be accommodated, identify which and its reasons.
    → THEN, IF NECESSARY, the question can be put to my practitioner properly.

 withdrawn. For the purpose of identifying controls, what matters is that the stressors exacerbate my condition

 I record that section 124(1) of the Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 provides that a person "must not ask another person,

 124(3) the defence requires the respondent to prove "that the information was reasonably required for a purpose that
 did not involve discrimination." Impairment is a protected attribute. I raise this not as a complaint but so that the Health
 Service can satisfy itself that each question it presses meets that standard.

 5.2 CORRECTION OF FACT
 Question 2 is premised on the statement that "the Health Service is not aware of any concerns being raised for
 appropriate management."

 That statement is incorrect. Concerns have been raised in writing on multiple occasions, including a public interest
 disclosure (PID 24-ESU-1130); a written patient safety report; correspondence to Human Resources over a period
 exceeding two years concerning fatigue, rostering and the management of directory information; a written complaint to
 the A/Director, Human Resources Business Partnering dated 3 October 2025; and the matters in WC/2024/227, in
 which the Health Service filed an objection dated 5 June 2026 under the signature of the Health Service Chief
 Executive.

 I do not ask the Health Service to agree with any of those concerns. I ask only that my treating practitioner not be asked
 to answer a question which assumes they were never made. I request that the correction be provided to Dr Ma in writing
 before he is asked to answer any question resting on that premise.

 PART 6 — DELEGATION AND CONFLICT OF INTEREST
 This is not a personal complaint about any individual. I make no allegation and I ask for no finding about anyone. My
 concern is with how the process is being run — who is deciding, on what material, and under what instrument — and
 with the support and adjustment that ordinarily apply when an employee is certified fit with restrictions. G03 clause 1.1
 provides for temporary adjustments so an employee may "continue work during their recovery"; the Workplace
 rehabilitation standard requires suitable duties to be actively sought and the worker's connection with the workplace
 maintained, for "either a work or non-work-related injury/illness". I obtained the checklist the Health Service required for
 that purpose. It certified me fit with restrictions. What followed was exclusion rather than adjustment.

 Due process is the other half: being told what power is being used and who decides; a fair opportunity to respond before
 a serious employment consequence; consultation on the matters in issue; deadlines that are not one-sided; and
 decisions made by an officer independent of the matters they concern — what the Managing the risk of psychosocial
 hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 calls organisational justice. I do not say any tribunal has found a denial of fair
 process; I say that process has not been applied, and I ask that it be.

 I asked on 28 July 2026 who is making decisions about me and whether any conflict of interest has been identified. I
 have not received a response. Both letters of 31 July 2026 are written in the first person of the decision-maker and
 signed by Mr Hughes, Director, Corporate Services; question 3 asks my doctor about the reporting arrangements within
 that same directorate, and the Manager who gave the advice of 2 July 2026 reports within it. The officer determining my
 return therefore sits within the arrangements in issue. I ask the Health Service to confirm: (a) the source and instrument
 of the delegation; (b) whether any conflict has been identified, declared and managed, and how; and (c) whether the
 decisions of 2 and 3 July 2026 were made with the knowledge or approval of the officer now determining my return.

 6.1 A PROPOSED MANAGEMENT OF THE CONFLICT
 I propose the ordinary separation of functions: the clinical material held exclusively by the Injury Management team on a
 medical-in-confidence basis — which is what the Checklist itself recommends at Additional Comments 4(c); any
 decision concerning my capacity or return made by an officer outside Corporate Services; and implementation —
 rostering, and putting the adjustments in place — retained within Corporate Services. The officer steps out of the
 decision, not out of the workplace. I record, because it bears on the assessment, that on 3 October 2025 I made a
 formal written request for review to the A/Director, HR Business Partnering concerning a process initiated by the officer
 who has signed the letters of 31 July 2026; I do not reopen it here. Code of Conduct clause 1.2 provides that a conflict is
 not wrongdoing in itself — failing to disclose and manage one is likely to be.

 7.1 DEADLINES IN THIS MATTER HAVE RUN IN ONE DIRECTION
 I met the deadline of 2:00pm on 3 July 2026; the checklist was provided at 2:32pm and certified me fit with restrictions.
 At 3:18pm I asked whether I should attend. Five weeks later that has not been answered, no instrument authorising my

 decision would be made, and on 30 July 2026 I was told the matter was "progressing for delegate approval" and that the
 Health Service was "unable to guarantee" my return.

 On 31 July 2026 the Director, Corporate Services set me seven calendar days, with a consequence: a decision
 regarding my ability to perform my role on the available information. The letter does not say what that decision is. I ask
 that it be identified — what decision, and under what instrument. If it is a decision that I return to work, I welcome it and
 no consequence arises. If it is a decision of another kind, I am entitled to know now, and to the procedural fairness that
 attaches to it. This is the second occasion an adverse position has been foreshadowed without an instrument: on 15
 July my return was said to "remain at the discretion of the Employer".

 I do not object to a deadline. I note only that I have met every deadline set for me, and in five weeks without income I
 have been given none in return. I ask for the extension below, and for a date by which the Health Service will tell me
 whether I am returning to work.

 7.2 THE EXTENSION
 The letter allows seven days, expiring 7 August 2026, and expressly contemplates a reasonable extension. I request
 one. The letter arrived at 11:43am on 31 July, two hours before a consultation with Dr Ma of which the Health Service
 had notice; because the question set is in issue I cancelled it rather than waste a cost, and will rebook once the set is
 settled. I propose two parts: (a) Dr Ma's questions — 21 days from the Health Service confirming the final question set;
 (b) specialist questions — on a timeframe set once it confirms which it presses and that it will meet the cost. I do not
 seek delay; the exclusion is costing me my income, and it cannot be reasonable to maintain an unpaid exclusion for a
 period created by the Health Service's own requirements.

 1. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS
 This document sets out my proposal for returning to work. It accompanies my response of today's date to the Request
 for Medical Information, and is presented separately so that it can be considered — and, internally, routed — on its own.
 The confirmations I seek are listed at Part 9 of the response. The proposal at section 3 below is also the subject of my
 separate request of today's date under clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement.

 2. THE PROPOSAL
 I have been held out of the workplace since 3 July 2026 without wages, with my accrued leave debited, and self-funding
 the medical costs of this process. G03 clause 1.1 contemplates temporary adjustments which allow an employee to
 "continue work during their recovery," and clause 1.1.1 confirms that workplace rehabilitation support is available to
 employees "who have an injury/illness impacting their current ability to perform their role, with no claim or entitlement to
 compensation (health management case)." Clause 1 provides that "Managers are responsible for ensuring work
 environments and work, do not unreasonably prevent employment for people."

 The Health Service's Workplace rehabilitation standard (QH-IMP-401-5, 7 January 2026) is also engaged. It provides
 that the line manager or delegate shall "identify and actively seek ... meaningful suitable duties, and ensure suitable
 duties are made available wherever reasonably practicable"; that the line manager "is best placed to be the primary
 contact for the worker wherever possible and facilitate the injured workers on-going connection with the workplace"; that
 "regular, transparent and timely communication" be maintained with the worker "whether at work or off work"; and that
 the worker be informed of "the appropriate dispute resolution process to follow in such cases where the worker does not
 agree with elements of a proposed workplace rehabilitation plan or suitable duties program". The standard applies to a
 worker requiring rehabilitation "for either a work or non-work-related injury/illness".

 I have been offered no suitable duties — interim duties were declined in any capacity. I have been held away from the
 workplace rather than connected to it. I have not been informed of any dispute resolution process. I ask that each of
 those be addressed.

 I also record that I was not consulted before the decision of 3 July 2026, or since. Section 47 of the Work Health and
 Safety Act 2011 requires consultation with workers who are "directly affected by a matter relating to work health or
 safety". Section 48 requires that I be given a reasonable opportunity "to contribute to the decision-making process
 relating to the matter". Section 49 requires consultation when identifying hazards and assessing risks, when deciding
 how to eliminate or minimise them, when proposing changes that may affect the health or safety of workers, and when
 making decisions about the procedures for monitoring the health of workers. The present request is a procedure for
 monitoring my health.

 Request for a change in the way I work
 Clause 10.3.2, Certified Agreement (No. 12) 2025 · s 27, Industrial Relations Act 2016 (Qld)
 Cory Lea Shepherd

 1. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS
 This is a request under clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement for a change in the way I work.

 I make it as a separate document, rather than within my response to the Request for Medical Information of 31 July
 2026, so that there is no question about what it is or when it was received.

 Clause 10.3.2 provides that, in accordance with the Industrial Relations Act 2016, an employee "may ask the employer
 for a change in the way the employee works, including the employee's ordinary hours of work". Section 27(1)(c) of that
 Act provides that the request may be for "a change to the way the employee works, for example, the use of different
 equipment as a result of a disability, illness or injury".

 Clause 10.3.3 requires that the request be in writing, state the change in sufficient detail to allow a decision to be made,
 and state the reasons. Parts 2 and 3 below do each of those things.

 I make the request under two separate limbs of section 27(1), and I ask that they be considered separately.

   (a) ORDINARY HOURS — Part 2.1. This is made under section 27(1)(a), which concerns "the employee's ordinary
      hours of work", and under clause 10.3.2, which is in the same terms. That limb stands on its own. It does not
      depend on illness or injury, and neither section 27, nor section 28, nor clause 10.3 makes medical information a
      precondition to making such a request or to deciding one. My reasons for it are matters of rostering history and are
      set out at Part 3.
   (b) THE WAY I WORK — Parts 2.2 to 2.5. These are made under section 27(1)(c), which concerns "a change to the
      way the employee works, for example, the use of different equipment as a result of a disability, illness or injury".
 I separate them because a decision on one is not a decision on the other, and because the question of my ordinary
 hours does not require, and should not await, information sought for a different purpose. If the Health Service is not in a
 position to decide (b) at present, I ask that it decide (a), and say so.

 2. THE CHANGE I AM ASKING FOR

 2.1 MY ORDINARY HOURS
 That my rostered pattern continue at the level at which it has in fact operated over the twelve months preceding the
 Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026 — approximately 0.6 of the shifts of my full-time permanent line of 76
 hours per fortnight, worked from within that line, being the average I have actually worked across those twelve months,
 with the precise figure to be established from the Health Service's own roster and payroll records as set out below. My
 appointment to that line is not varied by this request.

 The Employee Capabilities Checklist describes that level, at Additional Comments 3, as a "reduced pattern of
 approximately six shifts per fortnight", and records that it "is the pattern Mr Shepherd has in fact worked and tolerated
 over the past twelve months without deterioration, and maintaining rather than increasing it best supports recovery while
 minimising risk of exacerbation". The first page records the arrangement as a "continuation of existing arrangement".

 I am not asking for any reduction from the pattern I have been working. I am asking that the existing pattern continue. It
 was set by the Health Service, worked by me, and sustained across twelve months. No concern was raised with me at
 any time that it was insufficient, and no request was made that I work more.

 I record for completeness that my substantive appointment is full-time at 76 hours per fortnight, and that the pattern
 described above is less than that. It is, however, the pattern the Health Service in fact rostered and accepted throughout
 the twelve months in question, and the Employee Capabilities Checklist describes it as a "continuation of existing
 arrangement". Clause 10.3.2 expressly contemplates a request concerning "the employee's ordinary hours of work",

 4. THE DECISION, AND WHO SHOULD MAKE IT
 Clause 10.3.4 provides that the Health Service may grant this request, grant it in part or subject to conditions, or refuse
 it. Clause 10.3.5 provides that it may grant it in part or subject to conditions, or refuse it, "only on reasonable grounds".

 I ask that the decision be made by an officer outside Corporate Services.

 I do not ask that Corporate Services be removed from the management of my employment, and I make no allegation
 against any individual. Part of what this request concerns is the reporting arrangements within Corporate Services, and
 the officers who would otherwise decide it sit within those arrangements. Clause 1.2 of the Code of Conduct for the
 Queensland Public Service provides that a conflict of interest is not wrongdoing in itself, but that failing to disclose and
 manage one is likely to be wrongdoing. Section 89 of the Public Sector Act 2022 is to the same effect.

 The separation I propose is the ordinary one: the clinical material held by Injury Management on a
 medical-in-confidence basis; the decision made outside Corporate Services; implementation — rostering, and putting in
 place whatever is decided — retained within Corporate Services. The officer steps out of the decision, not out of the
 workplace. This requires no restructuring and no finding to be made about anyone.

 I ask that the officer who makes the decision be identified to me, together with the source of the delegation relied on.

 5. THE FRAMEWORK THE DECISION SITS IN
 I set this out for one reason only. Clause 10.3.5 permits the Health Service to grant the request in part or subject to
 conditions, or refuse it, "only on reasonable grounds". Grounds are reasonable against the whole of the law that applies,
 not against the agreement alone. If the request is refused in whole or in part, I would like to be able to understand the
 reasons given under clause 10.3.6 by reference to the same framework the Health Service is applying.

 5.1 THE OBLIGATION
 The Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 provides at section 15(1) that a person must not discriminate "in any variation of the
 terms of work", or "by treating a worker unfavourably in any way in connection with work". Section 15(2) provides that
 "dismissing includes ending the particular work of a person by forced retirement, failure to provide work or otherwise".

 Section 11 provides that indirect discrimination happens if a person imposes a term with which a person with an
 attribute does not or is not able to comply, and which is not reasonable. Impairment is a protected attribute under
 section 7.

 5.2 THE EXEMPTIONS, AND WHAT THEY REQUIRE
 Sections 35 and 36 provide that it is not unlawful to discriminate on the basis of impairment where the person would
 require special services or facilities and supplying them would impose unjustifiable hardship, or where the
 circumstances of the impairment would impose unjustifiable hardship.

 Those provisions are exemptions, and each of them turns on unjustifiable hardship. Section 5 provides that whether
 something would impose unjustifiable hardship depends on all the relevant circumstances of the case, including the
 nature of the services or facilities, their cost and the number of people who would benefit or be disadvantaged, the



Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Request under clause 10.3.2 — decision due within 21 days (cl 10.3.6)                 Page 3

>>> drafts/out/Shepherd_Documents_MSH-INJ-5795_3Aug2026.pdf :: page 17
 financial circumstances of the person, the disruption that supplying them might cause, and the nature of any benefit or
 detriment to all people concerned.

 HR Policy G03 puts the same test in the Health Service's own words, at clause 2: unjustifiable hardship is "tested
 against the whole organisation, not a division or unit within the organisation", and "the onus is on Queensland Health, as
 the employer, to prove an adjustment is unreasonable, not on the person to prove that it is reasonable".

 I would add that the Health Service is a public entity for the purposes of the Human Rights Act 2019, and section 58 of
 that Act requires a public entity to act and make decisions compatibly with human rights and to give proper
 consideration to relevant human rights in doing so.

 5.3 WHY I RAISE IT, AND WHAT I AM NOT DOING
 I have made no complaint under the Anti-Discrimination Act, and this letter is not one. I make no allegation against
 anyone and I ask for no finding to be made about anyone.

 I raise it because the measures at Part 2 are modest ones, and I would like the reasons for any refusal to engage with
 that. On the shifts I attend, the arrangement at 2.2 costs one telephone call. The roster at 2.1 is the roster the Health
 Service already sets. The complaint-handling arrangement at 2.4 is the Health Service's own established process. The
 correspondence routing at 2.5 is what the Employee Capabilities Checklist itself recommends.

 If the Health Service considers that any of the measures would impose unjustifiable hardship, I ask only that it identify
 which measure, and what the hardship is. That is the same thing clause 10.3.6 requires, expressed in the language of
 the Act.

 6. THE TIME FOR THE DECISION
 Clause 10.3.6 provides:

     "The employer must give the employee written notice about its decision within 21 days after receiving the request. If
     the employer decides to grant the request in part or subject to conditions or to refuse the request, the written notice
     about the decision must state the reasons for the decision, outlining the reasonable grounds for granting the request
     in part or subject to conditions or for the refusal."

 Section 28(3) of the Industrial Relations Act 2016 is in the same terms. Section 28(4) provides that a notice granting the
 request in part or subject to conditions, or refusing it, must state the written reasons outlining the reasonable grounds,
 and must state that the Commission has jurisdiction to hear and decide a dispute over the request under chapter 6.
 Section 29 provides that if the written notice is not given within 21 days after the request is received, the employer is
 taken to have decided to refuse the request.

 Twenty-one days from the date of this letter is Monday 24 August 2026.

 I record these provisions because a date has not been available in this matter at any stage. I have asked several times
 to be told when I would know whether I am returning to work, and I have not been given a date. The certified agreement
 provides one, and I would much prefer that the request be dealt with by agreement well before it.

 7. WHAT THIS REQUEST DOES NOT DO
 For completeness:

   (a) This request is separate from my response of the same date to the Request for Medical Information. The matters
      raised there are not made under clause 10.3 and are not answered by a decision under it.
   (b) This request is separate from any dispute notified under clause 1.11 of the certified agreement.
   (c) Nothing in this request is a concession that I am unfit to attend work. I remain willing and available to work, and
      have been since 3 July 2026. Identifying hazards and determining control measures is a function of the Health
      Service under Part 3.1 of the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011, and nothing here relieves the Health Service
      of that function or is offered as a substitute for the workplace assessment I have asked for.

 Conflict of interest, delegation, and the handling of my personal

 Section 89, Public Sector Act 2022 · Code of Conduct clause 1.2
 Cory Lea Shepherd

 Employee reference MSH-INJ-5795

 1. WHAT I AM ASKING, AND WHAT I AM NOT
 I am asking that the decisions being made about my capacity, my attendance and my return to duty be made by an
 officer outside Corporate Services, and that the clinical material be held only by the Injury Management team.

 I address this letter to you because section 89 of the Public Sector Act 2022 makes the chief executive the person to
 whom a conflict is disclosed, and the only person who may authorise an officer to continue to act in a matter affected by
 one. I do not raise it with you in order to escalate it. I raise it with you because, on the terms of the section, there is no
 one else who can answer the questions at Part 3.

 I am not asking that anyone be removed from the management of my employment. I am not asking that anyone be
 stood aside, investigated, or found to have done anything wrong. I make no allegation against any individual and I seek
 no finding about anyone.

 This is not a personal complaint. It is about how the process is being run when an employee is diagnosed with an illness
 and needs managerial support and reasonable adjustment.

 Clause 1.2 of the Code of Conduct for the Queensland Public Service records that having a conflict of interest is not of
 itself wrongdoing, and that what matters is whether it is disclosed and managed. I proceed on that basis, and I ask these
 questions in that spirit.

 2. THE POSITION AS I UNDERSTAND IT
   (a) The letters of 31 July 2026 are written in the first person of the decision-maker — "I am seeking further
      clarification", "I require further information", "I will make a decision regarding your ability to perform your role" — and
      are signed by Mr Scott Hughes, Director, Corporate Services.
   (b) Question 3 of the attached request asks my general practitioner to advise whether I am fit to return "under the
      existing reporting arrangements, including working with and reporting to [my] current line manager". Those reporting
      arrangements sit within Corporate Services.
   (c) The Manager, Switchboard Services — who on 2 July 2026 advised that my return could not be facilitated, and
      asked me to wait for advice as to my next returning shift — reports within that same directorate.
   (d) On 3 October 2025 I made a formal written request for review to the A/Director, Human Resources Business
      Partnering, concerning a process initiated by the officer who has signed the letters of 31 July 2026. My union was
      copied. I do not reopen that matter and I make no submission about it. I record it only because it bears on whether a
      conflict exists and how it must be managed.
   (e) The letter of 7 July 2026 records that my treating practitioner had advised of "unresolved workplace matters
      involving line management", and that the Health Service did not have sufficient information to assess whether they
      presented psychosocial hazards.
 The officer determining my return to duty is therefore the Director of the directorate in which the advice of 2 July 2026
 was given, to whom the officer who gave it reports, and whose own directorate is the subject matter of the
 reporting-arrangements question at question 3.

 I say only that this is a set of circumstances in which a conflict may exist. Whether it does, and how it has been
 managed, is not something I can determine.

 2A. WHAT THE "UNRESOLVED WORKPLACE MATTERS" ARE, AND WHY THEY ARE WORKPLACE MATTERS




Cory Lea Shepherd · MSH-INJ-5795 · Conflict of interest, delegation and information handling                                Page 1

>>> drafts/out/Shepherd_Documents_MSH-INJ-5795_3Aug2026.pdf :: page 24
 The letter of 7 July 2026 records that the Health Service does not have sufficient information to understand the nature of
 the unresolved matters involving line management, or to assess whether they present psychosocial hazards. I take that
 at face value, and I would rather close the gap than argue about it.

 The matters concern how the work is organised and decided, not the character of any officer. They are, in substance:

   (a) how patient safety concerns raised at the switchboard are escalated and answered;
   (b) how changes to the work, the roster and the on-call arrangements have been introduced, and whether affected
      staff were consulted before rather than told afterwards;
   (c) fatigue and recovery between shifts, and how rostering is managed against it; and
   (d) the ability of staff to have genuine input into decisions that affect the work — which the Managing the risk of
      psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 treats as a matter of work design and organisational justice,
      and therefore as a psychosocial hazard in its own right where it is absent.
 Each of those is a workplace matter. None of them can be answered by a medical practitioner writing about me.
 Sections 47 to 49 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 require the Health Service to consult workers who are directly
 affected when identifying hazards, when deciding how to control them, when proposing changes affecting health or
 safety, and when deciding the procedures for monitoring the health of workers. That consultation has not occurred at
 any point since 26 June 2026.

 I record, without argument, that the information gap the Health Service identifies is one only the Health Service can
 close, and that it is being used in the meantime to maintain my exclusion.

 2B. MANAGERIAL SUPPORT AND ADJUSTMENT WHILE I AM UNWELL

 When an employee is certified fit with restrictions, the Health Service's own policies contemplate managerial support
 and reasonable adjustment: G03 clause 1.1 (temporary adjustments so an employee may "continue work during their
 recovery"; clause 1.1.1 extends this to a "health management case" with no compensation claim), and QH-IMP-401-5
 (suitable duties identified and actively sought and "made available wherever reasonably practicable"; the worker's
 connection with the workplace maintained; the dispute resolution process advised — for "either a work or
 non-work-related injury/illness").

 I obtained the checklist the Health Service required in order to facilitate my return. It certified me fit with restrictions.
 What followed was exclusion rather than adjustment: interim duties were declined in any capacity on 15 July 2026, and
 no adjustment plan has been identified to me. The Health Service may seek medical information — but a medical
 process clarifies functional limits; it does not displace the duty to consider adjustments in the meantime. I ask that
 interim adjustments be identified and implemented under the restrictions already certified.

 2C. DUE PROCESS — HOW THE DECISIONS ARE MADE

 Support and adjustment are the substance; due process is how the decisions about them are made: being told what
 power is being used and who decides; a fair opportunity to respond before a serious consequence; a decision-maker
 independent of the matters in issue; consultation as sections 47 to 49 of the Work Health and Safety Act require; and
 deadlines that are not one-sided. On the last point I record only this: I was given seven calendar days on 7 July and
 again on 31 July, each with a consequence attached, while the Health Service advised on 15 July that it was unable to
 commit to a timeframe of its own and on 30 July that it was unable to guarantee my return. I have asked several times
 for a date and have not been given one.

 The Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 calls this organisational justice, and
 treats its absence — including a lack of procedural fairness — as a psychosocial hazard. I do not say any tribunal has
 found a denial of fair process. I say the process described has not been applied to me, and I ask that it be — which is
 what the separation at Part 4 is for.

 3. THE QUESTIONS I ASK
 Section 89(1) of the Public Sector Act 2022 provides that if a public sector employee has an interest that conflicts or
 may conflict with the discharge of the employee's duties, the employee:

      "(a) must disclose the nature of the interest and conflict to the employee's chief executive as soon as practicable
      after the relevant facts come to the employee's knowledge; and (b) must not take action or further action concerning
      a matter that is, or may be, affected by the conflict unless authorised by the employee's chief executive."

   duration. If a written authority is needed for Dr Ma to respond to a specific request, I am
   happy to provide one confined to that purpose.

2. WHAT I NEED IN ORDER TO DO THAT

   2.1 To put a request to Dr Ma, I need the request. Your email states that "further
   clarification is required regarding your functional capacity and the medical restrictions
   identified", but does not identify what is unclear. Dr Ma cannot respond to a request in
   those terms.

   2.2 Could you please provide, in writing:

   (a) the specific questions the Health Service asks Dr Ma to answer, set out as questions;

   (b) for each question, the duty or task to which it relates, identified by reference to the
   Administration Officer, Switchboard Services (AO3) role description, which Dr Ma reviewed
   before completing the checklist;

   (c) what in the 3 July Employee Capability Checklist is said to be insufficient - which
   entry requires clarification, and why the existing entry does not enable the assessment;
   and

   (d) who will consider Dr Ma's response, and the timeframe within which the decision about
   my duties will then be made.

3. WHY THAT SPECIFICITY IS NEEDED

   3.1 Your email states the request is made under the Health Service's obligation to assess
   the medical information "alongside the inherent requirements of the role". I accept that
   the Health Service has its own obligations. Five things follow.

>>> drafts/out/Shepherd_response_30July2026_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 2
  (a) The assessment is task-based, so the questions should be. QH-POL-210 directs
  adjustments to enabling an employee to safely perform the genuine occupational requirements
  of the role, tailored to their circumstances, and reflects the obligation under the Anti-
  Discrimination Act 1991 (Qld) to make reasonable adjustments for an employee with an
  impairment unless doing so would impose unjustifiable hardship. QH-IMP-401-5 makes managers
  responsible for identifying suitable duties, guided by medical information. Each operates
  at the level of identified duties. A refusal of all duties, without identifying which duty
  cannot be performed or adjusted, does not engage that assessment - and a question not tied
  to a duty cannot produce information that either instrument can use.

  (b) Assessing a risk requires identifying the risk. EB12 clause 7.2 and the Managing the
  risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 proceed by identifying a hazard,
  assessing the risk it presents, and considering controls. I am not presently able to
  identify what risk is said to arise, or from which duty - and without that I cannot
  meaningfully participate in the assessment, as consultation under sections 47 to 49 of the
  Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) contemplates.

  (c) The checklist is the Health Service's own instrument. It was required by the Health
  Service and completed by Dr Ma after he reviewed the AO3 role description. If it is now
  insufficient, the entry said to be insufficient should be identifiable, together with what
  the form did not capture.

  (d) The arrangement is not new. I worked in the role on reduced hours within my certified
  capacity for approximately twelve months before 3 July 2026, and the Health Service's
  correspondence of 7 July 2026 records that my restrictions were already being accommodated.
  Could the request please also identify what has changed - that is, which duty is now said
  to be affected in a way it was not during that period.

  (e) The framework identifies hazards in the work, not in the worker. The Code of Practice
  identifies psychosocial hazards by reference to features of work and its management - job
  demands, job control, support, role clarity, change management, workplace relationships and
  organisational justice. EB12 clause 7.2 correspondingly provides for risk assessments of
  workplaces, conducted using the Code and in consultation with workers and health and safety
  representatives. I therefore ask that any assessment framed in psychosocial terms be
  directed to the work and the work system, and that questions to Dr Ma be confined to my
  capacity to perform identified duties.

4. THE RESTRICTIONS AND THE DUTIES

  4.1 Since your email refers to the inherent requirements of the role, I have compared the
  restrictions certified on 3 July with the responsibilities set out in the AO3 role
  description.

  4.2 The role description lists the position's key responsibilities as: attending to
  telephone enquiries and maintaining call queues; collating information and maintaining the
  Omnivista database and SharePoint; supporting the allocation, coordination and fault repair
  of pager units; participating in the emergency response process in accordance with
  emergency code procedures; establishing and maintaining networks and records; exercising
  discretion and judgement to resolve problems within the scope of the role; interacting
  appropriately with the public and service providers; multitasking and operating under
  pressure; contributing to the team; working with limited supervision; treating patients and
  staff fairly; and following safety policies and procedures.

  4.3 First, the restriction on complaint-handling does not correspond to any responsibility
  listed in the role description. If the Health Service considers complaint-handling to be an
  inherent requirement of the position, could you please identify where it appears in the

>>> drafts/out/Shepherd_response_30July2026_MSH-INJ-5795.pdf :: page 3
  role description, or on what other basis it is said to be an inherent requirement.

  4.4 Second, the remaining restrictions - the limits on peak weekday day and afternoon
  shifts, predictable rostering, and a minimum ten-hour break between shifts - go to when I
  work, not to which duties I perform. They do not remove any of the responsibilities listed
  above.

  4.5 I note the role description records that the position is a continuous shift working
  role. I worked that role, on reduced hours and within my certified restrictions, for
  approximately twelve months prior to 3 July 2026, and the correspondence of 7 July 2026
  records that those restrictions were already being accommodated. If the rostering
  restrictions are now said to be incompatible with the role, could you please identify what
  has changed since that period.

  4.6 Third, a reduction in ordinary hours is an arrangement the industrial instruments
  expressly contemplate. Clause 8.2 of the Hospital and Health Service General Employees
  (Queensland Health) Award - State 2015 provides for part-time employment on a regular
  number of ordinary hours, pro rata to full-time conditions, with a minimum of eight
  ordinary hours per fortnight. EB12 clause 10.3 provides that an employee may request a
  change in the way they work, including their ordinary hours, that such a request may be
  refused only on reasonable grounds, and that the employer must give written notice of its
  decision, with reasons, within 21 days.

  4.7 A reduction in hours does not of itself remove any duty from the role, and where such
  an arrangement is made for reasons unrelated to health it does not ordinarily require
  medical clarification or absence from the workplace while it is considered. Could the
  Health Service please identify why the reduced hours certified on 3 July 2026 are treated
  differently - that is, what it is about those hours, as distinct from the reasons for them,
  that prevents the duties of the position from being performed.

  4.8 Accordingly, could the request to Dr Ma please identify which of the responsibilities
  listed at paragraph 4.2 the Health Service says I cannot perform, and which restriction is
  said to prevent it.

6. DECISION-MAKING

   6.1 The Code of Conduct for the Queensland Public Service, made under the Public Sector
