LETTER OF INSTRUCTION — MEDICO-LEGAL REPORT (WC/2024/227)
Cory Lea Shepherd, Appellant (self-represented) · HOLD until the rebooked consultation

To: Dr [Krishnaiah], Consultant Psychiatrist From: Cory Lea Shepherd — Appellant, QIRC matter
WC/2024/227 (self-represented) Re: Letter of instruction — medico-legal report (the "appeal report")

Dear Doctor,

I am the appellant in WC/2024/227 (Shepherd v Workers' Compensation Regulator), an appeal against the
rejection of my workers' compensation claim for a psychological injury. I ask you to prepare a medico-legal
report for that proceeding. This report is SEPARATE from any information provided to Metro South Health
for return-to-work purposes: this report may address causation; the workplace documents must not.

I enclose: (1) a chronology of the workplace events; (2) the pleaded stressors (Amended Statement of
Facts and Contentions, 7 April 2026); (3) the admitted facts extract (Form 24), including that I was rostered
a 7-hour break between shifts on 17–18 March 2024 against a 10-hour minimum, and that the Regulator's
own Reviewing Officer found that rostering "amounted to unreasonable management action" and was
"satisfied [my] employment was a significant contributing factor"; (4) your own clinical records as you hold
them.

The legal test: an injury is compensable if employment is "A SIGNIFICANT contributing factor" (s 32(1),
Workers' Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003). Employment need not be the only or main factor;
other contributors may coexist.

I ask that your report address, in your own clinical judgment:

1. Diagnosis, and the date of onset as best the clinical record establishes it (I note your record of 24
October 2024 and the escalation of medication at that time).

2. Whether my employment — in particular the pleaded matters: the rostering and fatigue events (including
the 17–18 March 2024 break), the sustained workload and complaint-exposure conditions of the
Switchboard role, and the non-response to the concerns and reports I raised — was A SIGNIFICANT
contributing factor to the onset of the condition, and your clinical reasoning.

3. CHRONOLOGY, expressly: the diagnosis was recorded on 24 October 2024. The personal events
sometimes referred to in my history (a separation and related matters) began in December 2024 and after.
Please state plainly the significance, if any, those later events could have for the ONSET of a condition
diagnosed before they occurred, and distinguish (if you consider it clinically appropriate) between the
CAUSE of onset and factors affecting the subsequent COURSE of the condition.

4. Any clinical observations relevant to the reliability of my account — including that I continued working a
reduced pattern against clinical advice through 2025, funding the shortfall from my own leave.

5. The mechanism: from a clinical perspective, how conditions of the kind described in the enclosures
(sustained high demand, low control, absent support, unresolved complaints, fatigue) contribute to
conditions of this kind.

Please do not address current work capacity or adjustments in this report — those are dealt with
separately. I am responsible for your fee for this report; please provide an estimate. I am conscious you
may be asked to produce your file in the proceeding; please write on the basis that the report and its
reasoning may be tested.

Yours sincerely, Cory Lea Shepherd · 0417 400 227 · coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

# CHANGELOG — consultation, support/adjustment and due process frame
**1 August 2026.** Applied to the two documents that carry the frame. **Nothing else changed.**
⚠️ **File naming:** the task named `LETTER_A_*` / `LETTER_B_*`. **Not created** — that would fork
the live layer and defeat `CURRENT.md`. The edits went into the existing equivalents:
**Letter A = document 1**, `RFMI_ALLOCATION_AND_PROPOSAL.txt`; **Letter B = document 4**,
`LETTER_CONFLICT_AND_INFORMATION.txt`.

---

## LETTER A — RFMI response (14pp, unchanged length)

| Where | What was added |
|---|---|
| **Part 4.2** (Q3) | The 7 July "insufficient information" quote, and that **the gap is closed by the employer consulting and assessing, not by a GP**. WHS ss 47–49. Then, in four lines and without a complaint history, **what the "unresolved workplace matters" actually are**: escalation of patient safety concerns; changes to work and roster introduced without consultation; fatigue and recovery; staff input into decisions. Framed as *why the assessment belongs with the Health Service* |
| **Part 6 opening** | ⭐ **"This is not a personal complaint about any individual."** No allegation, no finding sought. Concern is **how the process is being run** |
| **Part 6** | ⭐ **Managerial support and adjustment** — G03 cl 1.1 "continue work during their recovery"; QH-IMP-401-5 suitable duties actively sought and made available, connection maintained, **"either a work or non-work-related injury/illness"**. *"What followed was exclusion rather than adjustment."* Raised **as a question about process, not about people** |
| **Part 6** | ⭐ **Due process** — what power, who decides, opportunity to respond, consultation, deadlines not one-sided, independent decision-maker. Code 2022 **organisational justice**. ⛔ **"I do not say that any tribunal has found a denial of fair process."** |
| **Part 6** | Pointer to the separate Chief Executive letter, so the two are not read as duplicates |

## LETTER B — conflict of interest letter (3pp → **5pp**)

| Where | What was added |
|---|---|
| **Part 1** | *"This is not a personal complaint. It is about how the process is being run when an employee is diagnosed with an illness and needs managerial support and reasonable adjustment."* |
| ⭐ **New Part 2A** | **What the "unresolved workplace matters" are** — patient safety escalation; workplace, roster and on-call change without prior consultation; fatigue and recovery; **staff input into decisions**, which the Code treats as work design and organisational justice. Then **WHS ss 47–49**, and that **only the Health Service can close its own information gap** — which is meanwhile being used to maintain the exclusion |
| ⭐ **New Part 2B** | **Managerial support and adjustment while unwell** — G03 cll 1, 1.1, **1.1.1 "health management case"**; QH-IMP-401-5 §2.2 and §2.3. *"I obtained the checklist the Health Service required in order to facilitate my return. It certified me fit with restrictions. What followed was exclusion rather than adjustment."* Interim duties declined **15 July**. ⭐ *"a medical process clarifies functional limits; it does not displace the duty to consider adjustments in the meantime"* — **asks for interim adjustments now** |
| ⭐ **New Part 2C** | **Due process**, (a)–(e). Plus the **one-sided deadlines** point on the record: seven days on 7 July and again on 31 July, each with a consequence, against *"unable to commit to a timeframe"* (15 July) and *"unable to guarantee"* (30 July). ⛔ No claim of a finding |
| ⭐ **New Part 6.1** | **The careful paragraph.** Records that he has raised patient safety, workplace change, fatigue and staff-input concerns; that he is entitled to raise them and to be consulted; the detriment since 3 July and 13 July; that the matters remain unassessed while decisions sit in the directorate they concern. ⛔ **"I am not making a claim in this letter and I ask for no finding."** Union noted. *"I do not abandon my employment or any entitlement."* |

## ⚠️ ONE DEPARTURE FROM THE TASK, AND WHY
The task asked for the adverse-action paragraph **in both** documents. ⭐ **It is in Letter B only.**

**Letter A goes to Injury Management and is answered by clinicians.** General protections language in
a medical-information response is the wrong register, and it is the one paragraph most likely to be
forwarded onward out of context. **Letter B is copied to Petering and is where the process question
lives**, so the record is made there — once, carefully, and to the right readers. Letter A carries the
detriment as fact without the rights framing.

NOTICE OF DISPUTE — STAGE 1
Clause 1.11.2(a), Queensland Health Employing Office Certified Agreement (No. 12) 2025

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health

To:      Ms Chloe Taylor, Manager, Switchboard Services
         (immediate supervisor, for the purposes of clause 1.11.2(a))
         Human Resources, Logan Bayside Health Network — LBH.HRTeam1@health.qld.gov.au
Cc:      Ms Emily Petering, Industrial Officer, Together Queensland
         Mr Heath Moran, Together Queensland
Date:    3 August 2026
Subject: Notice of dispute under clause 1.11 — application of the certified agreement to my
         attendance, roster, leave and pay from 26 June 2026

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  WHAT THIS NOTICE IS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This notice informs you, as my immediate supervisor, of the existence of a dispute, in accordance
with clause 1.11.2(a) of the certified agreement.

Clause 1.11.2 provides that where there is "any disagreement between the parties as to the
interpretation, application or implementation of this Agreement", the procedure in that clause
applies. Clause 1.11.1 records that the objectives are "the avoidance and resolution of any
disputes … by measures based on the provision of information and explanation, consultation,
co-operation and negotiation", and that "the emphasis will be on finding a resolution at the
earliest possible stage in the process".

That is what I am seeking. I would prefer this resolved at Stage 1 and I am available to discuss
it at any time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  THE SUBJECT MATTER OF THE DISPUTE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The dispute concerns the application and implementation of the certified agreement to my
employment from 26 June 2026, in the following respects.

2.1  ATTENDANCE AND ROSTERED DUTY

I have not been permitted to attend my rostered shifts since 3 July 2026. On 2 July 2026 I was
advised that the Health Service was "unable to facilitate" my return until a completed Employee
Capacity Certificate was received, and asked to "wait for my advice to when your next returning
shift will be".

The Employee Capability Checklist was returned to the Injury Management team on 3 July 2026 at
2:30pm and, a section having been identified as missing, resubmitted at 3:06pm that afternoon.
The letter of 7 July 2026 records both times. The same letter records that "you have been
certified fit to return to work effective from 3 July 2026". I asked the same afternoon to be
told whether I should attend. I have not received an answer to that question.

The condition on which the advice of 2 July 2026 was expressed has therefore been satisfied. I
have asked which instrument is relied on to maintain the position since, and have not received an
answer.

2.2  LEAVE

Since 3 July 2026 my accrued leave has been debited, and from 13 July 2026 I have been recorded
as absent without pay, in respect of a period in which I have been willing and available to work
and have said so in writing. I dispute the application of the leave provisions of the certified
agreement to that period.

2.3  ROSTER

I dispute the position, so far as it is taken, that my rostered pattern over the preceding twelve
months is inconsistent with the requirements of my role. That pattern was set by the Health
Service and worked without any concern being raised with me.

2.4  WORK HEALTH AND SAFETY MATTERS RAISED

Clause 7.1.11 provides that "the parties commit to ensure that appropriate feedback is provided
to employees who raise workplace health and safety matters". Clause 7.1.5 records the parties'
agreement to address, among other issues, "management of ill or injured employees",
"psychosocial issues and implementation of Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code
of Practice 2022", and "injured workers to have the opportunity to be re-trained in alternative
areas/departments". I have raised matters within each of those descriptions and have not received
feedback on them.

2.5  PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK ASSESSMENT

Clause 7.2 provides for psychosocial risk assessments conducted using the resources in the
Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022, "in consultation with
workers and Health and Safety Representatives". I have asked for a workplace risk assessment and
none has been provided.

I record that the Health Service identified this itself. The letter of 7 July 2026 states:

     "it is noted that your treating medical practitioner has advised that there are unresolved
     workplace matters involving line management. At this stage, the Health Service does not have
     sufficient information to understand the nature of these matters or assess whether they
     present any psychosocial hazards or risks that may affect your proposed return to work."

That was written on 7 July 2026, with further information said to be required "to enable the
Health Service to assess any identified risks". So far as I am aware, no assessment has been
undertaken in the four weeks since. I ask that one be conducted, and that I be consulted in it,
as clause 7.2.2 contemplates.

2.6  THE PROCESS ITSELF

Since 26 June 2026 I have been asked to provide medical information about myself, held out of my
rostered shifts, had my accrued leave debited and then been recorded as absent without pay, and
told that a decision will be made regarding my ability to perform my role.

The letter of 15 July 2026 refers to employees "being managed through Health Management
processes". That is the only description of this process I have been given.

I have a phrase. I do not have a process.

I ask to be told, in relation to it:

  (a)  the instrument under which it is conducted — the Act, directive, clause of the certified
       agreement, or policy;
  (b)  what its steps are, and where they are published;
  (c)  who the decision-maker is; and
  (d)  what decision it ends in.

I am not raising this as a complaint about anyone. I raise it because I cannot follow a process
properly, or exercise whatever rights attach to it, without knowing those four things. If the
answer to any of them is that there is none, that is also something I need to know.

The Workplace rehabilitation standard (QH-IMP-401-5) requires that a worker be informed of "the
appropriate dispute resolution process to follow"; I have not been informed of any. Clause 1.11.1
makes "the provision of information and explanation" an objective of this procedure — this is a
request for exactly that, and it is the first one I make.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  THE STATUS QUO WHILE THE PROCEDURE IS FOLLOWED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Clause 1.11.4 provides:

     "Subject to legislation, while the dispute procedure is being followed, normal work is to
     continue except in the case of a genuine safety issue. The status quo existing before the
     emergence of a dispute is to continue whilst the procedure is being followed. No party shall
     be prejudiced as to the final settlement by the continuation of work."

The status quo before the emergence of this dispute was that I was rostered and working. I ask
that I be returned to my rostered shifts while the procedure is followed, in accordance with that
clause. I am not asking for anything to be decided in my favour by doing so; clause 1.11.4
expressly provides that no party is prejudiced as to the final settlement by the continuation of
work.

I anticipate the Health Service may say that the exception for "a genuine safety issue" applies.
If that position is taken, I ask that it be put in writing and that the following be identified,
so that it can be discussed at Stage 1:

  (a)  the hazard identified, and the assessment on which it was identified;
  (b)  the control measures considered, in the order required by section 36 of the Work Health
       and Safety Regulation 2011, and why each was rejected; and
  (c)  why the restrictions certified on the Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026 do
       not address it.

I record that I hold a current certificate addressing my capacity, that I have proposed controls
in writing, and that I have asked for the workplace assessment which would resolve the question.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  WHAT I ASK AT STAGE 1
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  (a)  That I be told, in relation to the "Health Management processes" referred to in the letter

  (b)  That I be told whether I am suspended from duty. If I am, I ask to be told by whom, under

REQUEST FOR A CHANGE IN THE WAY I WORK
Clause 10.3.2, Queensland Health Employing Office Certified Agreement (No. 12) 2025
Section 27, Industrial Relations Act 2016 (Qld)

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
Employee reference MSH-INJ-5795

To:      Human Resources, Logan Bayside Health Network
         LBH.HRTeam1@health.qld.gov.au
Date:    3 August 2026

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is a request under clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement for a change in the way I work.

I make it as a separate document, rather than within my response to the Request for Medical
Information of 31 July 2026, so that there is no question about what it is or when it was
received.

Clause 10.3.2 provides that, in accordance with the Industrial Relations Act 2016, an employee
"may ask the employer for a change in the way the employee works, including the employee's
ordinary hours of work". Section 27(1)(c) of that Act provides that the request may be for "a
change to the way the employee works, for example, the use of different equipment as a result of
a disability, illness or injury".

Clause 10.3.3 requires that the request be in writing, state the change in sufficient detail to
allow a decision to be made, and state the reasons. Parts 2 and 3 below do each of those things.

I make the request under two separate limbs of section 27(1), and I ask that they be considered
separately.

  (a)  ORDINARY HOURS — Part 2.1. This is made under section 27(1)(a), which concerns "the
       employee's ordinary hours of work", and under clause 10.3.2, which is in the same terms.
       That limb stands on its own. It does not depend on illness or injury, and neither section
       27, nor section 28, nor clause 10.3 makes medical information a precondition to making
       such a request or to deciding one. My reasons for it are matters of rostering history and
       are set out at Part 3.

  (b)  THE WAY I WORK — Parts 2.2 to 2.5. These are made under section 27(1)(c), which concerns
       "a change to the way the employee works, for example, the use of different equipment as a
       result of a disability, illness or injury".

I separate them because a decision on one is not a decision on the other, and because the
question of my ordinary hours does not require, and should not await, information sought for a
different purpose. If the Health Service is not in a position to decide (b) at present, I ask
that it decide (a), and say so.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  THE CHANGE I AM ASKING FOR
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2.1  MY ORDINARY HOURS

That my rostered pattern continue at the level at which it has in fact operated over the twelve
months preceding the Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026 — approximately 0.6 of the
shifts of my full-time permanent line of 76 hours per fortnight, worked from within that line,
being the average I have actually worked across those twelve months, with the precise figure to
be established from the Health Service's own roster and payroll records as set out below. My
appointment to that line is not varied by this request.

The Employee Capabilities Checklist describes that level, at Additional Comments 3, as a
"reduced pattern of approximately six shifts per fortnight", and records that it "is the pattern
Mr Shepherd has in fact worked and tolerated over the past twelve months without deterioration,
and maintaining rather than increasing it best supports recovery while minimising risk of
exacerbation". The first page records the arrangement as a "continuation of existing
arrangement".

I am not asking for any reduction from the pattern I have been working. I am asking that the
existing pattern continue. It was set by the Health Service, worked by me, and sustained across
twelve months. No concern was raised with me at any time that it was insufficient, and no request
was made that I work more.

I record for completeness that my substantive appointment is full-time at 76 hours per fortnight,
and that the pattern described above is less than that. It is, however, the pattern the Health
Service in fact rostered and accepted throughout the twelve months in question, and the Employee
Capabilities Checklist describes it as a "continuation of existing arrangement". Clause 10.3.2
expressly contemplates a request concerning "the employee's ordinary hours of work", which is why
I have made the request under that clause rather than assuming the position.

If the Health Service takes the view that the requirements of the role cannot be met on that
pattern, I ask that it identify what changed, and when, given that the pattern operated for twelve
months without any concern being raised with me.

The Health Service holds the roster and payroll records from which the precise figure can be
established. I ask that it be established from those records, and that the figure so established
be the one used.

I also record that a temporary reduction of hours was raised with me by the Health Service
itself, as a form of support, in the course of a discussion recorded in writing on 30 June 2025.
I did not take it up at the time. I mention it only to show that an adjustment of this kind has
been contemplated within Switchboard Services before, and is not a novel proposal.

2.2  THE WAY I WORK — ATTENDANCE CONFIRMATION

(a)  A telephone call one hour before each rostered shift, to confirm that I am attending.

(b)  If that call is not answered, or attendance is not confirmed, a second call.

(c)  If attendance is still not confirmed after the second call, the on-call operator is
     contacted and cover is arranged for the shift.

The measure is contingent, not standing. The on-call is engaged only if the two calls do not
produce a confirmation, so it carries no cost on any shift I attend. On the shifts I do attend,
which is most of them, the arrangement costs one telephone call.

An on-call arrangement already exists in the unit. On 15 April 2024 the team was advised that
after-hours on call had been added, with the days highlighted on the roster and a contact process
for urgent matters. What I am asking for is the application of a mechanism Switchboard Services
already operates, not the creation of a new one.

To be clear about what this is and is not: it is a confirmation of attendance, of the kind any
roster requires, made early enough to be useful. It is not an assessment of my condition, and I
am not asking that colleagues on shift observe, assess or report on my mental state. That would
place a burden on staff who are not qualified to carry it, would require my health information to
be known to co-workers, and would itself be a workplace stressor. No colleague needs to know
anything about my health for (a) to (c) to work. They need only know whether the shift is
confirmed.

2.3  THE WAY I WORK — IN-SHIFT ESCALATION

A defined escalation pathway which I may initiate during a shift if my condition is acutely
exacerbated — including who assumes the board and how the shift is closed out — so that the
response is planned rather than improvised.

2.4  THE WAY I WORK — COMPLAINT HANDLING

Continuation of the existing arrangement recorded in the Health Service's own correspondence:
immediate escalation of complaints received by Switchboard staff to the Client Liaison Officer
and/or the Manager, Switchboard Services. This is the Health Service's established process and it
requires no change to anything.

2.5  THE WAY I WORK — CORRESPONDENCE ROUTING

That injury management correspondence concerning me be directed through the Injury Management
team, Human Resources. This is what the Employee Capabilities Checklist itself recommends at
Additional Comments 4(c): "return-to-work coordination and correspondence through the Injury
Management team, Human Resources."

2.6  REVIEW

That the arrangement be reviewed at six weeks, or earlier if either party considers it necessary.

I am willing to discuss any of the above, and any alternative the Health Service or my treating
practitioners consider more appropriate. If the Health Service would prefer a graduated
commencement, I am willing to return on a graduated basis by agreement.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  THE REASONS FOR THE CHANGE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3.1  The pattern was sustained out of my own leave, and that is what ran out. The roster was
designed by the Health Service. Where my condition was exacerbated I managed it myself, by sick
or annual leave; no adjustment was sought and none was provided. That is why, on 3 July 2026, my
paid sick leave was exhausted — in the course of managing, without assistance, a condition
arising in the workplace.

3.2  The measures replace that with a process. They do not change the roster; they replace an
arrangement under which exacerbations are absorbed by my leave balances with one under which they
are managed. Distress rises as a rostered shift approaches, and there have been occasions where I
have called in at short notice; a late call leaves the board short and the preceding shift unable
to leave. The sequence at 2.2 establishes non-attendance an hour ahead instead.

3.3  It is directed at the only matter ever raised with me — attendance and lateness. No concern
about the quality of my work has ever been put to me, and the correspondence of 31 July 2026
records that the Health Service is not aware of any performance or conduct matters raised for
management. Had these measures been in place, they would have addressed a substantial part of the
attendance history in the correspondence of 8 September 2025.

3.4  The applicable policy contemplates exactly this. G03 clause 1.1 provides temporary
adjustments so an employee may "continue work during their recovery", and clause 1 makes managers
responsible for ensuring work environments "do not unreasonably prevent employment for people".
The adjustment is the thing that allows work to continue while recovery occurs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  THE DECISION, AND WHO SHOULD MAKE IT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Clause 10.3.4 provides that the Health Service may grant this request, grant it in part or
subject to conditions, or refuse it. Clause 10.3.5 provides that it may grant it in part or
subject to conditions, or refuse it, "only on reasonable grounds".

I ask that the decision be made by an officer outside Corporate Services.

I do not ask that Corporate Services be removed from the management of my employment, and I make
no allegation against any individual. Part of what this request concerns is the reporting
arrangements within Corporate Services, and the officers who would otherwise decide it sit within
those arrangements. Clause 1.2 of the Code of Conduct for the Queensland Public Service provides
that a conflict of interest is not wrongdoing in itself, but that failing to disclose and manage
one is likely to be wrongdoing. Section 89 of the Public Sector Act 2022 is to the same effect.

The separation I propose is the ordinary one: the clinical material held by Injury Management on
a medical-in-confidence basis; the decision made outside Corporate Services; implementation —
rostering, and putting in place whatever is decided — retained within Corporate Services. The
officer steps out of the decision, not out of the workplace. This requires no restructuring and
no finding to be made about anyone.

I ask that the officer who makes the decision be identified to me, together with the source of
the delegation relied on.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  THE FRAMEWORK THE DECISION SITS IN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I set this out for one reason only. Clause 10.3.5 permits the Health Service to grant the request
in part or subject to conditions, or refuse it, "only on reasonable grounds". Grounds are
reasonable against the whole of the law that applies, not against the agreement alone. If the
request is refused in whole or in part, I would like to be able to understand the reasons given
under clause 10.3.6 by reference to the same framework the Health Service is applying.

5.1  THE OBLIGATION

The Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 provides at section 15(1) that a person must not discriminate
"in any variation of the terms of work", or "by treating a worker unfavourably in any way in
connection with work". Section 15(2) provides that "dismissing includes ending the particular
work of a person by forced retirement, failure to provide work or otherwise".

Section 11 provides that indirect discrimination happens if a person imposes a term with which a
person with an attribute does not or is not able to comply, and which is not reasonable.
Impairment is a protected attribute under section 7.

5.2  THE EXEMPTIONS, AND WHAT THEY REQUIRE

Sections 35 and 36 provide that it is not unlawful to discriminate on the basis of impairment
where the person would require special services or facilities and supplying them would impose
unjustifiable hardship, or where the circumstances of the impairment would impose unjustifiable
hardship.

Those provisions are exemptions, and each of them turns on unjustifiable hardship. Section 5
provides that whether something would impose unjustifiable hardship depends on all the relevant
circumstances of the case, including the nature of the services or facilities, their cost and the
number of people who would benefit or be disadvantaged, the financial circumstances of the
person, the disruption that supplying them might cause, and the nature of any benefit or
detriment to all people concerned.

HR Policy G03 puts the same test in the Health Service's own words, at clause 2: unjustifiable
hardship is "tested against the whole organisation, not a division or unit within the
organisation", and "the onus is on Queensland Health, as the employer, to prove an adjustment is
unreasonable, not on the person to prove that it is reasonable".

I would add that the Health Service is a public entity for the purposes of the Human Rights Act
2019, and section 58 of that Act requires a public entity to act and make decisions compatibly
with human rights and to give proper consideration to relevant human rights in doing so.

5.3  WHY I RAISE IT, AND WHAT I AM NOT DOING

I have made no complaint under the Anti-Discrimination Act, and this letter is not one. I make no
allegation against anyone and I ask for no finding to be made about anyone.

I raise it because the measures at Part 2 are modest ones, and I would like the reasons for any
refusal to engage with that. On the shifts I attend, the arrangement at 2.2 costs one telephone
call. The roster at 2.1 is the roster the Health Service already sets. The complaint-handling
arrangement at 2.4 is the Health Service's own established process. The correspondence routing at
2.5 is what the Employee Capabilities Checklist itself recommends.

If the Health Service considers that any of the measures would impose unjustifiable hardship, I
ask only that it identify which measure, and what the hardship is. That is the same thing clause
10.3.6 requires, expressed in the language of the Act.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  THE TIME FOR THE DECISION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Clause 10.3.6 provides:

     "The employer must give the employee written notice about its decision within 21 days after
     receiving the request. If the employer decides to grant the request in part or subject to
     conditions or to refuse the request, the written notice about the decision must state the
     reasons for the decision, outlining the reasonable grounds for granting the request in part
     or subject to conditions or for the refusal."

Section 28(3) of the Industrial Relations Act 2016 is in the same terms. Section 28(4) provides
that a notice granting the request in part or subject to conditions, or refusing it, must state
the written reasons outlining the reasonable grounds, and must state that the Commission has
jurisdiction to hear and decide a dispute over the request under chapter 6. Section 29 provides
that if the written notice is not given within 21 days after the request is received, the
employer is taken to have decided to refuse the request.

Twenty-one days from the date of this letter is Monday 24 August 2026.

I record these provisions because a date has not been available in this matter at any stage. I
have asked several times to be told when I would know whether I am returning to work, and I have
not been given a date. The certified agreement provides one, and I would much prefer that the
request be dealt with by agreement well before it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  WHAT THIS REQUEST DOES NOT DO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

For completeness:

(a)  This request is separate from my response of the same date to the Request for Medical
     Information. The matters raised there are not made under clause 10.3 and are not answered by
     a decision under it.

(b)  This request is separate from any dispute notified under clause 1.11 of the certified
     agreement.

(c)  Nothing in this request is a concession that I am unfit to attend work. I remain willing and
     available to work, and have been since 3 July 2026. Identifying hazards and determining
     control measures is a function of the Health Service under Part 3.1 of the Work Health and
     Safety Regulation 2011, and nothing here relieves the Health Service of that function or is
     offered as a substitute for the workplace assessment I have asked for.

(d)  I make this request without waiver of any entitlement, and it is not to be treated as a
     request for leave of any kind.

(e)  For the avoidance of doubt, the request at Part 2.1 concerning my ordinary hours is not made
     conditional on the provision of any medical information, and I ask that it not be decided on
     that footing. If the Health Service considers it cannot decide Part 2.1 without medical
     information, I ask that it identify the provision that makes such information a
     precondition to a decision under clause 10.3.4.

I confirm again that I am engaging with this process and want to return to work.

Yours sincerely,


Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital

CONFLICT OF INTEREST, DELEGATION, AND THE HANDLING OF MY PERSONAL INFORMATION
Section 89, Public Sector Act 2022 — Code of Conduct clause 1.2

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health
Employee reference MSH-INJ-5795

To:      Ms Noelle Cridland, Chief Executive, Metro South Health
Date:    3 August 2026

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  WHAT I AM ASKING, AND WHAT I AM NOT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I am asking that the decisions being made about my capacity, my attendance and my return to duty
be made by an officer outside Corporate Services, and that the clinical material be held only by
the Injury Management team.

I address this letter to you because section 89 of the Public Sector Act 2022 makes the chief
executive the person to whom a conflict is disclosed, and the only person who may authorise an
officer to continue to act in a matter affected by one. I do not raise it with you in order to
escalate it. I raise it with you because, on the terms of the section, there is no one else who
can answer the questions at Part 3.

I am not asking that anyone be removed from the management of my employment. I am not asking that
anyone be stood aside, investigated, or found to have done anything wrong. I make no allegation
against any individual and I seek no finding about anyone.

This is not a personal complaint. It is about how the process is being run when an employee is
diagnosed with an illness and needs managerial support and reasonable adjustment.

Clause 1.2 of the Code of Conduct for the Queensland Public Service records that having a
conflict of interest is not of itself wrongdoing, and that what matters is whether it is
disclosed and managed. I proceed on that basis, and I ask these questions in that spirit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  THE POSITION AS I UNDERSTAND IT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  (a)  The letters of 31 July 2026 are written in the first person of the decision-maker — "I am
       seeking further clarification", "I require further information", "I will make a decision
       regarding your ability to perform your role" — and are signed by Mr Scott Hughes,
       Director, Corporate Services.

  (b)  Question 3 of the attached request asks my general practitioner to advise whether I am
       fit to return "under the existing reporting arrangements, including working with and
       reporting to [my] current line manager". Those reporting arrangements sit within
       Corporate Services.

  (c)  The Manager, Switchboard Services — who on 2 July 2026 advised that my return could not
       be facilitated, and asked me to wait for advice as to my next returning shift — reports
       within that same directorate.

  (d)  On 3 October 2025 I made a formal written request for review to the A/Director, Human
       Resources Business Partnering, concerning a process initiated by the officer who has
       signed the letters of 31 July 2026. My union was copied. I do not reopen that matter and
       I make no submission about it. I record it only because it bears on whether a conflict
       exists and how it must be managed.

  (e)  The letter of 7 July 2026 records that my treating practitioner had advised of
       "unresolved workplace matters involving line management", and that the Health Service did
       not have sufficient information to assess whether they presented psychosocial hazards.

The officer determining my return to duty is therefore the Director of the directorate in which
the advice of 2 July 2026 was given, to whom the officer who gave it reports, and whose own
directorate is the subject matter of the reporting-arrangements question at question 3.

I say only that this is a set of circumstances in which a conflict may exist. Whether it does,
and how it has been managed, is not something I can determine.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2A. WHAT THE "UNRESOLVED WORKPLACE MATTERS" ARE, AND WHY THEY ARE WORKPLACE MATTERS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The letter of 7 July 2026 records that the Health Service does not have sufficient information
to understand the nature of the unresolved matters involving line management, or to assess
whether they present psychosocial hazards. I take that at face value, and I would rather close
the gap than argue about it.

The matters concern how the work is organised and decided, not the character of any officer.
They are, in substance:

  (a)  how patient safety concerns raised at the switchboard are escalated and answered;

  (b)  how changes to the work, the roster and the on-call arrangements have been introduced,
       and whether affected staff were consulted before rather than told afterwards;

  (c)  fatigue and recovery between shifts, and how rostering is managed against it; and

  (d)  the ability of staff to have genuine input into decisions that affect the work — which
       the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 treats as a
       matter of work design and organisational justice, and therefore as a psychosocial hazard
       in its own right where it is absent.

Each of those is a workplace matter. None of them can be answered by a medical practitioner
writing about me. Sections 47 to 49 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 require the Health
Service to consult workers who are directly affected when identifying hazards, when deciding how
to control them, when proposing changes affecting health or safety, and when deciding the
procedures for monitoring the health of workers. That consultation has not occurred at any point
since 26 June 2026.

I record, without argument, that the information gap the Health Service identifies is one only
the Health Service can close, and that it is being used in the meantime to maintain my exclusion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2B. MANAGERIAL SUPPORT AND ADJUSTMENT WHILE I AM UNWELL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When an employee is certified fit with restrictions, the Health Service's own policies
contemplate managerial support and reasonable adjustment: G03 clause 1.1 (temporary adjustments
so an employee may "continue work during their recovery"; clause 1.1.1 extends this to a "health
management case" with no compensation claim), and QH-IMP-401-5 (suitable duties identified and
actively sought and "made available wherever reasonably practicable"; the worker's connection
with the workplace maintained; the dispute resolution process advised — for "either a work or
non-work-related injury/illness").

I obtained the checklist the Health Service required in order to facilitate my return. It
certified me fit with restrictions. What followed was exclusion rather than adjustment: interim
duties were declined in any capacity on 15 July 2026, and no adjustment plan has been identified
to me. The Health Service may seek medical information — but a medical process clarifies
functional limits; it does not displace the duty to consider adjustments in the meantime. I ask
that interim adjustments be identified and implemented under the restrictions already certified.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2C. DUE PROCESS — HOW THE DECISIONS ARE MADE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Support and adjustment are the substance; due process is how the decisions about them are made:
being told what power is being used and who decides; a fair opportunity to respond before a
serious consequence; a decision-maker independent of the matters in issue; consultation as
sections 47 to 49 of the Work Health and Safety Act require; and deadlines that are not
one-sided. On the last point I record only this: I was given seven calendar days on 7 July and
again on 31 July, each with a consequence attached, while the Health Service advised on 15 July
that it was unable to commit to a timeframe of its own and on 30 July that it was unable to
guarantee my return. I have asked several times for a date and have not been given one.

The Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice 2022 calls this
organisational justice, and treats its absence — including a lack of procedural fairness — as a
psychosocial hazard. I do not say any tribunal has found a denial of fair process. I say the
process described has not been applied to me, and I ask that it be — which is what the
separation at Part 4 is for.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  THE QUESTIONS I ASK
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section 89(1) of the Public Sector Act 2022 provides that if a public sector employee has an
interest that conflicts or may conflict with the discharge of the employee's duties, the
employee:

     "(a) must disclose the nature of the interest and conflict to the employee's chief executive
     as soon as practicable after the relevant facts come to the employee's knowledge; and
     (b) must not take action or further action concerning a matter that is, or may be, affected
     by the conflict unless authorised by the employee's chief executive."

I ask the Health Service to confirm:

  (a)  whether any disclosure has been made under section 89(1)(a) in relation to the decisions
       concerning my attendance, my pay and my return to duty;

  (b)  whether any authorisation has been given under section 89(1)(b) for an officer to take, or
       to continue to take, action concerning those matters;

  (c)  who holds the delegation for those decisions, and the source and instrument of that
       delegation;

  (d)  whether the advice of 2 July 2026 and the decision of 3 July 2026 were made with the
       knowledge or approval of the officer now determining my return to duty; and

  (e)  whether any conflict has been identified and recorded, and if so, how it is being managed.

I ask these questions in writing because I have asked them before, in my email of 28 July 2026,
and have not received an answer.

If no authorisation has been given under section 89(1)(b), I ask that you consider the direction
contemplated by section 89(2), and that in the meantime the decisions described at Part 2 be
allocated to an officer outside Corporate Services.

I am conscious that this is a request that you exercise a function under the Act, and not a
request that anything be found about anyone. If the answer to each of (a) to (e) is that the
matter has been dealt with, that answer will resolve it entirely and I will take it no further.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  THE SEPARATION I PROPOSE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I propose the ordinary separation of functions. It requires no restructuring, removes no one from
the management of my employment, and requires no finding to be made about anyone.

  (a)  THE CLINICAL MATERIAL — held exclusively by the Injury Management team, Human Resources,
       on a medical-in-confidence basis. Corporate Services would not hold, and would not have
       access to, the clinical material. This is what the Employee Capabilities Checklist itself
       recommends at Additional Comments 4(c): "return-to-work coordination and correspondence
       through the Injury Management team, Human Resources."

  (b)  THE DECISION — any decision concerning my capacity or my return to duty made by an officer
       outside Corporate Services.

  (c)  IMPLEMENTATION — Corporate Services retains the operational role: rostering me, putting in
       place whatever adjustments are decided, and the ordinary day-to-day management of my work.
       My line manager would receive the adjustments to be implemented, not the clinical
       information behind them.

The officer steps out of the decision, not out of the workplace.

Metro South Health is a large organisation and I do not anticipate that this would present any
difficulty.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  MY PERSONAL INFORMATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The information sought by the request of 31 July 2026 is sensitive health information about me.
I ask:

  (a)  that it be held by the Injury Management team, used only for the purpose for which it was
       collected, and not provided to Corporate Services — what Corporate Services requires in
       order to roster me and implement adjustments is the adjustments themselves, not the
       diagnosis or the clinical reasoning behind them;

  (b)  to be told who has had access to the medical material already held about me, who will
       have access to the further material, and whether it is proposed to provide any of it to
       any person outside the Health Service, and for what purpose; and

  (c)  that it not be used in connection with any other proceeding. I do not consent to that.

I make these requests under the Information Privacy Act 2009 and the Queensland Privacy
Principles, and consistently with the consent I have given, which is scoped in my response of the
same date.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  WHY IT MATTERS TO THE DECISION ITSELF
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I raise one further matter, neutrally.

A decision on my request for a change in the way I work may only be made, or refused, on
reasonable grounds. Whether grounds are reasonable is not only a question of what was decided; it
is also a question of who decided it and on what material. If the decision is made by an officer
within the arrangements the decision concerns, that is a matter which can be raised later, by
either of us, and I would rather it were dealt with now.

I would also note that the Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at work Code of Practice
2022 identifies poor organisational justice — including a lack of procedural fairness — as a
psychosocial hazard in its own right, and that HR Policy G03 requires proper consideration to be
given to that Code.

I therefore ask that this be resolved before the decisions are made, rather than after.

6.1  ONE MATTER I RECORD FOR THE FILE

I record the following once, neutrally, and I do not develop it here.

In the course of my employment I have raised concerns about patient safety, about changes to the
work and the roster, about fatigue, and about the ability of staff to have input into decisions
affecting the work. I am entitled to raise those matters, and to be consulted on work health and
safety matters that affect me.

Since 3 July 2026 I have been held out of the workplace, my accrued leave has been debited, and
from 13 July 2026 I have been without wages, while those matters remain unassessed by the Health
Service and while the decisions about my return sit within the directorate they concern. That is
a serious detriment to me.

I am not making a claim in this letter and I ask for no finding. I record it because it is a
matter I have raised with my union, and because I would rather it be dealt with by the Health
Service now than become an issue later. I do not abandon my employment or any entitlement.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  WHAT THIS LETTER DOES NOT DO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  (a)  It makes no allegation against any individual and asks for no finding about anyone.

  (b)  It does not ask that anyone be removed from the workplace, stood aside or investigated.

  (c)  It is separate from my response of the same date to the Request for Medical Information,
       from my request under clause 10.3.2, and from my notice of dispute under clause 1.11.
       A decision on any of those is not an answer to this.

  (d)  It is not a complaint under any Act, and it is not a grievance.

I confirm again that I am engaging with this process and want to return to work.

## ⭐⭐ WHY DOCUMENT 4 WAS PULLED OUT OF THE RESPONSE
**s 89(1)(b) is not a discretion. It is a bar:**
> *"[the employee] **must not take action or further action** concerning a matter that is, or may
> be, affected by the conflict **unless authorised by the employee's chief executive**."*

⇒ The only cure is **chief executive authorisation**. So the two questions at §3(a)–(b) —
*has a disclosure been made under s 89(1)(a)*, and *has the chief executive authorised continued
action under s 89(1)(b)* — have exactly two possible answers:
- **No** → decisions have been taken by an officer the section says must not take them.
- **Yes** → ⭐ **an authorisation document exists, and it can be asked for.**

**Buried in Part 6 of a 14-page response it could be answered in passing. Standing alone it has to
be answered on its own.**

## ⭐ HOW THE CONFLICT FEEDS THE AD ACT AND ADVERSE ACTION — WITHOUT BEING ALLEGED
**It is never argued. It operates by itself, because it goes to *who decided* and *on what*:**
- **cl 10.3.5** — refusal only on **reasonable grounds**. ⭐ Whether grounds are reasonable is partly
  a question of **who formed them**. Document 4 §6 says exactly that, neutrally.
- **AD Act ss 35–36** — the exemption requires **unjustifiable hardship**, judged under **s 5**
  against **the whole organisation** (**G03 cl 2**, onus on QH). A conflicted assessor makes that
  harder to sustain, not easier.
- ⭐⭐ **IR Act s 306** — **they must disprove the reason.** If the decision-maker is the officer the
  earlier complaints concern, **disproof is materially harder** — and he never has to say why.
- **s 571** — accessorial liability reaches whoever was *"involved in"* it.
- **PID s 40(5)** — enough that the disclosure is **a substantial ground**, *"even if there is
  another ground"*.

⇒ ⭐⭐⭐ **Document 4 asks two questions and makes no argument. The answers do the work in all three
regimes at once.**

# PART 7 — ⛔ THE FIVE THINGS THAT MUST NOT HAPPEN
1. ⛔ **No allegation of conspiracy, bad faith, targeting or unlawfulness** — anywhere, in anything.
   It re-opens the one lane that makes every other lane survivable for them.
2. ⛔ **Do not cite PS Act s 101, or ss 103–109, to MSH.** Naming them lets MSH issue a compliant
   notice tomorrow, dated tomorrow, and cure five weeks prospectively.
3. ⛔ **Do not cite AD Act s 129 or PID Act s 41.** Criminal penalties against individuals, for
   conduct not established, in a letter asking for a roster.
4. ⛔ **Do not re-send or restate the cl 10.3 request.** A fresh request restarts the 21 days.
5. ⛔ **Do not open the cl 1.12 grievance yet** — duplication/abeyance, and **PS Act s 132(4)(e)**
   narrows the fair treatment appeal to the outcome only.

# PART 7A — ⛔⛔ WHY IT DOES NOT GO TO MSH LEGAL
**The Chief Executive: yes. MSH Legal: no — and the distinction is not a fine one.**

**Metro South Health's legal team is the opposing party's legal team in WC/2024/227.** The objection
of **5 June 2026 (ref K-LM26/729)** was signed by the **Chief Executive**, with enquiries directed to
**Myla Ruttan, Principal Lawyer**. They are running the case against him **right now**, and the
**mention is 7 August 2026**.

| Sending the employment file to MSH Legal | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Collapses the separation of tracks** | Discipline rule 8. The employment track has been kept scrupulously apart from the appeal. **One email undoes it.** |
| **Hands them the whole employment picture** | They have the appeal. **They do not necessarily have the RFMI, the ECC, the exclusion correspondence, or the medical allocation** — some of which touches causation, which is in issue |
| ⚠️ **Six days before the mention** | The standing posture is that Dwyer discovers MSH's problems himself. **Volunteering the employment dispute to opposing lawyers days out is the opposite** |
| **Changes who answers** | HR and the CE answer as an employer, under employment instruments. **Lawyers answer as litigators.** ⭐ **He wants the employer's answers, not the lawyers'** |

⇒ ⭐⭐ **The CE is the right addressee because the Act says so — s 89 makes the chief executive the
person to whom a conflict is disclosed and the only person who may authorise continued action.**
**MSH Legal is the wrong addressee because they are the other side in live proceedings.**

⚠️ **One thing to know and accept:** the Chief Executive who must answer the s 89 questions is also
the officer who signed the objection in the appeal. **That is awkward and unavoidable** — she is the
statutory decision-maker regardless. ⭐ **Which is exactly why the letter is addressed to the office
and asks only that a statutory function be exercised**, makes no allegation, and offers to take it no
further if the answers show the matter has been dealt with.

⛔ **If MSH refers the letter to its lawyers, that is their choice and it is fine.** ⭐ **It must not
be his.**

## ⚠️ AND ON "THE CE ATTENDING TO THE OFFICERS"
⛔ **Do not ask for anyone to be dealt with, disciplined, investigated or stood aside.** That is a
request for a finding against named individuals, and it re-opens the tone lane (Part 7, item 1).

⭐ **Ask instead for the statutory function**, which the letter now does at §3:
> *"If no authorisation has been given under section 89(1)(b), I ask that you consider the direction
> contemplated by section 89(2), and that in the meantime the decisions described at Part 2 be
> allocated to an officer outside Corporate Services."*

⇒ ⭐⭐ **s 89(2) is the CE's own power to direct an officer to resolve a conflict. Asking the CE to
consider exercising it produces exactly the outcome he wants — the officers out of the decision —
without asking for a finding about anyone, and without a single adverse word.**

# PART 9 — ⭐ WHAT THIS ACHIEVES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

## 9.1 WHAT IT ACHIEVES
1. ⭐⭐ **It removes silence as a strategy.** For five weeks doing nothing cost MSH nothing.
   After Monday every available move — refuse, grant, condition, suspend, regularise, dismiss, or
   say nothing — **produces a dated document with an author and a stated reason, or a deemed
   decision.**
2. ⭐⭐ **It creates the first date in the matter.** He has asked repeatedly to be told when he
   would know. **24 August 2026 is a date MSH cannot decline to set, extend or park.**
3. ⭐ **It moves the onus, three times over.** cl 10.3.5 and **G03 cl 2** (prove it unreasonable,
   against the whole organisation) · **IR Act s 306** (disprove the reason) · **AD Act s 124(3)**
   (prove it was reasonably required).
4. ⭐⭐ **It protects him.** **s 284** workplace rights are now exercised on a dated record and
   **s 306** attaches to everything after it. **The abandonment route is closed** by four documents
   each recording that he is engaging and wants to return — which matters because **8 October 2024
   happened.**
5. ⭐ **It spends nothing.** No allegation, no finding sought, no characterisation. **The PID track,
   the AD Act complaint, the fair treatment appeal, the reprisal tort and the general protections
   application all remain available and unspent.**
6. ⭐ **It builds the appeal record without touching the appeal.** Everything MSH now writes is a
   document in a matter it is defending — **written in the employment track, where it is not being
   careful.**
7. **It converts an indefinite situation into a bounded one.** That is the real achievement.

## 9.2 ⚠️ WHAT IT DOES NOT ACHIEVE — SAY THIS PLAINLY
1. ⛔ **It does not get him back to work on Monday.** Nothing in it compels a return. **cl 1.11.4
   needs the Commission to enforce it.**
2. ⛔ **It does not get him paid this fortnight.** The pay question runs through Stage 1 → 2 → 3 → 4,
   or a separate route.
3. ⚠️ **They can grant the request and still hold him out** — Rank 2B.
4. ⚠️ **They can regularise under PS Act div 5.** The package does not prevent it; it only makes the
   five weeks unrecoverable for them.
5. ⛔ **It does not resolve the appeal.** Separate track, separate posture, 7 August.
6. ⚠️ **The weeks continue while the clocks run.** Realistically **the earliest structural change is
   mid-to-late August.**

## 9.3 THE HONEST BOTTOM LINE
**Before: no date, no instrument, no decision-maker, no leverage, no route — and every week of
silence worked in their favour.**

**After Monday: four clocks, three reversed onuses, a statutory decision-maker named on the
conflict, a protected record if they escalate, and no move left that does not require them to write
something down.**

⚠️ **That is not a remedy. It is a floor.** ⭐ **But it is the first floor there has been, and
everything after this is built on it.**

PROPOSAL FOR RETURN TO WORK
Accompanying the Response to the Request for Medical Information of 31 July 2026 — MSH-INJ-5795

Cory Lea Shepherd
AO3, Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital, Metro South Health

To:      Human Resources, Logan Bayside Health Network
         LBH.HRTeam1@health.qld.gov.au
Date:    3 August 2026

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This document sets out my proposal for returning to work. It accompanies my response of today's
date to the Request for Medical Information, and is presented separately so that it can be
considered — and, internally, routed — on its own. The confirmations I seek are listed at
Part 9 of the response. The proposal at section 3 below is also the subject of my separate
request of today's date under clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  THE PROPOSAL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I have been held out of the workplace since 3 July 2026 without wages, with my accrued leave
debited, and self-funding the medical costs of this process. G03 clause 1.1 contemplates
temporary adjustments which allow an employee to "continue work during their recovery," and
clause 1.1.1 confirms that workplace rehabilitation support is available to employees "who have
an injury/illness impacting their current ability to perform their role, with no claim or
entitlement to compensation (health management case)." Clause 1 provides that "Managers are
responsible for ensuring work environments and work, do not unreasonably prevent employment for
people."

The Health Service's Workplace rehabilitation standard (QH-IMP-401-5, 7 January 2026) is also
engaged. It provides that the line manager or delegate shall "identify and actively seek ...
meaningful suitable duties, and ensure suitable duties are made available wherever reasonably
practicable"; that the line manager "is best placed to be the primary contact for the worker
wherever possible and facilitate the injured workers on-going connection with the workplace";
that "regular, transparent and timely communication" be maintained with the worker "whether at
work or off work"; and that the worker be informed of "the appropriate dispute resolution
process to follow in such cases where the worker does not agree with elements of a proposed
workplace rehabilitation plan or suitable duties program". The standard applies to a worker
requiring rehabilitation "for either a work or non-work-related injury/illness".

I have been offered no suitable duties — interim duties were declined in any capacity. I have
been held away from the workplace rather than connected to it. I have not been informed of any
dispute resolution process. I ask that each of those be addressed.

I also record that I was not consulted before the decision of 3 July 2026, or since. Section 47
of the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 requires consultation with workers who are "directly
affected by a matter relating to work health or safety". Section 48 requires that I be given a
reasonable opportunity "to contribute to the decision-making process relating to the matter".
Section 49 requires consultation when identifying hazards and assessing risks, when deciding
how to eliminate or minimise them, when proposing changes that may affect the health or safety
of workers, and when making decisions about the procedures for monitoring the health of
workers. The present request is a procedure for monitoring my health.

I propose the following. Each item is within the Health Service's existing processes and, so
far as I can see, requires no material expenditure and no restructuring.

  (a) RETURN TO DUTY. That I return to my rostered shifts now, on the restrictions certified in
      the Employee Capabilities Checklist of 3 July 2026, while the balance of this inquiry is
      completed. If the exclusion is maintained, that the instrument relied on be identified,
      that the period be treated as paid special leave, and that the leave debited since 3 July
      2026 be reversed.

  (b) COMPLAINT HANDLING. That the Health Service confirm in writing that complaints received
      by Switchboard staff are escalated in accordance with the process it has itself
      described. This requires no change to anything.

  (c) ROSTER PREDICTABILITY. That my roster be published in accordance with the certified
      agreement and not altered without my agreement other than in an emergency.

  (d) ORDINARY PROCEDURAL FAIRNESS. That any concern about my performance or conduct be raised
      with me in writing, with particulars, in accordance with the applicable directive, and
      that I be afforded a support person.

  (e) A SEPARATE CONTACT POINT. That leave, injury management and human resources matters
      concerning me be handled by an officer outside Switchboard Services rather than by my
      line manager, who wrote to me on 2 July 2026 concerning leave types and my return to
      duty. This does not alter day-to-day supervision and involves no change to reporting
      lines.

  (f) WORKPLACE RISK ASSESSMENT. As set out at Part 4.2.

  (g) REVIEW. That the arrangements be reviewed at six weeks, or earlier if either party
      considers it necessary.

  (h) GRADUATED RETURN. If the Health Service prefers, I am willing to return on a graduated
      basis by agreement. I am not seeking to avoid any part of my role.

If any part of this proposal cannot be accommodated, I ask that the Health Service identify
which part and its reasons, having regard to G03 clause 2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  CONTROLS I WOULD BE WILLING TO SEE PUT IN PLACE

I record these subject to two qualifications I do not waive: identifying hazards and determining
controls is a function of the Health Service under Part 3.1 of the Work Health and Safety
Regulation 2011, not of the worker; and the controls that are appropriate are ultimately a matter
for clinical opinion, which question 1(d) of the Health Service's own request seeks.

  (a) A telephone call one hour before each rostered shift, to confirm I am attending; if
      unanswered or attendance is not confirmed, a second call; if still not confirmed, the
      on-call operator is contacted and cover arranged. The measure is contingent, not standing:
      on the shifts I attend — most of them — it costs one telephone call, and where I am not
      attending, that is established an hour ahead rather than at start time. An on-call
      arrangement has existed in the unit since 15 April 2024; this applies it, and would have
      addressed a substantial part of the attendance history recorded in the correspondence of
      8 September 2025. It is a confirmation of attendance, not an assessment of my condition —
      no colleague needs to know anything about my health for it to work.

  (b) A defined escalation pathway I may initiate during a shift if my condition is acutely
      exacerbated — who assumes the board, how the shift is closed out — so the response is
      planned rather than improvised.

  (c) Continuation of the existing complaint-handling arrangement recorded in the Health
      Service's own letter: immediate escalation to the Client Liaison Officer and/or Manager.
      This requires no change to anything.

  (d) Continuation of the rostered pattern that has applied over the preceding twelve months.
      The Checklist records it as "the pattern Mr Shepherd has in fact worked and tolerated over
      the past twelve months without deterioration" and a "continuation of existing arrangement".
      The Health Service set that roster; where my condition was exacerbated I managed it myself,
      from my own sick and annual leave — which is why, on 3 July 2026, my paid sick leave was
      exhausted. I am not asking for the pattern to be reduced. I am asking that it continue,
      with the variability managed by a process rather than by the exhaustion of my entitlements.
      If it is now said the role requires something different, I ask what changed, and when.

  (e) Injury management correspondence directed through the Injury Management team, consistent
      with the Checklist's own recommendation.

The only conduct matter ever raised with me is attendance and lateness; the measures at (a) and
(b) are directed at precisely that. If any measure cannot be accommodated I ask that the Health
Service identify which and why, noting G03 clause 2: unjustifiable hardship is "tested against
the whole organisation, not a division or unit", and "the onus is on Queensland Health, as the
employer, to prove an adjustment is unreasonable".

4.  THE STATUS OF THIS PROPOSAL — A REQUEST UNDER CLAUSE 10.3
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

So that the Health Service is not left to determine for itself what kind of document this is, I
identify the provision the proposal is made under.

Clause 10.3.2 of the certified agreement provides that, in accordance with the Industrial
Relations Act 2016, an employee "may ask the employer for a change in the way the employee
works, including the employee's ordinary hours of work." Section 27(1)(c) of that Act puts the
matter beyond doubt for a case such as this one: the request may be for "a change to the way the
employee works, for example, the use of different equipment as a result of a disability, illness
or injury."

The measures at sections 2 and 3 are a change in the way I work, sought as a result of an
illness. I have made that request formally, by a separate letter of today's date headed "Request
for a change in the way I work", so that there is no question about what it is or when it was
received. That letter sets the change out in the form clause 10.3.3 requires and states the
reasons for it. Sections 2 and 3 of this document are the fuller explanation of the same
proposal.

I ask that the two be read together, and that the request be dealt with under clauses 10.3.4 to
10.3.6. Nothing in this Part is intended to displace a discussion by agreement, which I would
much prefer, and I remain willing to consider any alternative the Health Service or my
practitioners consider more appropriate.

For completeness, the request under clause 10.3 is separate from, and does not answer, the
matters at Parts 4, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of this document, which are not made under that clause.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  MY SUBSTANTIVE POSITION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The letters of 31 July 2026 describe my employment as "Administration Officer (AO), Switchboard
Operations, Corporate Services, Logan Hospital (LH), Metro South Health (MSH) on a Permanent
Full-time basis 76 hours per fortnight."

I ask the Health Service to confirm:

  (a) that the position so described continues to be held for me, and that no permanent
      appointment to it has been made or is proposed to be made while I am held out of the
      workplace;

  (b) whether the shifts I would ordinarily work are being performed by another employee. I ask
      because it bears directly on Question 9. The Health Service has asked my doctor to advise
      whether I can safely return if it is "not able to accommodate the restrictions". If the
      duties I would perform are being performed by someone else, the work is available, and
      the premise of that question requires examination before it is put to anyone; and

  (c) what, if anything, has been communicated within the workplace about my absence.

I raise (c) because my absence has been the subject of enquiry among colleagues. I would prefer
that whatever is said about it is accurate.

I raise these matters only to have the position confirmed in writing.

I confirm again that I am engaging with this process and want to return to work.

Cory Lea Shepherd

PART 1 — THE ORIGIN OF THE REQUEST, AND THE TEST APPLIED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.1  THE ORIGIN AND STATED PURPOSE OF THE EMPLOYEE CAPABILITIES CHECKLIST

The letter of 31 July 2026 records the origin of the checklist in the Health Service's own
words:

    "your recently completed Employee Capabilities Checklist (ECC) (Attachment 1) completed by
    Dr Day Hong Ma on the 3 July 2026 which was provided to us to facilitate a Return to Work
    Plan."

That is correct, and the sequence was as follows.

  (a) On 5 May 2026 the Manager, Switchboard Services asked me to arrange for the Employee
      Capabilities Checklist to be completed, so that the Health Service could "provide the most
      appropriate support in the workplace" and "discuss the next steps to ensure you are
      supported and working safely". No condition was attached to my attendance.
  (b) On 21 May 2026 I advised that an appointment was booked for 5 June 2026. In the same email
      I arranged a swap for a shift I was rostered on the following day. I remained rostered and
      at work with the checklist outstanding, and no suggestion was made that I could not attend.
  (c) On 26 June 2026 the position changed. I was advised that "until we receive appropriate
      medical clearance, including a completed Employee Capacity Certificate (ECC), we are unable
      to facilitate your return to work", by reference to section 19 of the Work Health and Safety
      Act 2011, and that without the documentation I "will be unable to return to work".
  (d) That position was repeated on 2 July 2026, with a leave-type deadline of 2:00pm on Friday
      3 July 2026.
  (e) I obtained the checklist and provided it on 3 July 2026 at 2:32pm. It certified me fit to
      work with restrictions.
  (f) At 3:18pm on 3 July 2026 I asked the Health Service to confirm whether I was to attend, or
      otherwise to advise my next returning shift. That request has not been answered. My rostered
      shifts were charged to accrued leave, then to sick leave without pay, and from 13 July 2026
      to income protection without pay. I have not worked since.

The checklist was therefore required by the Health Service, for a purpose the Health Service
has itself stated — to facilitate a return to work — and, once provided, became the basis on
which work was refused. It did not certify me unfit. It certified me fit with restrictions.

I record this because it bears directly on the present request. The Health Service now seeks
further information about a document it required me to obtain in order to work, and which
certified that I could.

I am willing to provide clarification of that document. I ask that the clarification be
directed to identifying the adjustments which allow me to work — the purpose for which the
document was obtained, the purpose stated in the letter of 31 July 2026, and the purpose
contemplated by Human Resources Policy G03.

1.2  THE TEST APPLIED

The letter to Dr Ma states the purpose of the request:

    "to identify and implement any appropriate workplace controls or reasonable adjustments
    to support a safe and sustainable return to his substantive position."

Human Resources Policy G03 (QH-POL-210), which the Health Service has cited, sets the limit at
clause 3:

    "Reasonable adjustment may need to be supported by medical or rehabilitation information,
    where necessary, to either identify required workplace adjustments and/or assess the
    suitability of proposed adjustments."

I have applied that test to each question: is this information necessary to identify a required
adjustment, or to assess the suitability of a proposed one — and is the person being asked the
right person to answer it?

Applying that test, the nine questions divide four ways. I am not declining to provide
information. I am proposing that each question be directed to whoever is able to answer it.

1.3  THE CHECKLIST ALREADY ANSWERS MOST OF WHAT IS NOW ASKED

The Employee Capabilities Checklist is Attachment 1 to the Health Service's own letter. Read in
full, it already answers, in substance, most of the nine questions.

  Q1(d)  foreseeable risk and necessary controls — answered at Additional Comments 3 and 4,
         which set out the recommended work pattern with clinical reasoning for each shift type,
         and five specific workplace modifications.

  Q4     restrictions, clinical basis in functional terms, duration and review — answered at
         Additional Comments 2: "Episodic, with symptom exacerbation linked to stressor
         exposure. The restrictions below are expected to remain necessary for at least the next
         3-6 months, subject to treatment response and 8-weekly review." The review date is
         given on the first page as 28 August 2026.

  Q5     what "complaint handling" encompasses — answered: "complaints received at the
         Switchboard are to be logged and redirected to management/the dedicated complaints
         area, not actioned, resolved or absorbed by Mr Shepherd."

  Q6     the requirements of the role — answered: "Usual switchboard operational duties remain
         suitable; complaint-handling duties are excluded as below."

  Q7     working memory in functional terms — addressed under Memorising information ("Working
         memory affected under stress") and at Additional Comments 1 ("reduced concentration and
         working memory under sustained high-demand load"), with the roster controls which
         manage it.

  Q8     tasks and environments which exacerbate the condition — answered at Additional Comments
         1 and in the foreseeable-stressors response.

  Q2     capacity to follow a direction — the checklist records "Understanding instructions:
         Normal" and "Carrying out instructions accurately: Normal."

I do not raise this to refuse further clarification. I have set out at Part 3 what my
practitioners will provide. I raise it because I have been excluded from the workplace for five
weeks while information the Health Service has held since 3 July 2026 is sought again.

1.4  THREE MATTERS ON THE FACE OF THE CHECKLIST

  (a) **It records a continuation, not a return.** The first page states: "Fit to commence the
