# A PSYCHOSOCIAL RISK ASSESSMENT FRAMEWORK WITH WORKER INPUT
## What the law requires, how it is actually run, and what to ask Metro South Health

> Built 31 July 2026. **Every provision quoted verbatim from the in-force text filed in this repo.**
> **ATT24** WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld), current 29 March 2026 — downloaded and filed this session ·
> **ATT17** WHS Act 2011 (Qld) · **ATT05** Psychosocial Code of Practice 2022 · **ATT02** EB12.
>
> **The point of this document:** MSH's stated position is that it *cannot assess the risk*. The
> assessment is **mandatory**, the method is **prescribed**, and **worker input is a statutory
> element of it**. Asking for it is not a challenge — it is asking them to do the thing they say
> they are unable to do.

---

# PART 1 — IT IS NOT OPTIONAL

## 1.1 The duty
> **WHS Regulation 2011 s 55C(1):** "A person conducting a business or undertaking **must manage
> psychosocial risks under part 3.1**."

**Mandatory. No discretion. No threshold.** Not "may", not "should", not "where practicable".

## 1.2 What counts as a psychosocial hazard — and it covers this case exactly
> **s 55A:** "A psychosocial hazard is a hazard that— (a) arises from, or relates to— (i) **the
> design or management of work**; or (ii) a work environment; or (iii) plant at a workplace; or
> (iv) **workplace interactions or behaviours**; and (b) **may cause psychological harm**."

⇒ *"Unresolved workplace matters involving line management"* — the ECC's stressor (4) — is
**squarely** within s 55A(a)(i) and (iv).

## 1.3 The matters MSH is REQUIRED to consider
> **s 55D(2):** "In determining the control measures to implement, the person… **must have regard to
> all relevant matters, including**—
> (a) the **duration**, frequency or severity of the exposure of workers… to psychosocial hazards;
> (b) **how the psychosocial hazards may interact or combine**;
> (c) the design of work, including **job demands** and tasks;
> (d) the **systems of work, including how work is managed, organised and supported**;
> (e) the design and layout, and environmental conditions, of the workplace…;
> (h) **workplace interactions or behaviours**;
> (i) the **information, training, instruction and supervision** provided to workers."

⭐ **(d) and (h) are the case.** How work is *managed* and *supported*, and workplace *interactions*,
are matters MSH **must** have regard to. **(a) duration** captures a five-week exclusion.

## 1.4 The prescribed method — Part 3.1
| Reg | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **34** | "must **identify reasonably foreseeable hazards** that could give rise to risks" |
| **35** | "**eliminate** risks… so far as is reasonably practicable; and if not reasonably practicable to eliminate—**minimise** those risks" |
| **36** | **Hierarchy of control:** substitute → isolate the hazard → engineering → **then** administrative → **then** PPE |
| **37** | control measures must be **maintained** — fit for purpose, suitable for the nature and duration of the work |
| **38** | must **review and revise** controls — including **38(2)(c)** when *"a new relevant hazard or risk is identified"* and **38(2)(d)** when *"the results of consultation… indicate that a review is necessary"* |

⭐⭐ **Reg 36 is decisive on the exclusion.** The hierarchy requires **isolating the hazard** —
not the worker. Removing the person exposed is not a listed control at all. And administrative
controls come **only after** substitution, isolation and engineering have been considered.

## 1.5 ⭐⭐ WORKER INPUT IS A STATUTORY ELEMENT — NOT A COURTESY
> **WHS Act s 47(1):** "The person conducting a business or undertaking **must**, so far as is
> reasonably practicable, **consult**… with **workers**… who are, or are likely to be, **directly
> affected by a matter relating to work health or safety**. **Maximum penalty—200 penalty units.**"

> **s 48(1):** "Consultation under this division **requires**—
> (a) that **relevant information about the matter is shared with workers**; and
> (b) that workers be given **a reasonable opportunity**— (i) **to express their views** and to raise
> work health or safety issues…; and (ii) ⭐ **to contribute to the decision-making process**…; and
> (c) that **the views of workers are taken into account**…; and
> (d) that the workers consulted are **advised of the outcome of the consultation in a timely way**."

**Four mandatory elements. All four are enforceable. Section 47 carries a penalty.**
> **s 48(2)–(3):** consultation **must involve** the health and safety representative, or a
> representative the worker asks for.
> **s 48(6)(a):** but a representative need **not** be given access to *"personal or medical
> information concerning a worker"* — ⭐ **so worker participation and medical privacy coexist.**

---

# PART 2 — HOW IT IS ACTUALLY RUN

**Six steps. Each maps to a provision. Worker input is built into every one of them, because s 48
requires it.**

## STEP 1 — SCOPE AND CONVENE  *(s 47; s 48(2)–(3))*
- Define the unit assessed: **Switchboard Services, Logan Hospital**, all shifts including night and
  on-call.
- Convene: the **PCBU representative** (a manager **outside** the directorate whose conduct is in
  issue), the **HSR** if one exists, the **union representative** if requested, **Injury Management**,
  and **the affected worker**.
- ⚠️ **Nobody whose own conduct is a candidate hazard sits on the assessing group.** Consistent with
  **Code of Conduct cl 1.2**.
- Record who was invited, who attended, and who declined.

## STEP 2 — IDENTIFY HAZARDS  *(reg 34; s 48(1)(a)–(b))*
Sources, in order:
1. **Worker input** — structured, confidential, and *before* any management view is circulated
2. Existing records: incident reports, complaints, PIDs, grievances, injury and claims data
3. Absence, turnover and roster data
4. The **Code of Practice 2022** hazard list, worked through item by item

**Instrument:** short structured interviews plus an anonymous written return. Every worker in the
unit, not a sample. ⭐ **Anonymity matters where the hazard is management conduct** — otherwise the
instrument measures fear, not risk.

## STEP 3 — ASSESS RISK  *(reg 35; s 55D(2))*
For each hazard, record against **the s 55D(2) matters by name**:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Duration, frequency, severity** of exposure | s 55D(2)(a) |
| **Interaction and combination** of hazards | s 55D(2)(b) |
| **Job demands and task design** | s 55D(2)(c) |
| ⭐ **Systems of work — how work is managed, organised and supported** | s 55D(2)(d) |
| Workplace design, layout, environment | s 55D(2)(e) |
| ⭐ **Workplace interactions and behaviours** | s 55D(2)(h) |
| **Information, training, instruction, supervision** | s 55D(2)(i) |

⚠️ **A risk-matrix score is not an assessment.** The regulation requires *regard to the matters*.
Each must appear in the document by name, with reasoning.

## STEP 4 — CONTROL, IN THE PRESCRIBED ORDER  *(reg 36)*
| Order | Control | Applied here |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Substitute** the hazard | change the process, the workflow, the allocation of the task |
| 2 | ⭐ **Isolate the hazard** | separate the **source** — e.g. reporting line, decision-maker, complaint routing |
| 3 | **Engineering** | systems, escalation routing, call handling |
| 4 | **Administrative** — *only after 1–3* | procedures, training, supervision |
| 5 | **PPE** — last | rarely applicable to psychosocial risk |

⭐⭐ **"Isolating the hazard from any person exposed to it" (reg 36(3)(b)) means isolating the
HAZARD. Removing the worker is nowhere in the hierarchy.**

## STEP 5 — DOCUMENT AND REPORT BACK  *(s 48(1)(c)–(d))*
- Record **the views of workers and how they were taken into account** — s 48(1)(c)
- **Advise those consulted of the outcome in a timely way** — s 48(1)(d)
- ⚠️ **A consultation that is never reported back is not consultation.** It is data collection.

## STEP 6 — REVIEW  *(regs 37–38)*
Set a review date. Review **earlier** if any **reg 38(2)** trigger occurs, expressly including:
- **38(2)(c)** a new relevant hazard is identified
- **38(2)(d)** the results of consultation indicate a review is necessary
- **38(2)(e)** an HSR requests it

---

# PART 3 — THE REQUEST TO MSH

> **Framing: the clinicians need it to answer the Health Service's own questions.** Neutral,
> procedural, no accusation. **Refusal is the answer.**

**Draft:**

> To enable my treating practitioners to answer questions 1(d) and 3 of the Request for Medical
> Information — which ask whether identified stressors present a foreseeable risk, and what controls
> are medically necessary — I ask the Health Service to provide the following:
>
> 1. The **psychosocial risk assessment** conducted in respect of the AO3 Switchboard Services role
>    and work unit, and any **hazard register** for that unit.
> 2. The **control measures currently in place** for the psychosocial hazards identified, and the
>    record of how the **hierarchy of control at s 36 of the WHS Regulation 2011** was applied.
> 3. The record required by **s 55D(2)** of the matters had regard to in determining those controls.
> 4. ⭐ **The date on which the last psychosocial risk assessment for Switchboard Services was
>    conducted, and the date of the last such assessment that included input from the workers in
>    that unit** — together with the record of that consultation under **s 48(1)(c) and (d)** of the
>    WHS Act, being the workers' views, how they were taken into account, and how the outcome was
>    communicated.
> 5. The **review date** set under **s 38**, and whether any **s 38(2)** trigger has been assessed as
>    having occurred since.
> 6. Confirmation whether a **health and safety representative** is in place for the work unit.
>
> If any of the above has not been undertaken, I ask that the Health Service confirm that, so that
> my practitioners may proceed on an accurate understanding of the controls in place.

---

# PART 4 — WHAT EACH ANSWER DOES

| If MSH… | Then |
|---|---|
| **Produces an assessment** | ⭐ It is disclosable, testable, and **a specialist can evaluate it clinically** — which is exactly what Q1(d) invites |
| **Produces one with no worker input** | **s 47/48 breach on the face of it.** Consultation is mandatory and carries a penalty |
| **Produces one that never considered the s 55D(2)(d) and (h) matters** | The determination of controls did not have regard to matters the regulation **requires** |
| **Cannot identify when the last worker-input assessment occurred** | ⭐⭐ **The strongest outcome.** It confirms in writing that the mandatory process has not been run — and *"we do not have sufficient information to assess whether they present psychosocial hazards"* is answered: **the information does not exist because the assessment was never done** |
| **Refuses to answer** | A refusal to state whether a mandatory assessment exists, made to a worker excluded on the basis of an unassessed risk |

## ⭐ AND THE CENTRAL POINT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE CASE IN ONE LINE
MSH's stated reason for the exclusion is that it **cannot assess the psychosocial risk**.
**Assessing the psychosocial risk is a mandatory duty it owes — and the method requires the worker's
participation.**

⇒ **The Health Service excluded a worker because it had not performed a duty which, had it performed
it, would have required that worker's input.** The inability relied upon was self-created.

⇒ And **reg 36** answers the exclusion directly: **the hierarchy of control requires isolating the
hazard. Removing the worker is not a control measure known to the regulation.**

---

## ⚠️ HOW TO USE THIS
- **Attach it or don't** — but **ask the Part 3 questions**. The framework's value is that it makes
  the questions obviously reasonable and obviously answerable.
- **Never frame it as an allegation of breach.** Frame it as: *my clinicians need to know what
  controls exist.* Let the absence speak.
- **The "when was the last one with worker input" question is the sharpest.** It is a single date. A
  date, an "unknown", or a silence — all three help.
- ❌ **Do not put a penalty provision in the letter.** Citing "200 penalty units" at HR reads as a
  threat and forfeits the register. **Know it; don't write it.**

---

# PART 5 — THE HAZARDS IN THIS CASE, MAPPED TO THE CODE'S NAMED CATEGORIES

> **Every description below is quoted verbatim from the Code of Practice 2022 hazard table
> (ATT05, pp 14–16).** The fit is not analogy — it is the category description.

## 5.1 "Changes to the workplace without consultation or input"
> **POOR ORGANISATIONAL CHANGE MANAGEMENT** — *"Organisational change management that is poorly
> planned, communicated, supported, or managed. **Examples: not consulting workers on changes in the
> workplace that affect them** (e.g. not communicating with workers about the change or **genuinely
> considering their views**), lack of practical support for workers during implementation."*
> **LOW JOB CONTROL** — *"…**little or no involvement or input into decisions that affect workers**…"*

⭐ **A verbatim fit, and it is documented.** Taylor, **15 Apr 2024**, to all Switchboard staff:
*"Ellen and myself have added Afterhours on call… **This new process is effective from today.**"*
Cory to WorkCover, 29 Aug 2024: *"On April 15, 2024 **with no consultation** after hours on call
delegation was removed from switchboard… **without consulting those who were taking the call**."*
⚠️ **And MSH knows how to do it properly** — the 2022 8hr/10hr roster went out repeatedly *"for
Consultation"* across four months (pack 01). **The contrast is their own.**

## 5.2 "Responsible for patient safety"
> **HIGH JOB DEMANDS** — *"Sustained or intense high levels of physical, mental or **emotional job
> demands**… Examples: time pressure, role overload, unachievable deadlines, **high vigilance**,
> challenging work hours or **shift work**…"*
> **LOW JOB CONTROL** — *"Workers having **little or no control over what happens in their work
> environment**, how or when their work is done or the objectives they work towards."*
> **LOW ROLE CLARITY** — *"…where there are **conflicting job roles, responsibilities, or
> expectations**."*

⭐⭐ **High demand with low control is the classic psychosocial combination, and both are named
hazards.** The AO3 Role Description makes it *"a continuous shift working role… a roster which covers
multiple shifts over a **24/7** period"* — **high vigilance and shift work, from their own document.**
⇒ He carries responsibility for emergency call routing **without authority over the systems or the
process**. That is the definition of low control paired with high demand.
**Documented:** his email to WorkCover of **30 Aug 2024** — *"**Failure to consult putting patients at
risk**"*.

## 5.3 "Support in the workplace"
> **POOR SUPPORT** — *"Tasks or jobs where workers have **inadequate emotional and/or practical
> support from supervisors** and/or co-workers; **inadequate training or information** to support
> their work performance; or inadequate tools, equipment or resources… Examples: poorly maintained or
> inadequate access to equipment/tools or **supervisory support**, ⭐ **lack of functional or adequate
> IT systems**…"*

⭐⭐ **"Lack of functional or adequate IT systems" is a NAMED EXAMPLE in the Code.** It is not a
metaphor:
- **3 Mar 2025** — *"Cory SHEPHERD **is not currently assigned to a position in Access Manager**"*
- **4 Dec 2024** — mailbox **disabled and wiped**; viewable only from March 2025
- **8 Aug 2025** — restoration **"Rejected — approvals have expired"**
- **6 Aug 2025** — a meeting invitation sent to an account he could not access, forwarded 8 days late

**And supervisory support:** *"Noted thanks"* to a DV disclosure; **no union delegate since 2021**;
the complaint about the Director **never answered**.

## 5.4 "Persons not following procedures and lawful actions"
> **POOR ORGANISATIONAL JUSTICE** — *"A lack of **procedural fairness** (fair processes to reach
> decisions), **informational fairness** (keeping relevant people informed), or **interpersonal
> fairness** (treating people with dignity and respect). **Example: inconsistent, unfair,
> discriminatory or inequitable decisions and application of policies or procedures.**"*
> **POOR WORKPLACE RELATIONSHIPS INCLUDING INTERPERSONAL CONFLICT** — *"Examples: **Unresolved** and
> excessive conflict regarding work tasks, processes… interpersonal issues."*

⭐⭐⭐ ***"Inconsistent… application of policies or procedures"* is the entire case in five words.**
G03 cited and its test inverted · DFVL refused and recreational leave substituted · the ECC's
function reversed between May and June · **six shifting bases in five weeks** · a policy misnumbered
in the letter that relies on it.
⇒ And the ECC's stressor (4) — *"**unresolved** workplace matters involving line management"* — uses
**the Code's own word** for the relationships hazard.

---

## 5.5 ⭐⭐⭐ AND HERE IS WHAT THE MAPPING PROVES

**Read the Code's hazard list end to end. There is no category called "the worker".**

Every named psychosocial hazard is a feature of **work design**, **work systems**, **management**, or
**workplace relationships**:

> high/low job demands · low job control · poor support · low role clarity · **poor organisational
> change management** · low reward and recognition · **poor organisational justice** · **poor
> workplace relationships** · remote or isolated work · poor environmental conditions · traumatic
> events · violence and aggression · bullying · harassment

⇒ **Every hazard Cory has identified falls within a named organisational category. Not one of them
is about him.**
⇒ **So a control directed at the worker cannot be a response to any of them** — which is the
inversion at `THE-INVERSION-worker-as-hazard.md`, proved a second way and from a second instrument.

⚠️ **How to say it:** *"The matters I have raised fall within the hazard categories described in the
Code of Practice — organisational change management, job control, support, and organisational
justice. Each is a feature of the work. I would ask that they be assessed as such."*
**Neutral. Sourced. And it never once says that anyone did anything to him.**

---

# PART 6 — ⭐⭐⭐ WHAT IS ACTUALLY BEING ASKED FOR

## 6.1 The adjustment is not protection. It is participation.

**Cory's position, stated plainly:** he does not feel safe working in a unit where changes are made
without consultation or input, **when the core function of that unit is patient safety**. Being
included in decisions about the work he is accountable for is the thing that makes the work safe to
do.

⭐ **That is not a request to be shielded from work. It is a request to participate in it.** It is
the opposite of the incapacity narrative the questions assume.

## 6.2 And it is already a duty they owe — not an adjustment at all
> **WHS Act s 47(1):** the PCBU "**must**… consult… with **workers**… who are, or are likely to be,
> **directly affected by a matter relating to work health or safety**."
> **s 48(1):** consultation **requires** that information is **shared**; that workers have a
> reasonable opportunity ⭐ **"to contribute to the decision-making process"**; that their views are
> **taken into account**; and that they are **advised of the outcome**.

⇒ ⭐⭐ **The "adjustment" he needs is for the Health Service to do what section 47 already requires.**

**Say that, and the whole frame collapses in his favour:** five weeks of exclusion, unpaid, over a
restriction whose practical content is *consult me about the work I am responsible for* — which is
not an accommodation at all, but a statutory obligation the employer already owed and has not met.

## 6.3 The hazard categories it answers
| Named hazard (Code 2022) | Description | The control |
|---|---|---|
| **Low job control** | *"**little or no involvement or input into decisions that affect workers**"* | Include him in decisions affecting switchboard operations |
| **Poor organisational change management** | *"**not consulting workers on changes in the workplace that affect them**… or genuinely considering their views"* | Consult before change, per s 48 |
| **Low role clarity** | *"**conflicting job roles, responsibilities, or expectations**"* | Define what he is accountable for and what authority attends it |
| **Poor organisational justice** | *"lack of **procedural fairness**… **informational fairness** (keeping relevant people informed)"* | Decisions made on a stated basis and communicated |

⇒ **Four named hazards. One control. And the control is consultation.**

## 6.4 ⭐⭐ THE PATIENT SAFETY DIMENSION — his most credible asset
The unit routes **emergency and after-hours calls** for a hospital. The Role Description makes it
*"a continuous shift working role… a roster which covers multiple shifts over a **24/7** period"*.

**Changing call-routing or on-call arrangements without consulting the operators who action them is
a clinical risk, not merely an industrial one.** And this is his documented, contemporaneous
position — not a litigation position:
> **Cory → WorkCover, 30 Aug 2024:** *"**Failure to consult putting patients at risk**…"*
> **Cory → ESU, 15 May 2024:** *"…have severely impacted our workplace, department, staff members,
> and, **most critically, patient safety**."*
> **Taylor → all staff, 15 Apr 2024:** *"Ellen and myself have added Afterhours on call…
> **This new process is effective from today.**"*

⇒ **Two years before any of this, he was raising consultation as a patient safety issue.** That is
consistent conduct across the whole period and it is the least self-interested thing in the file.

⚠️ **State it as concern, never as leverage.** *"I have raised, since 2024, that changes to
switchboard processes made without consulting the operators create risk. That concern is unchanged."*
❌ **Never** frame current patient risk as a consequence of his own absence. It reads as a threat and
it is beneath the rest of the case.

## 6.5 ⭐ AND IT ANSWERS THE NINE QUESTIONS
The RFMI asks whether he can perform the role, whether he can follow directions, whether he is fit
under existing reporting arrangements, and what controls are medically necessary.

**On this framing the answers are simple, and the ECC already gives most of them:**
- *"**Usual switchboard operational duties remain suitable**"* — he is fit for the work
- *"Understanding instructions: **Normal**"* · *"Carrying out instructions accurately: **Normal**"*
- The restriction is that complaints be **escalated** — which MSH's own process already does
- **What remains is not a medical restriction at all. It is a workplace control: consultation.**

⇒ **A control the employer is already obliged to provide, which costs nothing, which no adjustment
process is needed to deliver, and which four separate named hazards are answered by.**

⇒ ⭐⭐⭐ **That is the answer to Q6 and Q9 in one line: the genuine occupational requirements can be
met, and the only adjustment sought is one the Work Health and Safety Act already requires.**

>>> skill/references/public-entity-obligations.md :: text
# MSH as a PUBLIC ENTITY — how the 28 July letter and its attachments bind them, and what a failure
# to apply them fairly/correctly amounts to

> Research-grounded (verified 28 Jul 2026 against EB12 source PDF, Directive 12/24, QH-POL-210,
> HRA 2019 ss 58/59 via legislation.qld.gov.au/austlii + QHRC). Strategy/union-brief use. NOT for the
> WC/64G track. Remedies section is deliberately honest about limits.

## 1. WHY "PUBLIC ENTITY" MATTERS
MSH (a Hospital and Health Service) is a **public entity** under the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld).
That adds a PUBLIC-LAW layer on top of the industrial layer. Private employers owe the contract,
award and agreement. A public entity owes those PLUS: statutory obligations under the PS Act and
directives, its own published policies (administrative-law consistency), and HRA s 58.

## 2. THE FOUR LAYERS ENGAGED BY THE 28 JULY LETTER (strongest → weakest)

### LAYER 1 — CERTIFIED AGREEMENT (the strongest; verified)
EB12 is a certified agreement under the IR Act 2016 — an **enforceable industrial instrument**, not a
policy. Verified provisions engaged:
- **6.1** Employment Security.
- **7.1.5** parties agree to ADDRESS: (b) fatigue risk management; **(f) injured workers to have the
  opportunity to be RE-TRAINED IN ALTERNATIVE AREAS/DEPARTMENTS**; (g) injury management; (h)
  management of ill or injured employees; (j) psychosocial issues + Code 2022; (k) security for
  administrative staff in frontline positions.
- **7.1.11** appropriate FEEDBACK to employees who raise WHS matters.
- **7.2.1** support for workplace audits/psychosocial risk assessments "as requested through a HCF
  either by an employer **or a union party**."
- **9.12.1** Directive 12/24 Special Leave "applies to all employees covered by this Agreement."
ENFORCEMENT: the agreement's **dispute-settling procedure** → QIRC (conciliation/arbitration). A
certified agreement is enforceable; breach can also attract IR Act contravention proceedings/penalties.
This is the layer with real teeth and the one the UNION runs.

### LAYER 2 — DIRECTIVE + POLICY (administrative-law consistency)
- **Directive 12/24 (Special Leave)** — made under s 223 PS Act; applies to HHS employees (cl 4.1(b)(ii)).
  ⚠️ **Discretionary** (cl 6.1 "may approve... any purpose"), BUT cl 6.5 makes the CE's considerations
  **mandatory**: reason, duration, and **the impact on the employee if the leave is not approved**.
  → Failing to consider those factors is a defective exercise of discretion (a reviewable error in
  administrative-law terms), even though the outcome itself is discretionary.
- **QH-POL-210 Reasonable Adjustment** — applies to **ALL** QH/HHS employees; covers TEMPORARY
  adjustment during rehabilitation/RTW and adjustment for capacity restriction. No accepted-claim limit.
- **QH-IMP-401-5 Workplace Rehabilitation Standard** — rehab/suitable duties may be provided to
  employees WITHOUT an accepted WC claim where operationally reasonable; managers responsible for
  identifying suitable duties.
PRINCIPLE: a public authority that departs from its own published policy, without reasons and without
considering the individual case, acts unreasonably/inconsistently — the classic administrative-law
criticism. Not usually a standalone cause of action in an employment setting, but powerful in the
QIRC dispute, before a union, and as evidence of unreasonableness.

### LAYER 3 — HUMAN RIGHTS ACT 2019 (Qld) s 58 (the "public entity" layer)
**s 58(1): it is UNLAWFUL for a public entity (a) to act or make a decision in a way NOT COMPATIBLE
with human rights; or (b) in making a decision, to FAIL TO GIVE PROPER CONSIDERATION to a human right
relevant to the decision.**
Rights plausibly engaged on these facts (each subject to the s 13 proportionality limit):
- **Recognition and equality before the law (s 15)** — differential treatment connected with an
  impairment; equal protection without discrimination.
- **Privacy and reputation (s 25)** — handling/disclosure of medical information; the framing of his
  condition as a workplace "psychosocial hazard."
- **Protection from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment (s 17)** — HIGH threshold; do
  NOT plead on these facts.
- (Property/work rights are NOT protected as such — Qld's HRA contains no free-standing right to work.
  Be accurate: the vehicle is equality + privacy, not "a right to my job.")
**s 58(5)-(6):** proper consideration means identifying the human rights that may be affected and
considering whether the decision would be compatible — practically, and without requiring legal
technicality.
→ APPLIED HERE: an indefinite, unpaid exclusion of a certified-fit employee, decided in 58 minutes,
with no consultation, no risk assessment, no timeframe, and no identified instrument, is a decision in
which there is **no evidence any human right was identified or considered at all**. That is the s 58(1)(b)
failure — and it is easier to establish than incompatibility itself.

### LAYER 4 — ANTI-DISCRIMINATION ACT 1991 (Qld)
Impairment is a protected attribute; work is a covered area; **positive duty in force since 1 July 2025**
to take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate discrimination. Blanket exclusion on
unparticularised assumed risk, against a treating doctor's fit-with-restrictions certificate, with no
individualised assessment, is the classic failure-to-adjust / direct-discrimination pattern. QHRC
complaint jurisdiction; QIRC for work-related complaints.

## 3. SO — IS A FAILURE TO APPLY THEM FAIRLY A "BREACH"? (honest answer)
- **Of the certified agreement** — YES, potentially a genuine, enforceable contravention. Strongest.
- **Of the directive/policies** — a failure to comply/consider; not usually a standalone action, but
  it is unlawfulness in the administrative sense and evidence of unreasonableness.
- **Of human rights (s 58)** — YES, s 58 expressly makes non-compatible conduct, and failure to give
  proper consideration, **UNLAWFUL**. But see the remedy catch below.
- **Of the AD Act** — arguable and independently actionable.

## 4. THE REMEDY CATCH (must be understood before anyone leans on the HRA)
**HRA s 59: there is NO free-standing cause of action for a s 58 breach, and NO damages.** A person may
"piggyback" the s 58 unlawfulness onto another proceeding in which they may seek relief for
unlawfulness — and may succeed on the human-rights ground even if the other ground fails — but
**s 59(3): the person is NOT entitled to be awarded damages** on the s 58 ground.
CONSEQUENCE / CORRECT USE:
1. **QHRC human-rights complaint** — the direct route (complaint about a s 58 contravention; conciliation-
   based). Available, low-cost, but conciliation, not compensation.
2. **Piggyback** — attach the s 58 argument to a proceeding that already exists (e.g. the QIRC dispute,
   or an AD Act complaint) to strengthen it.
3. **Leverage/persuasion** — for a PUBLIC HEALTH SERVICE, "you made a decision affecting an employee's
   equality and privacy rights without any evidence you considered them" is a serious internal
   compliance problem, even where damages are unavailable. It moves decision-makers.
→ So: the HRA is a **pressure and framing instrument**, and a real unlawfulness finding — but the
MONEY and the ORDERS come from the certified agreement (QIRC dispute) and, if ever needed, the AD Act
and general protections. Do NOT let anyone (including Cory) build the strategy on the HRA alone.

## 5. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE 28 JULY LETTER
The letter, without saying any of the above, has already put MSH in the position where each of the
four layers is engaged by their own answer (or non-answer):
- It cites the agreement clauses → Layer 1 engaged.
- It demands the delegate and instrument for each decision → forces a decision-maker to own the
  exercise of discretion → Layer 2 (and exposes whether cl 6.5 factors were considered).
- It asks them to identify what was considered and rejected → tests whether ANY consideration occurred
  → Layer 3 (s 58(1)(b) proper consideration).
- It records certified fitness + blanket refusal → Layer 4 evidence.
**Non-response is not neutral**: it is evidence that no considered decision exists to disclose.

## 6. DISCIPLINE
- Do NOT put the human-rights/AD Act framing into correspondence with MSH yet — the letter is
  strongest as an INSTRUMENT-COMPLIANCE demand. Rights framing is for the union brief and, if needed,
  the QHRC/AD Act route later (rule 8 sequencing).
- Never plead s 17 (cruel/inhuman/degrading) — wrong threshold, damages credibility.
- Verify any HRA section pinpoint before it enters a filing.

  documents/instruments/ATT02_EB12_CA_No12_2025.pdf.

# The Realization Cascade — what MSH/the Regulator come to understand, and WHEN

**Status:** reserve/strategy. How the opposing side's understanding evolves stage
by stage as the 64G runs — and the positions they lock themselves into. The bind
is sprung through the AFFIDAVIT + the RECORD, never argued as "they lied" (rule 1, 5).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
## THE CASCADE — what they realize, and when

**STAGE 1 — on SERVICE of the 64G (now):** MSH/Willson read the application +
draft order. First realization: *competent, grantable, Bunney/Scott-shaped — we
will likely be ordered substantially these terms.* They cannot easily resist.

**STAGE 2 — assessing the draft order (days):** production itself is SURVIVABLE
(confined, privacy-protected by ¶4). The EXPOSURE is order 6 — they will have to
put an officer ON OATH. Realization: *the affidavit, not the production, is the
problem.*

**STAGE 3 — deciding to abide vs fight:** the case law produces this order;
opposition costs more than compliance. The Regulator abides; MSH concedes the core
or fights only windows. Realization: *fighting is largely futile.*

**STAGE 4 — when the ORDER is made:** 14 days to PRODUCE + SWEAR. The real weight
lands: producing the manager's email/sign-in/swipe DOCUMENTS the vacuum; swearing
the non-existence answers LOCKS them on oath; ¶6(b) locks the FRMS vacuum; ¶6(c)
forces them to confront Item 20 against Annexure C. Realization: *we must put the
governance vacuum and our own answers onto oath.*

**STAGE 5 — choosing the DEPONENT (the distancing decision):** WHO swears reveals
posture AND carries personal false-verification exposure if the sworn statements
are contradicted by the produced records. Corporate officer = distancing; the
manager/Director = backing them. Realization: *whoever signs is personally exposed.*

**STAGE 6 — assembling the production (within 14 days):** they SEE what the records
show — absence (sign-in/swipe), directives (Item 10), complaints (Item 3),
no-changes (3(c)), institutional response (Item 20). The full picture assembles on
THEIR side of the table. Realization: *this is far stronger than a routine WC
matter; the appellant was right.*

**STAGE 7 — the SETTLEMENT realization:** a heard decision produces portable
adverse findings (vacuum, manner failure, FRMS gap); settlement produces payment
and NO findings. Realization: *resolve it.*

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
## THE "NO CHANGES" BIND (Item 3(c) sworn vs Item 10 produced) — the trap

Order ¶6(a) forces MSH to SWEAR that Item 3(c) — "consequential changes to
operating procedures" — does NOT exist ("no consequential changes" over the
period). Order ¶¶1–2 force MSH to PRODUCE Item 10 — the Line Manager's directives
(incl. the "effective immediately" sub-set). **These two collide:**

- **Branch A — the directives WERE procedural changes** → the sworn "no
  consequential changes" is FALSE, contradicted by MSH's own production. False
  verification exposure on the deponent.
- **Branch B — the directives were NOT procedural changes** → then the Line
  Manager was issuing unilateral disruptive directives (Item 10) while management
  made NO consequential procedural changes (3(c)) to FIX the operational-error
  complaints (Item 3(a)). i.e. **active, aware management that REMEDIATED NOTHING**
  — the manner/governance failure, proven on oath.

**Either branch hurts them.** Swearing "no changes" is a FIXED position that, set
against the produced directives AND the produced complaints, proves EITHER a false
statement OR a failure to remediate. And note: the "no changes" answer is ALREADY
damaging standing alone — it proves nothing was fixed despite the complaints (the
"complaints in / nothing out" black hole). The affidavit merely locks it onto oath
and the directives production adds the second blade.

**DISCIPLINE:** this is sprung by the RECORD (the sworn answer next to the produced
directives), discovered by the Commission — NEVER argued as "they are lying."
Discovered contradiction = evidence; alleged perjury = discounted + vexatious. The
affidavit (order 6) is the mechanism; the contradiction reveals itself.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
## THE LATTICE OF DOUBLE-BINDS — how many lose-lose choices order 6 forces

The verification affidavit is not one trap; it is a NETWORK of forced binaries,
each with two damaging exits. No clean version exists. Count:

**BIND 1 — Item 3(c) "no changes" vs Item 10 directives.** Swear "no consequential
procedural changes" → EITHER (A) FALSE, contradicted by the produced directives,
OR (B) true → management issued directives but REMEDIATED NOTHING. Falsity or
failure.

**BIND 2 — Items 4/5/7 FRMS vacuum (¶6(b)).** State whether ANY fatigue-management
requirement applied to Switchboard staff before 30 June 2024 → EITHER "none" →
the GOVERNANCE VACUUM sworn on oath (the spine), OR "some" → contradicts the 5
June letter AND admits a BREACH. Vacuum or breach.

**BIND 3 — Item 20 "does not exist" vs Annexure C (¶6(c)).** Maintain
non-existence → swearing it against MSH's OWN produced McGinley routing + its July
2025 production = FALSE VERIFICATION; OR abandon it and PRODUCE → the deflection /
institutional-response failure proven. Perjury-risk or production.

**BIND 4 — Item 14 device date (¶6(d)).** State when the LM got a QH device →
"~Q3 2024" confirms the LM ran a life-safety function with NO QH device in the
relevant period (records-management + equipment gap, sworn); OR responsive comms
exist on MSH systems → produce them. Gap admitted or comms produced.

**BIND 5 — Item 16 PRN reconciliation (¶6(e)).** Identify the process references →
reconcile the gap (may reveal more records); OR cannot → admit INCOMPLETE
production. Reveal or admit-gap.

**BIND 6 — Items 1–2 SPOK (¶6(a)).** Swear the paging records "do not exist" (system
upgrade) → admits LIFE-SAFETY paging records were NOT RETAINED through an upgrade
(a records-retention failure for the very system at issue). Clean-ish, but still an
adverse admission.

**STRUCTURAL BIND 7 — the deponent identity (the distancing decision).** Corporate
officer signs → DISTANCES the institution from the manager (confirmation by
distancing); manager/Director signs → BACKS them but personally exposed to
false-verification on the contradicted statements. Distance or expose.

**STRUCTURAL BIND 8 — the "direct knowledge" requirement.** Find an officer with
direct knowledge of the searches → that person swears the contradicted statements
(personal exposure); OR no one has direct knowledge → admits records so
disorganised they cannot properly verify. Expose or admit-disarray.

**COUNT: ~6 item-level binds + 2 structural binds = 8 forced lose-lose nodes**, all
on ONE document, on oath, simultaneously. Compounding effect: the ASSEMBLED
affidavit is a catalogue of falsity-or-failure at multiple points. There is no
construction that bleeds positive — every node bleeds negative both ways.

**WHY NO ONE WILL SIGN IT:** an officer asked to put their name to a document that
is false-or-damaging at 8 nodes, with personal false-verification exposure, will
BALK, seek advice, and the institution will prefer to RESOLVE before the affidavit
must be sworn. The affidavit's un-signability IS the settlement engine. (Sprung by
the RECORD + the affidavit, discovered by the Commission — NEVER argued as perjury;
rules 1, 5.)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
## WHERE TWO PEOPLE SIGN AGAINST EACH OTHER (Cory, 13 Jun) — the fractures

YES — the verification affidavit doesn't just trap one deponent; it forces FRACTURES
between deponents and between the allied parties. Three:

**FRACTURE 1 — the corporate officer vs the Line Manager (the distancing fracture; the sharpest).**
- Order 6 needs a deponent with DIRECT KNOWLEDGE to verify the searches/records
  honestly (false-verification exposure if not).
- The records that officer verifies — sign-in/swipe (absence), the directives
  (Item 10), the no-FRMS (4/5/7), the no-changes (3(c)) — CONTRADICT the Line
  Manager's account of her own conduct ("I was present / the roster was equitable
  / I managed properly").
- So a corporate officer who verifies the records HONESTLY (to avoid personal
  exposure) **signs against the manager**. The institution's self-protection
  throws its own manager under the bus.
- MSH CANNOT have BOTH a clean verification affidavit (records) AND clean witness
  statements (conduct) — the records impeach the conduct account. **One signs
  against the other.** This is BIND 7 made literal.

**FRACTURE 2 — MSH vs the Regulator (the seam, sworn).**
- MSH's order-6 affidavit on Item 20 ("does not exist") vs the REGULATOR's own
  disclosure of the McGinley routing (= the Item 20 subject matter) + its July
  2025 production of the same. The two NOMINALLY-ALLIED parties end up on opposite
  sides of a sworn-vs-documentary record. The joint defence cannibalises itself at
  the obligation layer (working-theories §4 — the seam).

**FRACTURE 3 — the 2025 witnesses vs the 2026 records (the contradiction matrix).**
- The 52MB July 2025 witness statements (Donovan-Taylor, Reese; "roster equitable")
  were committed BLIND, before the records existed. The Item 8/9 attendance records
  produced in 2026 IMPEACH them. The witnesses' sworn 2025 accounts vs the
  documentary record = the same person's earlier oath contradicted by the
  production an officer now verifies.

**THE STRUCTURAL CONSEQUENCE:** order 6 does not present MSH with one bad signature.
It forces the JOINT DEFENCE to fracture — corporate officer vs manager, MSH vs
Regulator, 2025 witnesses vs 2026 records. There is no configuration of deponents
in which everyone signs honestly AND consistently. Someone must sign against
someone. **That internal collision — not just the external case — is what makes
settlement (before any affidavit is sworn) the only exit that keeps the alliance
intact.** Sprung by the order + the record; never argued (rules 1, 5).

## CRITICAL CORRECTION (Cory, 13 Jun) — MSH is the NON-PARTY; it cannot settle the appeal

The roles, precisely:
- **Appeal = Cory (Appellant) v Workers' Compensation Regulator (Respondent).**
  Settles between THESE two only. (Regulator officer: Matheson; counsel: Willson.)
- **MSH = NON-PARTY** (employer holding the records; legal: Ruttan/Cridland). MSH
  is subject to the Form 29/64G disclosure but is NOT a party to the appeal and
  **CANNOT settle it.** The affidavit fractures are MSH's, but MSH has no settle
  button on the WC matter.

**So how the pressure actually flows:**
1. The 64G is Cory v MSH (a disclosure dispute). It compels MSH to PRODUCE.
2. The produced records feed the APPEAL (Cory v Regulator) — they arm Cory's case
   AGAINST THE REGULATOR, whose s 32(5)(a) defence DEPENDS on MSH's conduct being
   reasonable.
3. When MSH's forced production/affidavit documents the vacuum + fractures its own
   evidence, the REGULATOR's defence becomes unsustainable.
4. **The REGULATOR settles the appeal** (accepts the claim by consent) — NOT MSH.
   MSH's fractures are the LEVER; the Regulator is the one who can resolve.

**THE KEY CONSEQUENCE — the Regulator can SHORT-CIRCUIT the fractures:**
The Regulator can concede the appeal BEFORE the 64G production happens, to spare
MSH (the ally) the damaging production and the affidavit fractures. If the appeal
settles first, the 64G may become MOOT — MSH never produces, never swears, never
fractures. This PROTECTS THE ALLIANCE and resolves the WC matter — but it DEPRIVES
Cory of the production that would arm the PARALLEL tracks.

**THE STRATEGIC FORK FOR CORY:**
- **(A) Production-then-settle:** push for the 64G production to LAND before any WC
  settlement → arms the parallel reprisal/PID tracks (where MSH IS a defendant and
  the fractures actually bite) → but slower, and the Regulator may concede to avoid it.
- **(B) Settle the WC early:** take the compensation outcome now → but may forgo the
  production. MSH's fractures then live ONLY in the parallel tracks, which must be
  re-litigated to get the records.
- **RELEASE-SCOPE DISCIPLINE (rule 9):** whichever path, the WC settlement deed must
  release the COMPENSATION CLAIM ONLY — never MSH, never the reprisal tort — or the
  WC settlement buys MSH's escape from the fractures with Cory's compensation money.

**WHERE MSH'S FRACTURES ACTUALLY BITE:** not the WC appeal (MSH isn't a party) — the
PARALLEL tracks (s 40–42 PID tort, Issue 4712), where MSH IS a party/defendant and
the same production + affidavit fractures are sought again. The WC settlement does
NOT make MSH's affidavit problem disappear; it DEFERS it to the forum where MSH is
actually on the hook. (Sprung by the record; never argued — rules 1, 5.)

# ⚠️ CORRECTION — READ FIRST (recorded 31 Jul 2026, on Cory's instruction)

**The 14 January 2024 QPS matter was NOT an intimate-partner matter, and it was not about Cory.**

Cory's account **[A]** (refined 2 Aug 2026): it concerned his **sister, then 15**, who was
**running away, returning home, and picking on their mother** — the conduct was directed at the
**mother**, not at Cory. The police issued something **less than a Police Protection Notice** — a
good-behaviour direction — **against the sister**. He attended the police station at police
direction in relation to a **family** matter involving a child.

⭐ **Cory's role: neither aggrieved nor respondent.** The person the conduct targeted was his
mother; the person subject to the police direction was his sister. **He had no party status of any
kind** — he was the supporting adult family member. The ~10 days that followed (helping his mother
move her belongings; she went to NSW for a week) fit the same role: **the stabilising adult
assisting a parent, not a person in crisis.**

**Legal note (verified, ATT25):** even with the mother as the person needing protection,
s 22(2) still barred any DVO or PPN against the sister — mother–daughter is a *family*
relationship, and a child respondent is possible only in intimate-personal or informal-care
relationships. The non-DFVP good-behaviour direction was the only instrument available to police
**whoever the aggrieved was**.

⇒ **It is a wholly separate matter from the ex-partner matter of February–March 2025**, which is what
Hughes wrote about on 28 March 2025. **The two are unconnected.**

**And it lands in a file where the Regulator is running a pre-existing/non-work line.**

## 4. ⚠️ STRESS TEST — read this before deploying

**Taylor's conduct here is largely defensible. Do not overreach.**

1. **Matheson's request was legitimate.** The 14 Jan 2024 event is **paragraph 9 of Cory's own
   SOFAC** — he put it in issue. She was entitled to ask about it.
2. **Supplying the whole thread is defensible.** The text saying he would be late is *in* those
   messages. Redacting around it would have been selective. **"She leaked his DV" is not a
   sustainable characterisation and must not be advanced.**
3. **Taylor's texts read as measured, not callous.** "I hope everything is ok"; "I'm sorry to hear
   about your family situation"; she explains the two-on-the-board requirement and the night-shift
   impact. A Commissioner will read that as a manager handling a roster problem reasonably.
   **The value of this document is knowledge and the leave substitution — not her tone.**
4. **The privacy point — UPGRADED. See §4A.** Originally rejected; the correction above removes the
   relevance basis that made the over-supply defensible.
5. **The A/L-or-S/L offer was framed helpfully**, not as a refusal. The point is that the DFV
   entitlement was never put on the table — not that she said no to it.

⇒ **Deploy this as evidence, not as a complaint about Taylor's tone.** Its power is the knowledge
element, the leave substitution, and the over-supply — **not** the perpetrator point, which is
withdrawn.

## 4A. THE OVER-SUPPLY — REASSESSED

### What is now established
| | |
|---|---|
| **What was asked** | *"if there is an email or text from Mr Shepherd saying that he **was going to be late**"* (para 9 SOFAC) |
| **What was sent** | Two full screenshots of the whole thread, including a police attendance and a family matter concerning **a 15-year-old child** |
| **Relevance of the extra content to any pleaded issue** | **None** |
| **Was Taylor on notice of what it was?** | Yes — she replied *"I'm sorry to hear about your family situation"* and reported it to Reese the same morning |
| **Was a narrower response available?** | Yes — a cropped screenshot of the lateness message, or a transcription. Ordinary practice |

### The privacy analysis, honestly
- **IP Act sch 5** — the content is probably **not "sensitive information"**: it is not *criminal
  record* (no charge, no conviction, and not Cory's in any event) and not *health information*.
  It is plainly **personal information**.
- **QPP 6.1** — the text was collected for a **rostering/attendance** purpose. Disclosure to the
  Regulator for an **appeal** is a **secondary purpose**.
- **QPP 6.2(a)(ii)** — "the individual would reasonably expect… and the secondary purpose is
  **related to** the primary purpose". Arguable for the lateness message. **Much harder for the
  family and police content, which relates to nothing in the primary purpose.**
- **QPP 6.2(b)** — "**required or authorised** under an Australian law". The conferencing was
  **voluntary**, not compulsory, so "required" does not apply. "Authorised" is arguable but
  undecided.

### ⚠️ THE HONEST WEAKNESS — state it before anyone else does
**Cory put paragraph 9 in issue himself.** Matheson was entitled to ask; Taylor was obliged to
answer. An employer over-supplying in a litigation response is a common and usually forgiven fault,
and the OIC remedy would be limited. **This will not win anything on its own.**

### ⭐ SUPERSEDED BY THE AMENDED PLEADING — recorded 2 Aug 2026
**[A]** Per Cory: the **amended Form 9A of 8 April 2026** (the Neville pleading, Stressor 3(b) —
see confirmed-record.md) **does not plead the 14 January 2024 event at all**. ⚠️ Verify against the

If confirmed, the honest weakness above becomes **historical only**:

  relevance runs on the **live** issues, and the material now connects to **nothing pleaded by

### ⭐ THE CASE-THEORY FRAME (Cory, 2 Aug 2026) — occasion vs stressor
**[A]** Cory's clarifications: (1) he doubts even the *original* 9A touched the event — the para-9
hook was Matheson's citation of "**paragraph 9 SOFAC**" (the statement of facts and contentions,
a different document from the Form 9A — keep them distinct; verify both on ingest). (2) To the
extent the event was ever pleaded, **the stressor was Taylor's rostering decision — being rostered
out of a shift he had given notice for and insisted he would attend — a workplace management
action.** The family matter was only the **occasion**: the personal circumstance that should have
been *accommodated* (DFV leave), and instead was answered with a roster-out and a leave
substitution.

**Why this frame matters:**
- It means the family/police content was **never relevant at ANY point in the case's history** —
  even under the original pleading, only the notice/lateness message and the rostering response
  were in issue. Matheson's own narrow request ("a text saying he was going to be late")
  implicitly recognised exactly that boundary; Taylor's supply crossed it. ⇒ The confinement
  letter's position upgrades from "no longer relevant" to "**at no time relevant**".
- It is the same architecture as the whole 2026 employment file: **personal/medical circumstance →
  accommodation owed → management action instead.** Jan 2024 is the first instance of the pattern
  the July 2026 exclusion repeats at scale.
- ⚠️ s 32(5) discipline: framing any single event as "Taylor's decision-making" invites the
  reasonable-management-action defence on that event. The pleaded strength is the **pattern**
  (Stressor 1(a) erratic presence / roster inequity), not the reasonableness of one rostering
  call. The occasion-vs-stressor frame is for understanding and for the confinement letter's
  relevance point — not a new particular to plead.

**[A] The manner point (Cory, 2 Aug 2026):** the roster-out happened in a **slow hour, not a
high-volume call period** — undercutting the stated operational rationale ("two on the board",
"not fair on the night staff") on its own terms. If the early period was quiet, covering the
shift of a person who had *given notice and said he would attend* reads as unnecessary, and the
s 32(5) shield needs both a reasonable action AND a reasonable manner.
- Evidence that would prove it: **switchboard call-volume/activity logs for the morning of
  14 Jan 2024** — MSH-held. ⚠️ NOT currently worth an ask: the event is (per Cory) not pleaded
  in the amended documents; do not build evidence requests around a non-pleaded event. Banked
  in case Stressor 1(a) pattern evidence ever makes that morning material again.
- ⚠️ Tone discipline: do NOT run "insensitive" on her *texts* — on their face they read polite
  ("I'm sorry to hear...", "I hope everything is ok") and a Commissioner will read them that
  way (§4 above). The insensitivity, if ever run, lives in the **substance**: roster-out despite
  notice, in a quiet hour, with the DFV entitlement substituted — never in the wording.

### ⇒ WHERE IT ACTUALLY EARNS ITS KEEP

>>> skill/references/what-power-did-MSH-use.md :: text
# WHAT DID MSH THINK IT WAS USING? — the instruments, tested against the acts taken

> Primary sources downloaded 31 July 2026 from legislation.qld.gov.au and filed at
> `documents/instruments/ATT19–ATT21`. All quotations verified against the in-force text.

---

## 1. WHAT MSH ACTUALLY CITED

**31 July 2026, both letters:**
> "We are requesting this information in accordance with the provisions of the **Human Resources
> (HR) Policy G3: Reasonable Adjustment**, and **sections 17 and 19 of the Work Health and Safety
> Act 2011**."

**That is the entire stated basis.** Across five weeks and six positions, nothing else has ever been
identified.

---

## 2. THE MOST CHARITABLE RECONSTRUCTION OF THEIR THEORY

It is articulable, and Forrest stated it on **7 July 2026**:

> "your treating medical practitioner has advised that there are **unresolved workplace matters
> involving line management**. At this stage, the Health Service **does not have sufficient
> information to understand the nature of these matters or assess whether they present any
> psychosocial hazards or risks** that may affect your proposed return to work."

Reconstructed in full, MSH's position appears to be:

1. We hold a **WHS s 19** duty to ensure health and safety so far as reasonably practicable
2. The ECC identifies psychosocial stressors, including unresolved matters involving line management
3. We do not understand those matters, so we cannot assess the risk
4. Until we can assess it, we cannot safely permit a return
5. **G03** requires reasonable adjustment, and information is needed to identify what adjustments
6. Therefore we seek information under G03, in discharge of our s 19 duty

**That theory is coherent. It is not absurd. It should be engaged with, not dismissed.**

---

## 3. WHAT EACH INSTRUMENT ACTUALLY DOES

### G03 / QH-POL-210 — *supports the request; contradicts the exclusion*
| Provision | Effect |
|---|---|
| Purpose | "To **assist** employees requiring support to **meet the genuine occupational requirements** of their role" — an **enabling** policy |
| cl 1.1 | Temporary adjustments exist so employees "**continue work during their recovery**" |
| cl 1.1.1 | Support extends to employees "with **no claim or entitlement to compensation** (health management case)" |
| cl 1 | "Managers are responsible for ensuring work environments and work **do not unreasonably prevent employment for people**" |
| cl 3 | Supporting information permitted "**where necessary**, to either identify required workplace adjustments and/or assess the suitability of proposed adjustments" |
| cl 2 | Unjustifiable hardship "tested against **the whole organisation**"; "**the onus is on Queensland Health**… to prove an adjustment is unreasonable" |

⇒ **G03 can bear an information request.** It cannot bear an exclusion — it says the opposite.

### WHS ss 17 and 19 — *duties, not powers*
- **s 17**: a duty to ensure health and safety "requires the person to **eliminate** risks… or **minimise** those risks so far as is reasonably practicable"
- **s 19(1)**: a PCBU "must **ensure**, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers"

⇒ Both **impose obligations on MSH**. Neither confers any power over a worker. The way a PCBU
discharges s 19 in relation to a **psychosocial** hazard is to **assess and control the hazard** —
the Psychosocial Code 2022 treats hazards as features of the work, controlled by the PCBU.
**Removing the worker is not a control; it is an avoidance of the assessment.**

### ⭐ IP ACT 2009 — QPP 3.3 (NEW FINDING, verified 31 Jul 2026)
The Act now applies **Queensland Privacy Principles** (sch 3), current as at 1 July 2026 —
superseding the old IPP/NPP split. Earlier note on that question is obsolete.

> **QPP 3.3** An agency **must not collect sensitive information** about an individual unless—
> (a) **the individual consents** to the collection **and** the information is **reasonably
> necessary for, or directly related to,** 1 or more of the agency's functions or activities; or
> (b) QPP 3.4 applies [required by law; permitted general situation; permitted health situation;
> law enforcement].

**sch 5:** "sensitive information… means… **(b) health information about the individual**".
**health information** includes "the individual's **health at any time**" and "**a disability** of
the individual at any time".

⇒ **The RFMI collects sensitive information.** Absent QPP 3.4, MSH's lawful basis is **QPP 3.3(a):
consent plus reasonable necessity.**
⇒ **Cory's consent is therefore a statutory precondition, not a courtesy** — and consent may be
**scoped**. Declining option 2, and consenting question-by-question, is the operation of QPP 3.3, not
obstruction of a process.
⇒ **This is now the third independent necessity test**, alongside G03 cl 3 and **AD Act s 124(3)**
(which puts the onus on MSH to prove information was "reasonably required").

### ❌ PS ACT 2022 ch 3 pt 8 div 5 — **NEVER CITED**
The only statutory power to compel medical examination. Verified verbatim, current 1 July 2026:

> **s 103** This division applies… if— (a) the employee **is absent from duty** or the chief
> executive is reasonably satisfied the employee **is not performing** the employee's duties
> satisfactorily; **and** (b) the chief executive **reasonably suspects** that the absence or
> unsatisfactory performance **is caused by** mental or physical illness or disability.
> **s 104** The chief executive may (a) appoint a doctor… and (b) **require the employee to submit**
> to the medical examination.
> **s 105** The employee **must not be given sick leave** for any period during which the employee
> fails to comply with a requirement under section 104(b).

⇒ **MSH never invoked it.** And the gateway is problematic: no performance issue has ever been put
to Cory, which leaves absence — **and the absence is MSH's own act**.
⚠️ **s 105 is the only statutory link in the entire division between this process and leave** — and
it operates only where an s 104(b) requirement is not complied with. **Never invoked. So it supplies
no basis for the sick-leave debiting either.**

---

## 4. WHERE THE THEORY HOLDS, AND WHERE IT FAILS

### ✅ HOLDS
**The information request itself is defensible in principle.** Seeking medical information to assess
a psychosocial risk is a legitimate way to discharge s 19; G03 cl 3 permits it where necessary; and
QPP 3.3(a) permits it with consent. **MSH offered the consent mechanism** (options 1 and 2) —
operating the correct legal model, even if it never articulated it.

### ❌ FAILS — six ways

1. **The exclusion does not follow from anything cited.** G03 says adjustments exist so employees
   *continue work*. Neither WHS provision authorises removing a worker while information is
   gathered.
2. **They never assessed the risk.** If the theory is "we cannot assess it", the answer is to assess
   it. **WHS ss 47–49** require consultation when identifying hazards and assessing risks;
   **EB12 cl 7.2.1** supplies the mechanism. Five weeks; no assessment; no consultation.
3. ⭐ **The thing they say they do not understand is the thing they hold the file on.** "Unresolved
   workplace matters involving line management" is the PID (24-ESU-1130), the complaint about Hughes
   of 4 October 2025, the complaint of February 2026, and two years of correspondence.
   **MSH is the archive for the matter it is asking his doctor to explain.**
4. **Q3 inverts the duty** — asking a treating GP whether a workplace is safe, when s 19 puts that
   on the PCBU.
5. **Q6 applies the wrong test** under the very policy the same letter cites.
6. **Q9 asks the doctor to answer a question on which G03 cl 2 places the onus on MSH.**

---

## 5. ⭐ THE VERDICT

**MSH used G03 as the vehicle for an information request.** G03 can carry that.

**It then treated the exclusion as though it followed automatically.** Nothing it cited makes it
follow. G03 contemplates the opposite; the WHS provisions are duties; and the leave treatment has no
basis in either.

**And it never used the one power that would have authorised compulsion** — PS Act s 104 — because
the s 103 gateway is not met on facts of MSH's own making.

⇒ **So the answer to the question is split:**
- **For the request:** a policy was used, and it can bear the weight — subject to necessity under
  G03 cl 3, QPP 3.3 and AD Act s 124.
- **For the exclusion:** **nothing was used at all.** No instrument was identified in five weeks
  because none exists. The exclusion was not an exercise of a power. It was an act without one.

That is why the six shifting bases exist. **Each was an attempt to find, after the fact, an
authority for something already done.**

---

## 6. OPEN — NOT YET OBTAINED
- [ ] **Directive 03/20** (Support for employees affected by DFV) — not locatable by path on
      forgov; `health.qld.gov.au` returns 403. Still unread; the March 2025 DFVL point rests on it.
- [ ] **Directive 04/24** (Independent medical examinations) — same.
- [ ] **HR Policy C73** and **HR Policy E4** — attached by Hughes on 28 March 2025; not held.
- [ ] Whether any **permitted health situation** (IP Act sch 4 pt 2) could engage QPP 3.4(c) for an
      employment collection — unlikely, but unchecked.

| ATT20 | Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 | current as at 19 May 2025 — **confirms DV is not a s 7 attribute** |

# Working Theories — WC/2024/227

**Everything here is hypothesis, not confirmed fact.** Each carries a confidence level. These frames are analytically useful and shape strategy, but NONE may enter a filing as an asserted fact. When a theory is confirmed against a source, move it to `confirmed-record.md` and note it there. Keep this separation absolute — it is the point of the skill.

---

## 1. Two-stream disclosure model (confidence: moderate–high, but UNSETTLED by the Form 29 finding)

Collected early, packaged late, completeness to the Respondent, selectivity to the Appellant.

**Support:** metadata (see below) — WCRS bundle container 6 May 1:31 PM (= day 14 from Form 29 service); payroll report run 8 May 9:53 AM by operator 105777; then NO Cory-facing artifact until after 22 May (prints by "Renee Dawson" 25 May, Ruttan 29 May & 2 June, letter 5 June).

## 3. Motive of Renee Matheson's 11 June disclosure (confidence: individual self-protection ~dominant)

> **UPDATE 11 June 2026 — timing refinement (theory, but anchored to extracted
> facts):** "never identified" stopped being a safe assumption the moment MSH
> objected (5 June) asserting Item 20 documents "do not exist" while the
> Regulator held responsive internal MSH correspondence (container 6 May).
> Once the 64G compelled production, anything MSH produced became comparable
> against the Regulator's file — a dated, provable hold. The 5–12 June window
> was the last moment disclosure could read as voluntary discharge rather than
> compelled surrender; the 11 June 10:56 re-save (appending the email prints,
> 7 minutes before sending) is consistent with a same-morning decision about
> exactly what to put on the record before the application landed. Disclosure
> also moved the Regulator to the right side of the foreseeable verification-
> affidavit contradiction before MSH swore anything.

**MATERIAL CORRECTION (12 Jun, per Appellant):** the "never accused her" premise some reads rested on is WRONG. At the Form 4 / Form 20 stage (Feb 2026) Cory **personally accused Matheson of PID reprisal**, and lodged a "NOTICE OF STATUTORY REPRISAL & BREACH OF MODEL LITIGANT PRINCIPLES — WC/2024/227" re her conduct (→ OIR Issue 4712). So her carefulness is self-protection in the LITERAL sense: there is a LIVE personal complaint about her conduct. This (a) strengthens the §3 motive read (she discloses carefully because her own conduct is already under complaint), and (b) is a DISCIPLINE BREACH against parent rules 1 & 8 — the reprisal/personal-accusation framing bled into the WC track ahead of settlement. Consequence to weigh: it likely contributed to the disclosure pressure (leverage) BUT also hands the Regulator a vexatious-litigant framing lever and personally antagonised the officer with carriage. The 64G application itself stays clean (verified: no reprisal/Matheson accusation) — so the compulsion track is disciplined even though the earlier Form 4/20 was not. **Going forward: hold the line the 64G holds; do NOT add further personal accusations; let Issue 4712 run its own track behind the WC matter.**

**Theory:** Matheson disclosed primarily to clear her OWN professional position before Cory's 64G could implicate her — the continuing disclosure duty and model-litigant obligation are personally hers, and she has direct experience (the Feb application) that Cory attacks disclosure conduct. Not goodwill toward Cory (price none); not coordination with MSH against him (the no-CC to MSH and the metadata cut against it). The careful provenance clause is an experienced officer being accurate-but-careful.

**Wording analysis (12 Jun) — the cover sentence as a chosen instrument.** She had MSH's objection (incl. the Item 20 "does not exist") in hand from 5 June 3:02 PM and watched it for six days before disclosing. The sentence she then wrote — "As part of the Regulator's ongoing disclosure obligation in this matter, please see attached documentation received through Notice of Non-Party Disclosure request and conferencing" — does four things at once: (1) "ongoing disclosure obligation" frames the act as continuing-duty discharge, conceding no lateness; (2) "received through… and conferencing" attributes provenance to MSH's own channels — "MSH gave us this" — and volunteers the existence of the conferencing channel, which she did not have to name; (3) it makes NO reference to MSH's objection or Item 20 — the contradiction is placed on the record by juxtaposition, never stated (the same discovered-not-stated technique the 64G uses); (4) "Notice of Non-Party Disclosure request" is left deliberately unspecified as to whose — the precise ambiguity the index email asks about. Functional effect, whatever the motive: she moved the contradiction from inside her file (her problem) onto the record (MSH's problem) without taking a side. Counter-reading (keep live): the sentence could be template compliance wording; but day-6 timing + the same-morning append + six days of watching MSH's answer favours considered choice.

**REFINEMENT (Cory, 13 Jun) — the disclosure was ADVISED, not careless/isolated.** Correcting the "Willson out of the loop" inference: standing down from APPEARANCES (the 22 May mention) is not ceasing to ADVISE — counsel advises without appearing. The extreme care of Matheson's cover email (the precise "received through Notice of Non-Party Disclosure request and conferencing" provenance wording) is the FINGERPRINT of considered, advised drafting, not an officer acting alone. Synthesis (advice + duty are COMPATIBLE, not contradictory): advice on a continuing-disclosure obligation says "this is adverse and disclosable — you MUST disclose (the duty) — and here is HOW (careful, accurate provenance, position-protective)." So the careful wording = the advised EXECUTION of a COMPELLED disclosure. The decision to disclose was the duty; the care was the advice.

**The liability tell (Cory's inference, sound):** that advice was sought on LIABILITY means they ASSESSED the exposure before disclosing. A WHS-expert assessor (Willson) rating this case rates the liability as SIGNIFICANT (comparable-cases §7). So the disclosure happened in a context of RECOGNISED, ADVISED liability — they disclosed an adverse document, on advice, knowing it hurt them, because the duty compelled it AND because the careful execution managed the exposure. This is NOT goodwill; it is an advised model-litigant discharging a duty in a context where it has assessed its own liability as real. **Settlement-relevant intelligence: the careful, advised disclosure is evidence the Regulator has, on expert advice, assessed its liability exposure and found it material.**

**Operational consequence:** she will answer a *written* request because not answering recreates the exposure she just moved to avoid. The index email works on her specifically.
