>>> skill/sub-skills/advocacy-and-persuasion.md :: text
# Sub-skill: Written advocacy & persuasion (how to build and word an argument)

Load with the parent `SKILL.md`. This sub-skill is the **craft layer** — how to frame, structure, and word an argument so a QIRC member is persuaded. It sits above `drafting.md` (which holds Cory's specific document mechanics) and applies to every WC-track document: the 64G, submissions, the SOFC, an outline of argument, even an email. Apply ALL parent discipline rules — especially **neutral/procedural tone** (rule 5) and **let Dwyer discover** (a discovered pattern is evidence; a declared one is discounted argument).

> The original 64G voice is the benchmark. Everything below is a generalisation of why that voice works, so it can be reproduced deliberately.

---

## 1. The QIRC framework for putting an argument forward

**Where argument lives.** Three vehicles, kept distinct:
- **Application (Form 4) + affidavit (Form 20)** — the affidavit carries *facts* (sworn); the Form 4 carries *argument + relief*. Never argue in the affidavit (it invites "that's submission, not evidence"). Never swear facts only in the Form 4.
- **Statement of Facts and Contentions (Form 9A)** — the pleading; contentions, not evidence, not submission.
- **Outline of argument / written submissions** — the persuasion document, filed when ordered.

**QIRC submission format (PD 2/2023, Industrial Court / adopted in practice):**
- Title and file number of the proceeding; state on whose behalf filed; **dated**; if settled by counsel, counsel's name at the foot.
- **Logically arranged, with appropriate headings.** Active-voice, short, consistent headings.
- Electronic copy must **not** contain hyperlinks.
- Filing under **PD 3/2021**: ≤30pp goes by email to the Registry in business hours; >30pp lodge in hard copy and serve every party (here: Respondent/OIR **and** MSH as affected non-party).

**The de novo frame.** The appeal is heard afresh (s 550 WCRA). The Review Officer's findings are persuasive, not binding (Form 24 ¶34 reserves relevance "for the Commission"). So argument is pitched at *what the Commission should now find*, not at impeaching the review — except to adopt the findings that help (the "unreasonable management action" finding, Form 24 ¶2).

**The self-represented outline structure** (LawRight, adapted for an interlocutory application like the 64G):
1. **What this application is about** — one short paragraph.
2. **Background** — a few facts, by reference to the affidavit (not re-sworn).
3. **Issues** — what the Commission must decide.
4. **Grounds** — one heading each; within each, *state the rule, then apply it to the facts* (separate sentences).
5. **Orders sought** — exact, in the draft order.
Keep it short; legal argument only, not evidence; make each point **once**.

---

## 2. The architecture of a persuasive submission

**Frame the essential issue first.** The single most important technique. A well-framed issue *is* the roadmap — it tells the member what to decide and, by its framing, half-decides it. In this matter the issue is framed not as "should MSH be put to expense" but as "should a self-executing server-side export, offered subject to nil-result discharge, be ordered, or should a bare assertion of non-existence be accepted un-sworn." The framing builds in the answer.

**Put context before detail (the overview).** Open with a short roadmap — what the application is about, who must do what, the position taken — before any detail. The reader absorbs detail far better once oriented. (In the 64G this is Part A + the opening grounds.)

**One controlling theory, repeated structurally not verbally.** Decide the one thing the document is about and make every section serve it. Here: *the records sit only in MSH's systems; the request is bounded and self-executing; produce-or-swear resolves it either way.* Don't restate the theory in words — let the structure carry it.

**Signpost and sequence.** Headings in active voice; each does one job; the sequence is itself an argument (concessions → necessity → relevance → proportionality → the answer to each objection). A member who reads only the headings should get the case.

**Make the point once.** Repetition does not add persuasion; it signals weakness. Say it once, with best facts, move on.

---

## 3. Bar-table persuasion technique (the craft)

These are the moves top advocates use (Guberman, *Point Made*; Australian bench guidance). Each is mapped to how this matter already uses it.

- **Lead with the conclusion, then prove it.** Topic sentence states the point; the rest earns it. Never make the reader assemble the conclusion themselves.
- **Short, flat sentences for the kill.** After a long, qualified build-up, land the decisive point in a short declarative: *"That record is held only by MSH. I cannot produce it."* Varying rhythm — long/complex then short/blunt — is what makes the blunt sentence hit.
- **Precision as aggression.** Exact figures, timestamps, PRNs, dates, quoted words do the accusing. *"Submitted four times… declined twice… approved on the same evidence."* No adjectives. The fact is the argument. (Parent rule 5.)
- **Concession as credibility (the "restraint" move).** Lead with what you do *not* press. Conceding the available certifies the necessity of what remains and makes it grantable. A barrister who gives ground on the weak points is believed on the strong ones. (Parent rule 6; the 64G withdraws Items 8, 17, 18 and offers nil-result discharge.)
- **Use the opponent's own words.** The most powerful sentence in a submission is the other side's admission quoted back. *MSH's own letter: complaints come "directly to the Line Manager… solely via email"* → the 20,006-staff burden objection collapses on its own terms. Quote, then turn.
- **Anchor every assertion to an admitted fact.** Tie each contention to a Form 24 admission or a produced document on its face. An argument resting on admitted facts is nearly un-answerable. (The Relevance Anchor Table / Annexure B does exactly this.)
- **Let the reader discover.** State the facts neutrally and in sequence; let the member draw the adverse inference. A discovered contradiction is the member's own finding and is owned; a declared one is your argument and is discounted. (Parent rule 5 — the cardinal persuasion rule for Dwyer, a close reader who ran the failed conference.)
- **Frame relief as the easy, proportionate path.** Give the decision-maker a single bounded step that resolves everything (produce-or-swear). Judges take the orderly exit. Make your order that exit.
- **Active voice, strong verbs, no nominalisations.** "MSH controls the records," not "the records are within the control of MSH." "The roster determines whether the page reaches the clinician," not "there is a determination."
- **Cut intensifiers and hedges.** "Clearly", "plainly", "it is submitted that", "very", "extremely" subtract force. The fact should carry the weight; if it needs an adverb, it isn't proven yet.

---

## 4. Sentence- and paragraph-level rules

- **One idea per sentence; one point per paragraph.** Open the paragraph with its point (topic sentence); the member can then skim topic sentences and still follow.
- **Subject–verb–object, early and close together.** Front the actor and the action; push qualifications to the end, not the middle.
- **Length variation is the rhythm of persuasion.** Build with a longer sentence; resolve with a short one. Three long sentences in a row lose the reader; three short ones sound hectoring.
- **Parallel structure for lists of reasons.** "It is bounded; it is self-executing; it requires no review." Parallelism reads as control and completeness.
- **Quote sparingly and exactly.** A short exact quotation (the manager's words, the letter's words) is evidence; a long block quotation is skipped. Never paraphrase what you can quote in six words.
- **Defined terms once, then used.** "the Form 29", "the Amended 9A", "MSH" — define on first use, never re-explain.
- **Numbers as numerals in argument** (250–300 calls; 7-hour break; 25-day delay) — numerals catch the eye and carry the precision.

---

## 5. This matter's established voice (reproduce it deliberately)

The 64G voice = four signatures. Every WC-track document should pass all four:
1. **Concession-first architecture** — what is *not* fought comes first; it licenses what is.
2. **Precision as aggression** — exact data accuses; adjectives are deleted.
3. **Keystone, not perimeter** — the 7-hour break (and now the safety-critical role) is the anchor the whole course of conduct is measured against, not the boundary of the claim.
4. **Neutral, procedural, proportionate** — the member discovers; the page never argues motive, never says "fraud", never narrates conspiracy (parent rules 1, 2, 5).

**The role-as-standard move (current):** describe the role precisely (AO3; life-safety hub; 250–300 calls) and let its criticality *raise the reasonableness bar* the Regulator must clear — without ever arguing "they were unreasonable." The description does the work; the conclusion is left for the member.

---

## 6. Persuasion calibrated to the reader (Dwyer)

- He is a close reader who ran the failed conference — he will find the contradictions himself if you lay the facts in order. Do not point; arrange.
- He must not feel managed. Restraint, concessions, and a proportionate single-step order read as reasonableness and earn trust on the contested points.
- He summoned Ruttan to attend 7 August — he wants the objection answered, not rubber-stamped. The submission's job is to give him the principled basis (produce-or-swear; the model-litigant expectation; the un-sworn-assertion problem) to require it.
- Keep reprisal/PID and the medical-causation fight off this paper entirely — both are real, both are reserved, neither persuades on disclosure and both risk the neutral posture.

---

## 7. Pre-send checklist (every WC-track argument)

- [ ] Issue framed so the framing builds in the answer?
- [ ] One-paragraph overview before any detail?
- [ ] Each heading active-voice, one job, sequence tells the story?
- [ ] Facts in the affidavit; argument in the Form 4/submission; not crossed?
- [ ] Every contention anchored to an admitted fact or produced document?
- [ ] Opponent's own words quoted and turned where available?
- [ ] Adjectives, intensifiers, hedges cut? Precision left to carry it?
- [ ] Conclusions discovered by the reader, not declared by the writer?
- [ ] Relief = one bounded, proportionate step (the easy exit)?
- [ ] Each point made once?
- [ ] Reprisal / fraud / conspiracy / medical-causation kept off the page?
- [ ] PD 2/2023 form (title, file no., dated, headings, no hyperlinks); PD 3/2021 lodgement?

---

## Sources
- Justice Davies, "Effective and persuasive written advocacy" (Federal Court of Australia).
- "The Art of Written Submissions" and "Written Advocacy" (Hearsay, Bar Association of Queensland).
- "Use of Written Submissions" (Supreme Court of Tasmania, Legalwise seminar).
- Ross Guberman, *Point Made: How to Write Like the Nation's Top Advocates* (OUP).
- LawRight, "Drafting an outline of argument or submissions" (self-represented guide).
- QIRC/Industrial Court of Queensland Practice Direction No. 2 of 2023 (written submissions); PD 3/2021 (filing); QIRC Workers' Compensation Appeal Guide.

# Sub-skill: Drafting (64G, orders, submissions, emails)

Load with the parent SKILL.md and `references/documents-and-64g.md`. Apply ALL parent discipline rules — especially tone (neutral/procedural), the fraud-word ban, and Items 8–9 anchoring to 1(a) only.

## How Cory's documents are built (his voice)
- **Concession-first architecture** — lead with what is NOT being fought. Concessions certify the necessity of what remains.
- **Precision as aggression** — exact figures, timestamps, PRNs, device dates do the accusing; no adjectives.
- **Keystone, not perimeter** — the 7-hour break is the anchor, not the boundary; the inquiry is the whole course.
- **Discovered, not stated** — place findings for a close reader to find; never point. "The answer cannot stand against the document" beats a paragraph of argument.
- **Commit, don't hedge** — state the law and the position flatly. (The onus hedge was removed in v5 for this reason.)
- **Their records convict them** — build on Form 24 admissions, MSH's own answers, the Regulator's own disclosure.

## v5 structure (Sections A–J, continuous)
A Orders; B Jurisdiction/Timeliness; C Character of MSH's Response; D Role of Non-Party & Matter in Issue (keystone-not-perimeter; IRO point framed PERSUASIVE not binding per Form 24 ¶34); E Expense (cross-refs G); F Items Pressed; **G The Respondent's Disclosure of 11 June 2026** (three limbs: records exist / production frictionless / breadth confirmed — the centrepiece, built on Annexure C); H Verification (metadata trap; device date; PRN reconciliation); I Items Not Pressed/Pleadings; J Disposition.

## No case law (Cory's instruction)
v5 strips ALL case citations. "Directly relevant = tends to prove or disprove an allegation in issue" is stated as rule-text, no Robson. Statute/rules only (rr 64B/64C/64E/64G/64I, s 32(5)(a) WCRA, s 65 PID Act). Bunney [2020] QIRC 210 is held in reserve as the order template, not cited.

## Onus — corrected (was wrong pre-v5)
Appellant bears the onus of establishing the injury incl. excluding s 32(5)(a). The corrected onus is the STRONGER necessity argument: a party who must prove the character of conduct cannot be left without the records of it, held solely by the author. Severity goes to BOTH limbs.

## Filing-day checklist (12 June 2026)
1. Verify Form 24 pinpoints against the source — mind the numbering offset (Resp ¶34 = Notice ¶37, etc.).
2. Confirm the IRO point in Section D reads PERSUASIVE, not binding (¶34 reserves relevance to the Commission) — the one place v5 could overreach.
3. Confirm the onus paragraph matches the Appellant-onus position; confirm what the Regulator pleaded.
4. Fix any "1 July 2024" Hawes-certificate reference → 8 September 2024 (Form 24 ¶33).
5. Fill [street address] / [telephone] placeholders.
6. Confirm no live 9 Feb 2026 direction conflicts with the Items 8–9 regime.
7. Lodge by email to qirc.registry@qirc.qld.gov.au, business hours, <30pp (PD 3/2021). Cover line references K-LM26/729 and the 22 May direction.
8. Serve sealed copy on Regulator + MSH; TQ courtesy notice.
9. Then silence. Index email the day AFTER service, written only.

## Email discipline
- Registry filing email: factual, references the objection by identifiers, attaches the application + draft order.
- MSH/Regulator service email: "substantive correspondence in writing" shield; no merits.
- Index email (post-service): the Form 29 / 64D questions; neutral; two-to-four lines.
- Never phone the Regulator. Anything by phone → "please put that in an email."

## Reserve drafts
The asymmetry reply and the differential-answer inference live in `references/working-theories.md` §7. Deploy ONLY if MSH maintains the expense ground (~12.5%). Hold otherwise — an unfired weapon they never saw costs nothing.

## The contradiction matrix (priority build, post-order)

## THE PID-BETRAYAL ANATOMY — does the case have every aspect? (Cory, 13 Jun)

**Mapped against the recognised pattern of systemic betrayal of a protected
disclosure / whistleblower reprisal. This is PARALLEL-TRACK material (s 40–42 PID
tort, Issue 4712) — its strength is precisely WHY it must NOT enter the WC appeal
(rules 1, 2, 8). The WC appeal wins on the clean governance vacuum; the betrayal
narrative is the grievance/vexatious-framing bait.**

|---|---|---|---|

**Verdict:** the case exhibits ESSENTIALLY THE COMPLETE anatomy — and unusually, a
large share is DOCUMENTED or ADMITTED (1, 2, 5–7, 10), not merely asserted. The
textbook pattern is rarely this well-evidenced (the 6-minute routing and the
same-day retraction are extraordinary documentary anchors). Gaps are stages 3, 4,
8, 9 — provable via the WC production (Items 19, 20) + the ESU file + the
verification affidavit.

**THE DISCIPLINE (non-negotiable):** the completeness of this pattern is the
TRAP, not the win. It is powerful in the PID-reprisal tort and Issue 4712 — and
poison in the WC appeal, where it IS the "personal campaign / vexatious"
framing Willson needs. Rule 8: the reprisal track is sequenced BEHIND the WC
settlement; the WC production builds the fat record on which the betrayal case is
later run. Maximum accountability LATER; clean governance-vacuum win FIRST. Do
NOT let the betrayal narrative — however true and however complete — bleed into
the WC pleading, evidence, or closing. The injury is compensable on the vacuum;
the betrayal is litigated on its own track, on its own record, in its own time.

# Sub-skill: Settlement (Calderbank, the deed, release scope)

Load with the parent SKILL.md. Settlement is the modal outcome (~85–90% once production lands). The governing rule is parent rule 9 — release scope.

## Sequencing
- NO renewed Calderbank until production lands. Then price off the enlarged record.
- Conference protocol: writing only; nothing scheduled pre-filing; no merits by phone; agenda exchanged in advance; nothing without-prejudice unless Cory elects it.
- The 13 March conference failed on the THIN record. The renewed approach happens on the FAT record (production + sworn FRMS vacuum + the completed ledger).

## Why settlement is the shield (their incentive)
A HEARD appeal produces portable findings (unreasonable management action, reprisal chronology, FRMS vacuum) — usable in the s 42 tort, WHS space, CCC file. A SETTLED appeal produces payment and NO findings. So the respondent's endgame is to resolve precisely because of what a decision would seed elsewhere. This is leverage for Cory on quantum, but it means the deed will try to buy the parallel tracks.

## RELEASE SCOPE — the critical discipline
The WC appeal settles with the REGULATOR and releases the COMPENSATION CLAIM ONLY. Flag the moment any draft deed appears. WATCH FOR and resist:
- any release reaching Metro South HHS (a non-party to the appeal);
- any release of the s 40–42 PID reprisal tort;
- "all claims arising from employment" or equivalent global wording.
Any of these = buying their Layer 1–2 liability-shield immunity with Cory's compensation money. The compensation settlement does not require releasing the reprisal/criminal/privacy tracks.

## Likely landing
Acceptance of the claim by consent within ~3–4 months (orders 2–6 weeks, production 14 days, matrix, renewed Calderbank, resolution before listing). Statutory entitlements: weekly arrears from rejection, medical/rehab expenses, leave reinstatement — NOT common law. Own costs either way (QIRC default) — for a self-rep, time, already spent.

## Limitation watch
The reprisal events run May–Oct 2024. The s 42 pathway has notice/limitation clocks that may already be running — verify timing with rigour, soon, independent of settlement timing. Do not let a WC settlement deed quietly consume a live reprisal limitation.

Cyber Alert
Funds Transfer Critical Information

People across Australia have lost money when hackers have impersonated a law practice or another party involved in a legal matter
by altering electronic communications including email, fax, social media, text, instant messaging, applications, file sharing and
documents including PDF or Word documents. The following steps are critical to reduce this risk and if you are involved in a transfer
of funds these are our expectations of you in helping to reduce the risk of such loss.

To Stone Group Lawyers. In this matter, where payment details are contained in an electronic communication or document, I
acknowledge I:


X          MUST NOT


         Transfer any funds (send, deposit, pay or transfer) of more than $10,000 Australian dollars or its equivalent in any other
         currency without first telephoning the apparent sender to verbally confirm the account number, details and amounts by
         reading out and reading back the account and BSB numbers (or other specific payment details where applicable, e.g.,
         if not a bank account) and confirming any instructions; and


✓          MUST


         Give the same warnings to anyone else known to be connected to the matter and anticipated to be involved in transferring
         or receiving any funds (including but not limited to, agents, brokers, family members, accountants).

I must also:

•         when calling to check payment details above, ensure that I do not make contact using a phone number for the apparent
          sender listed in any communication or document that asks for money or sets out account numbers or details without
          first checking the phone number from a source that is different to that communication, for example a separate paper
          communication or checking the person’s website or white or yellow pages telephone listing;

•         contact the sender to check legitimacy before I open attachments, or click on hyperlinks or download buttons in unexpected
          emails; and

•         contact you immediately if in any doubt about emails or any other electronic communications that appear to have come from
          you.


    PLEASE NOTE: Stone Group Lawyers will not transfer money out of our practice until we are able to verify any bank account by a
    voice call to confirm those details (by reading out and reading back the account and BSB numbers or other specific payment
    details where applicable, e.g., if not a bank account). You must make sure you can be contacted if you need any funds
    transferred by a specific time, otherwise your objectives may not be met.

  Appellant:                                                         CORY LEA SHEPHERD



                                                                          V
  Respondent:                                        WORKERS’ COMPENSATION REGULATOR


 Facts




 1. At the time of lodging the application for workers’ compensation (‘application’) with WorkCover
       Queensland (‘WorkCover’) on 1 July 2024 for a psychological injury, the appellant was employed by the
       Metro South Hospital and Health Service as an Administration Officer, based at Logan Hospital.

 2. By decision dated 13 September 2024, WorkCover advised the appellant of the decision to not accept the
       application. The decision of WorkCover was confirmed by the respondent’s review unit by way of
       reasons for decision dated 24 October 2024.

 3. The appellant’s Notice of Appeal was filed on 26 November 2024.

 4. As this appeal is to be determined as a hearing de novo, the appellant bears the onus to prove that there
       was sustained an injury in accordance with the provisions of the Workers’ Compensation and
       Rehabilitation Act 2003 (‘WCRA’).

 5. To do so, the appellant must prove, on the balance of probabilities, that:
            (a) the appellant suffered a personal injury that is a psychiatric or psychological disorder;
            (b) the injury has arisen out of, or in the course of employment with the employer;
            (c) employment was a significant contributing factor to the injury; and
            (d) the injury did not arise out of, or in the course of:

 Allegation - Stressor 1, Victimisation in the workplace
 8. The respondent does not admit the allegations in paragraph 5 of the appellants statement because there
     are no particulars or details to respond to. The respondent does not admit that Ms Taylor or Ms Reese
     reacted negatively or inappropriately to workplace concerns raised by the appellant.

 9. With respect to paragraph 6 of the appellant’s statement, the regulator:
            (a) admits that the appellant did text Ms Taylor on or about 4 April 2023;
            (b) says this pay period involved the Easter weekend of 8 and 9 April 2023;
            (c) does not admit the remainder of the allegation because the text message itself provides the
                accurate information;
            (d) says that the appellant was rostered in an equitable way over the Easter period and that the
                appellant would not have earned $1,500.00 less than his colleagues;
            (e) says the actions of Ms Taylor were reasonable in all respects.

            (a) admits that the appellant sent an email dated 7 August 2023;
            (b) does not admit the remainder of the allegation because the email message itself provides the
                accurate information;
            (c) says that Ms Reese responded to this email and provided other emails to address the appellant’s
                concerns;
            (d) says Ms Reese met with the appellant on 10 August 2023 and sent follow-up emails on 29 August
                2023 and 8 September 2023 to address the appellant’s issues;
            (e) says that Ms Taylor emailed the appellant on 14 November 2023 to discuss compliance with shift
                and break time procedures and to arrange a meeting for 15 November 2023;
            (f) says the actions and responses from Ms Reese and Ms Taylor were reasonable in all respects.

 11. With respect to paragraph 8 of the appellant’s statement, the regulator:
            (a) admits that the Ms Taylor did remove pages from the Communication Book;
            (b) does not admit that this occurred in February 2024 because records show that this occurred on or
                around 6 June 2023;
            (c) says this event was reported from Ms Taylor to Ms Reese on 6 June 2023 via email;
            (d) says this event occurred after Ms Taylor sent an email to the Logan Switch team at 9.57 am with a
                reminder about the correct use of the Communications Book;
            (e) says the actions of Ms Taylor were reasonable in all respects.

 Facts




 1. At the time of lodging the application for workers’ compensation (‘application’) with WorkCover
       Queensland (‘WorkCover’) on 1 July 2024 for a psychological injury, the appellant was employed by the
       Metro South Hospital and Health Service as an Administration Officer, based at Logan Hospital.

 2. By decision dated 13 September 2024, WorkCover advised the appellant of the decision to not accept the
       application. The decision of WorkCover was confirmed by the respondent’s review unit by way of
       reasons for decision dated 24 October 2024.

 3. The appellant’s Notice of Appeal was filed on 26 November 2024.

 4. As this appeal is to be determined as a hearing de novo, the appellant bears the onus to prove that there
       was sustained an injury in accordance with the provisions of the Workers’ Compensation and
       Rehabilitation Act 2003 (‘WCRA’).

 5. To do so, the appellant must prove, on the balance of probabilities, that:
            (a) the appellant suffered a personal injury that is a psychiatric or psychological disorder;
            (b) the injury has arisen out of, or in the course of employment with the employer;
            (c) employment was a significant contributing factor to the injury; and
            (d) the injury did not arise out of, or in the course of:

Dear Commissioner Dwyer

WC/2024/227 – Cory Lea Shepherd v Workers’ Compensation Regulator

I refer to the Form 29 – Notice of non-party disclosure (the Notice) regarding the above matter. Mr
Shepherd is a current employee of Metro South Hospital and Health Service (Metro South Health)
as Switchboard Operator at Logan Hospital.

The Notice compels Metro South Health to produce various documents that Mr Shepherd claims to
require for his Workers’ Compensation Appeal.

Metro South Health has complied with some of the Items requested in the Notice as outlined below.
In accordance with Rule 64E(4) of the Industrial Relations (Tribunals) Rules 2011, our objections
to production/compliance with the Notice are also outlined below.

At the outset, it should be noted that Metro South Health is not in receipt of the Applicant’s Amended
Statement of Facts and Contentions (Form 9A). Throughout the Notice, the Applicant has
expressed various opinions and views about the relevance of the documents to the allegations and
stressors the subject of the appeal. While Metro South Health’s substantiative grounds of objection
to compliance with the Notice are outlined below, our ability to determine whether the requested
documents are ‘relevant’ to the proceeding (and therefore give rise to an objection under Rule
64E4(b)) has, to some extent been limited. We submit this ought to be taken into consideration by
the Commissioner.

Items 1 and 2 - SPOK emergency paging export and Aggregate SPOK activation counts

Metro South Health cannot comply with the request for Items 1 and 2. The requested records do
not exist. The system was upgraded in SPOK, and records predating that upgrade were not
retained. However, a spreadsheet of recorded MET calls is available for the period 17-18 March
2024.

Item 3(a) - Complaints received - server side exchange filter

Metro South Health objects to the production of Item 3(a). The reason for this objection is the
expense and inconvenience that Metro South Health will incur (Rule 64E(4)(a)).

>>> documents/2026-06-05_MSH_Objection_KLM26-729_Cridland.pdf :: page 2
All employee complaints relating to Logan Hospital Switchboard operational errors are made
directly to the Line Manager of Switch Board and managed solely via email or verbally with the
complainant.

Metro South Health’s core function is to provide health services to the public. Compliance with a
request of this date range would require approval from the Health Service Chief Executive to
engage external resources and assistance from eHealth Queensland at the Department of Health
to review and search individual staff member email accounts. This would have a significant
administrative and operational burden. Particularly as the date range requested is so broad
(between the period 1 December 2023 to 30 June 2024). In circumstances where the Matter in
Issue as pleaded in the Notice relates to “consecutive shifts of 17 to 18 March 2024”, Metro South
Health submits a search of the requested range and breadth will take an unreasonable amount of
time and resourcing and detract from our core functions of providing health care to the community.

Item 3(b) - Management discussion of complaints

Metro South Health relies on the same grounds for objection as for Item 3(a) above.

Item 3(c) - Consequential changes to operating procedures

Metro South Health cannot comply with the request for Item 3(c) because there have been no
‘consequential’ changes to operating procedures over the period requested.

Item 4 - FRMS risk assessment record

Metro South Health cannot comply with the Notice in relation to Item 4. This is because the
requested documents do not exist. Mandatory Fatigue Risk Management System training only
applies to health practitioners and clinical assistants. The Logan Hospital Switchboard staff are
non-clinical staff, and therefore there is no mandatory requirement for them to complete Fatigue
Risk Management System training.

Item 5 - FRMS training and competency records

Metro South Health cannot comply with the request in relation to Item 5. The implementation of
fatigue risk management assessment at Switchboard Logan Hospital occurred after 30 June 2024
in connection with an organisational change related to the reporting lines for Switchboard.

Item 6 – FRMS delegation and governance record

Metro South Health encloses the attached Role Description for Manager of Switchboard Services.

Item 7 - FRMS register entries and switchboard roster expectations

Metro South Health cannot comply with the Notice in relation to Item 7. This is because the
requested documents do not exist. Mandatory Fatigue Risk Management System training only
applies to health practitioners and clinical assistants.

Item 8 – Management System Log in records

Metro South Health objects to the production of Item 8. The reason for this objection is the expense
and inconvenience that Metro South Health will incur (Rule 64E(4)(a)).

Compliance with a request of this date range would require approval from the Health Service Chief
Executive to engage external resources and assistance from eHealth Queensland at the
Department of Health to review and search individual staff member email accounts. This would
have a significant administrative and operational burden, particularly as the date range requested
is so broad (between the period 1 December 2023 to 30 June 2024) and a search of the requested

Dear Jennifer and Louise,



Thank you for your correspondence.

I apologise for the delay in responding. I have been managing diagnosed Major Depressive
Disorder with anxious distress, which has significantly affected my capacity to manage
correspondence and competing demands on multiple threads causing me to shut down.
During this time, I have also been self‑representing in multiple legal proceedings without
legal assistance. I am responding now because I wish to resolve this matter.

There are two issues I need to address in this email.

The first concerns the apparent overpayment of my Income Protection benefit.
The second is a formal complaint regarding the handling, use and disclosure of my medical
information.

Apparent overpayment of Income Protection benefit

My concern is not merely that an overpayment may have occurred. Rather, it is that my
benefit does not appear to have been reviewed, adjusted or reconciled in a timely manner
after I returned to work at reduced capacity, despite ongoing employer contributions
continuing to be remitted to QSuper during that period.

During the period of my Income Protection claim, I was dismissed from Queensland Health. I
pursued an unfair dismissal matter, which resolved by consent, resulting in my reinstatement
with a partial payment for less than half of the period I had been stood down. I returned to
work against medical advice because, having already lost my job once, I felt I had no
practical alternative if I wished to retain it. That was not recovery. It was survival. Since
returning, I have only been able to work at approximately 60% of my full‑time capacity.

I acknowledge that my benefit entitlement required, or may have required, adjustment once I
resumed work in that reduced capacity. I also confirm that I have not received any
WorkCover benefits. My WorkCover claim was rejected, and my appeal remains pending
before the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission.

What concerns me is that active employer contributions continued throughout this period. At
a minimum, this information should have prompted a timely review of my classification and
benefit rate. Had such a review occurred earlier, any apparent overpayment may have been
identified and limited at a much earlier stage.

>>> documents/2026-07-14_QSuper_IP_RTW_Correspondence_Bundle.pdf :: page 14
In these circumstances, it is not reasonable for the entire burden of identifying and
quantifying any overpayment to now be placed on me, particularly by requiring me to compile
12 months of payslips before QSuper has first utilised the contribution, account and
employer information already available to it.

Accordingly, I ask QSuper to:

   1. use the contribution, account and employer‑related information already in its
      possession to calculate the apparent overpayment in the first instance;
   2. provide a written breakdown of that calculation, including the relevant period, the rate
      applied, and the basis on which QSuper says my entitlement should have changed;
   3. confirm whether my benefit should now be adjusted to reflect my partial work capacity,
      or whether it should cease;
   4. consider a recovery approach that takes into account the delay in identifying the issue,
      my current circumstances, and the fact that I returned to work under pressure and at
      reduced capacity rather than because I had recovered; and
   5. confirm whether any further documents are genuinely required after QSuper has
      reviewed the information already in its possession.

Formal complaint – handling and disclosure of medical information

The difficulty I have experienced in responding to requests for further medical material is not
abstract. I later became aware that personal disclosure I made to my psychiatrist which was
later information prepared by my treating psychiatrist for the purposes of my Income
Protection claim—containing highly sensitive and deeply personal information—had been
shared without my knowledge across various parties and used in a legal context for which it
was not provided. I did not consent to that use or disclosure. This disclosure was then
handed to the PID subjects of a substantive public interest disclosure.

That material later circulated back to me in circumstances I say were contrary to the
applicable WorkCover legislative framework and has since been sealed by the Commission.
This experience has had a serious impact on me and is the reason I am not prepared to
provide further medical information without clear, written limits on its use, disclosure and
handling.

Accordingly, I require QSuper and/or ART Life Insurance to confirm in writing:

   1. what medical information from my claim file has been disclosed;
   2. when that information was disclosed;
   3. to whom it was disclosed;
   4. the purpose for which it was disclosed;
   5. the legal or other basis on which that disclosure is said to have been authorised;
   6. what entities have had access to my claim file and medical information more generally;
      and
   7. what safeguards will apply to any further medical information I provide.

Before I provide any further medical material, I also require written confirmation that any
additional medical information will not be disclosed to any party involved in my legal
proceedings without my prior written consent, unless QSuper and/or ART contends that such
disclosure is required or authorised by law. In that event, I require the legal basis for that
position to be identified in writing.

If a current medical certificate is required to confirm my present work capacity, I expect to be
able to provide one following my upcoming psychiatrist appointment. However, given what

15 July (their letter): the request to my GP has no

asked the fund for written confirmation); interim

un-timetabled GP request; and my situation
"remains at the discretion of the Employer"
because I don't have an accepted workers'
compensation claim, with reference to employees
"being managed through Health Management
processes."

>>> documents/2026-07-17_Heath_still-reviewing_industrial-team.pdf :: page 3
Issue 1 — the situation is being mischaracterised
as a "return to work." I have been continuously
employed and working my shifts for the past year,
on hours I adjusted within my certified capacity.
Throughout that period I kept the fund side correct
myself: while the appeal was ongoing I asked
QSuper to assess my payslips and adjust my
benefit to partial payments reflecting the hours I
was actually working, and ultimately my income
protection payments stopped at my own request,
to prevent overpayment, because I was working.
On 3 July at about 2:32pm I provided the Employee
Capability Checklist my GP completed certifying
me fit to work with identified restrictions — as a
serving employee updating my medical information
as requested by my employer while finalising my
super matters, not as an application for permission
to work. I was rostered to work at that time. By
about 3:30pm the same day — under an hour — I
was held out of the workplace "pending review,"
with my rostered shifts "paid out of [my] available
sick leave." I have been out since, thirteen days
now, with no timeframe. Accurately described, I am
a working employee directed not to attend by my
employer while certified fit — not an absent
employee requesting to return. Their letters
(including to my super fund) describe me as "a
QSuper Claimant request[ing] to return to duties,"
which is wrong on both counts.



Issue 2 — pay and leave. I am, and at all times
since 3 July have been, ready, willing and able to
work my rostered shifts; the decision that I not
attend is the Health Service's, not mine. No stand-
down, suspension or other power has been
identified to me, yet the shifts are being debited
against my own sick leave — leave that exists to
cover incapacity, which on their own file I don't
have, and which I have already substantially
exhausted through my illness. Their stated basis for
refusing pay — that the fund is responsible — rests

>>> documents/2026-07-17_Heath_still-reviewing_industrial-team.pdf :: page 4
on a claim that is closed, and in any event an
insurance benefit is not wages.



Issue 3 — the policies and frameworks I believe are
being misapplied or ignored. Their letter treats the
absence of an accepted workers' compensation
claim as leaving everything to "the discretion of the
Employer." As I understand it, that is not a
complete statement of the position:
(a) Queensland Health's Workplace Rehabilitation
Standard (QH-IMP-401-5) provides that
rehabilitation, suitable duties and temporary
adjustments may be provided to employees
without an accepted workers' compensation claim
where operationally reasonable, and that
managers are responsible for identifying such
duties;
(b) Queensland Health's Reasonable Adjustment
policy (QH-POL-210) applies to my circumstances;
(c) the Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 (Qld),
including the positive duty in force since 1 July
2025, and the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) s 58,
apply to decisions the Health Service makes about
my employment;
(d) the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld), ss
47–49, requires consultation with me about
matters affecting my health and safety. There has
been none: the 3 July decision was made and

been consulted since — even though their letter
now frames the assessment in psychosocial-risk
terms.



Issue 4 — "Health Management processes." Their

ATTACHMENTS
ATT02 — Queensland Public Health Sector Certified

ATT03 — Hospital and Health Service General

ATT05 — Managing the risk of psychosocial hazards at

FACTS
The 3 July 2026 ECC certifies me fit for modified duties
and reduced hours from 3 July 2026 as a continuation of
the existing arrangement. The doctor viewed the AO3
Switchboard position description (ATT14) and recorded
that usual switchboard duties remain suitable with
stated modifications (including no complaint-handling;
limits on peak weekday day/afternoon shifts;
predictable rostering; minimum 10-hour break). I was
performing work consistent with those limits when I
provided the ECC. The same-day direction not to attend

ECC is a review of restrictions — not the start of

WHAT HAS BEEN WRONGLY APPLIED


1. "Current QSuper Income Protection claim" → ordinary
pay sits with ART (your 15 July email)


Wrong application.
• An IP file is not ordinary wages for a permanent
employee who is certified fit, ready and available, and
directed by the employer not to attend.

>>> documents/2026-07-28_Cory_to_HR_incorrect-application-EB12-Award-policies_SENT.pdf :: page 3
• On the material available to me notified by employee
(myself) May 2025 and February 2026 and now 3rd July
2026 certification of that partial capacity, ART put
benefit payments are not applied from 1 June 2026.
Treating the Fund as presently replacing ordinary pay is
incorrect on that record. Partial capacity and partial
payment does not dislodge this framing.
• IP administration is separate (Mr Zappia). It does not
displace ATT02 EB12 cl 6.1 (employment security) or
ATT02 EB12 cl 7.1.5(g)–(h) (injury management;
management of ill or injured employees).
• Coding "IP no pay" while held out after an ECC is not a
correct application of ATT02 or of ATT12/ATT13 (special
leave).


2. WCRA rehabilitation only if accepted claim; return
purely at "employer discretion" (your 15 July email)


Wrong application.
• Even if WCRA statutory rehab is limited to accepted
claims, that does not exhaust your duties under ATT02
(EB12), ATT03 (HHS Award), ATT10 (QH-POL-210) and
ATT09 (QH-IMP-401-5).
• ATT10 applies to all Queensland Health / HHS
employees and includes temporary reasonable
adjustment for rehabilitation/RTW and for capacity
restriction — not only accepted workers' compensation
claims.
• ATT02 EB12 cl 7.1.5 requires the parties to address
injury management, management of ill or injured
employees, fatigue, psychosocial issues and the Code
of Practice 2022 (ATT05), and security for administrative
staff in frontline positions.
• "Discretion" does not correctly authorise indefinite
exclusion, refusal of interim duties "in any capacity,"
and non-payment without applying ATT09, ATT10 and
ATT02 Parts 6 and 7.


3. Further medical framing me as the psychosocial risk
before return "in any capacity" (your 13–15 July emails)


Wrong application of ATT05 and ATT02.
• ATT05 and ATT02 EB12 cl 7.2 require assessment of
psychosocial hazards in the workplace and work
system (including workplace risk assessments as
requested through an HCF by employer or union).
• The 3 July ECC already identifies workplace stressors
(complaint-handling; blame for others' failures;

>>> documents/2026-07-28_Cory_to_HR_incorrect-application-EB12-Award-policies_SENT.pdf :: page 4
rostering/fatigue; unresolved line-management
matters). Those are workplace issues under ATT05 and

what is unclear. Dr Ma cannot respond to a request in
those terms.

4. THE ORIGIN OF THE REQUIREMENT

4.2 Could you also please confirm the outcome of that
request to reduce my hours, and if no decision has been
made, when one will be made and by whom. EB12
clause 10.3 provides that an employee may ask for a
change in the way they work, including their ordinary
hours of work; that the request may be refused only on
reasonable grounds; and that the employer must give
written notice of its decision, with reasons, within 21
days.

5. THE RESTRICTIONS AND THE DUTIES (Attachment 1)


5.1 Since your email refers to the inherent requirements
of the role, I have compared the restrictions certified on
3 July with the responsibilities set out in the AO3 role
description, which Dr Ma reviewed before completing
the checklist. Attachment 1 lists those twelve
responsibilities as they appear in that document.


5.2 First, complaint-handling. The ECC of 3 July 2026
records: no complaint-handling duties; complaints
received at the Switchboard to be logged and
redirected, not actioned or resolved by me. That
restriction has already been addressed in
correspondence. In her email of 7 July 2026, Ms Forrest
stated that the established process is for patient
concerns to be redirected to Consumer Liaison
Services (CLS); that there is no expectation for
Switchboard operators to manage or deal with those
matters; and that where a consumer raises concerns
about a Switchboard employee, those concerns are
referred to the Manager, Switchboard or, in her absence,
CLS. My reply of 9 July 2026 noted that this
confirmation, together with existing rostering practice,
appears to accommodate that ECC recommendation. I
treat complaint-handling as closed on the Health
Service's own account of the role. It does not need to be
reopened with Dr Ma, and it is not a basis for refusing all
duties in Attachment 1.


5.3 Second, the remaining restrictions — the limits on
peak weekday day and afternoon shifts, predictable
rostering, and a minimum ten-hour break between
shifts — go to when I work, not to which duties I
perform. They remove none of the responsibilities listed
in Attachment 1.


5.4 I note the role description records the position as
continuous shift work. I performed that role, on reduced
hours and within my certified restrictions, for
approximately twelve months, and the Health Service's
correspondence of 7 July 2026 records that my
restrictions were already being accommodated. If the

>>> documents/2026-07-30_Harrison_holding_reply_RFMI_delegate_approval.pdf :: page 8
rostering restrictions are now said to be incompatible
with the role, when they were not during that period,
could you please identify what has changed.


5.5 Third, reduced ordinary hours are expressly
contemplated by the industrial instruments. Clause 8.2
of the Hospital and Health Service General Employees
(Queensland Health) Award – State 2015 provides for
part-time employment on a regular number of ordinary
hours, pro rata to full-time conditions, with a minimum
of eight ordinary hours per fortnight. A reduction in
hours does not of itself remove any duty from the role.
Could you please identify why the reduced hours
certified on 3 July are treated differently — that is, what
it is about those hours, as distinct from the reasons for
them, that prevents the duties of the position from
being performed.


5.6 QH-POL-210 applies to all Queensland Health and
Hospital and Health Service employees and directs
adjustments — including temporary adjustment for
rehabilitation and return to work, and for capacity
restriction — to enabling an employee to safely perform
the genuine occupational requirements of the role. It
reflects the Anti-Discrimination Act 1991 (Qld), which
contemplates reasonable terms and special conditions
where job capacity is restricted by impairment (s 34)
and permits departure only where unjustifiable
hardship is established (ss 5, 35). QH-IMP-401-5 makes
managers responsible for identifying suitable duties,
guided by medical information, and its application is
not limited to accepted workers' compensation claims.
Each operates at the level of identified duties, which is
what Attachment 1 is directed to.

Administration Officer, Switchboard Services (RD)
     Job Ad Reference:
     Status:                       Administration Officer, Switchboard Services
     Unit/Department:              Switchboard, Corporate Services
     Location:                     Logan Hospital, Metro South Hospital and Health Service
     Contact:                      Chloe Taylor                            Salary range:

Purpose of the role
To provide a highly effective and efficient communication service to the public and staff of the Logan Hospital within
Metro South Hospital and Health Service.
The occupant of this position is required to work continuous shift work over the full 24-hour period, 7 days a week


Your key responsibilities
 ▪    This position reports to the Switchboard Manager, Corporate Services, Logan Hospital.
 ▪    Attend courteously to all telephone enquiries and clients’ requests, displaying tact, diplomacy and
      interpersonal skills of a high standard when dealing with the public and members of staff. Maintain call
      queues to minimum at all times.
 ▪    Collate information and maintain Omnivista database and SharePoint to ensure information held within
      Switchboard Services is accurate and appropriate.
 ▪    Provide a service to support hospital staff in the allocation, coordination, and fault repair of all pager
      units for the hospital. This includes allocating pagers to hospital staff and submitting paging units for
      repair, maintaining database and registers with accurate and current information.
 ▪    Participate in the Emergency Response process by receiving emergency response notifications and
      distributing them to the appropriate response groups, dependent on the category of emergency, as per
      emergency code procedures, strictly adhering to protocols and timeframes.
 ▪    Ability to communicate at all levels and effectively establish and foster networks throughout the hospital
      to maintain accurate and current records for effective switchboard operations.
 ▪    Maintain discretion and exercise judgement where necessary to resolve problems within the scope of
      your role; in situations where precedence have not been set and procedures not defined.
 ▪    Interact in a sensitive, timely, effective, and appropriate manner with members of the general public and
      service providers, maintaining strict confidentiality at all times.
 ▪    The ability to multitask and operate under pressure, particularly where high volume call traffic is
      concerned.
 ▪    Contribute to a cohesive team environment by sharing information, supporting and assisting colleagues
      in a proactive manner.
 ▪    Ability to work effectively as an individual with limited supervision to meet deadlines and establish work
      priorities, and work as a member of a multi-disciplinary team in a changing environment.
 ▪    Ensure patients and other staff are treated fairly and with mutual respect and understanding, regardless
      of cultural, religious, ethnic and linguistic backgrounds, gender, identity, ages or abilities.

We are Metro South Health
We are the major public healthcare provider for Brisbane’s south side, Logan, Redlands and the Scenic Rim. We
operate five major hospitals and a range of community, specialty and state-wide healthcare services. We are
renowned for teaching and research excellence.
We are truly dedicated people who care about our community. We come to work to make a difference. We save
lives, changes lives and make the world a better place. We overcome the many challenges that come our way by
going above and beyond and achieve the best possible outcomes by working together. We are bold, innovative,
collaborative, inspiring.
We are part of and proud of the community we serve. We are better together.

Our values
Our values of Integrity, Compassion, Accountability, Respect, Engagement and Excellence, shape our
culture. Our values guide our day-to-day decision making and are fundamental to what we care about as a health
service, how we behave, how we interact with each other and provide care to the many patients who come through
our doors every day.




Diversity and inclusion
We are the most culturally diverse area of Queensland with 28.5% of the community born overseas and 16% from
non-English speaking countries. Our employees proudly reflect the community in which they work. At Metro South
Health 20.5% of staff identify as coming from non-English speaking backgrounds.
Having a workforce that reflects and understands the needs and expectations of our community is important to
delivering safe, kinder, and more inclusive care.
We recognise our strength comes from the diversity of our people and so we encourage people of all genders,
ethnicities, ages, abilities, languages, sexual orientation and family responsibilities to apply.
We are committed to creating a diverse and inclusive workplace for our people and our community.


Flexible working arrangements
Metro South Health supports and encourages work-life balance for the mutual benefit of Metro South Health and its
employees. Work-life balance is about a person’s ability to manage their paid work commitments with their career
goals, personal, community and cultural responsibilities. Through flexible working arrangements such as leave, flex
time accrual or a reduction in working hours, there is an opportunity to match the individual’s requirements with
those of the workplace – delivering quality health services.


Additional information
For further information about this opportunity and the benefits and conditions of working at Metro South Health
please refer to the Information for Applicants document attached with this Smart Jobs advertised vacancy.

Collection notice:
Metro South Health is collecting your information in order to support rehabilitation and return to work processes. Personal information collected is
handled in accordance with the Information Privacy Act         . With your consent, the health agency’s Rehabilitation and Return to Work Coordinator or
representative will contact your treating medical practitioners and health care providers, as well as authorised WorkCover Queensland representatives
and authorised QSuper or other income protection insurer representatives where relevant, in order to obtain and communicate information about your
current injury/illness, to assist the planning and management of your workplace rehabilitation and return to work.
All personal information will be securely stored and only accessible by appropriately authorised officers of Metro South Health involved in your workplace
rehabilitation, such as your workplace supervisor, Rehabilitation and Return to Work Coordinator, Human Resources and other authorised
representatives. Your personal information may be disclosed to WorkCover Queensland, QSuper or other income protection insurers for the purposes
of your workplace rehabilitation program. Your personal information will not be disclosed to other third parties without consent, unless the disclosure is
authorised or required by or under law. If you do not provide all the personal information requested in the form, the health agency may not be able to
fully support your workplace rehabilitation for your current injury/illness, due to the requirement for this information to address any work health and
safety concerns.
For any questions regarding this collection notice, please contact your local health and safety or rehabilitation contact. For information about how Metro
South Health protects your personal information, how to access or correct your own personal information, or how to make a complaint about a breach
of the privacy principles and learn how we deal with such a complaint, please refer to:
Metro South Health’s privacy policy.

 Facts




 1. At the time of lodging the application for workers’ compensation (‘application’) with WorkCover
       Queensland (‘WorkCover’) on 1 July 2024 for a psychological injury, the appellant was employed by the
       Metro South Hospital and Health Service as an Administration Officer, based at Logan Hospital.

 2. By decision dated 13 September 2024, WorkCover advised the appellant of the decision to not accept the
       application. The decision of WorkCover was confirmed by the respondent’s review unit by way of
       reasons for decision dated 24 October 2024.

 3. The appellant’s Notice of Appeal was filed on 26 November 2024.

 4. As this appeal is to be determined as a hearing de novo, the appellant bears the onus to prove that there
       was sustained an injury in accordance with the provisions of the Workers’ Compensation and
       Rehabilitation Act 2003 (‘WCRA’).

 5. To do so, the appellant must prove, on the balance of probabilities, that:
            (a) the appellant suffered a personal injury that is a psychiatric or psychological disorder;
            (b) the injury has arisen out of, or in the course of employment with the employer;
            (c) employment was a significant contributing factor to the injury; and
            (d) the injury did not arise out of, or in the course of:

  Prizeman v Q-Comp - [2005] QIC 53




BarNet publication information - Date: Sunday, 07.06.2026 - - Publication number: 00002 - - User: coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

>>> documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf :: page 2
                                                                                                    View this document in a browser




                                      Attribution
                                      Original court site URL:                    file://[2005] QIC 53.rtf
                                      Content retrieved:                          June 12, 2020
                                      Download/print date:                        June 07, 2026



                                        INDUSTRIAL COURT OF QUEENSLAND



Worker’s Compensation and Rehabilitation Act 2003 – s. 561 – appeal against decision of industrial
                                          magistrate



                                               Merle Prizeman AND Q-COMP
                                                         (C/2005/30)



PRESIDENT HALL 14 September 2005



                                                                 DECISION



By a letter dated 2 March 2004, a self insurer rejected Ms Prizeman’s application for compensation
under the WorkCover Queensland Act 1996 . The claim was rejected because the psychiatric
/psychological disorder relied upon was withdrawn from the definition of “injury” by the operation
of s. 34(5)(a) of the WorkCover Queensland Act 1996 (s. 32 of the Workers’ Compensation and
Rehabilitation Act 2003 replicates s. 34 of the WorkCover Queensland Act 1996 however it is
unnecessary to determine which Act applies). Ms Prizeman sought a statutory review. By a letter of
4 June 2004 Q-COMP confirmed the decision of the self insurer. Ms Prizeman then appealed to the
Industrial Magistrates Court. Her Appeal was unsuccessful. She now Appeals to this Court.



It is useful to make some preliminary observations.



One. Because Ms Prizeman had experienced significant stressors in her life which were entirely
unrelated to her employment with Coles Myer Ltd, there was initially some apprehension that her


 BarNet publication information - Date: Sunday, 07.06.2026 - - Publication number: 00002 - - User: coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

>>> documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf :: page 3
admitted condition was not a condition to which her employment had been a significant contributing
factor. A conclusion that the employment was not a significant contributing factor to the physical
injury would have been fatal to the submission that Ms Prizeman suffered an “injury” for the
purposes of the WorkCover Queensland Act 1996 . In her dealings with the self insurer and in her
dealings with Q-COMP and subsequently on the Appeal to the Industrial Magistrates Court, Ms
Prizeman relied heavily on an opinion from a psychologist “Ms Dormer”. By her report of 5
January 2003 Ms Dormer observed, inter alia:



“Ms Prizeman’s work history will be covered in the questions following. It is important to note
though that it appears that Ms Prizeman’s attitude to her work was one of dedication and
enjoyment. It is apparent that her work was an integral part of her identity and that it offered her
stability and outside support in some fairly difficult times in her personal life. She states that she
has worked throughout her adult life and is reportedly a long term employee of Coles Myer.



… “As stated above and from the information that I have at this time, I consider the situation at Ms
Prizeman’s employment is a significant contributing factor to her anxiety and depression.”.



Importantly, Ms Dormer also observed:



“From my interview with her and from the documentation that I have read, it appears that Ms
Prizeman perceived that a situation developed between Ms Sturgess, the Store Manager, and herself
over the first half of 2003 (sic.) … However it is important to note that it is Ms Prizeman’s
interpretation of events and her method of handling the events must be taken into consideration.”.



Ms Dormer then went on to list particular dealings which Ms Prizeman had informed her had proved
stressful. I do not repeat the list, because the list relied upon before the Industrial Magistrate was
marginally different. But it was plainly that list which triggered concern that the “injury” had been
withdrawn from the definition by s. 34(5)(a) of the WorkCover Queensland Act 1996 . And it must
be remembered that it is a consequence of s. 34(5)(b) of the WorkCover Queensland Act 1996 that,
in determining whether action was reasonable management action taken in a reasonable way by the
employer in connection with the worker’s employment, it is the reality of the employer’s conduct
and not the employee’s perception of it which must be taken into account.



Two. The case developed at first instance was that each of the work related stressors relied upon by
Ms Prizeman was withdrawn from consideration because it arose in the course of reasonable
management action taken in a reasonable way. In light of the subsequent decision in Q-COMP v
Education Queensland (2005) 179 QGIG 491, that approach may well be argued to be flawed. It
will be necessary to return to that matter subsequently. However, for present purposes, it is


 BarNet publication information - Date: Sunday, 07.06.2026 - - Publication number: 00002 - - User: coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

>>> documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf :: page 4
important to note that the case developed at first instance let in a side issue viz. whether any
particular stressor had in fact contributed to Ms Prizeman’s decompensation. Some of the language
in the Industrial Magistrates Decision is, in my view, properly to be understood as developing that
alternative basis for putting a particular stressor aside.



Three. Very early on in His Honour’s decision, the Industrial Magistrate records that on an
“overall” basis the evidence of Ms Prizeman was to be preferred to the evidence of Ms Sturgess. It
has been contended that the Industrial Magistrate did not resolve conflicts in the evidence in
accordance with that finding. In my view, the Industrial Magistrate did resolve conflicts in the
evidence in accordance with that finding. His Honour did accept that dealings identified by Ms
Prizeman did occur. The point at which the Industrial Magistrate (on some occasions) declined to
act upon the evidence of Ms Prizeman was in terms of the detail about that which had occurred. The
Industrial Magistrate was simply distinguishing between Ms Prizeman’s perceptions and that which
had in fact occurred. And there is no suggestion that in taking that course, the Industrial Magistrate
was acting on the view that the perceptions and/or recollections of perceptions of a person who has
decompensated are inherently unreliable.



Four. The Industrial Magistrate examined the alleged stressful situations seriatim. For convenience,
I shall follow that course. However, I do wish to stress, that at the end of the day the Industrial
Magistrate (consistently with His Honour’s preliminary observations) rolled the dealings together
and made a global inquiry about whether the case fell within s. 34(5)(a) of the WorkCover
Queensland Act 1996 .



Five. Consistently with decisions such as Delaney v Q-COMP (2005) 178 QGIG 197, I stress that
the Appeal against the decision of Q-COMP is an Appeal to the Industrial Magistrates Court. The
further Appeal to this Court is an Appeal for the purposes of correction of error. Conclusions upon
factual matters reasonably open to the Industrial Magistrate are not to be interfered with. Subject to
the limitations developed in Fox v Percy (2003) 214 CLR 118, the findings of primary fact based on
an evaluation of a witness seen and heard by the Industrial Magistrate are not to be departed from. I
turn then to the dealings examined by the Industrial Magistrate. At the outset, the Industrial
Magistrate summarised the dealings relied upon as follows:



“The main incidents, apparently initially relied upon by the Appellant, are as follows:



   1. the so-called “Black dress” matter.
   2. the initial staff meeting held by Ms Sturgess when she advised the staff, inter alia, that their
      jobs were on the line.
   3. the one-on-one meeting of 2/6/03 about the need for spot balances – the discussion planner
      document, the discrepancy of $40.00, and the attitude and demeanour of Ms Sturgess during
      that meeting.
   4.
 BarNet publication information - Date: Sunday, 07.06.2026 - - Publication number: 00002 - - User: coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

>>> documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf :: page 5
   4. the “red basket” incident.
   5. the spillage on the floor, on the same date.

   6. the claims made about Ms Sturgess, calling her into her office, one Friday, and asking her if
      she wanted her job or not, before she commenced recreation leave.”.

In the end result, the transactions labelled 1 and 2 were not relied upon before the Industrial
Magistrate. Neither were they relied upon on the Appeal to this Court. I put them aside.



The transaction labelled 3 was a serious one and was treated as such by the Industrial
Magistrate. His Honour reviewed the evidence over six pages. There is no doubt that Ms Prizeman
felt that she was being accused of stealing. There is equally no doubt that Ms Prizeman did not steal
the money. Neither is there any doubt that she was not being accused of stealing the money. The
evidence of Ms Prizeman was that she became very upset. (The evidence was corroborated). The
Industrial Magistrate concluded:



“It is the case though, that in the final analysis, in relation to the meeting conducted in the manner it
was, the following points emerge:



(a) the meeting itself was completely justified, for the reason stated.
(b)       the appellant whilst addressed firmly, and with authority by her manager, was not
      spoken to aggressively, or in any abusive manner.
(c)       the appellant was given the opportunity to reply, to comment on the issue under
      discussion, but for the greater part, for reasons not revealed, chose not to.
(d)       a satisfactory resolution was reached, and the appellant did sign off on what was
      agreed, although she seems to suggest now, that signing off was not entirely voluntary or
      that she at least had some misgivings about doing so.
(e)       the perception, of the appellant is that she was indirectly being accused of acting
      inappropriately – dishonestly, in connection with the missing cash, and this was unfair.
(f)      the perception, of the appellant that with there being no review, that she was thereby
      going to suffer some unfairness, in relation to this issue, at some later date.



How the appellant considered any unfairness actually manifested itself was not expanded upon by
the appellant. I am not sure if she at any time actually referred to the situation being one that
resulted in unfairness to her. I accept that she considered her integrity and reputation might be
impugned because of (e), but in reality the respondent never any time suggested any punitive action
being taken against her, and had plans to continue with her employment, after she stopped work
with her illness, and at no time, in fact, considered she was dishonest. Any such argument, therefore
lacks a degree of substance, in reality. As to (f), the unfairness she perceived, was also not
detailed. I take it that, it was just the fact that a review was not specifically provided for, as is
normally the case that gave her some cause for concern, rather than any specific issue as such. It
was a general concern on her behalf. It seems that she considered that this might have the potential,


 BarNet publication information - Date: Sunday, 07.06.2026 - - Publication number: 00002 - - User: coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

>>> documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf :: page 6
in some way, to disadvantage her, at some future date, in relation to circumstances not able to be
specified. Again, in the absence of other material, of the proof of that unfairness or unjust situation,
this argument is not a compelling one.”.



Granted that it was Ms Prizeman who carried the onus of proof in the approach taken by the
Industrial Magistrate and the findings which His Honour made seem to me to be entirely
understandable and, indeed, predictable.



The transactions labelled 4 and 5 were potentially significant because both occurred on the same day
and because both involved Ms Sturgess causing embarrassment to Ms Prizeman in the presence of
customers. The “red basket incident” concerned Ms Sturgess chiding Ms Prizeman in the presence
of customers about a red plastic basket belonging to the employer which she (Ms Sturgess) had
located in the car park. The latter incident concerned Ms Sturgess chastising Ms Prizeman in the
presence of others about a spillage of water from defective refrigeration equipment. In relation to
both incidents, the Industrial Magistrate was comfortable with finding that in taking action about the
“red basket” and about the “spillage” Ms Sturgess was engaging in reasonable management
action. That view, particularly in the case of the “water spillage” which gave rise to safety issues,
was plainly open to the Industrial Magistrate. The critical issue was whether the reasonable
management action was “reasonably taken”. Although the Industrial Magistrate was critical of the
way in which Ms Sturgess had conducted herself, on balance, His Honour came to the view that the
lapses from “proper or reasonable staff treatment” were but “blemishes”. Consistently with that
view and (I think) giving consideration to the issue whether the stressors should be put aside in any
event, the Industrial Magistrate commented that “neither incident was of long duration” and that it
was “difficult to assess the actual effect that same had on the appellant, based on comparatively brief
evidence provided to the court in relation to both incidents.”. Notwithstanding the skill with which
Mr Lippett has argued his case I am unable to conclude that the Industrial Magistrates’ conclusions
were not reasonably open to His Honour.



The transaction labelled 6 was a matter of major significance. In the event, though expressly (once
again) preferring the evidence of Ms Prizeman that the transaction had occurred to the evidence of
Ms Sturgess that it had not occurred, the Industrial Magistrate concluded:



“In the absence of some corroboration of the claim, I find that I cannot be satisfied that the appellant
was spoken to when and in the manner alleged.”.



I have gone to the transcript. The transcript shows that Ms Prizeman twice said that she had been
left with the “impression” that Ms Sturgess “didn’t want me in that position” and Ms Prizeman said
that she was “shocked”. There is also evidence of Ms Prizeman that Ms Sturgess had asked her to
“think if I wanted my job or not” and asked Ms Prizeman “whether I wanted a job or not”. The
evidence has to be read also with Ms Prizeman’s inability to articulate what she had found upsetting


 BarNet publication information - Date: Sunday, 07.06.2026 - - Publication number: 00002 - - User: coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

>>> documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf :: page 7
about the meeting of 2 June 2003. On one view the noun “impression” was not Ms Prizeman’s
language but was suggested by a leading question. There was certainly a fresh complaint. But the
fresh complaint stifled an attack upon the evidence about the incident. It does not go to what was
said. At the end of the day in an issue about the reliability of evidence I must defer to the Industrial
Magistrate who saw and observed the witness over quite a period of time.



(For completeness, I should add that the Industrial Magistrate also considered a transaction outside
the original list relating to the cleanliness of the tills and service area but concluded that any
stressors arising from the transaction were not an issue. Having regard to the transcript and the way
in which the matter was argued on appeal, that conclusion seems to me to have been correct).



Having considered each of the items separately, the Industrial Magistrate then entered upon a global
consideration of three incidents, viz. the transactions labelled 3, 4 and 5. On His Honour’s findings
about the transaction labelled 6 it was inevitable that His Honour would leave that issue out of
account. Having referred to the item involving the “red basket” and the item involving “spillage on
the floor” as “blemishes”, the Industrial Magistrate returned to the points which His Honour had
found to emerge from the evidence about the pre-recreation leave meeting (set about above),
reiterated that there was nothing untoward about points (a) to (d), returned to the point that any
“unfairness” said to arrive out of (e) and (f) had not been identified and concluded spelling the word
in higher case that “overall”, the Appellant had failed to prove that the incidents were other than
reasonable management action taken reasonably. Given the findings of primary fact, I am unable to
conclude that the Industrial Magistrate’s decision was not open to His Honour.



I should return briefly to the decision in Q-COMP v Education Queensland (2005) 179 QGIG
491. I do so because an Appeal by way of rehearing is to be determined on the basis of the law as it
is understood to be at the time that the Appeal is determined, Victorian Stevedoring and General
Contracting Co Pty Ltd and Meakes v Dignan (1931) 46 CLR 73 at 107 per Dixon J.



With hindsight, the Industrial Magistrate’s inability to make findings about what was said and done
at the pre-recreation leave meeting labelled 6 is decisive. Although Ms Dormer’s report seems to
suggest that it was the combination of stressors which caused Ms Prizeman to decompensate, in re-
examination the following exchange occurred between Mr Lippett (for Ms Prizeman) and Ms
Dormer:



“Q. Was it just the changes that seemed to make her anxious or was it a combination of things?
A. No, it was mostly the request that – that did she still want her job?”.




 BarNet publication information - Date: Sunday, 07.06.2026 - - Publication number: 00002 - - User: coryshepherd1@hotmail.com

>>> documents/Prizeman_v_QComp_2005_QIC_53.pdf :: page 8
The Industrial Magistrate’s inability to make a finding about what was said in the course of the
meeting makes it impossible to class the transaction as other than “reasonable management action
reasonably taken” and on the test in Q-COMP v Education Queensland, op cit, that was sufficient to
remove the psychiatric/psychological disorder from the definition of “injury”.



I dismiss the Appeal.



I reserve all questions as to costs.



Dated 14 September 2005.



D.R. HALL, President.                       Appearances:

                                            the Appellant.

Neale v Workers' Compensation Regulator [2023] QIRC 9 (16 January 2023) (Pidgeon IC)

      [199]       The Respondent says that the failure to implement the draft return-to-work plan is at best
      a 'blemish' [281] as far as Mr Neale's case goes. The Respondent says that an imperfection in
      management action will not automatically result in characterising the action as management
      action which is unreasonable. [282] The Respondent goes on to say that management action need
      not be perfect [283] and that in determining whether the action in this case was reasonable or not,
      'it is the reality of the employer's conduct and not the employee's perception of it which must be
      taken into account'. [284]
